title: Iran War: Hormuz flows near-normal
message:
**1. Forecast Question**  
Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each horizon: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months.

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
Functional normality requires a sustained multi-domain condition (observed for at least 2–4 consecutive weeks) meeting all of the following observable thresholds:  

- **Direct military activity**: No significant kinetic exchanges (airstrikes, missile/drone barrages, or naval engagements) between US/Israeli forces and Iranian forces or assets.  
- **Proxy activity**: Major Iranian proxies (especially Houthis, Iraqi PMF elements, residual Hezbollah capacity) not conducting large-scale attacks on commercial shipping, Gulf energy infrastructure, or US/Israeli targets that materially disrupt Gulf operations.  
- **Shipping security (Hormuz and nearby waters)**: Waters free of active mine-laying or effective IRGC interdiction; commercial vessels can transit without routine high-intensity military escort as the default operating mode.  
- **Commercial transit levels**: Combined AIS-visible and dark commercial traffic (particularly tankers) consistently at ≥70% of the pre-February 2026 baseline (roughly ≥60 equivalent daily commercial crossings).  
- **War-risk insurance**: Additional premiums for Hormuz/Gulf transits reduced to ≤1–2% of hull value (or broadly available at rates no more than 5–10× peacetime levels) with restored market capacity; not dependent on exceptional sovereign backstops as the primary mechanism.  
- **Oil and LNG export continuity**: Non-Iranian Gulf oil exports and Qatari LNG at ≥90% of pre-war levels without major force majeures or sustained port/export disruptions.  
- **Energy market stress and volatility**: War-risk premium largely priced out of crude (Brent not persistently elevated solely by Hormuz risk; material reduction from current ~$100–115 range toward levels consistent with other fundamentals).  
- **Force posture of major actors**: Significant reduction in dedicated US carrier/strike-group and escort/blockade presence; Iranian IRGC naval and coastal forces not in sustained high-alert denial posture.  
- **Absence of major new escalation triggers**: No new high-profile attacks, leadership strikes, nuclear-related escalations, or proxy surges that restart the disruption cycle.  

A temporary ceasefire, battlefield pause, or lower oil prices alone does not meet the definition. Commercial and insurance normalization are gating requirements.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 2 November 2026)**  
The conflict began 28 February 2026 with US-Israeli strikes (Operation Epic Fury / Roaring Lion); Ali Khamenei was killed early. It is now Day ~248 of the Hormuz crisis. An April ceasefire and June Islamabad Memorandum collapsed by early July; the dual-blockade dynamic (US blockade of Iranian ports + Iranian restrictions/attacks on shipping) has persisted with intermittent managed flows.  

AIS-visible commercial traffic is ~9–10/day versus ~85 pre-crisis (≈10% of normal). Hundreds of vessels remain waiting on both sides of the strait. Attacks (projectiles, claimed mines, hull explosives) continued through October and into early November; October was among the worst months for shipping incidents. Iran claims control via a Persian Gulf Strait Authority and requires coordination/permits; US CENTCOM coordinates some transits and maintains blockade pressure on Iranian exports.  

Total Middle East oil exports (including pipelines/bypasses and offshore transfers) have recovered to near or above pre-war levels (~24 mbd in mid-October Kpler data). Hormuz clearance itself remains lower and variable (roughly 8–14 mbd depending on the window and whether dark shipping is fully captured—40–80% of pre-war). War-risk premiums are elevated at 6–10% of hull value (roughly 30–60× peacetime); cumulative claims exceed $2 billion. A US DFC-linked reinsurance facility exists but has not fully normalized private capacity.  

Diplomacy continues via Qatar (Iran has floated a shortened two-day plan); Trump has publicly ruled out US strikes before the 3 November midterms. Preparations and messaging point to elevated risk of a short, intense US campaign afterward if talks do not progress. Proxies remain active: Houthis continue pressure on Saudi infrastructure and Red Sea/Bab al-Mandeb routes. Energy prices remain stressed (Brent ~$110 range). Sources include live AIS trackers (hormuz.now and equivalents), Kpler/Vortexa reporting, UKMTO/JMIC, insurer/broker commentary, and major news organizations. Some attack attributions and exact transit volumes remain disputed between CENTCOM and Iranian claims.

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**  

Relevant historical reference classes:  
- **1980s Tanker War (Iran–Iraq)**: Closest analog for sustained anti-shipping campaigns in the Gulf. Lasted years; US naval intervention degraded Iranian naval capacity (Praying Mantis) but shipping risk and insurance friction persisted until the broader war ended. Suggests 12–36+ months for functional commercial stabilization without political settlement. Breaks down due to different nuclear/proxy density, modern surveillance, and US precision-strike advantages.  
- **2019–2020 Iran–US maritime tensions (tanker attacks, Abqaiq)**: Short spikes in risk and insurance; partial recovery in weeks to a few months after de-escalation. Suggests 1–6 months if attacks cease and political signaling stabilizes. Breaks down because current case is a multi-month open war with leadership decapitation and dual blockades.  
- **Red Sea Houthi campaign (2023–present)**: Proxy denial of a chokepoint; insurance elevated and rerouting persistent for many months despite air campaigns and escorts. Partial recovery possible in 6–18 months; full commercial normality slower. Highly relevant for proxy effects and insurance stickiness.  
- **Black Sea shipping corridors (Russia–Ukraine)**: Severe initial disruption followed by managed corridors and partial recovery over several months with external protection. Suggests 3–12 months for functional flows under escort or temporary arrangements.  
- **Short intense Gulf wars (1990–91, 2003 Iraq)**: Rapid post-conflict commercial recovery for non-belligerent Gulf producers once major combat ended (weeks to a few months). Breaks down because Iran retains significant residual denial capacity and the conflict has not produced decisive regime change.  

**Base-rate prior (outside-in, before heavy case-specific adjustment)**:  
- 1 week: ~5%  
- 1 month: ~10–15%  
- 3 months: ~25%  
- 6 months: ~35–40%  
- 1 year: ~50–55%  
- 18 months: ~60–65%  

These reflect that chokepoint commercial and insurance normalization typically lags military pauses, with insurance and shipping behavior especially sticky.

**5. Evidence Ledger**  

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| AIS commercial traffic ~9–10/day (~10% of pre-crisis) | Live AIS trackers (hormuz.now, IMF PortWatch) | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| Hormuz oil clearance variable ~8–14 mbd; total Gulf exports near/above pre-war via bypasses | Kpler and similar trackers | Mixed (physical resilience positive; Hormuz-specific negative) | Medium-High | Confirmed/inferred on dark shipping |
| Ongoing shipping attacks in October–early November (projectiles, claimed mines) | UKMTO, news, Iranian claims vs CENTCOM | Strongly negative | High on occurrence; Medium on attribution | Confirmed incidents; disputed perpetrators |
| War-risk premiums 6–10% hull value; claims >$2B | Broker/insurer commentary, Lloyd’s List, FT-derived | Strongly negative (sticky) | High | Confirmed |
| Qatar-mediated talks; Iran two-day plan on table | Al Jazeera, Gulf media, Iranian statements | Mildly positive (near-term window) | Medium | Confirmed statements; outcome uncertain |
| US no-strike pledge before 3 Nov midterms; post-midterm strike options prepared | Trump statements, WSJ/Gulf official reporting | Mixed (short-term positive; medium-term risk) | Medium-High | Confirmed pledge; inferred preparation |
| US DFC reinsurance facility and naval coordination/escorts | Official and market reporting | Mildly positive for managed flows | Medium | Confirmed |
| Houthi activity vs Saudi and secondary chokepoints | Conflict monitors (ISW, FDD, news) | Negative | Medium-High | Confirmed |
| Islamabad Memorandum long collapsed | Multiple reporting, timeline | Negative | High | Confirmed |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**  
1. Physical adaptation already achieved (dark shipping, STS transfers, pipeline bypasses, US coordination) — reduces absolute dependence on a full political deal for oil continuity.  
2. Economic and political pressure on both sides (high energy costs, US midterms, Iranian export constraints and domestic strain).  
3. Active mediation (Qatar and others) and explicit short-horizon proposals.  
4. US capacity to degrade Iranian coastal denial assets if it chooses.  
5. Insurance markets’ historical ability to reprice downward once attack frequency drops for several weeks.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**  
1. Unresolved core issues (nuclear constraints, sanctions, blockade, Iranian claims of sovereignty over Hormuz).  
2. Insurance stickiness and capacity withdrawal — often the last domain to normalize.  
3. Residual Iranian denial capacity and demonstrated willingness to attack shipping even under escort pressure.  
4. Post-midterm escalation risk (short intense campaign possible).  
5. Proxy activity (Houthis especially) providing secondary pressure and complicating Gulf-state calculations.  
6. Eight months of established disruption already; confidence rebuilding requires sustained calm.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts** (probabilities of the component being in a “normalized enough” state by each horizon; these are inputs, not the final joint probability)  

Rough directional estimates:  
- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 15%, 1m 30%, 3m 50%, 6m 65%, 1y 75%, 18m 80%.  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (security + volume): 1w 5%, 1m 10%, 3m 25%, 6m 40%, 1y 55%, 18m 65%.  
- Meaningful insurance normalization: 1w 5%, 1m 8%, 3m 20%, 6m 35%, 1y 50%, 18m 60%.  
- Oil/LNG export recovery (already partially achieved): 1w 60%, 1m 65%, 3m 75%, 6m 80%, 1y 85%, 18m 88%.  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 20%, 1m 25%, 3m 35%, 6m 45%, 1y 55%, 18m 65%.  
- Force drawdown: 1w 10%, 1m 15%, 3m 30%, 6m 45%, 1y 60%, 18m 70%.  
- No major new escalation trigger: 1w 40%, 1m 35%, 3m 40%, 6m 50%, 1y 60%, 18m 65%.  

Insurance, transit security/volume, and absence of escalation are the primary gating factors. Export continuity is already closer to satisfied and is less binding.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**  

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 5%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~5%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly downward (active attacks, midterm window, no sustained calm yet).  
- Core rationale: Too short for confidence rebuilding, insurance re-pricing, or force posture changes. Any quiet is likely tactical.  
- Main gating factor: Shipping security and insurance.  
- What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate, verified multi-day halt in all attacks plus explicit dual announcements of transit coordination.  
- What would lower this forecast materially: Fresh high-profile shipping incident or post-election strike announcement.  
- Confidence in this estimate: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 12%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~10–15%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Roughly neutral to slightly downward.  
- Core rationale: Possible post-midterm quiet or limited deal window exists, but insurance and commercial behavior lag. Escalation risk remains material.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance normalization and sustained transit security.  
- What would raise this forecast materially: Successful implementation of a short coordinated reopening plan with no attacks for 2+ weeks and visible premium declines.  
- What would lower this forecast materially: Resumption of large-scale strikes or continued weekly attack cadence.  
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 25%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~25%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Roughly neutral.  
- Core rationale: Enough time for a managed de-escalation or limited agreement to produce measurable commercial recovery if attack frequency collapses. Still requires the political issues not to re-escalate.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance capacity and absence of new escalation.  
- What would raise this forecast materially: Multi-week calm plus clear US force reduction signals and insurance quotes moving below 3–4%.  
- What would lower this forecast materially: Post-midterm intense campaign or proxy surge that keeps premiums elevated.  
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~35–40%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly upward (adaptation already demonstrated; economic pressure).  
- Core rationale: Managed or partial political settlement becomes more plausible; physical flows can support higher volumes. Insurance remains the slower variable.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance normalization and force posture.  
- What would raise this forecast materially: Sustained 8–12 weeks of low attack rates and visible market capacity returning.  
- What would lower this forecast materially: Renewed high-intensity phase or breakdown of mediation.  
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~50–55%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Roughly neutral.  
- Core rationale: Sufficient time for either a political arrangement or durable managed normalization under residual risk. Long-horizon uncertainty on Iranian residual capabilities and US political will remains.  
- Main gating factor: Resolution or durable management of the core political disputes.  
- What would raise this forecast materially: Formal or de-facto agreement that lifts blockade elements and produces multi-month calm.  
- What would lower this forecast materially: Prolonged low-level denial campaign or new nuclear-related crisis.  
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium-Low  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 62%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~60–65%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly upward (historical tendency for commercial systems to adapt even without full political resolution).  
- Core rationale: By this horizon, either a settlement, regime fatigue, or structural adaptation (pipelines, insurance markets, escort regimes) is more likely to have produced functional normality under the definition. Still far from certain.  
- Main gating factor: Absence of a new major escalation cycle.  
- What would raise this forecast materially: Clear multi-quarter trend of declining incidents and premiums.  
- What would lower this forecast materially: Evidence of Iranian reconstitution of denial capabilities or renewed large-scale war.  
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium-Low  

**10. Most Likely Path**  
Continued managed but restricted operations through early 2027, with intermittent attacks, elevated insurance, and partial oil flows sustained by dark shipping, bypasses, and US coordination. A limited or fragile diplomatic arrangement is possible after the midterms, but full multi-domain normality (especially insurance and force posture) is more likely in the 6–18 month window than earlier. Physical export continuity improves faster than perceived security and insurance.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**  
Post-midterm deal or durable de-escalation within weeks; attack frequency collapses; insurers re-enter aggressively within 4–8 weeks; US begins visible drawdown. Probability of functional normality by 3 months rises to ~40–45% under this scenario. Load-bearing assumption: both sides prioritize economic relief over maximalist demands.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**  
Post-midterm strikes restart a higher-intensity phase; Iran maintains low-cost denial; proxies keep secondary pressure; insurance remains elevated for 12+ months. Probability of functional normality stays below 30% even at 12 months. Load-bearing assumption: residual Iranian coastal and proxy capabilities plus unresolved nuclear/sanctions issues sustain the disruption.

**13. Red-Team Critique**  
Strongest case that this forecast underestimates speed: Physical oil flows have already demonstrated surprising resilience; a political pause could produce faster commercial re-entry than insurance history suggests if the US backstop expands and attack rates drop sharply. Strongest case that it overestimates speed: Insurance markets and shipowner risk tolerance are stickier than military pauses; eight months of established disruption plus proxy activity and post-midterm optionality make early normalization harder than reference classes imply. Load-bearing assumptions include the continued efficacy of US escort/coordination and the absence of a major new escalation trigger after 3 November.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**  
- Daily/weekly AIS and dark-shipping transit counts and attack frequency (UKMTO/JMIC).  
- War-risk premium quotes and capacity (broker reports).  
- Hormuz oil clearance volumes (Kpler and equivalents) versus total Gulf exports.  
- US force movements and Iranian coastal activity post-3 November.  
- Status of Qatari or other mediation and any formal coordination mechanisms.  
- Houthi and other proxy attack rates on Saudi or secondary routes.  
- LNG force majeure status and Asian/European buyer behavior.

**15. Final Summary Table**  

| Horizon | Probability | Confidence | Main gating factor |
|---------|-------------|------------|--------------------|
| 1 week | 5% | High | Shipping security & insurance |
| 1 month | 12% | Medium-High | Insurance & sustained security |
| 3 months | 25% | Medium | Insurance & escalation absence |
| 6 months | 38% | Medium | Insurance & force posture |
| 1 year | 52% | Medium-Low | Core political resolution/management |
| 18 months | 62% | Medium-Low | Avoidance of new escalation cycle |

These probabilities are calibrated judgments built from reference-class base rates updated by the eight-month evidence base. They treat commercial and insurance normalization as distinct from, and slower than, military pauses. Major updates would follow sustained changes in attack rates, insurance pricing, or the political trajectory after the US midterms.

title: Iran War: Probabilities Updated
message:
**1. Forecast Question**  
Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each horizon: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months.

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
Functional normality requires simultaneous, sustained satisfaction of the following observable conditions for at least 30 consecutive days (or 60 days for insurance and transit metrics where specified). It is not a temporary ceasefire, a price dip, or a pause in major strikes:

- Direct military activity: No kinetic strikes by the US, Israel, or Iran on each other’s territory, forces, or assets.  
- Proxy activity: Houthi, Iraqi militia, and other proxy attacks on shipping, energy infrastructure, or bases at or below pre-February 2026 baseline frequency and severity.  
- Shipping security (Strait of Hormuz and adjacent waters): No attacks, mines, or harassment for 60 days; free transit without mandatory Iranian permits, routine US escorts, or systematic AIS-dark operations as the commercial standard.  
- Commercial transit levels: Total (AIS + estimated dark) oil, product, LNG, and container volumes ≥90% of 2025 pre-war daily averages through Hormuz and Gulf terminals.  
- War-risk insurance: Additional premiums ≤1% of hull value (roughly 4× pre-war ~0.25%) and available on standard commercial terms without primary reliance on special government facilities.  
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf exports (including pipeline bypasses) at ≥95% of pre-war capacity with no widespread force-majeure declarations.  
- Energy market stress: Brent crude and related volatility driven by non-crisis fundamentals rather than sustained war-risk premia (no multi-month levels >$90 solely from Gulf disruption risk).  
- Force posture: US blockade and escort operations reduced to routine presence; Iranian naval/IRGC posture non-aggressive and without formal exclusion zones or Strait Authority control mechanisms.  
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No new nuclear breakout moves, regime-targeting campaigns, or major proxy escalations that reintroduce systemic risk.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 1 November 2026)**  
The conflict began 28 February 2026 with US-Israeli strikes. It is now ~8 months old, characterized by cycles of direct strikes, pauses (including a Trump pledge of no US attacks before the 3 November midterms), and persistent Iranian maritime pressure.<grok:render card_id="637b02" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">0</argument></grok:render>  

AIS-visible commercial transits average ~8–12 ships/day (~10% of the ~85 pre-war baseline). Oil flows have recovered to roughly 65–80% of pre-war levels in some recent weeks (~11–14 mb/d) via dark AIS operations, ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, US-coordinated shuttles, and increased bypass pipeline use, but remain volatile and attack-sensitive. Port activity inside the Gulf is well below normal.<grok:render card_id="399c76" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">40</argument></grok:render>  

War-risk insurance is 6–10% of hull value (vs. ~0.25% pre-war), equating to millions of dollars per VLCC voyage and remaining a binding constraint even when physical passage is possible.<grok:render card_id="86adc7" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">61</argument></grok:render>  

Iran continues intermittent attacks and mine claims; the US maintains a blockade of Iranian ports and provides protective cover. Diplomacy via Qatar and others is active but stalled on sequencing (blockade/sanctions relief vs. nuclear and Strait control issues). Multiple reports indicate US preparations for possible intensified operations after the midterms. Proxy activity (including Houthis) continues. Brent is elevated (~$115–117 range in recent reporting).<grok:render card_id="e969c7" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">26</argument></grok:render>  

Confirmed facts include the attack tempo, insurance levels, and partial volume recovery via non-standard means. Disputed or inferred items include the precise efficacy of US mine-clearing, the durability of any post-midterm pause, and the exact contribution of dark shipping to totals.

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**  
- **Tanker War (1984–1988)**: Multi-year campaign of attacks on shipping during the Iran-Iraq War. Traffic continued but at reduced volumes; full commercial normalization required the broader ceasefire. Relevant because of Iranian maritime disruption capability and US escorts. Breaks down: different political end-state and no nuclear dimension. Suggests 12–36+ months for functional recovery once hostilities end.  
- **Houthi Red Sea disruption (2023–present)**: Persistent threat capability produced multi-year elevated insurance, rerouting, and incomplete volume recovery even during lulls. Relevant for insurance lag and commercial risk aversion. Breaks down: lower volume stakes and different geography. Suggests 12–24 months for partial normalization after sustained quiet.  
- **2019 Gulf/Hormuz incidents**: Brief attacks produced short insurance and price spikes that normalized within weeks once the immediate threat subsided. Relevant for rapid market response to discrete events. Breaks down: no sustained campaign or dual blockade dynamic. Suggests weeks to low months.  
- **Post-ceasefire phases of limited regional conflicts (e.g., various Gulf skirmishes)**: Insurance and transit often lag military pauses by 1–3 months. Relevant for second-order commercial effects.  

**Base-rate prior (before case-specific evidence)**:  
1 week: ~5%; 1 month: ~10%; 3 months: ~20%; 6 months: ~35%; 1 year: ~50%; 18 months: ~60%. These reflect the historical difficulty of simultaneous multi-domain recovery when threat capability and political incentives for disruption persist.

**5. Evidence Ledger**  

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| AIS-visible transits ~10% of normal; oil volumes 65–80% via dark/STS/escorts | AIS trackers, Kpler, CENTCOM | Negative (non-standard ops required) | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk insurance 6–10% of hull | Brokers, FT, Marsh via trade press | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| Ongoing Iranian attacks/mines claims and US protective operations | UKMTO, CENTCOM, Iranian statements | Negative | High | Confirmed (claims partly disputed) |
| Stalled diplomacy; Iranian conditions on blockade/sanctions; US nuclear demands | Reuters, mediators, official statements | Negative | Medium-High | Confirmed contacts, outcomes disputed |
| Reports of US post-midterm intensification planning | WSJ, CNN, official briefings | Strongly negative (near-term) | Medium | Reported, not executed |
| Partial volume recovery and continued (non-normal) flows | Kpler, CENTCOM | Mildly positive for continuity | Medium | Confirmed |
| Proxy activity (Houthis et al.) | Open reporting | Negative | Medium | Confirmed incidents |
| Elevated energy prices and market stress | Market data | Negative | High | Confirmed |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**  
- Mutual economic pain (Iranian export blockade + elevated global energy costs) creating incentives for de-escalation.  
- Active mediation and some shared interest in avoiding full collapse of flows.  
- Demonstrated ability to move significant volumes under protection, reducing absolute scarcity.  
- Historical pattern that insurance and transit recover once a credible multi-month quiet period is established.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**  
- Persistent Iranian capability and demonstrated willingness to impose costs on shipping to retain leverage.  
- High probability of renewed US/Israeli kinetic action after midterms if talks stall.  
- Insurance market lag and risk aversion (requires sustained quiet far longer than a ceasefire).  
- Unresolved core issues (nuclear, Strait control, sanctions) that make temporary pauses fragile.  
- Proxy residual capacity and second-order effects on Gulf state posture and buyer confidence.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts** (probabilities of each component being in place by horizon)  
- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 15%, 1m 25%, 3m 40%, 6m 55%, 1y 70%, 18m 75%.  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (no special measures): 1w 5%, 1m 10%, 3m 20%, 6m 35%, 1y 50%, 18m 60%.  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤1%): 1w 2%, 1m 5%, 3m 12%, 6m 25%, 1y 40%, 18m 55%.  
- Oil/LNG export recovery to ≥95% without force majeure: 1w 10%, 1m 20%, 3m 35%, 6m 50%, 1y 65%, 18m 75%.  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 20%, 1m 30%, 3m 45%, 6m 55%, 1y 65%, 18m 70%.  
- Force drawdown (blockade/escorts to routine): 1w 5%, 1m 10%, 3m 20%, 6m 30%, 1y 45%, 18m 55%.  
- No major new escalation trigger: 1w 40%, 1m 35%, 3m 30%, 6m 40%, 1y 50%, 18m 55%.  

Insurance normalization, sustained safe transit without special measures, and force drawdown are the tightest gating factors. Military pauses alone do not unlock them.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**  

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 3%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~5%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Downward (ongoing attacks, midterm window, insurance levels).  
- Core rationale: Immediate conditions fail nearly all definitional criteria.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance and transit security.  
- What would raise: Immediate multi-day quiet + credible deal announcement.  
- What would lower: Any confirmed attack or strike.  
- Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 6%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~10%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Downward (post-midterm risk, stalled talks).  
- Core rationale: Even a temporary pause would not produce insurance or commercial normalization within 30 days.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance pricing lag.  
- What would raise: Sustained no-attack period + clear diplomatic sequencing agreement.  
- What would lower: Post-midterm kinetic resumption.  
- Confidence: High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 12%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~20%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Downward (capability persistence, political incentives).  
- Core rationale: Requires both military de-escalation and several weeks of clean commercial operations to begin shifting underwriter and operator behavior.  
- Main gating factor: Credible multi-week security of transit.  
- What would raise: Formal agreement with verified implementation and force adjustments.  
- What would lower: Renewed attacks or major proxy escalation.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~35%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Downward (historical insurance lag, unresolved core disputes).  
- Core rationale: Possible if a durable pause holds and volumes normalize, but force posture and insurance thresholds remain demanding.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance ≤1% and force drawdown.  
- What would raise: Verified 90+ day quiet + sanctions/blockade relief steps.  
- What would lower: Escalation cycle or new nuclear-related triggers.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~50%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Downward (persistent leverage incentives, proxy residual risk).  
- Core rationale: Longer horizon allows more room for negotiated end-states or exhaustion-driven de-escalation, but full multi-domain recovery is not the modal outcome.  
- Main gating factor: Sustained absence of disruption capability use.  
- What would raise: Comprehensive agreement covering nuclear, Strait, and sanctions.  
- What would lower: Prolonged low-level maritime campaign.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~60%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mildly downward (second-order commercial and political scars).  
- Core rationale: Approaching the range where historical cases show substantial recovery if the acute phase ends, but residual risk premia and posture changes can persist.  
- Main gating factor: Commercial confidence and insurance.  
- What would raise: End of active conflict plus 6+ months of clean operations.  
- What would lower: New escalation or regime-level instability.  
- Confidence: Low-Medium  

**10. Most Likely Path**  
Continued low-to-moderate intensity maritime pressure and intermittent kinetic exchanges through at least early 2027, with partial volume recovery under protection but persistently elevated insurance and non-normal operating practices. A durable political settlement remains possible but not the base case within 12 months.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**  
A post-midterm agreement that sequences blockade relief, limited nuclear steps, and verified Strait free-passage, followed by 60+ days of zero attacks. Insurance begins falling within weeks of clean data; volumes and posture normalize by 3–6 months. Probability of this path: ~15–20%.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**  
Renewed high-intensity campaign after midterms, Iranian retention of maritime disruption tools, and proxy activation. Insurance stays elevated, volumes remain dependent on special measures, and commercial normality is deferred beyond 18 months. Probability of this path: ~30–35%.

**13. Red-Team Critique**  
Strongest case that probabilities are too low: Economic pain and mediation could produce a faster political deal than historical reference classes suggest, and partial volume recovery already shows adaptation. Strongest case that probabilities are too high: Iranian strategic incentives to retain Strait leverage, US political dynamics, and the demonstrated multi-month lag between military quiet and insurance/commercial normalization. Load-bearing assumptions include the durability of any post-midterm pause and the continued relevance of the Tanker War/Houthi insurance lag. Evidence that would falsify the forecast: a verified 60-day attack-free period with insurance falling below 2% and free transit becoming the norm, or the opposite (major new campaign).

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**  
- Daily/weekly AIS + dark-adjusted transit and oil-flow data (Kpler, PortWatch, CENTCOM).  
- Broker quotes for war-risk additional premiums.  
- Confirmed attack frequency (UKMTO, open sources).  
- US force movements and official statements post-3 November.  
- Mediator statements and any verified implementation steps on blockade/Strait.  
- Proxy incident rates and Gulf state infrastructure status.  
- Brent volatility attributable to physical vs. risk premia.

**15. Final Summary Table**  

| Horizon | Probability | Base-rate anchor | Adjustment | Main gating factor | Confidence |
|---------|-------------|------------------|------------|--------------------|------------|
| 1 week | 3% | ~5% | Down | Insurance & security | High |
| 1 month | 6% | ~10% | Down | Insurance lag | High |
| 3 months | 12% | ~20% | Down | Sustained clean transit | Medium |
| 6 months | 22% | ~35% | Down | Insurance + force posture | Medium |
| 1 year | 38% | ~50% | Down | Absence of disruption use | Medium-Low |
| 18 months | 52% | ~60% | Mild down | Commercial confidence | Low-Medium |

These estimates treat full multi-domain functional normality as a high bar. Military pauses and partial volume recovery under special measures do not meet it.

title: Iran War: 3% 1-week normality
message:
**1. Forecast Question**  
Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each horizon: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months.

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
Functional normality requires simultaneous, sustained satisfaction of the following observable thresholds for at least 14 consecutive days (longer for the 6-month+ horizons):

- **Direct military activity**: No significant US/Israeli airstrikes, missile/drone barrages, or naval engagements against Iranian territory, forces, or assets, and reciprocal Iranian restraint beyond sporadic low-level incidents. No active blockade enforcement that prevents normal commercial traffic.
- **Proxy activity**: Houthi, Iraqi militia, and other proxy attacks on Gulf shipping, energy infrastructure, or states reduced to pre-February 2026 baseline levels (near-zero for Gulf-directed kinetic attacks).
- **Shipping security (Strait of Hormuz and adjacent waters)**: UKMTO/IMO/JMIC threat level downgraded from “severe”; no successful attacks on commercial vessels in a rolling 14-day window; mines cleared from primary shipping lanes with third-party verification; no IRGC “unauthorized route” enforcement or limpet-mine operations.
- **Commercial transit levels**: Daily AIS-visible commercial transits (tankers + cargo) averaging ≥70% of the pre-war baseline (~60+ of the ~85–90 daily average), with outbound oil/LNG tankers at ≥80% of pre-war volumes without mandatory US naval escorts as the dominant mode.
- **War-risk insurance**: Additional premiums for Hormuz/Gulf transits ≤1% of hull value (from current 6–10%), with standard 7-day cover widely available and no mass cancellation or exclusion clauses.
- **Oil and LNG export continuity**: Combined Gulf oil exports through Hormuz ≥15–16 mb/d (near pre-war ~17–18 mb/d including Iranian volumes where permitted) and LNG flows restored without systematic disruption; no major port or terminal damage constraining loadings.
- **Energy market stress and volatility**: Brent crude in a sustained range of $70–85/bbl (near or modestly above pre-war ~$60–75) with implied volatility and forward-curve backwardation/contango returning to non-crisis norms; no emergency stock releases required.
- **Force posture of major actors**: US carrier strike groups and amphibious forces reduced from peak wartime levels; Iranian IRGC Navy and missile forces at non-heightened readiness; no active US blockade of Iranian ports.
- **Absence of major new escalation triggers**: No new leadership decapitation attempts, nuclear-related strikes, large-scale proxy activation, or mine-laying campaigns that reset the above metrics.

A temporary ceasefire, partial oil-flow rebound under escorts, or price dips alone do not qualify. Normality is commercial and multi-domain, not merely a battlefield pause.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot** (as of 31 October 2026, ~Day 245–246)  
The war began 28 February 2026 with US/Israeli Operation Epic Fury strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. An April ceasefire and June Islamabad MOU (60-day negotiation window, Hormuz reopening provisions) collapsed in early July after renewed Iranian shipping attacks and Trump’s declaration that the MOU was “over.” US strikes on Iranian territory have been paused by Trump’s pledge until after the 3 November midterms; Iran has not reciprocated. October has been the highest month for maritime attacks (UKMTO/IMO: 25–30+ incidents, bringing cumulative regional incidents to ~120–145 since March, with ~24 seafarer deaths). AIS-visible traffic is severely depressed (~7–10% of baseline in recent daily counts; some escort-facilitated oil flows reported at 50–80% of pre-war in weekly averages by Kpler/CENTCOM). War-risk premiums remain 6–10% of hull value. Brent is ~$114–117. Qatari mediation continues; Iran insists on its seven-point conditions (including ending the US blockade and sequencing). US force posture is expanding (third carrier, additional Marines, aircraft to Qatar/Israel). Houthis remain active against Saudi targets. Confirmed facts (UKMTO, CENTCOM statements, Kpler volumes, IMO incident counts) are distinguished from claims (IRGC “closure” assertions, disputed mine-clearing success). Disputed: exact daily transit volumes (AIS dark activity) and whether US escorts have fully neutralized mine threats.<grok:render card_id="b46d24" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">0</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="14b45f" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">1</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="dec4db" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">6</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**  
- **Tanker War (1984–1988)**: Relevant as sustained IRGC/Iraqi anti-shipping campaign in the same waters with US escorts eventually containing but not immediately ending attacks. Breakdown: embedded in a larger land war that ended only after years of attrition and UN ceasefire. Suggests 2–4+ years for functional commercial normalization while hostilities continue; partial recovery under escorts within 6–12 months of dedicated naval protection.
- **Red Sea/Houthi crisis (2023–ongoing)**: Relevant for proxy-driven chokepoint disruption with insurance spikes and traffic diversion. Breakdown: lower volume of oil and alternative routing available. Suggests multi-year residual disruption and elevated premiums until the underlying conflict ends; traffic recovery lagged political de-escalation by many months.
- **1990–91 Gulf War**: Relevant for rapid US-led resolution of a Gulf crisis with energy implications. Breakdown: short, decisive conventional campaign against a conventional state actor, not a resilient missile/proxy power. Suggests commercial recovery within 1–3 months after hostilities cease.
- **Suez closures (1956 ~5 months; 1967–75 8 years; 2021 Ever Given 6 days)**: Relevant for pure chokepoint physical or political closure effects on trade. Breakdown: Suez has substitutes; Hormuz for Gulf oil largely does not. Suggests recovery within weeks after physical clearance if political will exists, or years if political closure persists.
- **Post-2020 COVID / Red Sea traffic hysteresis**: Relevant for lingering commercial caution and insurance lag after acute shocks. Suggests 3–9 months of residual under-utilization even after security improves.

**Base-rate prior** (before current-case adjustment): 1 week <5%; 1 month 5–10%; 3 months 10–15%; 6 months 20–30%; 1 year 35–45%; 18 months 50–60%. These reflect that durable multi-domain commercial normalization in Hormuz-class crises has historically required either war termination or sustained naval dominance plus political settlement, which typically takes many months to years.

**5. Evidence Ledger**  

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| War start 28 Feb 2026; ~245 days elapsed; MOU collapsed July | News / official timelines | Against (protracted) | High | Confirmed |
| US strikes paused until after 3 Nov midterms; Iran continues shipping attacks | Trump statements, UKMTO, ISW | Mixed (pause near-term; attacks ongoing) | High | Confirmed |
