| No major US/Israeli strikes on Iranian territory in recent days; lower intensity than peak | Daily military updates | Mildly toward (pause) | Medium | Confirmed for window |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

Ranked: (1) Economic and political incentives for all sides (Iran needs revenue; Gulf states and Asian buyers need volume; US political costs of prolonged disruption); (2) demonstrated operational adaptation (dark shuttles + pipelines already restoring much oil volume); (3) active regional mediation; (4) fatigue after 8 months and election timing that may favor de-escalation windows; (5) historical pattern that protected corridors eventually allow partial commercial recovery.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

Ranked: (1) Iran’s residual capacity and demonstrated willingness to attack shipping to retain leverage over Hormuz and extract concessions (nuclear, sanctions, “new realities”); (2) post-election risk of renewed major US/Israeli strikes; (3) insurance market conservatism and lag (premiums remain elevated even during quieter periods); (4) proxy persistence (Houthis, possible Iraqi/Hezbollah reactivation); (5) force-posture inertia and mutual distrust preventing rapid drawdown or full reopening; (6) absence of a comprehensive political settlement addressing nuclear and Strait control issues.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Probabilities of each component being largely achieved by the horizon (rough, calibrated judgments):

- Major reduction in direct strikes (sustained): 1w 5%; 1m 15%; 3m 35%; 6m 55%; 1y 70%; 18m 80%.
- Sustained safe commercial transit (no systematic attacks, high volume): 1w 3%; 1m 8%; 3m 20%; 6m 40%; 1y 60%; 18m 75%.
- Meaningful insurance normalization (premiums ≤1–2% or low multiples, broad availability): 1w 2%; 1m 5%; 3m 15%; 6m 35%; 1y 55%; 18m 70%.
- Oil/LNG export recovery on normal routes/volumes: 1w 10% (already partial); 1m 20%; 3m 40%; 6m 60%; 1y 75%; 18m 85%.
- Proxy restraint: 1w 10%; 1m 20%; 3m 40%; 6m 55%; 1y 70%; 18m 80%.
- Force drawdown: 1w 2%; 1m 5%; 3m 15%; 6m 35%; 1y 55%; 18m 70%.
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 40%; 1m 30%; 3m 45%; 6m 55%; 1y 65%; 18m 70%.

Insurance, safe unrestricted transit, and force posture are typically the slowest; oil volume can recover faster via workarounds.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

• **1 Week**  
Probability: 3%  
Base-rate anchor: 2–5%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Downward (active attacks, election window, elevated premiums, restricted AIS traffic).  
Core rationale: Immediate military and commercial conditions remain far from the definition; post-election strike risk and ongoing incidents dominate.  
Main gating factor: Ongoing ship attacks and absence of any durable pause.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate comprehensive ceasefire with verified end to attacks and public transit reopening.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Confirmed major strike or sharp rise in attacks.  
Confidence in this estimate: High  

• **1 Month**  
Probability: 8%  
Base-rate anchor: 5–10%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly downward (mediation exists but no breakthrough; attack tempo high; election uncertainty).  
Core rationale: Possible short pause after elections, but commercial and insurance lags, plus residual IRGC capability, make full normality improbable.  
Main gating factor: Insurance pricing and unrestricted transit security.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Verified 2–3 week attack-free period plus early premium decline and transit surge.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Renewed major kinetic exchanges or proxy surge.  
Confidence in this estimate: Medium-High  

• **3 Months**  
Probability: 22%  
Base-rate anchor: 15–25%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slightly downward (adaptation in oil flows is real, but political settlement and insurance lag remain large).  
Core rationale: Possible de-escalation window if post-election diplomacy advances, but historical lags and Iran’s leverage incentives keep full multi-domain normality low-probability.  
Main gating factor: Durable end to systematic shipping attacks and insurance normalization.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Formal agreement reopening Hormuz on near-pre-war terms plus 60+ days of low incidents.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Renewed major campaign or persistent high-tempo IRGC activity.  
Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

• **6 Months**  
Probability: 38%  
Base-rate anchor: 30–45%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly upward on oil adaptation, downward on political and insurance inertia.  
Core rationale: Enough time for a freeze or limited deal to produce visible commercial recovery, but full insurance, force posture, and proxy restraint often take longer; residual risk common in reference classes.  
Main gating factor: Insurance market repricing and force drawdown.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Sustained low-incident period plus premium collapse and high AIS transit recovery.  
What would lower this forecast materially: New escalation cycle or Iranian rejection of any reopening formula.  
Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

• **1 Year**  
Probability: 58%  
Base-rate anchor: 50–65%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Mildly downward (nuclear and Strait-control issues unresolved; proxy capacity durable).  
Core rationale: Most reference classes show substantial commercial recovery by this horizon after a military pause, but the demanding definition (insurance, force posture, no residual systematic threat) and case-specific leverage dynamics keep it below 65%.  
Main gating factor: Political settlement durability and insurance/force normalization.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Comprehensive deal implemented with verified multi-month normality.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Frozen conflict with continued low-level attacks or renewed major fighting.  
Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

• **18 Months**  
Probability: 68%  
Base-rate anchor: 60–75%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Mildly downward (long-term Iranian residual capability and mutual distrust).  
Core rationale: Extended time favors adaptation and economic pressure for recovery, yet full functional normality (especially insurance and unrestricted security without escorts) remains incomplete in prolonged chokepoint cases; residual risk is the modal outcome.  
Main gating factor: Elimination of systematic residual threat and full insurance normalization.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Multi-year stability under a durable agreement.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Recurrent escalation cycles or permanent “managed risk” regime.  
Confidence in this estimate: Low-Medium  

**10. Most Likely Path**

A post-election period of heightened risk (possible limited strikes or intensified maritime pressure) followed by a fragile freeze or limited arrangement by early-to-mid 2027. Oil volumes continue via adapted routes at elevated cost; AIS-visible traffic recovers slowly; insurance premiums decline only gradually. Full multi-domain normality remains incomplete at 12–18 months, with residual risk premia, selective escorts or dark operations, and proxy activity. Probability mass concentrates on partial, managed recovery rather than clean return to pre-war conditions.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Strongest case: Rapid post-election diplomacy produces a durable reopening formula; Iran prioritizes revenue and accepts constrained Hormuz status; US draws down surge forces; premiums collapse within 60–90 days of verified quiet; AIS traffic rebounds above 70%. This path is possible if economic pain and regional mediation outweigh leverage calculations. It would push 6-month probability above 55% and 1-year above 75%.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Strongest case: Post-election strikes restart a high-intensity phase; Iran sustains or escalates maritime attacks and proxy activation; no political settlement on nuclear or Strait issues; insurance remains punitive; traffic stays depressed with permanent workarounds. Reference-class Red Sea and Tanker War tails support this. It would keep 6-month probability below 20% and 18-month below 45%.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

The forecast may overestimate normalization speed by underweighting Iran’s demonstrated ability to impose costs at low intensity and the conservatism of insurance markets (which lagged even the June MOU). It may underestimate normalization if oil-volume adaptation already signals that commercial actors will accept elevated risk faster than the definition assumes, or if election outcomes create a strong de-escalation window. Load-bearing assumptions are that residual IRGC maritime capability persists and that insurance/force posture lag military pauses by months. Evidence of a verified multi-month attack-free period with rising AIS traffic would force an upward revision; a new major strike campaign would force a downward one.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

Daily/weekly AIS and JMIC transit counts versus baseline; UKMTO/IMO incident logs and attribution; war-risk premium quotes from brokers; Brent and freight-rate levels; official statements on blockade status and Hormuz rules; force-posture announcements (carrier movements, escort reductions); proxy attack frequency on Saudi/Gulf targets; progress or collapse of mediation channels; post-election US/Israeli strike decisions.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon | Probability | Confidence | Main Gating Factor |
|---------|-------------|------------|--------------------|
| 1 week | 3% | High | Ongoing attacks & election risk |
| 1 month | 8% | Medium-High | Insurance & unrestricted transit |
| 3 months | 22% | Medium | Durable shipping security |
| 6 months | 38% | Medium | Insurance & force posture |
| 1 year | 58% | Medium | Settlement durability |
| 18 months | 68% | Low-Medium | Residual threat elimination |

These probabilities are calibrated judgments grounded in reference-class base rates, updated by the current evidence of restricted traffic, elevated premiums, partial oil adaptation, and unresolved political/military drivers. They treat commercial and insurance normalization as lagging any military pause and remain below 70% even at 18 months because the operational definition is deliberately demanding.

title: Iran War: 2% 1-week normality
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each horizon: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (from 26 October 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

“Return to functional normality” requires concurrent, sustained (at least 30 consecutive days) satisfaction of all of the following observable conditions across military, maritime, commercial, and market domains. Partial or temporary improvements do not count.

- **Direct military activity**: No large-scale US/Israeli strikes on Iranian territory or forces, and no Iranian large-scale missile/drone barrages on US bases, Gulf states, or Israel. Sporadic isolated incidents (<2 per week with no casualties or infrastructure damage) are tolerable only if they do not trigger retaliation cycles.
- **Proxy activity**: Houthi and other Iran-aligned forces conducting no more than residual, low-intensity attacks (≤1 significant incident per week) on Saudi/UAE targets or Bab el-Mandeb shipping. No active maritime embargo declarations.
- **Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters**: Commercial vessel attacks ≤1 per week for 30 days; no active mining or credible mine threats in main transit corridors; no Iranian requirement for permits, fees, or “authorized” routes enforced by fire.
- **Commercial transit levels**: Average daily transits (AIS-visible + dark/facilitated) ≥80–100 vessels (roughly 70–80% of pre-war ~120–140 baseline), with the majority broadcasting AIS normally and no large anchorage backlogs outside the strait.
- **War-risk insurance conditions**: Additional war-risk premiums for Gulf/Hormuz tankers ≤1% of hull value (near pre-war ~0.25%), with broad market availability and no reliance on special US/Saudi government backstops or 7-day cancellation clauses dominating pricing.
- **Oil and LNG export continuity**: Combined Gulf (Saudi, UAE, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, and residual Iranian) crude and LNG outflows at ≥85% of pre-war volumes without major reliance on high-cost “dark shuttle,” STS transfers, or pipeline bypasses as the primary mechanism. Iranian seaborne exports restored if sanctions are adjusted, or stably zero if under durable agreement.
- **Energy market stress and volatility**: Brent crude sustained in a $70–95 range (or equivalent real-term normal) with 30-day realized volatility near historical non-crisis levels; no persistent $20+ geopolitical risk premium.
- **Force posture of major actors**: US naval blockade of Iranian ports lifted or reduced to routine sanctions enforcement; no dedicated multi-carrier strike groups permanently postured solely for Hormuz/Gulf interdiction; Iranian IRGC naval forces not actively interdicting or declaring routes “illegal.”
- **Absence of major new escalation triggers**: No assassination of senior leadership, strikes on nuclear/missile production infrastructure that restart high-intensity air campaigns, or attacks that destroy major export terminals.

A temporary ceasefire, a battlefield pause, or lower oil prices alone do not meet the standard. Commercial and insurance normalization must be independently verified.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 26 October 2026, ~Day 241)**

The war began with US-Israeli strikes on 28 February 2026. An April ceasefire and a June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding both collapsed. Major land/air campaigns have paused (Trump has publicly held off on strikes until after 3 November midterms), but the maritime domain remains active. Iran continues frequent attacks on commercial shipping (October has the highest monthly total since the opening phase—dozens of incidents, including drones, projectiles, and claimed mines). The US maintains a naval blockade of Iranian ports (reimposed mid-July). AIS-visible transit is severely reduced (~8% of pre-war in some trackers); US-facilitated “dark” transits and pipeline bypasses have kept non-Iranian Gulf crude flows closer to pre-war levels at high cost. Hundreds of vessels wait outside the strait. War-risk premiums stand at 6–10% of hull value (up from ~0.25%). Brent is ~$114–117. Diplomacy continues via Pakistan/Qatar mediators, but stalled on nuclear constraints, Hormuz control, and blockade terms. Houthi activity against Saudi targets persists. Force posture remains elevated (additional US carrier movements reported). Confirmed facts are distinguished from IRGC claims (many mine/tanker-hit assertions remain unverified or disputed by US officials).

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant cases:

- **Tanker War (1984–1988)**: Sustained attacks on shipping during Iran-Iraq War; traffic continued under US escort (Operation Earnest Will) but with elevated risk and premiums. Full commercial normalization followed the August 1988 ceasefire and political end of hostilities. Suggests multi-year disruption possible while kinetic pressure and political disputes persist; stabilization within months after durable ceasefire.
- **2011–12 Hormuz threats**: Verbal Iranian closure threats and drills; no sustained kinetic closure or major insurance spike. Rapid return to baseline once threats receded. Suggests short timelines when kinetic action is absent.
- **Red Sea/Houthi campaign (2023–ongoing)**: Multi-month to multi-year partial disruption; rerouting, elevated premiums, and incomplete commercial normalization even after some tactical pauses. Suggests commercial adaptation lags military pauses by months.
- **Brief Iran-US tanker incidents (2019) and Soleimani aftermath (2020)**: Short spikes in risk premiums and force posture; return to functional normality within weeks to a few months once direct escalation stopped.
- **Post-ceasefire recovery after limited Gulf conflicts**: Insurance and traffic typically recover over 1–3 months once attacks cease and political signals stabilize, but slower when mines, residual proxy activity, or unresolved political claims remain.

Base-rate prior (before case-specific update): Low near-term probability of full functional normality in an active kinetic maritime campaign with unresolved political demands. Rough prior: 1 week <5%; 1 month ~10%; 3 months ~20–25%; 6 months ~35–40%; 1 year ~50–55%; 18 months ~60–65%. These are then adjusted upward or downward by current evidence.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence Item | Source Type | Direction on Normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| October highest attack month (27+ commercial incidents) | Maritime monitors (UKMTO, IMO, USNI, Lloyd’s List) | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| AIS-visible traffic ~8% of pre-war; hundreds of vessels waiting | Vessel tracking (hormuz.now, JMIC, Windward) | Strongly against | High | Confirmed (AIS); facilitated dark transits partially offset |
| War-risk premiums 6–10% of hull value | Brokers/insurers (Marsh, FT, Insurance Business) | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports active since mid-July | Official US statements, tracking | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Non-Iranian Gulf crude flows near pre-war via shuttles/pipelines | Energy data (Kpler, Vortexa, Bessent claims) | Mildly toward (partial) | Medium | Partially confirmed; disputed vs. transit counts |
| Brent ~$114–117; elevated volatility | Market data | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Trump pause on major strikes until after 3 Nov midterms | Official statements | Mildly toward (near-term) | High | Confirmed |
| Ongoing mediation (Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi/Turkish delegations in Tehran) | Diplomatic reporting (AP, Al Jazeera) | Mildly toward | Medium | Confirmed activity; outcome uncertain |
| IRGC claims of multiple mine/tanker hits; US disputes some | Conflicting official statements | Against | Medium | Disputed |
| Houthi attacks on Saudi targets continuing | Saudi coalition, Houthi claims | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Iranian insistence Hormuz stays restricted until US terms accepted | Iranian officials (Araghchi) | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

Ranked: (1) US political calendar and post-midterm deal incentives (Trump statements leave open “nice big beautiful agreement”); (2) Sustained mediation channels and Gulf state interest in de-escalation; (3) Market and shipping adaptation already keeping partial oil flows moving; (4) Mutual interest in avoiding full resumption of high-intensity air campaign; (5) Potential for limited technical arrangements on transit lanes even short of full political settlement.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

Ranked: (1) Iranian demonstrated capacity and willingness to sustain shipping attacks as leverage (highest October rate); (2) Unresolved core disputes (nuclear constraints, blockade lift, Hormuz control/permits); (3) Elevated war-risk insurance pricing and commercial risk aversion that lag any military pause; (4) Residual proxy (Houthi) activity and mine threats; (5) Force posture and blockade continuity; (6) History of collapsed MOUs and ceasefires in this conflict.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities that each component reaches the operational threshold by horizon (not mechanical averages):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: High by 1 month if pause holds (~70%), but fragile thereafter.
- Sustained safe commercial transit through Hormuz: Very low near-term; rises meaningfully only after political signal + 1–3 months of low attacks.
- Meaningful insurance normalization: Lags transit recovery by weeks to months; low until attacks stay near zero.
- Oil/LNG export recovery (functional, not just partial): Partial already; full threshold requires transit + insurance + political clarity.
- Proxy restraint: Medium near-term, dependent on Iranian direction and Saudi responses.
- Force drawdown: Low until political settlement.
- No new major escalation trigger: Medium-high in next 1–2 weeks (election timing); lower thereafter.

Gating factors are shipping security + insurance + sustained low attacks. Partial oil flows and military pauses are insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
• Probability: 2%  
• Base-rate anchor: Near-zero in active kinetic maritime phases of Tanker War analogs.  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Downward; highest October attack rate, premiums elevated, blockade and Iranian conditions unchanged.  
• Core rationale: Active interdiction and commercial disruption continue; no mechanism for multi-domain recovery in days.  
• Main gating factor: Shipping attacks and insurance.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate verified ceasefire on shipping + premium collapse (extremely unlikely).  
• What would lower this forecast materially: New major strike or mass casualty shipping incident.  
• Confidence in this estimate: High  

**1 Month**  
• Probability: 8%  
• Base-rate anchor: Low single digits to low teens in unresolved kinetic chokepoint cases.  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly upward from pure base rate due to election pause and mediation, but offset by attack tempo.  
• Core rationale: Post-midterm window could produce a limited pause, but commercial and insurance lags plus Iranian leverage make full normality improbable.  
• Main gating factor: Sustained attack reduction + insurance response.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Verified multi-week shipping pause + rapid premium drop below 2% + transit surge.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Resumption of major US/Israeli strikes or accelerated Iranian attacks.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
• Probability: 18%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~20–25% from mixed chokepoint and post-ceasefire recoveries.  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Downward; history of collapsed agreements in this war and persistent Iranian maritime capacity.  
• Core rationale: Possible limited deal or de-escalation after elections, but multi-domain requirements (especially insurance and free transit) typically require more time once attacks stop.  
• Main gating factor: Political settlement durability and commercial follow-through.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Durable MOU with observed attack cessation and transit recovery >60% of baseline.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Escalation cycle or mine/residual threat confirmation.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**6 Months**  
• Probability: 32%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~35–40% from Tanker War partial recoveries and Red Sea adaptation timelines.  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mildly downward given unresolved core issues and demonstrated Iranian resilience.  
• Core rationale: Sufficient time for a political deal to translate into attack reduction, transit recovery, and insurance normalization if incentives align; still substantial risk of continued leverage campaign.  
• Main gating factor: Iranian decision to trade maritime pressure for sanctions/blockade relief.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Verified free transit regime + premiums <1.5% for 60+ days.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: New escalation or breakdown of mediation.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**1 Year**  
• Probability: 48%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~50–55%.  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mildly downward; long-horizon political and proxy risks remain.  
• Core rationale: Higher chance of either a negotiated end-state or market/shipping adaptation that meets the operational threshold, but not guaranteed.  
• Main gating factor: Absence of renewed high-intensity campaign and residual threats.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Formal political settlement with observed multi-domain recovery.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Regime instability in Iran or expanded regional proxy war.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium-Low  

**18 Months**  
• Probability: 58%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~60–65%.  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mildly downward.  
• Core rationale: Most kinetic maritime campaigns eventually produce some form of commercial normalization or durable political arrangement within this window, but residual risks and possible incomplete settlements keep it below high confidence.  
• Main gating factor: Long-term political durability.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Full settlement and force posture normalization.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Entrenched low-level maritime conflict or new regional war.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Low-Medium  

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued elevated maritime pressure and partial oil flows through protected/dark mechanisms through the US midterms and into early 2027. Limited diplomatic progress produces occasional tactical pauses but not durable multi-domain normality until a broader political trade (nuclear constraints vs. blockade/sanctions relief) is reached or one side’s costs become prohibitive. Full functional normality more likely in the 9–18 month window than sooner.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Post-election deal that includes Iranian restraint on shipping, US blockade adjustment, and rapid technical demining/transit protocols. Insurance markets reprice within weeks of verified attack cessation. Probability weighted lower because prior MOUs collapsed and core issues remain hard.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Iran sustains intermittent attacks as leverage; US maintains blockade and periodic strikes; proxies remain active; insurance and commercial traffic stay suppressed. Partial oil flows continue at high cost indefinitely. Higher probability than the fastest case given current attack tempo and history.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

The forecast may overestimate near-term normalization by weighting the election pause and mediation more heavily than Iranian demonstrated capacity and the lag between military signals and commercial/insurance recovery. It may underestimate longer-horizon normality if a political settlement proves more durable than prior attempts or if markets fully adapt via bypasses and alternative routes. Load-bearing assumptions are that Iran retains effective maritime interdiction capacity and that commercial actors require sustained low-attack periods before premiums and volumes normalize.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

Weekly commercial attack counts (UKMTO/IMO); AIS + facilitated transit volumes; war-risk premium quotes; status of US blockade and Iranian permit regime; mediation outcomes and any verified technical transit agreements; Houthi activity levels; Brent volatility and Gulf export data; force posture changes (carrier movements, blockade enforcement).

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon | Probability | Main Gating Factor | Confidence |
|---------|-------------|--------------------|------------|
| 1 Week | 2% | Active attacks & insurance | High |

title: October 25 forecast: 3% 1-week normality
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each of these horizons: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months.

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

Functional normality requires simultaneous, sustained (minimum 30 consecutive days of observation for the shorter horizons; longer for the extended ones) multi-domain conditions. It is not a ceasefire, not lower oil prices alone, and not a battlefield pause while commercial risk remains elevated.

- **Direct military activity**: No sustained large-scale US/Israeli strikes on Iranian territory or major Iranian counterstrikes on US/Gulf state assets or shipping. Minor isolated incidents do not disqualify if they do not restart the prior tempo.
- **Proxy activity**: Houthi attacks on Saudi energy, infrastructure, airports, or shipping reduced to sporadic/low levels (well below current multi-incident weekly rates). No major new or expanded activation of Iraqi, Lebanese, or other proxies that materially affects Gulf shipping or energy.
- **Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters**: AIS-visible plus confirmed total commercial transits return to ≥70% of pre-crisis levels (pre-crisis roughly 80–90 commercial vessels per day). Attack frequency falls below roughly two significant incidents per week with no sinkings. Mine threats are cleared or demonstrably negligible.
- **Commercial transit levels**: Sustained high volumes of ordinary commercial traffic without primary reliance on military escorts or widespread “dark” (AIS-off) operations for the majority of vessels.
- **War-risk insurance conditions**: Additional war-risk premiums fall below 1% of hull value for routine tankers/LNG carriers (versus current 6–10%), with broad market availability and no requirement for large-scale government backstops for ordinary voyages.
- **Oil and LNG export continuity**: Non-Iranian Gulf crude exports (via Hormuz plus bypass pipelines) at or above pre-war levels on a sustained basis. Qatar/UAE LNG flows approach pre-war volumes. Iranian seaborne exports are not required for this definition.
- **Energy market stress and volatility**: Brent not persistently elevated solely by Hormuz-specific risk premia (sustained movement toward a range consistent with non-war fundamentals). Volatility metrics normalize.
- **Force posture of major actors**: US naval blockade of Iranian ports lifted or converted to routine presence. Major US carrier/strike assets reduced from crisis levels. Iranian naval forces not postured for active interdiction of non-Iranian traffic.
- **Absence of major new escalation triggers**: No new leadership targeting, nuclear-related provocations that restart large-scale strikes, or territorial seizures that reopen high-intensity fighting.

Temporary workarounds (US-facilitated corridors, pipeline bypasses, elevated insurance that still allows some traffic) do not constitute normality.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot** (as of ~25 October 2026)

The war began on 28 February 2026 with joint US-Israeli strikes (Operation Epic Fury / Roaring Lion) that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran retaliated with missiles and drones and restricted the Strait of Hormuz. An April pause and the June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding produced a temporary lift of the US blockade and a partial traffic rebound; the arrangement collapsed in July, the blockade was reimposed on 14 July, and the MOU expired in mid-August.

As of late October (roughly Day 240 of the Hormuz crisis):
- US blockade of Iranian ports remains active (CENTCOM reports prevention of ~$25 billion in Iranian oil exports; no meaningful Iranian seaborne crude loadings for months).
- US forces facilitate “dark” and escorted transits for non-Iranian traffic via a southern corridor near Oman. AIS-visible commercial traffic is ~7% of pre-crisis (~5–6 vessels/day versus ~85). Actual facilitated volumes are higher (reports of dozens per day or hundreds in some weekly windows).
- Iranian/IRGC attacks on commercial shipping reached their highest monthly total of the war in October (UKMTO/IMO and maritime trackers report 20–28+ incidents; some ships sunk). Claims of mines versus projectiles are disputed; US statements treat many IRGC claims as exaggerated or false.
- Non-Iranian Gulf crude flows have recovered to or above pre-war levels excluding Iran via a combination of Hormuz (often 70–80+% of pre-war in recent weeks) plus increased pipeline bypasses (Saudi East-West and UAE routes now carrying a much larger share). LNG remains more constrained. Brent has traded in the $100–115 range recently (pre-war ~$70).
- War-risk premiums for Gulf tanker voyages stand at 6–10% of hull value (versus ~0.25% pre-crisis), equating to multi-million-dollar costs per VLCC transit. Coverage is available but commercially prohibitive for ordinary traffic.
- Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, energy facilities, and related targets continue at elevated levels, with reports of interceptor shortages and ground fighting in Yemen.
- Indirect talks continue via mediators; Iranian conditions for reopening Hormuz remain extensive (end blockade, sanctions relief, force withdrawals, compensation). Trump has publicly pledged no strikes on Iran before the 3 November US midterms. US naval presence remains large.

Confirmed facts are distinguished from claims: attack counts and traffic data come from UKMTO, Lloyd’s List, Kpler/Vortexa-type trackers, IMO, and CENTCOM statements; Iranian claims of control or specific mine hits are frequently contested by US reporting.

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

- **Tanker War (Iran–Iraq, ~1984–1988)**: Relevant as the closest sustained maritime campaign against Gulf shipping with US escort operations (Earnest Will from 1987). Traffic never fully stopped; insurance rates rose sharply (peaks in the several-percent range) and declined after the August 1988 ceasefire, with more complete normalization over the following 1–2 years. Breakdown: current conflict involves direct US–Iran state-on-state fighting, a formal blockade, drones/missiles at higher volume, and proxy dimensions absent or weaker then. Suggests commercial stabilization lags military intensity reduction by months, with full insurance and force normalization often taking 6–18 months after intensity drops.
- **Red Sea / Houthi disruptions (2023–2025)**: Relevant for asymmetric attacks raising insurance and diverting traffic without full physical closure. Traffic remained depressed for over a year in many segments; insurance stayed elevated until attack frequency fell materially. Partial returns occurred only after sustained quiet periods. Breakdown: Hormuz has far less viable bypass capacity than the Cape route. Suggests multi-month to multi-quarter lags even after attacks decline.
- **Brief 2019 Gulf tanker incidents and 2019–2020 US–Iran tensions**: Relevant for short, limited disruptions resolved by diplomacy or restraint within weeks to a few months. Breakdown: scale and duration of the 2026 war are larger.
- **1991 Gulf War oil recovery**: Relevant for rapid export rebound once military conditions stabilized, aided by alternative routes. Breakdown: different political and military end-state.
- **Historical chokepoint physical closures (e.g., Suez)**: Physical clearance can enable recovery in weeks once the obstacle is removed, but risk perception and insurance lag.

**Base-rate prior** (before current-case updates, reflecting typical lags in comparable chokepoint/maritime war cases):  
1 week ~5%; 1 month ~10–12%; 3 months ~25%; 6 months ~40%; 1 year ~55–60%; 18 months ~70–75%.  
These embed the observed pattern that commercial and insurance normalization trail military de-escalation by 3–12+ months and that low-level residual risk can persist.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| Highest monthly shipping attacks in October (20–28+) | UKMTO, IMO, Lloyd’s List, USNI | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| AIS-visible traffic ~7% of pre-crisis | Vessel tracking / hormuz.now-type | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Non-Iranian crude flows recovered to/above pre-war via Hormuz + bypasses | Kpler, Vortexa, Reuters, WSJ | Toward (physical resilience) | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk premiums 6–10% of hull | Brokers, Financial Times, Insurance Business | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports active since 14 July; ~$25B prevented | CENTCOM | Against full normality (force posture) | High | Confirmed |
| US-facilitated dark/escorted corridor operating | CENTCOM, Windward, Lloyd’s | Partial toward (volumes) but not normality | High | Confirmed |
| Houthi attacks on Saudi airports/energy continuing | Reuters, ISW, regional reporting | Against (proxy) | High | Confirmed |
| MOU expired; Iranian conditions for Hormuz reopening extensive | Official statements, JINSA trackers | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Trump pledge no strikes before midterms | Public statements | Mixed (short-term restraint, post-election risk) | Medium | Confirmed |
| Some IRGC mine/attack claims disputed by CENTCOM | CENTCOM vs IRGC | Reduces Iranian narrative of total control | Medium | Disputed |
| LNG flows remain more constrained than crude | Kpler-type reporting | Against | Medium | Inferred from tracking gaps and volume data |
| Insurance market has paid out ~$2B range in claims | IUMI / Howden-type estimates | Against (pricing stickiness) | Medium | Reported |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

1. Physical oil-flow resilience via US-protected corridor + pipeline bypasses (reduces immediate economic pressure for a deal).  
2. High cumulative cost of the blockade to Iran and demonstrated US capacity to sustain it.  
3. Mutual interest in avoiding full resumption of large-scale strikes (US domestic politics; Iranian reconstruction needs).  
4. Historical pattern that sustained quiet produces insurance and traffic recovery within quarters.  
5. Ongoing (if stalled) mediation channels.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

1. Iranian use of shipping attacks as leverage while the blockade continues (current tempo highest of the war).  
2. Insurance pricing stickiness and commercial aversion even after partial quiet (Red Sea and Tanker War precedents).  
3. Active Houthi campaign against Saudi targets and ground fighting in Yemen.  
4. Trust deficit, expired MOU, and expansive Iranian conditions.  
5. Elevated US force posture and post-midterm strike risk.  
6. Regime incentives under Mojtaba Khamenei to demonstrate resistance capability.

Ranked importance: shipping-attack tempo and insurance pricing are the tightest short-term gates; proxy and force-posture issues dominate medium-to-long-term risk.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities of each component being satisfied by the horizon (not independent; gated by military intensity and attack tempo):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 40%; 1m 55%; 3m 70%; 6m 80%; 1y 85%; 18m 90%.  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥70% levels, low attacks): 1w 5%; 1m 12%; 3m 25%; 6m 40%; 1y 60%; 18m 75%.  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (<1%): 1w 3%; 1m 8%; 3m 18%; 6m 35%; 1y 55%; 18m 70%.  
- Oil/LNG export recovery (non-Iranian sustained): already largely met for crude; LNG lags. Overall 1w 60%; 1m 65%; 3m 75%; 6m 85%; 1y 90%; 18m 92%.  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 15%; 1m 25%; 3m 40%; 6m 55%; 1y 70%; 18m 80%.  
- Force drawdown / blockade lift: 1w 5%; 1m 10%; 3m 20%; 6m 35%; 1y 55%; 18m 70%.  
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 70%; 1m 60%; 3m 55%; 6m 60%; 1y 65%; 18m 70%.

Shipping security and insurance are the primary gating factors for the composite definition. Oil recovery has already advanced further than commercial normality.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
• Probability: 3%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~5%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Down (peak October attacks, elevated insurance, active blockade and Houthi activity).  
• Core rationale: Current tempo of shipping attacks and insurance pricing make multi-domain normality impossible in one week.  
• Main gating factor: Shipping security and insurance.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate, verified halt to all shipping attacks plus public de-escalation commitments.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Additional sinkings or resumption of large-scale strikes.  
• Confidence in this estimate: High

**1 Month**  
• Probability: 8%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~10–12%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Down (attacks still elevated; midterm politics constrain but do not resolve).  
• Core rationale: One month is insufficient for insurance markets and commercial operators to treat the corridor as reliable even if attacks drop sharply.  
• Main gating factor: Insurance normalization and sustained safe transit.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Documented multi-week drop in attacks plus visible insurance quotes falling toward 2%.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Post-midterm strike resumption or Houthi intensification.  
• Confidence in this estimate: High

**3 Months**  
• Probability: 20%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~25%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Down (insurance stickiness and proxy activity).  
• Core rationale: Possible if a durable quiet period begins immediately after midterms and holds, but insurance and commercial return typically lag by additional weeks to months.  
• Main gating factor: Transition from escorted/dark traffic to ordinary commercial volumes with falling premiums.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Formal or de facto ceasefire holding through January with attack rates near zero.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Continued or renewed high-frequency attacks.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium

**6 Months**  
• Probability: 35%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~40%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mildly down (current intensity and trust deficit).  
• Core rationale: Aligns with Tanker War and Red Sea patterns in which partial commercial recovery occurs within two quarters of sustained intensity reduction, provided proxies also quiet.  
• Main gating factor: Insurance falling below ~2% and force posture beginning to ease.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Blockade conversion to routine presence plus proxy restraint.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: New escalation cycle or persistent low-level attacks that keep premiums elevated.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium

**1 Year**  
• Probability: 55%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~55–60%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Roughly neutral to mildly down.  
• Core rationale: Historical cases show substantial normalization within a year once high-intensity fighting ends, but residual political and proxy risks remain material. Oil resilience reduces the urgency of a comprehensive deal.  
• Main gating factor: Durable political arrangement or sustained mutual restraint sufficient for insurance and force drawdown.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Verified multi-month quiet plus partial sanctions or blockade relief.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Renewed large-scale strikes or expanded Houthi campaign.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium

**18 Months**  
• Probability: 70%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~70–75%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mildly down (possibility of prolonged low-level attrition).  
• Core rationale: Most comparable chokepoint disruptions resolve commercially within 12–18 months of intensity reduction. Long-horizon residual risk of episodic attacks or political reversals prevents higher probability.  
• Main gating factor: Absence of new escalation triggers and insurance market memory of losses.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Formal settlement and visible force reductions.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Entrenched low-intensity conflict that keeps premiums structurally higher.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium

**10. Most Likely Path**

Attacks remain elevated through the US midterms. A period of relative military quiet follows, possibly with continued low-level Iranian shipping harassment and Houthi activity. US-facilitated corridors and pipeline bypasses keep non-Iranian oil volumes near pre-war levels. Insurance declines only gradually. Full multi-domain normality (ordinary traffic, sub-1% insurance, reduced force posture, proxy restraint) is more likely in the 9–18 month window than earlier, contingent on no major post-election escalation.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Post-midterm negotiations produce a limited, holding arrangement that includes attack halt, partial blockade relief, and proxy de-escalation. Insurance markets reprice within 6–8 weeks of verified quiet. Ordinary commercial traffic returns above 70% by month 4–5. Probability mass shifts upward by 15–25 points at the 6-month and 1-year horizons.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Iran maintains intermittent shipping attacks as leverage; Houthis continue pressure on Saudi targets; post-election US strikes resume or the blockade hardens. Insurance remains structurally elevated; commercial operators treat Hormuz as permanently higher-risk. Normality probabilities fall 15–20 points at the 1-year and 18-month horizons, with functional recovery extending beyond 18 months.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Strongest case for faster normalization: Oil physical flows have already recovered substantially, reducing the economic cost of delay and increasing the chance that both sides accept a messy, incomplete status quo that markets eventually treat as normal enough. Insurance can reprice faster than historical averages if attack data improve sharply.  
Strongest case for prolonged instability: The current attack tempo demonstrates Iranian capability and willingness eight months in; insurance losses already exceed $2 billion range; proxies have independent incentives; political trust is lower than in the Tanker War.  
Where the forecast may overestimate normalization: Residual “acceptable” risk pricing and partial dark-traffic norms may become semi-permanent, so the operational definition is never fully met even if volumes are high.  
Where it may underestimate: A sharp post-election political breakthrough or Iranian internal constraints could produce faster quiet than base rates imply.  
Load-bearing assumptions: Attack tempo is responsive to US restraint/blockade status; insurance lags but does not freeze; proxies can be influenced by Iran.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Weekly UKMTO/IMO/Lloyd’s attack counts and confirmed sinkings.  
- AIS-visible and estimated total (including dark) transit volumes.  
- Broker-quoted war-risk premiums (% of hull).  
- Kpler/Vortexa-type crude and LNG export volumes through Hormuz versus bypasses.  
- CENTCOM statements on blockade enforcement and escort operations.  
- Houthi attack frequency and Saudi interceptor consumption.  
- Post-3 November US statements on strike intentions and Iranian responses.  
- Any verified multi-week period of near-zero shipping incidents.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon | Probability | Primary Gating Factor | Confidence |
|---------|-------------|-----------------------|------------|
| 1 week | 3% | Shipping security + insurance | High |
| 1 month | 8% | Insurance + sustained quiet | High |
| 3 months | 20% | Transition to ordinary traffic | Medium |
| 6 months | 35% | Insurance decline + force posture | Medium |
| 1 year | 55% | Durable restraint or partial deal | Medium |
| 18 months | 70% | Absence of new escalation cycles | Medium |

The gap between military pauses (or oil-volume recovery via workarounds) and multi-domain commercial normality is the central reason short-horizon probabilities remain low. Historical reference classes support gradual recovery once intensity falls, but current evidence of elevated attacks, insurance pricing, and proxy activity keeps the near-term outlook constrained.

title: Iran War: 4% 1-week normality
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each of these horizons: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months. (As of 24 October 2026; war began 28 February 2026, ~day 238.)

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

“Return to functional normality” requires sustained, observable multi-domain conditions over a continuous 14-day window (to exclude temporary pauses), meeting all of the following thresholds simultaneously:

- **Direct military activity**: No large-scale U.S./Israeli strikes on Iranian territory or Iranian ballistic/cruise missile or large drone barrages against regional targets (isolated residual incidents <5% of peak rates acceptable if not escalating).
- **Proxy activity**: Houthi and other Iran-linked proxy attacks on shipping, energy infrastructure, or Gulf states reduced to sporadic/low-intensity levels (≤2 confirmed incidents per week across the region) with no coordinated campaigns.
- **Shipping security (Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters)**: AIS-visible commercial transits averaging ≥60% of pre-war baseline (~85/day); no systematic mining, drone/missile attacks on commercial vessels, or IRGC “authorization” enforcement that effectively deters non-coordinated traffic; dark/escorted lanes not required as the dominant mode.
- **Commercial transit levels**: Sustained volumes of crude, products, LNG, and dry bulk through Hormuz and Gulf ports at ≥70% of pre-war levels (adjusting for bypasses like East-West pipeline).
- **War-risk insurance**: Premiums for Hormuz/Gulf transits ≤1.5–2× pre-war baseline (~0.25–0.5% of hull value per voyage) with broad underwriter availability and no mass P&I cancellations or force-majeure clustering by majors.
- **Oil and LNG export continuity**: Aggregate Gulf crude/condensate exports ≥16–17 Mb/d (near pre-war); Iranian crude loadings resumed at commercial scale without blockade; Qatari LNG force majeure largely lifted and exports ≥70% of pre-war.
- **Energy market stress and volatility**: Brent sustained below ~$85–90 (absent major non-Gulf shocks), with realized volatility and freight as % of FOB price returning near pre-war norms; no systemic buyer stockpiling or force-majeure cascade.
- **Force posture of major actors**: U.S. carrier/amphibious presence and blockade posture reduced from wartime peaks; Iranian IRGC Navy not enforcing exclusion zones; no active mutual high-alert nuclear/missile postures.
- **Absence of major new escalation triggers**: No new large strikes, mine campaigns, proxy offensives, or diplomatic collapses that reset the above within the window.

Temporary ceasefires, price dips alone, or battlefield pauses without commercial/insurance/export recovery do **not** count. The definition is demanding by design: commercial normalization lags military pauses.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot**

War ongoing without formal ceasefire. Trump has pledged no U.S. strikes before 3 November midterms, but blockade of Iranian ports (reimposed ~14 July) continues and preparations for post-election options are reported. October has seen the highest ship-attack tempo of the war (~26–28 incidents per UKMTO/Lloyd’s/JINSA/USNI). AIS-visible Hormuz transits are extremely low (~5–6% of normal in some trackers; higher for dark/US-escorted shuttle operations). Crude flows through Hormuz and bypasses partially recovered (reports of 8.5–16+ Mb/d depending on source and period; bypasses elevated). Iranian crude exports near zero since September under blockade. LNG from Qatar remains heavily constrained with ongoing force majeure. Brent ~$110–117. War-risk insurance 6–10% of hull value. Houthi activity against Saudi targets continues. Diplomacy via Qatar/Pakistan mediators is active but stalled on sequencing (blockade lift vs. Hormuz opening vs. nuclear constraints). Claims of control and attack attribution are contested; confirmed high attack rate and low visible traffic are robust.

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant classes (3–6):

- **1984–88 Tanker War (Iran-Iraq)**: ~450 ship attacks over years; strait never fully closed; flows largely maintained via reflagging/escorts (Operation Earnest Will 1987–88). Relevant for persistence of low-level attacks without total closure. Breaks down: no sustained U.S. blockade of one side’s ports; different power balance. Suggests multi-year partial disruption possible but commercial flows resilient under protection. Stabilization of attacks only with broader ceasefire (1988).
- **2019 Gulf of Oman/Hormuz incidents**: Short spike in attacks and war-risk premia (10× jump); traffic continued. Relevant for rapid insurance reaction and resilience. Breaks down: far lower intensity and no blockade or sustained campaign. Timeline: weeks to months for premia to ease once incidents stopped.
- **2023–24 Red Sea/Houthi campaign**: Months of attacks reducing Red Sea transits sharply; insurance elevated; partial recovery only with naval protection and later intensity drop. Relevant for proxy maritime disruption and slow commercial return. Breaks down: not a full great-power war or Hormuz-scale oil volume. Timeline: 6–12+ months for meaningful normalization even after intensity falls.
- **Post-ceasefire maritime recovery in other conflicts (e.g., limited Iran-Iraq pauses, or historical chokepoint reopenings)**: Insurance and traffic lag military pauses by weeks–months due to residual risk, mines, and underwriter caution. Suggests 1–3 months minimum after credible de-escalation for partial commercial recovery; 6–12+ for full.
- **Sustained great-power naval blockade or high-intensity Gulf campaigns**: Rare full analogues; historical blockades (e.g., earlier Iran-Iraq phases) show prolonged export disruption until political resolution. Suggests low probability of quick full normality without deal.

**Base-rate prior** (before current evidence, averaging across classes with weight on Tanker War resilience + modern insurance sensitivity + proxy persistence):

- 1 week: ~2–5%
- 1 month: ~8–12%
- 3 months: ~20–30%
- 6 months: ~40–50%
- 1 year: ~55–65%
- 18 months: ~65–75%

These reflect that full multi-domain commercial normality is slow even after intensity drops, and Gulf oil systems show resilience under protection but insurance/traffic lag.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence Item | Source Type | Direction on Normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| Highest October ship attacks (~26–28) | UKMTO, Lloyd’s, JINSA, USNI | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| AIS-visible transits ~5–6% of normal | hormuz.now, PortWatch, Windward | Strongly against | High | Confirmed (AIS limitation noted) |
| Dark/US-escorted flows continuing; some crude recovery via bypasses | CENTCOM, Kpler, Lloyd’s | Mildly toward (partial resilience) | Medium-High | Confirmed |
| Iranian crude exports ~0 since Sept under blockade | Kpler, UANI, AGBI | Against | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk 6–10% hull; P&I issues | Marsh, FT, brokers | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Brent $110–117 | Market data | Against (stress) | High | Confirmed |
| Qatar LNG force majeure ongoing; low exports | Kpler, reports | Against | High | Confirmed |
| No formal ceasefire; Trump no-strike pledge pre-Nov 3 | Official statements, reporting | Neutral/near-term pause | High | Confirmed |
| Active mediation (Qatar/Pakistan); proposals on table but stalled | Diplomatic reporting | Mildly toward | Medium | Confirmed |
| Houthi attacks on Saudi continuing | Saudi coalition, reporting | Against | High | Confirmed |
| US force buildup (carriers, ARG) | Official/reporting | Against (posture) | Medium-High | Reported |
| Contested claims (mines, control, exact flows) | IRGC vs. CENTCOM | Uncertainty | Low-Medium | Disputed |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

1. Economic and political exhaustion on both sides (Iran revenue hit hard; U.S. midterms and domestic costs).
2. Active mediation tracks and repeated proposals (even if stalled).
3. Demonstrated resilience of partial flows via escorts, dark shipping, and bypasses.
4. Trump’s explicit pre-midterm pause and stated preference for a deal over indefinite war.
5. Shared interest among Gulf producers and Asian buyers in restoring volumes.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

1. Ongoing high-tempo shipping attacks and Iranian enforcement attempts (gating for insurance and traffic).
2. U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and zero Iranian crude exports (core leverage and revenue pressure).
3. Proxy (Houthi) activity and risk of further activation.
4. Deep distrust, sequencing disputes (blockade lift vs. Hormuz control vs. nuclear), and post-election strike options.
5. Elevated force postures and residual mine/drone risk that keep underwriters cautious even after pauses.
6. LNG and refined-product systems less flexible than crude bypasses.

Ranked by importance: shipping security/attacks and insurance lag > blockade and export continuity > proxy and force posture > diplomacy.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities of each sub-component being met by horizon (gating ones dominate synthesis):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 70%, 1m 55%, 3m 45%, 6m 60%, 1y 75%, 18m 80% (pause possible but not durable).
- Sustained safe commercial transit (AIS + low attacks): 1w 5%, 1m 10%, 3m 25%, 6m 45%, 1y 65%, 18m 75%.
- Meaningful insurance normalization: 1w 3%, 1m 8%, 3m 20%, 6m 40%, 1y 60%, 18m 70%.
- Oil/LNG export recovery to thresholds: 1w 15% (partial crude), 1m 25%, 3m 40%, 6m 55%, 1y 70%, 18m 80%.
- Proxy restraint: 1w 20%, 1m 30%, 3m 40%, 6m 55%, 1y 70%, 18m 75%.
- Force drawdown: 1w 10%, 1m 20%, 3m 35%, 6m 50%, 1y 65%, 18m 75%.
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 40%, 1m 30%, 3m 35%, 6m 45%, 1y 55%, 18m 60%.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**
- Probability: 4%
- Base-rate anchor: ~3%
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly higher due to pre-midterm pause, but attacks and insurance dominate.
- Core rationale: High October attack rate, 6–10% war risk, AIS traffic near floor, blockade intact, and no deal. Pause in large strikes is insufficient under the definition.
- Main gating factor: Shipping security and insurance.
- What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate verified cessation of all attacks + public underwriter signals.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Further sinkings or U.S. strike resumption.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

**1 Month**
- Probability: 10%
- Base-rate anchor: ~10%
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral; mediation and pause offset by attack tempo and blockade.
- Core rationale: Midterms pass; residual risk and underwriter caution keep commercial normalization low. Partial crude flows do not equal full definition.
- Main gating factor: Sustained attack cessation + insurance reopening.
- What would raise this forecast materially: Credible deal or durable attack halt by late November.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Post-election strikes or Houthi escalation.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium-High

**3 Months**
- Probability: 28%
- Base-rate anchor: ~25%
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly higher on mediation and resilience signals.
- Core rationale: Window for post-midterm deal or exhaustion-driven de-escalation; still low odds of simultaneous insurance, traffic, LNG, and proxy thresholds.
- Main gating factor: Insurance and commercial transit recovery (lags military pause).
- What would raise this forecast materially: Deal that lifts blockade and stops attacks, followed by underwriter response.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Renewed large-scale strikes or mine campaign.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

**6 Months**
- Probability: 48%
- Base-rate anchor: ~45%
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild upward for economic pressure and bypass resilience.
- Core rationale: Higher chance of political resolution or attritional reduction in attacks; commercial systems can recover if risk drops for 1–2 months.
- Main gating factor: Durable reduction in attacks and proxy activity enabling insurance normalization.
- What would raise this forecast materially: Formal or de-facto ceasefire with verified Hormuz safety by early 2027.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Prolonged low-intensity attack campaign or renewed blockade intensification.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

**1 Year**
- Probability: 62%
- Base-rate anchor: ~60%
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight upward on exhaustion incentives.
- Core rationale: Sufficient time for deal, regime adaptation, or attritional de-escalation; residual risks (proxies, distrust) keep it well below certainty.
- Main gating factor: Absence of new escalation and insurance/traffic recovery.
- What would raise this forecast materially: Comprehensive agreement or clear Iranian inability to sustain attacks.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Regime change dynamics, expanded proxy war, or frozen conflict with intermittent attacks.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

**18 Months**
- Probability: 72%
- Base-rate anchor: ~70%
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild upward.
- Core rationale: Long enough for most reference-class recoveries if intensity falls; still non-trivial residual risk of frozen maritime contest or renewed crisis.
- Main gating factor: Sustained political resolution or exhaustion.
- What would raise this forecast materially: Stable post-deal environment with full commercial return.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Persistent low-level attacks or new regional trigger.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium-Low

Synthesis note: Probabilities are not mechanical averages. Shipping security + insurance are hard gates (must both clear); oil/LNG recovery is somewhat more flexible via bypasses; force posture and proxies are secondary but can re-gate. Long horizons discount certainty because residual risk persists.

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued contested Hormuz with elevated but not total disruption through early 2027. Partial crude flows persist via escorts/bypasses; Iranian exports stay constrained until a deal or blockade adjustment. Insurance remains high until attack rate drops for weeks. Post-midterm diplomacy produces a limited or temporary understanding by spring 2027 that reduces large strikes and some attacks, allowing gradual (not full) commercial recovery by mid-2027. Proxies continue at lower intensity. Full multi-domain normality only after sustained de-escalation, not immediately.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Post-midterm deal that sequences blockade relief with verified Hormuz opening and nuclear restraints; attack cessation verified within days; underwriters respond within 2–4 weeks; Gulf states and buyers rapidly restore volumes. Probability mass concentrated in 3–6 month window. Requires high trust and rapid verification that current evidence does not strongly support.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Post-election strikes resume; Iran sustains intermittent shipping attacks and proxy pressure as leverage; blockade remains; insurance stays elevated indefinitely; traffic and LNG recover only partially. Frozen conflict resembling prolonged Tanker War phase or Red Sea campaign. Extends high disruption beyond 12–18 months.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Overestimation of normalization risk: May underweight Iranian ability to sustain low-cost shipping harassment and proxy activation even under pressure, and underwriter conservatism (claims already ~$2B+). AIS undercounts dark traffic, so resilience may be higher than visible data suggest—potentially raising near-term probabilities. Underestimation of normalization: May overweight current attack tempo as permanent rather than tactical (pre-midterm); economic exhaustion and mediation could produce faster political resolution than base rates. Load-bearing assumptions: Attack rate is the dominant commercial gate; blockade remains leverage until a deal; no sudden regime or leadership shock. Falsifiers: Sustained attack halt + insurance drop within weeks (raises all near horizons); major post-election campaign or new mine barrage (lowers all).

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily/weekly UKMTO/Lloyd’s/IMO attack counts and sinkings.
- AIS + dark/escorted transit volumes (PortWatch, Kpler, Windward, CENTCOM claims).
- War-risk quotes and P&I notices (Marsh, brokers).
- Iranian crude loadings and Qatari LNG nominations/force-majeure status.
- Brent and freight rates; bypass pipeline utilization.
- Mediation outcomes and any blockade/Hormuz sequencing announcements.
- U.S. carrier movements and post-midterm statements; Houthi incident rate.
- Any verified mine clearance or exclusion-zone changes.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon | Probability | Confidence | Main Gating Factor | Key Upside Trigger | Key Downside Trigger |
|---------|-------------|------------|--------------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| 1 week | 4% | High | Shipping/insurance | Attack cessation + underwriter signal | Further sinkings/strikes |
| 1 month | 10% | Medium-High | Attack halt + insurance | Durable post-midterm pause/deal | Post-election strikes |
| 3 months | 28% | Medium | Insurance/transit recovery | Deal + verified safety | Renewed large campaign |
| 6 months | 48% | Medium | Durable risk reduction | Formal/de-facto ceasefire | Persistent low-level attacks |
| 1 year | 62% | Medium | Political resolution | Comprehensive agreement | Frozen intermittent conflict |
| 18 months | 72% | Medium-Low | Sustained exhaustion/resolution | Stable commercial return | New regional trigger |

These probabilities are calibrated to the demanding operational definition and current evidence. They will update sharply on verified attack-rate changes, insurance signals, or diplomatic breakthroughs.

title: Hormuz attacks peak, normality 3%
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each horizon (1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months), measured from 23 October 2026.

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

Functional normality requires a sustained (multi-week) multi-domain state, not a ceasefire, price dip, or temporary traffic spike. All of the following must hold simultaneously:

- Direct military activity: Average confirmed attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman, and nearby waters <1 per week, with no sinkings, major engine-room hits, or confirmed mine damage in the preceding 3–4 weeks.
- Proxy activity: Near-zero attacks by Iran-aligned groups (Houthis and others) on Gulf shipping, ports, or energy infrastructure in the preceding month.
- Shipping security: AIS-visible commercial transits through Hormuz at ≥60–70% of the pre-crisis baseline of ~85/day (IMF PortWatch/hormuz.now figures), without routine US naval escorts or widespread dark sailing as the primary safety method. Iran does not maintain a functional permit/control regime that ships must observe.
- Commercial transit levels: Consistent with the above; not reliant on opaque ship-to-ship transfers or extreme risk tolerance by a minority of operators.
- War-risk insurance: Additional premiums for Hormuz/Gulf tankers ≤1% of hull value (or ≤4× the pre-war ~0.25% baseline), widely available on standard terms without special government facilities or 7-day cancellation clauses dominating pricing.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Flows through Hormuz (including dark/STS where relevant) at ≥80% of the ~17–21 mb/d pre-war liquids baseline for a sustained period; LNG carriers operating normally. Bypass pipelines remain available but are not the dominant workaround forced by risk.
- Energy market stress: Brent (or equivalent) risk premium largely dissipated; prices driven primarily by fundamentals rather than acute war-risk spikes above ~$10–15/bbl attributable to Hormuz.
- Force posture: US naval blockade of Iranian ports lifted or substantially eased; major combatant naval presence reduced from wartime levels; no active Iranian claim of exclusive control over the strait that is enforced by force.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No large-scale strikes on land infrastructure, nuclear-related moves, undersea cable attacks, or equivalent new fronts in the preceding month.

Temporary pauses, partial traffic under escort, or oil price moves alone do not meet the threshold.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 23 October 2026)**

The conflict began ~28 February 2026 (~Day 238 of the Hormuz crisis). A June 2026 US-Iran MOU collapsed in July. Indirect talks via Qatar and Pakistan continue but remain stalled on sequencing (Iran demands blockade/sanctions relief and related conditions first; US prioritizes strait reopening and related security steps). Trump has indicated no major US strikes on Iran before the 3 November midterms.

AIS-visible commercial traffic is ~4% of the ~85/day pre-crisis baseline (3.6/day recent 7-day average; hormuz.now). CENTCOM and Lloyd’s List report higher numbers of facilitated or non-Iranian-linked transits in some weeks (e.g., claims of ~400 in a week or 100+ non-Iranian in mid-October periods), largely under US coordination, often dark, hugging Omani routes, or via STS transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Iran claims control, maintains a non-compliance list, and requires permits. October has seen the highest attack numbers of the war (IMO/USNI: 27 commercial ship attacks so far in October; multiple reports of 12–15 in single weeks; at least two sinkings including GFS Pride). Mine claims by IRGC are frequent but often disputed by CENTCOM (primary lanes reported cleared). 

Oil flows through Hormuz (including dark/STS) have recovered to roughly 70–82% of pre-war levels in recent Kpler/related estimates (~11–14 mb/d range in various weekly figures), with overall Middle East exports sometimes matching or exceeding pre-war totals via bypass pipelines (Saudi East-West, Emirati). Tanker freight rates remain extremely elevated (~12× pre-war for some routes). Brent is in the $108–113 range (five-month highs), well above pre-war ~$70–80 levels, with a clear war-risk premium. 

War-risk insurance for regional tankers is 6–10% of hull value (up from ~0.25% pre-war; multiple of 15–40× reported in various broker/FT/Insurance Business accounts), with claims estimated in the $2–3 billion range. Cover is available at a price. Houthi activity has expanded threats into the Red Sea and against Saudi infrastructure. US forces continue escorts, mine clearance, and the Iranian blockade; IRGC remains active. Evidence quality is mixed: AIS undercounts dark traffic; attack numbers and mine claims are partially disputed; oil flow trackers diverge; official statements from both sides are maximalist.

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant classes (outside-in):

- 1980s Tanker War (Iran-Iraq, ~1984–88): Sustained attacks on neutral shipping (hundreds of incidents), high insurance, US reflagging/escorts (Operation Earnest Will 1987–88). Shipping continued at reduced/risk-adjusted levels. Full political end came with the August 1988 ceasefire; escorts wound down shortly after. Recovery of commercial normality took months post-ceasefire. Relevant for endurance of maritime pressure and role of escorts; breaks down because it was a bilateral regional war without a nuclear dimension or modern drone/missile density, and ended via mutual exhaustion + UN process. Suggests multi-year disruption possible; functional shipping recovery mainly after political settlement.
- 2023–24 Red Sea Houthi campaign: Prolonged elevated risk, insurance spikes, partial rerouting (Cape), naval escorts, incomplete normalization even after a year. Relevant for proxy persistence and insurer caution; breaks down because Hormuz has fewer easy bypasses and higher oil concentration. Suggests 12–18+ months of elevated disruption is common absent resolution.
- Brief 2019–20 Iran tanker incidents and similar spikes: Insurance and traffic normalized within weeks to a few months once kinetic activity subsided. Relevant for rapid reversion if activity stops; breaks down for sustained multi-month wars.
- 1991 Gulf War: Short, high-intensity; shipping recovered quickly post-conflict. Relevant for rapid post-war reversion; less applicable to a prolonged, attritional, multi-domain standoff.
- Suez Canal closures (1956, 1967–75): Multi-year physical or effective closures with permanent rerouting adaptations. Relevant for chokepoint duration; less so for a contested but not fully closed Hormuz.

Base-rate prior (before current-evidence adjustment), for a multi-month active chokepoint conflict involving a nuclear-capable state, proxies, and a major power: very low short-term probability of the full operational definition being met; rising slowly with time conditional on de-escalation. Approximate prior: 1 week ~2%, 1 month ~5%, 3 months ~12%, 6 months ~25%, 1 year ~40%, 18 months ~55%. These reflect historical tendency for such disruptions to outlast initial expectations and for commercial/insurance normalization to lag military pauses.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status  
---|---|---|---|---  
AIS traffic ~4% of baseline (3.6/day) | AIS trackers (hormuz.now, IMF PortWatch) | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed (AIS only)  
CENTCOM/Lloyd’s higher facilitated transit claims | Official/military + trade press | Mildly positive (partial flow) | Medium | Partially confirmed/disputed interpretation  
October attack peak (27+ ships; multiple weekly highs) | IMO, USNI, UKMTO, Lloyd’s | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed counts, attribution mostly Iran  
War-risk premiums 6–10% hull (~15–40×) | Brokers, FT, Insurance Business, Howden | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed market reports  
Oil flows ~70–82% pre-war via Hormuz + bypasses | Kpler and related | Mildly positive (partial recovery) | Medium | Estimated/inferred from trackers  
Brent ~$108–113 with clear risk premium | Market data | Negative | High | Confirmed  
June MOU collapsed; talks stalled on sequencing | Multiple news + official statements | Negative | High | Confirmed  
Trump no major strikes pre-midterms | Reporting | Mildly positive short-term | Medium | Reported  
Houthi expansion to Red Sea/Saudi | Reporting + claims | Negative | Medium-High | Confirmed activity, some claims disputed  
Mine claims frequent but lanes reported cleared | IRGC vs CENTCOM | Negative (threat perception) | Medium | Disputed  
US blockade and escorts ongoing | Official | Negative for full normality | High | Confirmed  

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

Ranked: (1) Mutual exhaustion and economic costs (high insurance, lost Iranian export revenue, elevated global energy prices); (2) US electoral calendar creating a window for de-escalation post-midterms; (3) Partial technical success of US escorts/STS/bypass systems keeping some oil moving and reducing urgency for total closure; (4) Continued mediation channels (Qatar, Pakistan).

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

Ranked: (1) Iranian incentive to maintain Hormuz leverage as primary bargaining chip (explicit conditions for reopening); (2) Demonstrated Iranian capacity and willingness to sustain attacks (October peak eight months in); (3) Proxy activation and multi-front risk (Houthis); (4) Insurer and operator caution that lags any military pause; (5) Sequencing distrust and history of MOU collapse; (6) Risk of post-election escalation.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Rough probabilities that the sub-component is met by each horizon (these are inputs, not averages):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 5%, 1m 15%, 3m 30%, 6m 45%, 1y 60%, 18m 70%.
- Sustained safe commercial transit ≥60–70% without routine escorts: 1w 2%, 1m 8%, 3m 20%, 6m 35%, 1y 50%, 18m 65%.
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤1% / ≤4×): 1w 1%, 1m 5%, 3m 15%, 6m 30%, 1y 45%, 18m 60%.
- Oil/LNG export recovery to definition: 1w 10%, 1m 25%, 3m 40%, 6m 55%, 1y 70%, 18m 75% (partial recovery already exists).
- Proxy restraint: 1w 10%, 1m 20%, 3m 35%, 6m 50%, 1y 60%, 18m 70%.
- Force drawdown (blockade lift + reduced posture): 1w 2%, 1m 8%, 3m 20%, 6m 35%, 1y 50%, 18m 60%.
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 40%, 1m 35%, 3m 40%, 6m 50%, 1y 55%, 18m 60%.

Gating factors are insurance normalization, transit without escorts, and force posture/blockade—these lag kinetic pauses and require sustained political settlement. Oil flows are the least gating.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
Probability: 3%  
Base-rate anchor: ~2%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly upward from partial oil flow but offset by October attack peak and stalled talks.  
Core rationale: Active high-tempo attacks, restricted AIS traffic, elevated insurance, and no political breakthrough make the full definition effectively impossible in days.  
Main gating factor: Ongoing direct attacks and insurance pricing.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate verified multi-day halt in attacks + rapid insurance quotes falling.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Further sinkings or confirmed mine damage.  
Confidence in this estimate: High  

**1 Month**  
Probability: 8%  
Base-rate anchor: ~5%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Modest upward for possible post-midterm (early November) de-escalation window, but October data and sequencing deadlock dominate.  
Core rationale: Even a short pause would not clear insurance, escort dependence, or force-posture criteria within a month. Historical lags are longer.  
Main gating factor: Insurance and sustained transit without escorts.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Documented deal or verified attack halt lasting weeks with early insurance movement.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Post-election escalation or new proxy front.  
Confidence in this estimate: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
Probability: 18%  
Base-rate anchor: ~12%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Upward for electoral calendar and partial flow resilience; downward for demonstrated Iranian capacity and Houthi activity.  
Core rationale: Possible limited de-escalation after midterms, but commercial and insurance normalization requires sustained quiet that is not yet in evidence. Gating components remain low.  
Main gating factor: Force posture/blockade and insurance.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Framework agreement that includes blockade relief and verified attack reduction.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Resumed large-scale strikes or undersea/infrastructure attacks.  
Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**6 Months**  
Probability: 32%  
Base-rate anchor: ~25%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Upward on cumulative economic pressure and possible diplomatic progress; downward on history of MOU collapse and proxy persistence.  
Core rationale: Enough time for a political deal to begin translating into reduced attacks and early commercial recovery, but full multi-domain criteria (especially insurance and unescorted high-volume transit) still face significant lag risk.  
Main gating factor: Sustained political settlement translating into insurer and operator behavior.  
What would raise this forecast materially: Verified multi-month attack reduction + measurable insurance premium decline.  
What would lower this forecast materially: Escalation after any temporary pause.  
Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**1 Year**  
Probability: 48%  
Base-rate anchor: ~40%  
Current-evidence adjustment: Upward on exhaustion incentives and bypass adaptations; tempered by multi-front risks and sequencing distrust.
