- No major new escalation trigger: 1w 20%, 1m 35%, 3m 50%, 6m 60%, 1y 70%, 18m 75%.

Gating factors are shipping security + insurance + transit volumes; military pauses alone are insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**• 1 Week**  
• Probability: 2%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~5%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Strongly downward (active high-tempo attacks, traffic at 10%, premiums extreme).  
• Core rationale: No pathway exists for multi-domain thresholds in days.  
• Main gating factor: Immediate cessation of attacks and insurance response.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate, verified full ceasefire plus rapid attack halt.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Further sinkings or major escalation.  
• Confidence in this estimate: High  

**• 1 Month**  
• Probability: 5%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~10%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Downward.  
• Core rationale: Midterm pause may limit US strikes, but Iranian shipping campaign and blockade persist; insurance and traffic do not normalize on this timescale.  
• Main gating factor: Attack tempo and commercial confidence.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Verified multi-week attack halt plus traffic rebound above 50%.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Sustained or escalating attacks post-midterms.  
• Confidence in this estimate: High  

**• 3 Months**  
• Probability: 12%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~20%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Downward (ongoing denial campaign, no settlement).  
• Core rationale: Possible limited de-escalation after midterms, but historical analogues show commercial and insurance normalization lag kinetic pauses by months.  
• Main gating factor: Durable reduction in attacks + insurance pricing response.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Formal ceasefire or major attack cessation sustained for weeks with traffic >50% and premiums falling.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Post-midterm US escalation or Iranian mine/attack surge.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**• 6 Months**  
• Probability: 25%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~35%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Moderately downward.  
• Core rationale: Window for political deal or mutual restraint exists, but current trajectory (blockade, proxy activity, insurance hysteresis) makes full multi-domain recovery less than base-rate.  
• Main gating factor: Political settlement or sustained restraint enabling commercial return.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Agreement that ends blockade and attack campaign, with traffic recovering above 70%.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Continued or renewed high-tempo denial.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**• 1 Year**  
• Probability: 45%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~55%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Moderately downward.  
• Core rationale: Longer horizon allows for deal, exhaustion, or partial accommodation; residual insurance and behavioral effects still probable.  
• Main gating factor: Existence of a durable political/military settlement.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Early settlement with verified compliance on shipping and blockade.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Prolonged stalemate or new escalation.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**• 18 Months**  
• Probability: 60%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~70%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Moderately downward.  
• Core rationale: Most historical high-intensity chokepoint wars of this type resolve or de-escalate enough for functional commercial normality within this window, though residual effects remain possible. Full normality still demanding given definition.  
• Main gating factor: Resolution or stable low-intensity equilibrium.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Clear end-state agreement by mid-2027.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Entrenched stalemate or repeated escalation cycles.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Low-Medium  

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued elevated military and proxy activity through and immediately after US midterms, with intermittent oil-flow recoveries interrupted by attack surges. Commercial traffic and insurance remain severely constrained for months. A political deal or mutual restraint becomes more plausible in H1 2027, enabling gradual protected or selective transit recovery, followed by slower insurance and behavioral normalization. Full multi-domain functional normality is more likely in the 12–18 month window than earlier, contingent on settlement.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Rapid post-midterm deal that ends the blockade, halts Iranian shipping attacks, and restrains proxies. Traffic rebounds above 70% within weeks of compliance; insurance premiums fall sharply as loss experience improves. Probability of this path is low (~10–15% cumulative by 6 months) given current maximalist positions and attack incentives.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Post-midterm US escalation, Iranian mine-laying or sustained high-tempo denial, proxy surge, or breakdown of any talks. Traffic stays depressed, premiums remain extreme, and force postures stay high for 12+ months. This path has material probability (~25–35% that normality is not reached even by 18 months).

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Strongest critique of faster-normalization bias: The definition is demanding (insurance + transit + proxies + force posture simultaneously). Current attack surge and blockade show Iran retains effective denial capacity; commercial actors respond to risk faster than governments. Historical Tanker War lasted years.  
Strongest critique of underestimating normalization: Mutual economic pain is severe; US political incentives to declare success and reduce oil prices are high; partial protected transit has occurred before and could scale if attack tempo drops even without full political settlement. Insurance markets reprice quickly once loss experience improves. Load-bearing assumptions are that Iranian attack incentives remain high while the blockade continues, and that commercial/insurance hysteresis is substantial.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily AIS-visible Hormuz transit counts and oil-flow volumes (Kpler, PortWatch).  
- UKMTO/JMIC threat assessments and confirmed attack frequency.  
- War-risk premium quotes (hull % per voyage).  
- Status of US blockade and any formal talks or MOUs.  
- Houthi activity levels against shipping and Gulf energy.  
- Brent volatility and geopolitical premium.  
- Force movements (carriers, escorts).

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence | Main Gating Factor                  |
|-----------|-------------|------------|-------------------------------------|
| 1 Week    | 2%         | High      | Immediate attack cessation         |
| 1 Month   | 5%         | High      | Attack tempo & commercial response |
| 3 Months  | 12%        | Medium    | Sustained restraint + insurance    |
| 6 Months  | 25%        | Medium    | Political settlement or restraint  |
| 1 Year    | 45%        | Medium    | Durable end-state                  |
| 18 Months | 60%        | Low-Medium| Resolution or stable equilibrium   |

These probabilities are internally consistent with the decomposition: early horizons are gated by the currently active denial campaign; longer horizons rise as the probability of settlement or exhaustion increases, but remain below base rates because of insurance hysteresis, residual force postures, and the demanding multi-domain definition.

title: Hormuz traffic holds at 10%
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each of these horizons: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months.

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

Functional normality requires simultaneous, sustained satisfaction of the following observable criteria for a continuous period of at least 30 days (longer for insurance and market confidence metrics). A temporary ceasefire, price dip, or partial shuttle recovery does not qualify.

- **Direct military activity**: No sustained campaign of US, Israeli, or Iranian strikes on each other’s forces, infrastructure, or territory. Isolated incidents do not disqualify, but ongoing exchanges of fire do.
- **Proxy activity**: Houthi and other Iran-aligned proxy attacks on Saudi, Emirati, or other Gulf infrastructure, airports, energy facilities, and shipping reduced to pre-February 2026 baseline levels (sporadic or none). No major territorial advances in Yemen that expand pressure on the Bab el-Mandeb.
- **Shipping security**: JMIC/UKMTO threat assessment for Hormuz and adjacent waters no higher than moderate. Fewer than one confirmed significant attack on commercial vessels per week, sustained for four weeks. No enforced Iranian permit/fee/“illegal route” regime that systematically deters traffic.
- **Commercial transit levels**: Combined AIS-visible and estimated dark traffic averaging at least 70–80% of the 2025 baseline (~85–100+ commercial vessels/day depending on counting method; PortWatch-style ~60+). Free or lightly coordinated transit without routine naval escort as the primary enabler.
- **War-risk insurance**: Additional war-risk premiums ≤2–3× peacetime baseline (roughly ≤0.3–0.5% of hull value per voyage vs. current multiples of 15× or higher in some quotes), with broad commercial availability and no dependence on ad-hoc US government backstops as the main capacity source.
- **Oil and LNG export continuity**: Middle East crude and LNG exports via normal Hormuz routes at ≥90% of pre-war levels on a sustained basis, without reliance on high-risk dark/shuttle/bypass arrangements as the dominant mode. Refinery and terminal operations largely restored.
- **Energy market stress**: Brent risk premium attributable to Gulf disruption ≤10–15%; volatility normalized relative to other fundamentals. No persistent physical shortages or extreme freight spikes driven by Hormuz.
- **Force posture**: US/coalition forces able to sustain or reduce elevated presence without crisis-driven surge; Iranian forces not actively enforcing a de facto closure or high-intensity interdiction.
- **Absence of major new escalation triggers**: No new nuclear breakout signals, major attacks on third-country infrastructure, or opening of additional fronts that reset the risk environment.

This is a high bar by design. Military pauses and partial oil recovery via protected shuttles fall short.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot** (as of 14 October 2026)

The war began with US-Israeli strikes on 28 February 2026. A June Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for a 60-day negotiating window and partial Hormuz reopening collapsed by early July; the US naval blockade of Iranian ports resumed and remains in force. President Trump has publicly paused US strikes on Iran until after the 3 November midterm elections while describing discussions as productive; Iranian officials have called US responses to their Hormuz conditions inadequate and insist Hormuz issues precede nuclear talks. Indirect talks continue via mediators (Qatar, Pakistan, Oman).

Maritime conditions remain severe. AIS-visible commercial traffic is roughly 10% of the 2025 baseline (recent 7-day averages ~8–14 crossings/day vs. ~85). Hundreds of vessels are loitering. Iran continues high-tempo attacks on tankers (record weekly totals in early October, including off Qatar and near the UAE), using mines, projectiles, drones, and new spotter tactics, while claiming control and targeting “illegal” southern-corridor/shuttle traffic. US forces facilitate some dark and escorted movements; oil flows have partially recovered (estimates vary widely: Hormuz crude often 40%+ below normal in recent weeks, overall ME exports closer to 70–90% in some Kpler/other counts via bypasses and dark ships) but remain disrupted and costly. Brent trades in the $100–107 range. War-risk premiums are elevated (reported multiples of 15× or higher; cover available but expensive). Houthis have escalated against Saudi Arabia, including deadly airport strikes in Riyadh. US naval posture emphasizes blockade outside the Gulf plus air/unmanned protection; a third carrier strike group is en route. Confirmed facts and claims by parties frequently diverge on traffic volumes and control.<grok:render card_id="bc277e" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">0</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="f03476" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">1</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="88ef6e" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">2</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="27540c" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">5</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="d1bee8" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">8</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="afbfe4" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">35</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="6de8b9" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">36</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="1a0633" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">45</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant classes (adjusted for differences in intensity, technology, and stakes):

- **1980s Tanker War (Iran-Iraq)**: ~4 years of systematic tanker/mine/missile attacks; shipping continued at reduced levels under risk; US escorts (Earnest Will) raised costs but did not end attacks. Full commercial normalization followed the 1988 ceasefire. Suggests multi-year disruption while conflict persists; faster recovery once hostilities end. Breaks down: lower missile/drone density, no modern dark-shipping/AIS opacity, different political stakes.
- **2019 Gulf tanker attacks and seizures**: Short, limited campaign; insurance spiked briefly then eased; traffic largely recovered within weeks to months once attacks stopped. Suggests rapid commercial recovery if interdiction ceases. Breaks down: far lower intensity and no full war.
- **Red Sea Houthi campaign (2023–2025)**: Months of diversion, elevated insurance, and reduced traffic despite escorts; partial normalization only after pressure reduced. Suggests commercial recovery lags military de-escalation by 3–12 months. Relevant for proxy and insurance dynamics.
- **1990–91 Gulf War**: Rapid military resolution; shipping recovered quickly post-liberation. Suggests short timelines after decisive end. Breaks down: conventional land war with clear endpoint vs. current hybrid attrition.
- **Ukraine Black Sea grain/shipping disruptions**: Prolonged risk, insurance issues, and reduced volumes lasting years despite partial corridors. Suggests sticky commercial effects. Breaks down: different geography and actors.
- **Prior Hormuz threats (2011–12, intermittent seizures)**: Traffic rarely collapsed fully; recovery within weeks to months once threats receded. Suggests resilience when no sustained interdiction.

**Base-rate prior** (before case-specific adjustment; rough midpoint of comparable disruption timelines):

- 1 week: ~2–5%
- 1 month: ~5–10%
- 3 months: ~15–25%
- 6 months: ~30–45%
- 1 year: ~50–65%
- 18 months: ~60–75%

These reflect that functional commercial/insurance normality typically trails military pauses and requires demonstrated security for months.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence Item | Source Type | Direction on Normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| AIS-visible traffic ~10% of baseline; hundreds waiting | AIS trackers (hormuz.now, PortWatch-related) | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| Record tanker attacks early Oct; ongoing strikes including off Qatar/UAE | UKMTO, JMIC, Reuters, Windward | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed (some IRGC claims unverified) |
| Trump pause on US strikes until post-midterms; productive talks | Official statements, news | Mildly positive (near-term) | High | Confirmed |
| Iranian officials call US Hormuz response inadequate; 7 conditions | Iranian statements via Reuters/Al Jazeera | Negative | Medium-High | Confirmed claims |
| Partial oil flow recovery via dark/shuttle/bypass (estimates 40–90% depending on metric) | Kpler, other trackers, reporting | Mildly positive | Medium | Partially confirmed; disputed volumes |
| War-risk premiums elevated (15× or higher reports) | Brokers, Lloyd’s-related, underwriter commentary | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed directionally |
| Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport (13+ killed); Yemen fighting | News, Saudi statements | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports active; third CSG en route | Official/news reporting | Negative (sustains tension) | High | Confirmed |
| June MOU collapsed; talks deadlocked on sequencing | Multiple outlets | Negative | High | Confirmed |
| Iran using new spotter tactics; claims control | Reuters (Iranian officials), IRGC | Negative | Medium | Claims + corroborating incidents |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

Ranked: (1) US political calendar and stated preference to avoid pre-midterm escalation plus mutual interest in lower oil prices; (2) demonstrated partial recovery of oil flows via workarounds, showing commercial adaptability; (3) ongoing mediated talks and mutual exhaustion after ~7.5 months; (4) US air/unmanned protection enabling some dark transit.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

Ranked: (1) Persistent Iranian interdiction capability and demonstrated willingness to attack even as flows partially recover (core leverage); (2) high war-risk insurance costs and insurer caution that lag any military pause; (3) Houthi/proxy escalation and second-front risk in Yemen/Red Sea; (4) unresolved political terms (Iranian conditions on Hormuz control, sanctions, frozen assets, nuclear sequencing); (5) US blockade and elevated force posture that sustain Iranian incentives to disrupt.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts** (probability that each sub-condition is largely met by the horizon)

These are not averaged; gating factors (especially sustained shipping security + insurance normalization + proxy restraint) dominate the joint probability.

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w ~40%; 1m ~55%; 3m ~65%; 6m ~75%; 1y ~80%; 18m ~85%. (US pause helps near-term; longer depends on deal.)
- Sustained safe commercial transit (low attacks + high volume): 1w ~5%; 1m ~10%; 3m ~20%; 6m ~35%; 1y ~55%; 18m ~65%.
- Meaningful insurance normalization: 1w ~3%; 1m ~8%; 3m ~18%; 6m ~35%; 1y ~55%; 18m ~70%.
- Oil/LNG export recovery to high sustained levels via normal routes: 1w ~15%; 1m ~25%; 3m ~40%; 6m ~55%; 1y ~70%; 18m ~75%.
- Proxy restraint: 1w ~10%; 1m ~15%; 3m ~25%; 6m ~40%; 1y ~55%; 18m ~65%.
- Force drawdown/posture stabilization: 1w ~20%; 1m ~30%; 3m ~45%; 6m ~60%; 1y ~70%; 18m ~75%.
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w ~70%; 1m ~60%; 3m ~55%; 6m ~50%; 1y ~45%; 18m ~40%. (Risk accumulates.)

Gating: Transit security and insurance are the binding constraints. Oil can partially recover under protection without full normality.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
• Probability: 4%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~2–5%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight upward from US strike pause, but attacks and insurance dominate.  
• Core rationale: Ongoing high-tempo attacks, restricted traffic, elevated premiums, and Houthi activity make functional normality impossible in days.  
• Main gating factor: Shipping security and attacks.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate verified ceasefire on shipping + sharp traffic jump.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Major new attack or escalation.  
• Confidence in this estimate: High  

**1 Month**  
• Probability: 8%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~5–10%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Modest upward from pause and talks; downward from attack intensity and insurance stickiness.  
• Core rationale: Midterms may keep US strikes paused, but Iranian interdiction and commercial caution will not clear the multi-domain bar.  
• Main gating factor: Sustained low attacks + traffic recovery.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Verified deal implementing Hormuz reopening with security guarantees.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Post-midterm US strikes or intensified Iranian campaign.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
• Probability: 18%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~15–25%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Near base rate; pause and partial oil recovery offset by deadlock and proxies.  
• Core rationale: Possible post-election de-escalation or limited deal, but insurance and commercial normalization lag; proxy risks persist.  
• Main gating factor: Insurance normalization and sustained safe transit.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Broad deal with verification and rapid insurance easing.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Failed talks and renewed high-intensity strikes.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**6 Months**  
• Probability: 32%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~30–45%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly below base due to demonstrated Iranian resilience and multi-front risks.  
• Core rationale: More time for political resolution or attrition-driven accommodation, but commercial confidence and proxy restraint remain uncertain.  
• Main gating factor: Proxy restraint + insurance market shift.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Durable ceasefire with verified low attacks and traffic >70%.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: New front or collapse of talks into sustained campaign.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium  

**1 Year**  
• Probability: 48%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~50–65%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Downward for unresolved political terms and sticky commercial effects.  
• Core rationale: Higher chance of negotiated end or mutual de-escalation under economic pressure, but full multi-domain normality is not assured even then.  
• Main gating factor: Political settlement enabling force and insurance normalization.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Comprehensive deal covering Hormuz, sanctions, and proxies.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Prolonged stalemate or Iranian nuclear advance.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Medium-Low  

**18 Months**  
• Probability: 58%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~60–75%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Downward for risk of frozen conflict and commercial hysteresis.  
• Core rationale: Most comparable disruptions resolve or stabilize within this window, but current hybrid character and leverage incentives support residual risk.  
• Main gating factor: Absence of new escalation + commercial re-adaptation.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Clear end to hostilities with verification.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Entrenched low-level interdiction or new regional war.  
• Confidence in this estimate: Low-Medium  

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued intermittent talks, US restraint around the midterms, partial oil recovery via protected/dark/shuttle means, and persistent Iranian maritime pressure plus Houthi activity. Full functional normality is unlikely before late 2027 without a political breakthrough. Oil markets price elevated risk; commercial shipping remains cautious.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Post-midterm US priority on lower energy prices + Iranian economic pressure produces a sequenced deal (Hormuz first, limited nuclear steps). Attacks drop sharply, traffic rebounds within weeks, insurers reprice within 1–2 months. Probability mass shifts earlier (e.g., 3-month ~35–40%). Requires both sides to accept partial wins.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Talks fail; post-election US strikes resume; Iran maintains high-tempo interdiction and expands proxies. Traffic stays suppressed, insurance remains punitive, bypasses face attacks. Frozen conflict with chronic disruption through 2027–28. Probabilities fall (1-year ~25–30%).

**13. Red-Team Critique**

I may be underestimating near-term normalization if a narrow shipping deal is struck quickly and insurers follow traffic data aggressively, or if Iranian capability degrades faster than reported. I may be overestimating longer-term probabilities if the conflict settles into a durable low-intensity interdiction equilibrium (as in parts of the Tanker War or Red Sea) that keeps premiums and volumes permanently lower, or if Houthi pressure on Saudi creates cascading Gulf instability. Load-bearing assumptions: Iranian interdiction remains effective and politically valuable; insurance markets are slower to normalize than military facts; no decisive military outcome ends the war abruptly.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily AIS + estimated dark transit counts and attack frequency (UKMTO/JMIC).
- War-risk premium quotes and insurer capacity statements.
- Oil export volumes by route (Kpler-style).
- Status of mediated talks and any public terms.
- Houthi attack tempo and Saudi responses.
- US force posture and any post-midterm strike decisions.
- Iranian statements on permits/control and blockade incidents.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon | Probability | Confidence | Main Gating Factor |
|---------|-------------|------------|--------------------|
| 1 week | 4% | High | Shipping attacks & security |
| 1 month | 8% | Medium-High | Sustained safe transit |
| 3 months | 18% | Medium | Insurance + transit recovery |
| 6 months | 32% | Medium | Proxy restraint + insurance |
| 1 year | 48% | Medium-Low | Political settlement |
| 18 months | 58% | Low-Medium | No new escalation + commercial hysteresis |

These probabilities are calibrated to the demanding multi-domain definition and current evidence of active interdiction, elevated insurance, and unresolved political terms. They would update sharply on a verified drop in attacks combined with traffic and premium data.

title: Hormuz traffic at 10%
message:
**Forecast Question**  
Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each horizon: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (from 13 October 2026).

**Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
All of the following must hold simultaneously and be observable/sustained (not a temporary pause or price dip):

- Direct military activity: No sustained direct kinetic exchanges between US/Israeli forces and Iranian territory or forces (excluding isolated enforcement of any residual blockade). No Iranian ballistic/drone strikes on Gulf host-state targets.
- Proxy activity: Sustained restraint by major Iran-aligned groups (especially Houthis) — no major attacks on Gulf state infrastructure, airports, or shipping for multiple weeks.
- Shipping security (Strait of Hormuz and adjacent waters): Threat level assessed “low” or equivalent by JMIC/UKMTO/CENTCOM; no attacks on commercial vessels for ≥2–4 weeks; free commercial transit without requiring special US naval coordination, Iranian permits, or dark/AIS-off operations as the norm.
- Commercial transit levels: AIS-visible (plus dark-adjusted) commercial transits at ≥70–80% of pre-crisis baseline (~85–125+ vessels/day), including tankers, LNG, and containers, on routine routes.
- War-risk insurance: Premiums returned to near-pre-crisis multiples (low single-digit % of hull or less for standard transits); broad availability of cover without single-voyage negotiation, exclusions, or 10–30× loadings as the market standard.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf (non-Iranian) crude, products, and LNG exports near pre-war volumes and reliability without force majeure, shuttle-only, or heavy pipeline-bypass dependence as the primary mode. Iranian exports unblocked if part of any settlement.
- Energy market stress: Brent (and LNG benchmarks) not persistently elevated solely by Hormuz risk premium; volatility normalized; no structural supply shortfall driven by the conflict.
- Force posture: Material drawdown of elevated US naval/air assets dedicated to Hormuz escorts, blockade enforcement, and surge presence; regional actors not maintaining wartime alert postures.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No fresh nuclear, proxy, or territorial incidents that re-close the strait or re-spike insurance/shipping.

A temporary ceasefire, lower spot oil prices alone, or battlefield pause without commercial/insurance recovery does **not** meet the definition.

**Current Situation Snapshot** (as of 13 October 2026, ~Day 228 of Hormuz crisis; war began 28 February 2026)  
Strait of Hormuz is severely restricted. AIS-visible commercial traffic is ~10% of pre-crisis (~8–14 vessels/day vs ~85–138). Many vessels run dark under US coordination or southern-corridor shuttles; Iran claims control and requires permits via its Strait Authority. Recent weeks saw the highest attack rates on shipping since the war began (dozens of tankers/LNG/containers hit or threatened in early–mid October, including outside the strait near Qatar/Sohar/Fujairah). US naval blockade of Iranian ports remains “ironclad”; CENTCOM reports redirecting 130+ vessels, disabling several, and destroying IRGC-linked tankers — no Iranian crude has crossed the blockade line for months. Gulf non-Iranian oil exports show partial recovery (Kpler and others cite ~60–80% of some pre-war metrics in September via mix of dark/escorted transits + bypass pipelines), but LNG remains >75% below pre-war, products lag, and stranded cargo value is high (~$20bn cited). Brent ~$105–107. War-risk insurance is extreme: single-voyage only, high multiples (reports of 30×), widespread restrictions/cancellations by clubs, rendering normal transit uneconomic for most operators. Direct US/Israeli strikes on Iranian territory have been paused (Trump: none before 3 November midterms); Iranian ballistic/drone attacks on host states are limited recently, but shipping attacks continue. Proxies are active: Houthis have escalated against Saudi Arabia (multiple strikes on Riyadh and other airports, dozens killed, Saudi low on interceptors). Diplomacy is stalled (June Islamabad MOU collapsed; Iran’s conditions unmet). Elevated US force posture (carriers, blockade) persists. Sources include hormuz.now, Windward, Kpler, JINSA updates, UKMTO, CENTCOM, Al Jazeera, CNN, Reuters-linked reporting.

**Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**  
Relevant classes (3–6):

- **1984–88 Tanker War (Iran–Iraq War maritime phase)**: Closest analog — sustained anti-shipping campaign in the Gulf/Hormuz for years. Oil flows reduced but continued (with hazard pay and later US escorts in Operation Earnest Will). Full commercial normalization only after the broader ceasefire. Suggests multi-year partial disruption possible even with escorts. Breaks down: No modern insurance market freeze of this severity; lower absolute volumes then.
- **2019 Gulf of Oman/Hormuz attacks**: Short-lived kinetic incidents produced sharp insurance spikes (×10) but traffic largely continued and recovered within weeks–months after de-escalation. Suggests rapid recovery possible after clear stop to attacks. Breaks down: Far lower intensity/duration than 2026.
- **2023–present Red Sea/Houthi disruption**: Sustained threat → large traffic drop, rerouting, elevated insurance for years; partial recovery with escorts but not full normality. Suggests 12–24+ months for commercial confidence even after partial pauses. Breaks down: Alternative routes exist (Cape); Hormuz has none.
- **Temporary chokepoint closures (Ever Given 2021, COVID port shocks)**: Physical short blocks recover in weeks, but commercial/insurance/positioning lags months. Suggests hysteresis. Breaks down: Not war-driven.
- **Broader regional wars with energy chokepoints**: Normalization tracks political settlement of the land war more than pure maritime events.

**Base-rate prior** (pre-current-evidence adjustment, conditional on a major sustained Gulf maritime war of this type already 7+ months old): 1 week ~2–5%; 1 month ~5–10%; 3 months ~10–20%; 6 months ~20–35%; 1 year ~35–50%; 18 months ~45–60%. Full functional normality (especially insurance + unrestricted transit) is slow; military pauses alone are insufficient.

**Evidence Ledger** (selected high-impact items)

| Evidence Item | Source Type | Direction | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|-----------|------------|--------|
| AIS traffic ~10% of baseline; dark/shuttle heavy | AIS trackers (hormuz.now, Windward) | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Highest weekly shipping attacks since war start (early Oct) | UKMTO, maritime firms, news | Against | High | Confirmed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports effective; no Iranian oil out | CENTCOM, Kpler | Against (for full normality) | High | Confirmed |
