| CENTCOM says traffic and crude are flowing; Iran says strait is closed | Official claims | Mixed; supports militarized passage only | Medium | Disputed interpretation |
| September crude exports roughly 70–80 percent of pre-war, then late dip | Kpler, Reuters | Mildly toward on oil volumes; not on security | Medium | Estimated, dark fleet missing |
| Brent about $101–104 versus about $72 in February | Market data | Against market normality | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk still many times peacetime; June drop to about 2 percent did not last as a regime | Brokers, FT, trackers | Against | Medium | Confirmed for June; current level inferred from trackers and attacks |
| Ras Laffan: two trains, repairs cited at about three years; little LNG moving | QatarEnergy CEO, Reuters | Against LNG continuity | High on damage, medium on repair duration | Confirmed damage; repair timeline official claim |
| Pentagon preparing strike options before 3 November; no decision | Axios, Atlantic, via reporting | Against near-term | Medium | Reported, not officially confirmed |
| Houthis pressure Bab al-Mandab and Saudi bypass | Think-tank and wire reporting | Against | Medium | Reported |
| Mediation and Oman route talks continue | Iranian MFA, wire reporting | Mildly toward | Low | Claim plus talks |
| Bypass pipelines and Fujairah offset some crude | Kpler, CSIS | Toward oil adaptation, not Hormuz normality | Medium | Confirmed direction |

## 6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization

1. Fatigue and mediation. Eight months of cost, ongoing Oman-linked talks, and repeated US statements that a deal is the preferred end state keep a political off-ramp open.
2. Oil adaptation. Pipelines, Fujairah, and dark or facilitated transits have already restored a large share of crude. That reduces the incentive for Gulf producers to demand total closure and shows physical flows can rebound quickly once risk falls.
3. Iranian constraint. A US blockade has cut Iranian loadings sharply relative to neighbors. Tehran has a reason to trade strait harassment for sanctions or blockade relief, if it can sell that at home.
4. Insurance elasticity. The June quote drop showed underwriters reprice within days of a credible pause. The lag is weeks, not years, if incidents actually stop.
5. US political calendar. A pre-midterm deal that lowers oil is a plausible incentive. It is not the base case.

## 7. Key Drivers Against Normalization

1. No settlement of the political object. Nuclear limits, sanctions, blockade, and regime aims are unresolved. The last MoU addressed transit and not the war.
2. Iran’s remaining leverage is the strait. As neighbors’ exports recover and Iran’s do not, harassment is the cheap way to reimpose costs. That logic points to more attacks, not fewer, while the blockade holds.
3. Live escalation machinery. Strike options are being prepared. Recent attacks already broke the last pause. A new round before or after the midterms resets the insurance clock.
4. Proxies and bypasses. Houthi pressure on the Red Sea reduces the Saudi bypass and spreads the war geographically.
5. Infrastructure and trust. Ras Laffan damage caps LNG for years. Owners who returned and were struck will not treat the next communiqué as normality.
6. Force posture. Passage still depends on US facilitation and a southern corridor. That is a wartime operating mode.

Ranked gating order: political durability of a ceasefire, then a clean incident window, then insurance, then traffic. Oil volumes are not the gate.

## 8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts

Probabilities that each condition is met by the horizon:

| Sub-question | 1 week | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 1 year | 18 months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Major reduction in direct strikes, sustained | 8% | 18% | 35% | 48% | 60% | 68% |
| Sustained safe commercial Hormuz transit at ≥70% baseline | 1% | 5% | 14% | 26% | 40% | 52% |
| Insurance near peacetime terms | 1% | 4% | 12% | 24% | 38% | 50% |
| Oil export recovery to ≥90% of pre-war non-Iranian flows | 15% | 30% | 45% | 55% | 65% | 72% |
| LNG continuity from operable capacity | 3% | 8% | 18% | 30% | 45% | 55% |
| Proxy restraint at baseline | 5% | 12% | 25% | 38% | 50% | 58% |
| US and Iranian force posture de-escalated | 2% | 8% | 18% | 30% | 45% | 55% |
| No new major escalation trigger in the window | 25% | 20% | 30% | 40% | 48% | 55% |

Oil recovery is the easiest sub-condition and is already partly met. Insurance, transit, and posture move together and lag any ceasefire. The joint event is closer to the minimum of the gating items than to the average.

## 9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon

### 1 week

- Probability: 1%
- Base-rate anchor: 3 percent, cut for an active attack surge.
- Current-evidence adjustment: Down. Eleven ships struck in eight days, waivers revoked, strike options in preparation, traffic near 12 percent of baseline.
- Core rationale: The definition cannot be met inside 14 clean days when the last week failed the incident test.
- Main gating factor: Ongoing strikes and militarized passage.
- What would raise this forecast materially: Nothing plausible inside seven days.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Already near the floor.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 1 month

- Probability: 4%
- Base-rate anchor: 8 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: Down. A new MoU would still need a clean incident window that has not started, and insurance repricing lags.
- Core rationale: Even a sudden deal around the midterms would leave traffic, premia, and posture outside the definition by early November. A decision to resume major combat would zero the path.
- Main gating factor: No credible, incident-free settlement window.
- What would raise this forecast materially: An immediate, verified stop to ship attacks plus a published transit regime both sides honor.
- What would lower this forecast materially: US strikes before 3 November or a formal Iranian prohibited zone.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 3 months

- Probability: 12%
- Base-rate anchor: 15 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly down. Mediation exists, but the last pause failed in under a month and proxies are active.
- Core rationale: This is the first horizon on which a deal, a 4–8 week clean window, and partial insurance normalization could theoretically stack. The base case is another cycle of pause and strikes. January 2027 still sits inside the wartime reference class, not the post-Tanker-War class.
- Main gating factor: Durability of any ceasefire past the first incident.
- What would raise this forecast materially: A written transit and sanctions arrangement that survives 30 days without ship strikes.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Renewed major combat or Houthi closure pressure on Bab al-Mandab.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 6 months

- Probability: 22%
- Base-rate anchor: 28 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: Down. Adaptation in crude is real, but Tehran’s incentive to harass rises as neighbors export and Iran cannot. LNG and Red Sea risk keep the system abnormal even if Hormuz volumes rise.
- Core rationale: By April 2027 a settlement is plausible, not likely. If it arrives early in the window, insurance and traffic can catch up. If it arrives late, the 14-day test is met but the commercial regime may still be short of 70 percent transit and peacetime premia.
- Main gating factor: Political settlement early enough to leave a commercial lag inside the horizon.
- What would raise this forecast materially: End of the blockade and ship attacks together, with underwriters cutting quotes toward 0.5 percent.
- What would lower this forecast materially: A mine incident or a second Ras Laffan-scale strike.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 1 year

- Probability: 38%
- Base-rate anchor: 42 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly down. Wars of this type often last longer than governments predict. Partial oil recovery reduces urgency. Residual Iranian capability keeps a harassment option alive after any paper deal.
- Core rationale: A year is long enough for war exhaustion, a post-midterm policy reset, and one or two failed pauses to produce a more durable arrangement. It is not long enough to treat normalization as the default. The Red Sea case is the warning: threat persistence blocks commercial return even when headline fighting dips.
- Main gating factor: Whether Iran still uses Hormuz as leverage in October 2027.
- What would raise this forecast materially: A monitored ceasefire with six clean months and AIS traffic above 50 percent and rising.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Frozen conflict with episodic strikes, the Tanker War pattern.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

### 18 months

- Probability: 52%
- Base-rate anchor: 55 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly down. Physical LNG damage does not by itself block the definition, but a frozen conflict with retained Iranian sea-denial capability can.
- Core rationale: By April 2028 the modal outcome is a messy political arrangement or a de facto stalemate that has stopped routine ship attacks. Just over half is the judgment that exhaustion wins more often than not by then, with a wide band. It is not a claim that the pre-2026 Gulf returns.
- Main gating factor: Conversion of a stalemate into behavior underwriters will price as peacetime.
- What would raise this forecast materially: Verified drawdown of coastal anti-ship systems and a year of baseline proxy activity.
- What would lower this forecast materially: Institutionalized wartime routing, as in the Red Sea, still in place in 2028.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

Long-range figures stay near 50 percent because the definition still requires insurance, uncoerced transit, and posture change. Oil-flow recovery alone would have produced higher numbers and would have been the wrong target.

## 10. Most Likely Path

The next one to three months stay in the current regime: militarized partial transit, episodic IRGC attacks, US retaliation, crude moving at a discount to normal via a mix of facilitated Hormuz passages and bypasses, LNG largely offline, and premia elevated. A negotiating spike around the US midterms is likely. A durable deal is not. The modal path through mid-2027 is oscillation, with traffic sometimes reaching 20–40 percent of baseline and then falling after the next incident. Functional normality, if it arrives inside 18 months, arrives after a settlement that markets believe, not after the next quiet week. Oil volumes normalize before insurance and before LNG.

## 11. Faster Normalization Case

A pre- or post-midterm deal trades nuclear limits and a US blockade pause for an Iranian stop to ship attacks and proxy restraint. Incidents cease for six weeks. Underwriters cut quotes. Facilitated transit becomes ordinary transit. By three to six months the definition is met even though Ras Laffan is still damaged and Brent has not fully mean-reverted. Probability mass on this path is what supports the 12 percent at three months and the upper half of the one-year figure. It requires Iranian decision-makers to prefer revenue over leverage, and Washington to accept less than “wiped out.”

## 12. Prolonged Instability Case

Major combat resumes, or the current harassment equilibrium hardens. Iran keeps a permit and strike regime. The United States keeps a blockade and escort regime. Houthis tax the Red Sea bypass. Owners treat every reopening as temporary, which is already the Kpler description of the last MoU. Insurance never approaches peacetime. By 18 months the Gulf looks like a managed wartime chokepoint, with crude adapted through pipelines and dark fleets and LNG structurally impaired. This path is why the 18-month probability is only slightly above half.

## 13. Red-Team Critique

The forecast may be too low if adaptation is smuggled into the definition. September crude already near 70–80 percent of pre-war, plus a US-run corridor, could be called functional by traders who only need barrels. That reading is rejected here because insurance, uncoerced transit, and posture fail. If the user only cares about barrels, add roughly 15–25 points at the 6- to 18-month horizons.

The forecast may be too high at one year and 18 months. The Tanker War lasted four years. Iran’s incentive to harass strengthens as neighbors recover. US domestic politics can sustain a low-intensity conflict. A frozen conflict with retained coastal missiles is the strongest reason these figures should not be above 60 percent. The 52 percent at 18 months is the softest number in the set.

Load-bearing assumptions: Iran retains sea-denial capability; underwriters need about a month of clean transits; proxies do not become the main barrier once state strikes stop; dark-fleet crude does not count as commercial normality.

## 14. Critical Signals to Monitor

- UKMTO and CENTCOM incident counts in Hormuz, weekly. Two clean weeks would raise the one-month figure. Another double-digit strike week would cut the three-month figure.
- AIS commercial crossings versus the 85-a-day baseline, and the share that is US-facilitated or dark.
- Hull war-risk quotes from Lloyd’s and major brokers, not freight anecdotes.
- Whether the US blockade of Iranian ports is on or off, and whether Iranian loadings at Kharg resume.
- Qatar LNG cargo count. Security normality can return before volume normality.
- Houthi incidents at Bab al-Mandab and status of the East–West pipeline.
- A dated, mutual transit protocol versus another unsigned pause.
- Any Pentagon execution of prepared strike options.

## 15. Final Summary Table

| Horizon | P(functional normality) | Confidence | Gating factor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | 1% | High | Active strikes, traffic about 12% of baseline |
| 1 month | 4% | High | No clean window; strike options live |
| 3 months | 12% | Medium | Ceasefire durability after the next incident |
| 6 months | 22% | Medium | Settlement early enough for insurance lag |
| 1 year | 38% | Low | Whether Hormuz is still used as leverage |
| 18 months | 52% | Low | Stalemate versus priced peacetime behavior |

Bottom line: military pauses and partial crude recovery are already in the data and do not constitute normality. The probability that the full operational definition is met is about 1 percent within a week, 4 percent within a month, 12 percent within three months, 22 percent within six months, 38 percent within a year, and 52 percent within 18 months.

title: Hormuz traffic at 10%
message:
I will ground the forecast in current reporting on the 2026 Iran War and Gulf maritime conditions, then build the probabilities from reference classes and a decomposed evidence ledger.

The Persian Gulf is not functionally normal on day 222 of the Hormuz crisis. Direct and proxy-linked shipping attacks are still occurring, commercial transit is a fraction of the pre-crisis baseline, and war-risk pricing remains a multiple of peacetime. A June memorandum has not produced a durable settlement.

## 1. Forecast Question

What is the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality, under the operational definition below, by each horizon from 7 October 2026: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months?

## 2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”

All eight conditions must hold together for at least 14 consecutive days. A ceasefire, a lower oil price, or a temporary lull is not sufficient.

- Direct military activity: no confirmed kinetic strikes by the United States, Israel, or Iran against each other’s territory, forces, or commercial shipping in the Gulf theater.
- Proxy activity: no confirmed attacks on Gulf energy, port, or shipping targets attributable to IRGC-linked groups.
- Shipping security: no new mining, seizure, or projectile attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman approaches, or main Gulf anchorages.
- Commercial transit: AIS-visible commercial crossings at or above 70 percent of the 2025 baseline of about 85 ships a day, so roughly 60 or more a day, and not dependent on military coordination or Iranian permits as the normal mode.
- Insurance: additional hull war-risk premium at or below about 2 times the pre-crisis baseline, with International Group clubs writing Gulf cover without extraordinary cancellation notices. Pre-crisis was roughly 0.1–0.25 percent of hull value per voyage.
- Oil and LNG continuity: combined Gulf crude, products, and LNG export flows at or above 85 percent of the February 2026 baseline, without relying primarily on AIS-dark, sanctioned, or shuttle systems.
- Market stress: the war-specific risk premium and freight distortion largely unwound. A price level alone does not qualify.
- Force posture and triggers: no active blockade of Iranian ports, no active Iranian interdiction posture, no continuous US strike campaign in the Gulf, and no new major trigger such as a capital-ship hit, mass-casualty strike on a Gulf state, formal closure order, or nuclear breakout move.

## 3. Current Situation Snapshot

The war began around 28 February 2026. A 14-point US–Iran memorandum signed around 17 June was meant to pause hostilities and reopen Hormuz. It did not hold. Tit-for-tat strikes resumed within days, including attacks on shipping and on US-linked sites in Gulf states. As of early October, proximity talks and draft proposals to revive the memorandum are still being exchanged, including an Iranian offer to reopen the strait in exchange for lifting a US blockade of Iranian ports. Washington has described earlier versions as rejected. That diplomatic track is real and unresolved, not a settlement.

Maritime conditions remain abnormal. Independent AIS monitors on 7 October put the strait at “restricted,” day 222, with about 8–9 commercial crossings a day over the past week against a pre-crisis baseline near 85, or roughly 10 percent. IMF PortWatch-style counts for early October are even lower on some days. Hundreds of commercial ships are waiting near Fujairah, Sohar, and Gulf anchorages. UKMTO-reported attacks have accelerated: nine in the waterway already in October, about half of September’s combined Hormuz and Gulf total, with reports on 7 October of injured crew, including Indian seafarers, after a tanker attack off Oman. Bloomberg reported Iran increasing tanker attacks even as some oil and gas flow measures rose.

Oil is the partial exception and should not be read as normality. Kpler and related trackers put September Middle East crude exports near 16.3 million barrels a day, just under 80 percent of the February level of about 19.5 million, still about 3.2 million barrels a day short. Those flows use longer voyages, ship-to-ship transfers, dark transits, and a US-facilitated southern corridor in Omani waters. Container lines largely rerouted from March. War-risk pricing is disputed by source and date, but the live range is still extreme: tracker estimates around 15 times peacetime, other situation reports near 30 times, with voyage quotes for large hulls in the millions of dollars. Brent was reported near $101 on 7 October. Mines, residual threat, and insurer behavior remain binding constraints even when barrels move.

Confirmed versus disputed: the existence of a June memorandum, later breakdown, continued shipping attacks, very low AIS-visible transit, and elevated war-risk premia are well supported across Reuters, maritime monitors, and trade press. The exact oil-flow recovery rate and the share of dark traffic are tracker-dependent and should be treated as approximate. Iranian claims of control and permit requirements, and US claims about the scale of escorted transit, conflict; the observable result is a thin, insecure flow, not an open strait.

## 4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior

The Tanker War, 1984–88, is the closest kinetic analogue. Iran and Iraq attacked hundreds of commercial ships over years. Insurance stayed elevated. The US escort operation Earnest Will from 1987 raised throughput but did not restore normality. Commercial confidence returned only after the August 1988 ceasefire, and even then over months. It breaks down because today’s volume, insurance market, and missile and drone threat are larger, and a nuclear file sits behind the maritime fight. It implies little chance of functional normality while attacks continue, and a multi-month lag after a real stop.

The Red Sea and Houthi campaign from late 2023 into 2025 is the closest commercial analogue. Major carriers diverted for more than a year. Naval presence did not restore Suez traffic. Insurance and routing normalized only as the attack rate fell and a political off-ramp appeared. It breaks down because Hormuz has fewer practical alternatives and the chokepoint state is a principal belligerent. It implies 6–18 months after attacks actually stop before the definition here is met.

The 2019 Gulf tanker and Abqaiq crisis was short. Premia spiked and eased within weeks to a few months once the acute phase passed. It breaks down because it was not a general war and did not include a blockade or sustained mining threat. It is an upper bound on speed only if the current war ends cleanly.

The 1990–91 Gulf War kept Hormuz open and commercial recovery after Desert Storm was relatively fast. It breaks down because Iran was not the maritime belligerent closing the strait. It is a weak prior for this case.

The Black Sea grain corridor, 2022–23, shows an insurance-backed, politically fragile corridor can move cargo without equaling peacetime normality. It breaks down because volumes and the alternative geography differ. It supports treating escorted or politically licensed transit as not normal.

Outside-in prior, before this week’s evidence, for functional normality by each horizon: 1 week 2 percent; 1 month 6 percent; 3 months 12 percent; 6 months 22 percent; 1 year 40 percent; 18 months 55 percent. The prior assumes wars involving the chokepoint state itself rarely produce commercial normality inside a quarter, and that even after a ceasefire the insurance and carrier lag is measured in months.

## 5. Evidence Ledger

| Evidence | Source type | Direction | Confidence | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Crisis day 222; AIS commercial transits about 9 a day vs about 85 baseline | AIS aggregators, IMF PortWatch-style counts, 7 Oct | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Hundreds of ships waiting at Fujairah, Sohar, Gulf anchorages | AIS monitors, 7 Oct | Against | High | Confirmed |
| UKMTO and press: attack pace up in early October; crew injuries 7 Oct | UKMTO via news, Splash, Indian outlets | Strongly against | Medium-high | Confirmed incidents; attribution sometimes disputed |
| September crude exports near 80 percent of February, still short about 3 million b/d | Kpler via Al Jazeera, trade press | Mildly toward partial recovery, not normality | Medium | Tracker estimate |
| June 17 MOU collapsed within days; talks continue into early October | Reuters, CENTCOM-linked reporting | Mixed: diplomacy alive, settlement absent | High | Confirmed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports cited in Iranian proposal and shipping updates | Reuters, UANI shipping update | Against | Medium | Policy claimed by both sides; scope disputed |
| War-risk still about 15–30 times peacetime | Broker commentary, situation trackers | Strongly against | Medium | Level disputed, elevation confirmed |
| Brent near $100; risk premium still priced | Market reports, 6–7 Oct | Against | Medium | Confirmed price, inferred premium |
| Container majors rerouted since March | Carrier status compilations | Against | Medium | Confirmed for most large lines |
| Mines and narrow corridors still cited as constraints | Energy-policy and maritime analysis | Against | Medium | Inferred from official and trade reporting |

## 6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization

Ranked: mutual incentive to stop an economically costly war, visible in repeated attempts to revive the June memorandum; partial physical oil recovery, which shows the strait is not physically sealed; Gulf states’ interest in de-escalation after strikes on their territory; US political sensitivity to fuel prices ahead of midterms; insurer willingness to return capacity quickly once a real attack pause is observed, as briefly seen after the June deal.

## 7. Key Drivers Against Normalization

Ranked: Hormuz remains Iran’s principal leverage, so Tehran has a structural reason to keep threat and intermittent attacks alive until a political price is paid; the attack series is current, not historical, with a visible acceleration in early October; insurance, not naval escort, is the binding constraint, and premia reprice on incidents within hours; force postures are still wartime, including a US blockade claim and Iranian permit claims; proxy and Lebanon-Israel dynamics can break a Gulf pause from outside; mine and corridor risk clears slowly; buyers and carriers will not treat a two-week lull as a regime change.

## 8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts

Probabilities that each component is true at that horizon, not that it has been true for 14 days together. The joint outcome is tighter than any single row.

| Component | 1 week | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 1 year | 18 months |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Major reduction in direct strikes | 15% | 30% | 45% | 55% | 65% | 72% |
| Sustained safe commercial transit near the definition | 2% | 6% | 15% | 28% | 45% | 58% |
| Insurance near peacetime terms | 1% | 4% | 12% | 25% | 42% | 55% |
| Oil and LNG exports near the definition | 8% | 18% | 35% | 50% | 62% | 70% |
| Proxy restraint on Gulf targets | 25% | 35% | 45% | 55% | 62% | 68% |
| Force drawdown, no blockade or interdiction posture | 5% | 12% | 25% | 38% | 52% | 60% |
| No new major escalation trigger in the period | 55% | 40% | 35% | 40% | 45% | 48% |

Oil recovery is the easiest component and is not gating. Insurance and unescorted transit are gating. A new trigger can reset the clock at every horizon.

## 9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon

Synthesis rule: functional normality requires the hard components together. Near-term probabilities sit near the insurance and transit estimates, not the average. From six months out, a political deal becomes plausible enough to lift the joint probability, with an explicit lag of roughly one to three months between a credible attack halt and insurance and carrier normalization.

- Probability: 1%
- Base-rate anchor: 2%
- Current-evidence adjustment: down, because attacks were reported this week and transit is about 10 percent of normal.
- Core rationale: the definition cannot be met inside seven days from this starting point.
- Main gating factor: live attack series and war-risk pricing.
- What would raise this forecast materially: an immediate, verified mutual stand-down plus a public insurer reopening. Even then 14 clean days cannot finish inside this window.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a capital-ship or mass-casualty incident.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

- Probability: 3%
- Base-rate anchor: 6%
- Current-evidence adjustment: down. Talks exist, but October incidents dominate.
- Core rationale: a deal could be announced; commercial and insurance normalization cannot be completed and held for 14 days inside a month from here.
- Main gating factor: insurer and carrier response time after any pause.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a signed revival of the memorandum, zero incidents for three weeks, and quoted premia cut by more than half.
- What would lower this forecast materially: another September-scale tanker exchange or a Gulf-state strike.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

- Probability: 8%
- Base-rate anchor: 12%
- Current-evidence adjustment: down modestly. Diplomacy is a path, not a base case.
- Core rationale: three months is enough for a ceasefire to stick and for premia to fall, but the base rate for that sequence in a chokepoint war is low, and Iran still has reason to keep leverage.
- Main gating factor: whether talks produce a monitored pause rather than another June-style breakdown.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a ceasefire that survives 30 days and transit sustained above 40 a day without a fresh attack.
- What would lower this forecast materially: collapse of the current proposal track or renewed mining.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

- Probability: 18%
- Base-rate anchor: 22%
- Current-evidence adjustment: slightly down. Partial oil recovery prevents a deeper cut.
- Core rationale: six months can cover a deal, demining, and the start of insurance normalization. It is still more likely that the strait is in a managed, high-premium regime than at the definition.
- Main gating factor: political settlement durable enough that carriers re-enter on ordinary cover.
- What would raise this forecast materially: premia near 0.5 percent of hull and transit above 50 a day for a month.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a second winter of episodic attacks, or a Lebanon-Israel shock that Tehran treats as a breach.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

- Probability: 35%
- Base-rate anchor: 40%
- Current-evidence adjustment: down. The war is already eight months old without a stable maritime regime, which lengthens the tail.
- Core rationale: a year is long enough for war fatigue, a limited nuclear deferral, and commercial catch-up. It is not long enough to treat normalization as the base case while Hormuz leverage remains unresolved.
- Main gating factor: whether a second-phase nuclear and security bargain removes Iran’s incentive to tax the strait.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a written security arrangement for the strait plus club cover restored.
- What would lower this forecast materially: frozen talks and a normalized pattern of monthly shipping attacks.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low-medium

- Probability: 48%
- Base-rate anchor: 55%
- Current-evidence adjustment: down. Prolonged coercion can become the new operating system, as in the Red Sea case.
- Core rationale: just under even odds. Fatigue and cost push toward a deal; leverage, proxies, and the nuclear file keep a large residual. Above 80 percent would require assuming the political conflict ends and markets forget faster than the reference classes allow.
- Main gating factor: absence of a new escalation cycle in months 12–18.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a year of incident-free transit already banked by spring 2027.
- What would lower this forecast materially: regime crisis in Tehran, a US capital-ship loss, or a formal long-term Iranian claim enforced by periodic attacks.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

## 10. Most Likely Path

Episodic attacks and talks continue through late 2026. Oil moves in a reduced, expensive, partly dark system at roughly 60–80 percent of pre-war volumes. A more durable pause is more plausible in the first half of 2027 than this quarter, but insurance and carrier behavior trail any military pause by one to three months. The modal state at 12–18 months is a politically managed, still-premium strait, not the definition above. Functional normality is a plausible outcome by 18 months, not the central one.

## 11. Faster Normalization Case

A revived memorandum holds, attacks stop for 45 days, mines are declared cleared in the Omani corridor, and hull premia fall toward 0.5 percent. Gulf states press both sides. Carriers return in stages. That path can meet the definition around six to nine months. It requires Iran to trade immediate Hormuz leverage for sanctions and blockade relief, which it has not yet done on enforceable terms. Probability mass on this path is real but minority, on the order of one in five by month six and higher thereafter.

## 12. Prolonged Instability Case

Talks fail, the blockade remains, and Iran keeps a tanker-for-tanker doctrine. Monthly incidents hold premia in double-digit multiples. Transit oscillates between 5 and 30 percent of normal on AIS. A Lebanon or Iraq shock restarts direct strikes. This path can still export a large share of oil and still fail every commercial clause of the definition through 18 months. It is the main reason the 18-month probability stays below 50 percent.

## 13. Red-Team Critique

The forecast may understate normalization if dark and escorted flows are already closer to a workable system than AIS implies, and if insurers reprice faster than the Red Sea analogue once a pause is credible. The June premium drop shows that speed. It may overstate later normalization by treating war fatigue as likely to produce a bargain. Iran’s leverage rises when the strait is insecure, and US domestic pressure cuts both ways: it can force a deal or another round of strikes. The load-bearing assumption is that insurance and ordinary transit, not barrels moved, define the target. If a user substituted “oil is flowing,” these probabilities would be too low.

## 14. Critical Signals to Monitor

UKMTO incident frequency and casualties. AIS and PortWatch daily transits versus the 60-a-day threshold. Quoted hull war-risk as a percent of value. Whether the US blockade and Iranian permit regime are formally lifted. Mine-clearance statements from Oman, the US, or the IMO. Gulf-state strike claims. Hezbollah-Israel incidents tied by either side to the Gulf file. Any published text of a revived memorandum.

## 15. Final Summary Table

| Horizon | Probability | Confidence | Gating factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 week | 1% | High | Attacks this week; definition needs 14 clean days |
| 1 month | 3% | High | Insurance and carrier lag |
| 3 months | 8% | Medium | Deal must survive, not merely be announced |
| 6 months | 18% | Medium | Settlement durable enough for ordinary cover |
| 1 year | 35% | Low-medium | Nuclear and security bargain still open |
| 18 months | 48% | Low | Residual coercion risk remains large |

Bottom line: near-term functional normality is very unlikely. Even at 18 months it is about even odds, because a military pause is not the same thing as an open, insurable, unescorted strait.

title: Hormuz traffic at 10%
message:
I will ground this in current reporting on the 2026 Iran War, Hormuz traffic, insurance, and energy flows, then build the forecast from reference classes outward.The Gulf is not functionally normal on 6 October 2026, day 219–221 of the crisis that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on 28 February. Oil barrels have partially recovered through dark shipping, escorts, and bypass routes. The operating regime has not.

## 1. Forecast Question

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality, as defined below, by each horizon from 6 October 2026: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months.

## 2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”

All of the following must hold at the horizon date, not merely a ceasefire headline or a lower oil price.

- Direct military activity: no sustained U.S.–Iran or Israel–Iran kinetic exchanges affecting Gulf waters, ports, or energy infrastructure for at least 14 consecutive days, and no active campaign of strikes on shipping.
- Proxy activity: attacks by Iranian-aligned groups on Gulf shipping or energy infrastructure at near-peacetime frequency, not a live Lebanon, Yemen, or Iraqi-militia front that is still hitting Gulf targets.
- Shipping security: transit through Hormuz and nearby waters does not depend on a wartime permit, toll, or convoy regime as the normal mode. Residual naval presence is acceptable; a dual-control system is not.
- Commercial transit: AIS-visible plus dark commercial transits at or above about 70 percent of the pre-crisis baseline (roughly 85 commercial crossings a day on IMF PortWatch-type counts; about 130–140 vessels a day on broader industry counts). Container services largely restored, not still rerouted via the Cape.
- War-risk insurance: mainstream hull and P&I war cover available without blanket exclusions; additional war-risk premium at or below about 0.75 percent of hull value, versus roughly 0.125–0.25 percent before the war and 3–10 percent in 2026.
- Oil and LNG continuity: Gulf crude, products, and Qatari LNG moving on ordinary commercial terms through normal load ports and Hormuz, not primarily via Yanbu, Fujairah workarounds, ship-to-ship transfers, and AIS-dark shuttle tankers. Iranian exports unblocked if the political settlement that defines normality includes an end to the naval blockade.
- Energy-market stress: the wartime risk premium largely gone. A Brent price near $80–100 is not itself evidence of normality if backwardation, freight, and insurance still price a closure option.
- Force posture: U.S. posture reduced from a wartime surge built to force the strait open. A standing carrier-and-blockade regime fails this test.
- Escalation triggers: no fresh major trigger in the prior two weeks — new mine campaign, infrastructure strike series, declared re-closure, or collapse of the political channel into renewed general war.

A temporary ceasefire, a week of escorted tankers, or regional export totals flattered by bypass pipelines do not qualify.

## 3. Current Situation Snapshot

Confirmed or well-supported as of 6 October 2026:

- The war began on 28 February 2026. Iran declared the strait closed to “hostile” shipping in early March. Day count is about 219–221.
- A U.S.–Iran memorandum of understanding was signed around 17–18 June 2026, with a demining window and an intended reopening. It did not hold. Later strikes, tanker attacks, and a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports followed. Talks have resumed intermittently; they are not a settlement.
- AIS-visible commercial traffic is about 10 percent of normal: roughly 8.4 crossings a day over the past week versus 84.8 before the crisis. Last-24-hour counts are in the single digits. Status trackers mark the strait “restricted,” threat level severe. Iran claims a permit regime through a Persian Gulf Strait Authority; U.S. Central Command has said the strait remains open for transit. Both descriptions can be true at once: passage is arranged, not free.
- Oil volumes are higher than AIS implies because many tankers run dark and because Saudi Arabia and the UAE are using bypass routes. Kpler put Hormuz oil-and-product clearance near 13 million barrels a day in late September against a 17 million barrel pre-war baseline on its measure, and regional exports at times near or above the pre-war average once Red Sea and Gulf of Oman loadings are included. Other trackers (Vortexa, TankerTrackers) have been lower on strait crude. The gap is disputed and material.
- Attacks have not stopped. The Council on Foreign Relations, citing U.S. Maritime Trade Operations, counts at least seven strikes on ships since 28 September. Times of Israel reporting on 5 October also notes at least seven recent tanker attacks even as some export averages look recovered.
- Insurance has not normalized. Pre-war additional war risk was about 0.125–0.25 percent of hull. 2026 quotes have run from 3 to 10 percent; late-summer and October commentary still puts the multiple near 30 times normal, with claims on the order of $2 billion. Early in the war, International Group P&I clubs cancelled war-risk extensions after reinsurance support was withdrawn. A June consortium improved availability briefly; it did not restore peacetime pricing.
- Container networks remain broken. Major carriers have been rerouting since early March. Xeneta’s summer assessment was that disruption would not reverse quickly even after a political reopening.
- Brent is near $100 on one 6 October tracker, elevated but far below the March spike. Kpler has treated the confrontation as the market’s operating environment at least through year-end.
- Force posture remains wartime: carrier presence and a blockade of Iranian oil are still part of the operating picture. That deployment is expensive and, on the CFR’s reading, not a durable way to keep the strait open without a deal.
- Proxy fronts are not closed. Hezbollah and Israel have continued to trade fire; Houthis remain a live risk to Saudi targets; some Iraqi militias have struck during the war. Soufan Center’s 5 October brief treats Iran’s non-state network as weakened but not retired, with the Houthis still relevant.

Disputed: exact daily oil flow through the strait; whether lanes are fully clear of mines; whether October carrier and Marine movements are a new surge or continuation; how much of the June MOU still binds either side. Belligerent claims of victory or of effective closure should be discounted relative to ship-tracking, insurer behavior, and attack logs.

## 4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior

1. Iran–Iraq Tanker War, 1984–88. Relevant because it is the same waterway, with state attacks on tankers, elevated war risk, and partial continuation of exports under threat. It breaks down because both belligerents wanted oil revenue and outside naval escorts eventually constrained the campaign. Traffic never fully stopped; premiums and risk stayed high until the August 1988 ceasefire, with commercial confidence returning over roughly 6–12 months. Suggests a long tail even after shooting declines.

2. 2019 Gulf tanker and Abqaiq attacks. Relevant for insurance and owner behavior after limited strikes. It breaks down because there was no general war and no closure declaration. Premia rose for weeks and eased over one to three months once the attack tempo stopped. Suggests fast normalization only if the political contest ends.

3. Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, late 2023–2025. Relevant because insurers and liner companies rerouted and stayed rerouted while attacks continued, even when the waterway was not legally closed. It breaks down because the Houthis are not a littoral state controlling both shores of Hormuz. Diversions and premia persisted for more than a year. Suggests 6–18 months of commercial abnormality after the political signal turns.

4. Kuwait crisis and Desert Storm, 1990–91. Relevant for oil-shock duration and postwar force posture. Hormuz itself was not the closure point. Price stress faded within months; U.S. posture did not. Suggests energy prices can normalize before the security regime does.

5. Suez closures, 1956 and 1967–75. Relevant because a chokepoint can remain politically closed or semi-closed for months to years when sovereignty is the issue. It breaks down because alternative routes existed and the legal status of Hormuz is different. Suggests that an unresolved control contest dominates the calendar.

6. June 2026 Hormuz false start. Internal reference. Transits recovered toward a fraction of normal within days of the MOU, then reversed when strikes resumed. Insurers reprice in days; owners return only under escort; both reverse on the next incident.

Base-rate prior before this week’s evidence, for this definition: 1 week 3 percent; 1 month 8 percent; 3 months 15 percent; 6 months 28 percent; 1 year 42 percent; 18 months 55 percent. The prior already assumes that chokepoint wars with an open political dispute do not normalize on a ceasefire announcement.

## 5. Evidence Ledger

| Evidence | Source type | Direction | Confidence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| War started 28 Feb 2026; day ~220 | News, trackers | Against | High | Confirmed |
| June 17–18 MOU, later breakdown | Official reporting, think-tank updates | Mixed | High | Confirmed, terms disputed |
| AIS traffic ~10% of baseline this week | AIS aggregators | Against | High | Confirmed for AIS only |
| Hormuz oil flows ~70–80% of baseline in late September by some trackers | Kpler via NYT, CNN, Gulf News | Toward barrels, not regime | Medium | Disputed across trackers |
| Regional exports near pre-war via bypass | Kpler, Reuters | Toward energy continuity, against “normal route” | Medium | Confirmed directionally |
| ≥7 ship strikes since 28 Sep | CFR citing UKMTO; press | Against | Medium-high | Reported, attribution often unclear |
| War-risk still ~3–10%, ~30× pre-war | Marsh, trade press, broker commentary | Against | High | Confirmed range, not a single quote |
| ~$2bn war-risk claims | Trade press | Against | Medium | Reported |
| Major liners still rerouting | Carrier advisories, Xeneta | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Iran permit and fee claims; U.S. says open | Belligerents, trackers | Against free transit | Medium | Disputed control narrative |
| U.S. blockade of Iranian exports; carrier presence | CFR, news | Against drawdown | Medium-high | Reported |
| Talks channel still exists | News, Sept–Oct reporting | Toward | Medium | Confirmed intermittent |
| Hezbollah–Israel fire; Houthi risk | News, conflict monitors | Against | Medium | Confirmed activity, scale varies |
| Brent near $100, not a March-style spike | Price reporting | Weakly toward market function | High | Confirmed price, not normality |

June articles republished on shipping aggregators with October datelines are treated as historical, not as the current traffic picture.

## 6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization

1. Both sides have already accepted, in the June MOU, that reopening Hormuz is negotiable. The channel has not died.
2. Gulf producers have shown they can move large volumes under escort and via bypass. Physical impossibility is not the constraint.
3. Insurers will write the risk when a pause looks real, as they did within days of the June deal. Pricing is reversible.
4. The wartime U.S. naval posture is costly. Washington has a reason to trade force presence for a transit regime.
5. Buyers in Asia have adapted with stocks, dark barrels, and non-Gulf supply. That reduces panic but also reduces pressure for a perfect settlement.

## 7. Key Drivers Against Normalization

1. Iran treats the ability to condition Hormuz as its remaining strategic lever. A permit-and-fee system is a political objective, not an accident.
2. Attack tempo in late September and early October shows the pause is not yet self-sustaining.
3. Insurance and liner behavior ratchet. Cover was withdrawn in 72 hours in March; restoring peacetime terms requires a clean period measured in months, not days.
4. Bypass infrastructure and dark-fleet practices will outlast the war. “Normal” route share may not return even if barrels do.
5. Lebanon, Yemen, and militia theaters can re-trigger Gulf strikes without a new decision in Tehran to reopen general war.
6. No agreed end-state on nuclear limits, sanctions, or the blockade. Force drawdown without that deal is unlikely.

Ranked gating items: attack pause, insurance terms, and the transit regime. Oil volumes are not gating. Prices are not gating.

## 8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts

Probabilities that each component meets the operational bar at that horizon.

| Component | 1 week | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 1 year | 18 months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Major reduction in direct strikes | 20% | 35% | 48% | 58% | 67% | 72% |
| Safe commercial transit ≥70%, no wartime regime | 3% | 7% | 14% | 24% | 40% | 52% |
| Insurance near peacetime terms | 2% | 5% | 12% | 22% | 36% | 48% |
| Oil and LNG on ordinary routes | 8% | 16% | 28% | 40% | 55% | 64% |
| Proxy restraint on Gulf targets | 25% | 33% | 42% | 50% | 58% | 63% |
| Force drawdown from wartime surge | 4% | 10% | 20% | 32% | 46% | 55% |
| No new major escalation trigger | 45% | 40% | 42% | 48% | 52% | 55% |

These are correlated. A real political deal moves transit, insurance, and posture together. A mere fire pause moves the strike line and little else. The joint probability is therefore well below the strike-pause line and close to the insurance and regime lines.

## 9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon

### 1 week
- Probability: 2%
- Base-rate anchor: 3%
- Current-evidence adjustment: −1 point. Attacks this week, AIS near 10 percent, premia still crisis-level.
- Core rationale: Nothing in the current operating picture can flip to the joint definition inside seven days. A ceasefire headline would not qualify.
- Main gating factor: insurance and transit regime.
- What would raise this forecast materially: not applicable inside the window; a total stop in attacks would still leave premia and permits in place.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a new mine-laying claim or a declared re-closure.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 1 month
- Probability: 5%
- Base-rate anchor: 8%
- Current-evidence adjustment: −3 points. The June false start showed that a month is enough for a partial traffic bounce and not enough for insurer or owner normalization after fresh strikes.
- Core rationale: Talks can produce another pause. Owners will not treat a permit-and-escort system as normal, and underwriters will not cut premia to under 0.75 percent while UKMTO logs are still active.
- Main gating factor: a clean attack record long enough for reinsurers.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a signed reopening protocol, published mine-clearance completion, and two weeks with zero ship strikes.
- What would lower this forecast materially: carrier strikes on coastal launch sites or another Bahrain/Kuwait-style exchange.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 3 months
- Probability: 11%
- Base-rate anchor: 15%
- Current-evidence adjustment: −4 points. Late-September attack tempo and the still-open Lebanon file make a clean quarter unlikely. Bypass economics also reduce urgency.
- Core rationale: By early January a deal could reopen traffic on paper. Historical insurer behavior says premia and liner networks lag the paper by months. Three months is enough for a supervised corridor, not for this definition.
- Main gating factor: political settlement credible enough to end the permit regime.
- What would raise this forecast materially: blockade lifted, Iranian fees withdrawn, and mainstream P&I clubs restoring war extensions.
- What would lower this forecast materially: collapse of the talks channel or a Houthi or militia campaign against Gulf energy assets.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 6 months
- Probability: 20%
- Base-rate anchor: 28%
- Current-evidence adjustment: −8 points. Half a year is the first horizon at which mine clearance, liner repositioning, and a reinsurer review could coincide, but only if the political file is actually closed. Current evidence does not show that path as the base case.
- Core rationale: Red Sea experience says rerouting sticks for at least two quarters after attacks fade. The Tanker War says risk premia outlast the last shot. Both apply unless a formal transit settlement removes the closure option.
- Main gating factor: durable U.S.–Iran restraint plus insurer re-entry.
- What would raise this forecast materially: 90 days without a ship strike and war-risk quotes under 1 percent.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a decision in Washington to keep the blockade as the strategy through mid-2027, or an Iranian choice to keep fees as the price of passage.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 1 year
- Probability: 34%
- Base-rate anchor: 42%
- Current-evidence adjustment: −8 points. A year is long enough for fatigue, Asian buyer pressure, and cost of the naval surge to produce a deal. It is also long enough for another round of strikes. The unresolved control contest keeps this below the prior.
- Core rationale: The modal path is a messy supervised regime, not full normality. Full normality requires flag-neutral transit, ordinary insurance, and a reduced force posture. One of those three is likely still missing in October 2027.
- Main gating factor: whether the strait’s political status is settled or merely managed.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a written transit regime with no tolls, sanctions relief tied to compliance, and visible carrier drawdown.
- What would lower this forecast materially: renewed general war or a frozen conflict in which dark convoys become the permanent system.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

### 18 months
- Probability: 46%
- Base-rate anchor: 55%
- Current-evidence adjustment: −9 points. Time raises the chance of a settlement and of commercial habituation, but the definition excludes habituation to a wartime regime. Suez-length political closures and the Tanker War tail argue against crossing 50 percent without a deal.
- Core rationale: By April 2028 either a settlement has reopened ordinary commerce or a semi-closed, escorted, high-premium system has become the new baseline. Those two outcomes are close. The second fails the definition, so the probability stays under half.
- Main gating factor: settlement versus institutionalized restriction.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a year of peacetime premia and pre-war container service counts.
- What would lower this forecast materially: evidence that Iranian permit authority has been accepted by major flag states, or a second war cycle.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

Long-horizon figures stay below 80 percent because the definition requires the closure option to be removed, not merely unused. Current evidence does not show that removal as the likely state even at 18 months.

## 10. Most Likely Path

Through late 2026, intermittent talks and intermittent strikes. Oil moves in bursts under escort and via bypass; AIS-visible traffic stays a fraction of normal; premia stay several percent of hull. Container lines do not restore Gulf strings. Into 2027, the modal outcome is a supervised corridor: fewer attacks, more barrels, insurance still several times pre-war, U.S. naval presence still the condition of passage, Iranian political claims over the strait unresolved. That path is partial stabilization. It is not functional normality under the definition used here. A true settlement is plausible inside a year and more plausible by 18 months, but it is not the base case.

## 11. Faster Normalization Case

Washington and Tehran trade sanctions relief and a nuclear pause for an end to the blockade and to transit fees. Mine clearance is certified. Thirty to sixty days pass without a ship strike. Reinsurers reopen war extensions; premia fall under 1 percent; liners announce Gulf strings. Proxies are told to hold. On that path, the definition could be met around the six-month horizon and would likely be met by a year. Probability of this path inside six months is about 15 percent; inside a year about 30 percent. The June bounce shows the commercial system can move quickly once the political signal is believed. It also shows how fast the signal can be revoked.

## 12. Prolonged Instability Case

Talks fail, the blockade stays, and Iran keeps a permit regime backed by sporadic missile and drone attacks. A Lebanon or Yemen flare-up produces another round of coastal strikes. Insurers keep the Gulf in a listed high-risk area. Bypass pipelines and dark fleets become semi-permanent. Premia never sustainably break 2 percent. This path leaves the definition unmet at 18 months. Probability of still failing the definition at 18 months is the complement of the headline forecast, about 54 percent. The load-bearing piece is Iran’s incentive to retain a demonstrated closure option.

## 13. Red-Team Critique

The forecast may be too low if “functional normality” is interpreted by markets as “barrels flow and Brent is under $100.” On that weaker test, late-September export data would already justify much higher probabilities by six months. It may be too high if the control contest is structural: once a state has closed Hormuz and charged for passage, peacetime insurance terms may not return for years, as with prolonged chokepoint politicization. Dark-fleet measurement also cuts both ways. If true commercial transits are already far above AIS, the traffic gap is smaller than the 10 percent figure implies, but the security regime is worse, because ships are transiting only with transponders off. The estimate is most exposed to a single political event, not to a gradual operational improvement.

## 14. Critical Signals to Monitor

- UKMTO and JMIC incident counts, and whether seven-day ship-strike counts go to zero.
- Additional war-risk quotes for a standard VLCC, and whether International Group clubs restore war extensions without carve-outs.
- IMF PortWatch and AIS daily commercial crossings versus the pre-crisis ~85, plus the share of dark tankers.
- Kpler, Vortexa, and TankerTrackers Hormuz clearance versus bypass loadings. Convergence of those series matters more than any one print.
- Formal status of the blockade and of any Iranian fee or permit requirement.
- Carrier and destroyer days in the Gulf and Gulf of Oman.
- Hezbollah, Houthi, and Iraqi-militia attack logs against Gulf targets.
- Qatari LNG liftings through Hormuz rather than swap or shutdown arrangements.
- A written transit annex, not a communiqué. That is the single highest-value update.

## 15. Final Summary Table

| Horizon | Probability of functional normality | Confidence | Gating factor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | 2% | High | Insurance and regime cannot reset |
| 1 month | 5% | High | Clean attack record |
| 3 months | 11% | Medium | Credible end to permit regime |
| 6 months | 20% | Medium | Insurer re-entry after a real pause |
| 1 year | 34% | Low | Settlement versus managed restriction |
| 18 months | 46% | Low | Whether closure option is removed |

Bottom line: partial oil recovery is already underway and should not be mistaken for normality. Under a definition that requires ordinary transit, ordinary insurance, proxy restraint, and a reduced force posture, the probability stays in single digits through one month, about one in five at six months, and still under half at 18 months.

title: Hormuz traffic at 9%
message:
I will ground the forecast in current reporting on the 2026 Iran War and Hormuz conditions, then build the probabilities from reference classes outward.The Gulf is not near functional normality on 5 October 2026. Oil is moving again under extraordinary risk; the maritime system is not.

## 1. Forecast Question

What is the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality, as defined below, by each horizon from 5 October 2026: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months?

## 2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”

Normality requires all of the following, sustained for at least 14 consecutive days before the horizon date. A ceasefire, a lower oil price, or a pause in high-intensity bombardment is not sufficient.

- Direct military activity: no state-on-state strikes among Iran, the United States, Israel, and Gulf states in that window, and no active declared strike campaign.
- Proxy activity: no multi-day campaign by Houthis, Iraqi militias, or other Iran-linked groups against Gulf shipping, ports, pipelines, or energy facilities. Isolated incidents at or below the 2023–early 2025 baseline do not by themselves fail the test.
- Shipping security: Strait of Hormuz and nearby Gulf of Oman lanes open to commercial traffic without Iranian transit permits, tolls, or selective denial, and without mines as an active operational hazard. US or coalition convoy escort is not the default mode.
- Commercial transit: AIS-visible or otherwise confirmed commercial crossings at or above 70 percent of the pre-crisis baseline of roughly 85–130 ships a day, including a broad return of container lines and product tankers, not only risk-tolerant crude tankers.
- War-risk insurance: additional war-risk premium at or below about 1 percent of hull value (roughly four times the pre-war 0.25 percent), with cover widely available from the commercial market without a government backstop as the main mechanism.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf crude, products, and LNG moving at or above 85 percent of pre-war volumes on ordinary seaborne routes. Pipeline bypass and ship-to-ship transfers may supplement flows; they cannot be the system’s backbone.
- Energy-market stress: the wartime risk premium and extreme freight or insurance pass-through have faded. A price level alone does not qualify.
- Force posture: US and partner naval and air posture reduced from wartime surge; Iranian forces not exercising de facto closure authority.
- Escalation triggers: no fresh mine campaign, declared re-closure, major attack on Gulf-state territory, or new front that re-prices the route.

## 3. Current Situation Snapshot

The war began with US-Israeli strikes on 28 February 2026. This is about day 220 of the Hormuz crisis. A June memorandum of understanding produced a short traffic and insurance improvement, then collapsed. Early October reporting describes talks as stalled, US strikes paused but threatened, and an economic blockade of Iranian oil still in force.

Confirmed or well-corroborated:

- hormuz.now, using AIS and IMF PortWatch, rates the strait Restricted on 5 October: about 7.9 AIS-visible commercial ships a day over the past week versus 84.8 before the crisis, roughly 9 percent. Iran claims permit authority; ships that move do so under US naval coordination.
- Oil volumes have recovered more than ship counts. Kpler and related reporting put September Middle East crude exports near 16 million barrels a day, with roughly 10 million through Hormuz and several million via bypass, against about 17–20 million barrels a day pre-war through the strait. Dark AIS means barrel counts and ship counts diverge. The New York Times reported on 4 October that Iran is still attacking ships in the strait practically every day, while more tankers accept the risk.
- War-risk pricing remains crisis-level. Pre-war additional premiums were about 0.125–0.25 percent of hull. Peak quotes reached 3–10 percent. A June ceasefire cut some quotes toward 2 percent; that did not hold. Lloyd’s List and UKMTO reporting in late September and early October still show tanker strikes, including a Kuwait Oil Tanker Company vessel and an unidentified projectile strike reported on 4 October. Marine insurers have reported on the order of $2 billion in war-risk losses.
- Major container lines have not returned. Product tankers are more deterred than crude tankers because freight does not cover premiums.
- A second front is active. From July, and sharply in September, the Houthis resumed attacks on Saudi-linked shipping and energy sites, seized ground on the Red Sea coast including Mokha, and put pressure on Bab el-Mandeb. Iraqi militia attacks took the Saudi East-West pipeline offline in September. That bypass had been a main shock absorber.

Disputed: exact daily oil flow (US official figures have run hotter than tracker estimates), whether mines remain an active rather than residual hazard, and each side’s account of who fires first. Belligerent claims of control or openness are treated as positions, not facts.

## 4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior

1. Tanker War, 1984–88. Relevant because it is the last sustained Iranian mining and small-craft campaign against Gulf shipping under US convoy. It breaks down because traffic mostly continued, oil volumes stayed broadly intact, and the political end came with the August 1988 ceasefire. Insurance normalized over the following months into 1989–90, then was reset by the 1990 Kuwait crisis. Partial function can coexist with attacks; full commercial normality lagged the ceasefire by months.

2. Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, late 2023–2025. Relevant because a capable non-state actor diverted major container and some energy traffic for more than a year despite intermittent pauses and Western strikes. It breaks down because Hormuz is a harder geographic and energy chokepoint and a state actor is the principal threat. Suggested timeline: 12–24 months after the threat is credibly reduced, not after the first pause.

3. 2019 Gulf tanker and Abqaiq attacks. Relevant as an insurance and routing shock without war. Traffic largely continued; premia eased within weeks to a couple of months once the acute threat receded. Too mild for this case. Suggests the floor for a contained incident, not a war.

4. Black Sea grain corridor, 2022–23. Relevant as a negotiated, reversible maritime corridor inside an ongoing war. Flows resumed in weeks under a deal and collapsed when the deal died. Insurance and routing never returned to peacetime while the war continued. Suggests fragile partial function within 1–3 months of a deal, and reversal risk for as long as the war lasts.

5. 1991 Gulf War shipping shock. Relevant because Hormuz itself stayed open and the oil-price spike was short. It breaks down because Iraq could not interdict the strait and Kuwaiti production, not the lane, was the multi-year loss. Useful as an upper bound on how fast prices can normalize if the lane is not the contested object.

6. Suez closure, 1967–75. Relevant only as the extreme case of a closed chokepoint without a political settlement. Eight years is the wrong central estimate here, but it warns against assuming geography reopens on a military timetable.

Outside-in prior, before this week’s evidence, for full functional normality after a still-unsettled chokepoint war: 1 week 3 percent; 1 month 6 percent; 3 months 14 percent; 6 months 25 percent; 1 year 42 percent; 18 months 55 percent. The prior assumes settlement odds rise with time and that commercial normalization lags a deal by one to three months.

| War-risk quotes still several percent of hull; about $2 billion insurer losses | Brokers, IUMI, trade press | Against | Medium-high | Confirmed elevated; point quotes vary |
| June MOU produced a brief transit and premium improvement, then failed | FT, official statements | Against durability of pauses | High | Confirmed |
| Talks stalled; US demands open strait without tolls; Iran ties reopening to sanctions and Yemen terms | Official statements, Soufan, CBS | Against near-term deal | Medium | Confirmed impasse; terms disputed |

## 6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization

1. Oil is already moving at a large fraction of pre-war volume, so the physical system is not at zero and can scale if risk falls.
2. Both sides have accepted, in practice, that a pure military decision is unlikely. That raises the chance of another corridor deal.
3. Gulf producers and Asian buyers have a strong incentive to pay for risk reduction. Freight has been high enough to pull some crude tonnage back in.
4. US escort has shown that Iran cannot cheaply keep the strait at zero.
5. Insurers reprice within days of a credible quiet period, as June showed.

## 7. Key Drivers Against Normalization

1. No durable political settlement. The June framework already failed once.
2. Iran still treats Hormuz access as leverage and is still striking ships.
3. Insurance, not naval permission, is the binding commercial constraint, and losses have been large.
4. The Houthi and Iraqi-militia front threatens the bypass system that made partial oil recovery possible.
5. Container and product markets have rerouted via the Cape. Reversing that requires months of quiet, not a headline.
6. Mines, permit claims, and dark-fleet practices slow any return to ordinary lane use.
7. US blockade of Iranian exports and Iranian demands on sanctions and Yemen are linked. Solving one without the other is unstable.

Ranked: settlement failure and continued ship attacks are the primary blockers; insurance and the Yemen front are the main propagators into commercial non-normality.

## 8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts

Probabilities are for each condition being true at the horizon, not for it happening at some point before.

| Component | 1 week | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 1 year | 18 months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sustained major reduction in direct strikes | 30% | 42% | 55% | 64% | 74% | 80% |
| Hormuz commercial transit at or above 70% baseline, broad operator return | 2% | 6% | 14% | 24% | 40% | 52% |
| Insurance near the normality threshold | 1% | 4% | 11% | 20% | 34% | 46% |
| Oil and LNG on ordinary routes at or above 85% | 8% | 14% | 24% | 34% | 48% | 58% |
| Proxy restraint on Gulf energy and shipping | 18% | 22% | 30% | 36% | 46% | 54% |
| Wartime force-posture drawdown | 5% | 9% | 16% | 26% | 40% | 50% |
| No new major escalation trigger in the window | 45% | 38% | 42% | 46% | 50% | 55% |

Transit, insurance, and proxy restraint are the gating set. Oil recovery can lead them. Strike reduction can lead them further. Normality does not hold unless the gating set holds together.

## 9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon

Synthesis rule: the forecast is close to the joint probability of the gating set, with a small upward adjustment because success on transit, insurance, and proxies is correlated through a political deal. It is not an average of the sub-forecasts. Oil recovery is treated as necessary but not sufficient.

### 1 week
- Probability: 2%
- Base-rate anchor: 3 percent, from the outside prior for an unsettled chokepoint war.
- Current-evidence adjustment: down 1 point. AIS traffic near 9 percent, strikes this week, and talks at an impasse make a 14-day clean window almost unavailable inside seven days.
- Core rationale: even a sudden deal cannot clear mines, reopen insurance at scale, and bring liner operators back inside a week.
- Main gating factor: insurance and operator behavior.
- What would raise this forecast materially: an immediate, verified mutual halt plus a published demining and open-transit protocol already being executed.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a further declared closure or a strike on a Gulf-state port or energy site.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 1 month
- Probability: 5%
- Base-rate anchor: 6 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: down 1 point. June showed a deal can move traffic within days, but also that it can break. Yemen is an active second constraint.
- Core rationale: a corridor arrangement could lift crude flows further. It would not meet the 70 percent broad-transit and insurance tests for 14 straight days by early November unless attacks stop immediately and stay stopped.
- Main gating factor: continued ship attacks and absence of a deal.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a signed transit protocol, seven or more quiet days, and quoted premiums falling through 2 percent toward 1 percent.
- What would lower this forecast materially: another failed round plus a Houthi or Iraqi strike that keeps the East-West pipeline down.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 3 months
- Probability: 12%
- Base-rate anchor: 14 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: down 2 points. Seven months of failed or fragile pauses, and a widening Yemen front, outweigh the partial oil recovery.
- Core rationale: this is the first horizon at which a serious deal could be followed by demining, a premium cut, and a partial liner return. The base case is still a managed, attacked, or selectively permitted lane.
- Main gating factor: political settlement durable enough for underwriters.
- What would raise this forecast materially: 30 continuous days without a transit attack and premiums sustained under 1.5 percent.
- What would lower this forecast materially: renewed high-intensity strikes or Bab el-Mandeb effectively risk-priced like Hormuz.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 6 months
- Probability: 21%
- Base-rate anchor: 25 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: down 4 points. The second front and the sanctions-for-strait linkage make a clean six-month path less likely than the generic unsettled-war prior.
- Core rationale: by April 2027, fatigue, Gulf mediation, and the cost of the Iranian oil blockade could produce a wider arrangement. Insurance and container networks would still lag. A little over one in five paths clears the full definition.
- Main gating factor: Yemen and militia restraint tied to any US-Iran deal.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a deal that explicitly covers Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, and pipeline security, followed by six quiet weeks.
- What would lower this forecast materially: collapse of Saudi Red Sea exports or a new mine campaign.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 1 year
- Probability: 35%
- Base-rate anchor: 42 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: down 7 points. The war has already lasted seven months without a stable end state, and Iran has retained denial capability. That is closer to the Red Sea reference class than to 1991.
- Core rationale: a year is long enough for a settlement, demining, and commercial re-entry if the political war ends. It is not long enough to treat that end as likely. Residual force posture and episodic proxy fire can still fail the definition even if oil looks normal.
- Main gating factor: whether Iranian denial capability is politically traded away or only paused.
- What would raise this forecast materially: verified lane clearance, liner return, and premiums near pre-war multiples for a full quarter.
- What would lower this forecast materially: regime or succession crisis in Tehran that increases, rather than reduces, IRGC control of the strait.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low-medium

### 18 months
- Probability: 48%
- Base-rate anchor: 55 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: down 7 points. Long-horizon settlement odds are real, but the operational bar stays high, and the Red Sea case shows diversion can outlast several diplomatic cycles.
- Core rationale: just under half. The central path is a messy political arrangement sometime in 2027, with commercial normality arriving later and incompletely. Paths that never settle, or that settle and relapse, still account for about half the distribution. The figure stays below 80 percent because mines, proxies, insurer memory, and force posture can fail the definition even after a ceasefire.
- Main gating factor: durability of whatever arrangement ends the maritime campaign.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a year of attack-free transit and insurance inside the defined band by spring 2027, which would pull the 18-month number up sharply.
- What would lower this forecast materially: entrenchment of a permit-or-toll regime, or a second sustained closure episode.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

## 10. Most Likely Path

Through early 2027 the lane stays restricted and contested. Crude continues to move on risk-tolerant tonnage, dark AIS, escorts, and partial bypass, with volumes fluctuating between roughly half and four-fifths of normal. Container and much product trade stay on the Cape route. Insurance remains several times peacetime. Talks recur and break. Yemen remains a parallel risk. A more stable arrangement is more plausible in the second half of 2027 than in the next quarter, and commercial normality, if it comes, arrives one to three months after attacks actually stop, not when a communiqué is issued.

## 11. Faster Normalization Case

A US-Iran arrangement in the next one to two months trades sanctions relief and a Yemen de-escalation for verified open transit and joint or third-party demining. June showed premiums can halve within days. If that quiet lasts 45 days, crude and products can normalize inside a quarter and liners can begin to return inside six months. This case puts six-month normality near 40 percent and 18-month normality near 70 percent. It requires Iranian leadership to spend Hormuz leverage and the Houthis to accept a pause. That combination has not held once already.

## 12. Prolonged Instability Case

Talks stay deadlocked, ship attacks continue at a low but priced level, and the Red Sea bypass remains impaired. Insurers keep the region in a high-risk area. Operators treat the Cape as semi-permanent for containers. Oil flows persist but never meet the ordinary-route test. Under that case, 18-month normality is closer to 20–25 percent. The 1987–88 and 2023–25 reference classes both support this if the actor with denial capability is not politically constrained.

## 13. Red-Team Critique

The forecast may understate normalization if dark-fleet and escorted crude flows are a leading indicator rather than a substitute, and if Asian buyers force a commercial return faster than underwriters want. It may overstate it if the definition is treated as too close to “oil is moving.” The 48 percent at 18 months is the soft number: settlement odds are not directly observed, and a permit regime with high volumes could look like recovery in market data while failing the definition. The 2 and 5 percent near-term numbers are the hard numbers.

Load-bearing assumptions: Iran keeps denial capability; insurers will not normalize while attacks continue; a Hormuz deal does not automatically restrain the Houthis; 14 days of broad commercial function is the right bar.

What would prove this view wrong: either a verified open lane, sub-1 percent premiums, and liner return inside 90 days, or a fresh full closure that drives even the 18-month figure below 30 percent.

## 14. Critical Signals to Monitor

- AIS and PortWatch daily crossings, split by crude, products, and containers, not barrel headlines alone.
- UKMTO and Lloyd’s List incident log, and whether attribution stabilizes.
- Quoted additional war-risk premium and whether the US or Saudi backstop is still required.
- Status of the East-West pipeline and Yanbu loadings.
- Houthi actions at Bab el-Mandeb and any Iraqi militia fire on Gulf energy assets.
- A written transit protocol that drops Iranian permit authority.
- Announced demining and independent confirmation that lanes are clear.
- Return of a top-five container line to a published Hormuz rotation.

## 15. Final Summary Table

| Horizon | Probability | Confidence | Binding constraint |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | 2% | High | No time for insurance or operator return |
| 1 month | 5% | High | Attacks and no durable deal |
| 3 months | 12% | Medium | Underwriters need a quiet month, not a headline |
| 6 months | 21% | Medium | Yemen front plus sanctions-for-strait linkage |
| 1 year | 35% | Low-medium | Denial capability paused versus traded away |
| 18 months | 48% | Low | Durability after any settlement |

The operational gap that matters is between barrels moving and a normal maritime system. As of 5 October 2026, the first is partly true and the second is not.

title: Gulf normality odds steady
message:
I will ground the forecast in current reporting on the 2026 Iran conflict, Hormuz traffic, war-risk insurance, and energy flows before setting base rates and horizon probabilities.The Persian Gulf is not functionally normal on 4 October 2026, day 217–219 of the Hormuz crisis. A fragile June memorandum, partial crude recovery, and intermittent stand-downs have not restored open commercial navigation.

## 1. Forecast Question

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each horizon: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months. Horizons are measured from 4 October 2026.

## 2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”

All of the following must hold at the same time, and have held for at least 21 consecutive days (so a weekend pause or a single escorted convoy does not count):

- Direct military activity: no US–Iran or Iran–Gulf-state kinetic exchanges against military or commercial targets in the Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, or Gulf of Oman, and no active blockade of Iranian or other Gulf ports.
- Proxy activity: Houthi and other Iran-linked attacks on Gulf energy, ports, or shipping at or below pre-February 2026 sporadic levels, not wartime campaign intensity.
