- Shipping security: the traffic separation scheme in routine commercial use; no permit, toll, or selective-authorization regime; residual mine risk assessed by UKMTO/JMIC as low rather than severe; naval escort optional rather than the operating system.
- Commercial transit: AIS-visible commercial crossings averaging at least 60 per day, against a pre-crisis baseline of about 85 (roughly 70 percent). Current run-rate is about 6 per day.
- War-risk insurance: standard hull war-risk additional premium at or below about 0.5 percent of hull value on renewable terms, not crisis single-voyage pricing in the several-percent or reported ~10–40× band, and available from ordinary market capacity without a government backstop as the binding constraint.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf crude, products, and LNG exports by sea near pre-war volumes without dependence on a wartime escort or bypass-only system. Products matter as much as crude.
- Energy-market stress: the war-risk premium in Brent largely unwound and realized volatility back toward pre-crisis ranges. A price level alone does not qualify. Brent near $100–102 still embeds a large risk premium.
- Force posture: US and Iranian force postures reduced from wartime surge and blockade footing; no standing threat of immediate re-closure as the price of talks.
- Escalation triggers: no new major trigger in the prior 21 days (tanker strike campaign, mine reseeding, missile/drone salvo on Gulf hosts, or collapse of the diplomatic channel into renewed general hostilities).

A ceasefire, a lower oil price, or a battlefield pause is not normality. Partial crude flow under escort is not normality.

## 3. Current Situation Snapshot

The crisis dates from about 28 February 2026. As of 4 October, live AIS trackers put commercial crossings at about 5–6 per day over the past week, roughly 7 percent of the pre-crisis 85, with hundreds of commercial ships stationary on both sides of the strait. Iran says the strait stays shut until seven conditions in the June Islamabad memorandum are met, including sanctions relief and a stop to hostilities. The United States maintains a blockade of Iranian ports and has rejected Tehran’s seven-day reopening proposal. Talks continue through Qatar; a full October reopening is widely judged unlikely.

Kinetic activity has not stopped. Over the weekend of 3–4 October, US forces struck Iranian tankers and Iranian forces struck tankers and US vessels; traffic fell to the lowest since May. Mines have been reported cleared from the main traffic scheme, but maritime authorities still warn of drifting mines and attack risk, and shipowner bodies say clearance alone will not restore traffic. War-risk cover is available only on tight, often single-voyage terms at multiples of peacetime rates.

Oil is the partial exception. September tracking put Hormuz crude movements and bypass-pipeline flows together at a large fraction of pre-war regional exports — estimates range from roughly 7–10 million b/d through the strait plus several million via bypass, with some analysts near 80 percent of regional crude exports. Refined-product exports remain deeply depressed. Brent is about $100–102, up sharply on the year. In Yemen, the Houthis have retaken the Red Sea coast and Bab al-Mandab and are striking Saudi targets, including a claimed hit on an Aramco facility near Riyadh this weekend. That is a second chokepoint and a live proxy front.

Confirmed versus disputed: the low AIS transit count, the blockade, the rejected seven-day plan, weekend tanker strikes, and elevated insurance are well supported. Exact barrel counts differ by tracker and are partly inferred. Iranian claims of lawful control and US claims of a cleared, usable strait are both political; the commercial outcome is the better measure.

## 4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior

- Tanker War, 1984–88. Relevant because it is the closest Gulf shipping-war case: attacks, escorts, high war-risk premia, and continued but distorted trade. It breaks down because it was attrition inside an existing war, not a US–Iran state war with a port blockade and a nuclear file. Shipping stabilized within weeks to a few months after the 1988 ceasefire once attacks stopped, but political normality took longer. Suggests commercial function can return in 1–3 months after a real stop to attacks, not before.
- 2019 Gulf attacks and Abqaiq. Relevant as a short shock with insurance and freight spikes and no general war. Breaks down because there was no closure, no mines campaign, and no blockade. Partial normalization in weeks. Suggests the fast tail if this war ends cleanly, which it has not.
- Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab, late 2023–2025. Relevant for insurer and liner behavior: diversions persisted long after individual lulls, and carriers did not treat a pause as a reopening. Breaks down because volumes were smaller than Hormuz and alternative routing existed. Suggests 6–18 months of sub-normal traffic and premia even after intensity falls.
- Black Sea grain corridor, 2022–23. Relevant for mines, contested control, and insurance lag behind military pauses. Breaks down because it was a negotiated corridor for one commodity. Suggests repeated false reopenings and multi-month lags.
- 1990–91 Gulf War. Relevant for Gulf host-state risk and energy-price overshoot. Breaks down because Hormuz itself stayed open. Suggests the strait can function in a regional war if the local threat to shipping is removed — a condition not met here.
- Hormuz crisis to date, March–October 2026. The internal reference: a June memorandum produced a brief traffic spike (about 50 transits on 24 June in one series) and then relapse to low single digits by August–October. Suggests political announcements move traffic for days, not quarters.

Base-rate prior before case-specific update, for the demanding definition above:

- 1 week: 3 percent
- 1 month: 8 percent
- 3 months: 15 percent
- 6 months: 28 percent
- 1 year: 42 percent
- 18 months: 55 percent

The prior already assumes most chokepoint wars do not normalize inside a month, and that insurance and carrier behavior lag the last attack.

## 5. Evidence Ledger

| Evidence | Source type | Direction | Confidence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AIS commercial crossings ~6/day vs ~85 baseline; day 217–219 | Live AIS trackers (hormuz.now), IMF PortWatch lag | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Hundreds of commercial ships stationary near the strait | AIS trackers | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Iran: strait stays closed until seven MOU conditions met; US rejected seven-day plan | Iranian officials, US statements, wire reporting | Against | High | Confirmed as claims; political positions confirmed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports in force; Iran crude exports effectively interdicted | CENTCOM statements, UANI tracking | Against | Medium-high | Confirmed policy; export figure inferred |
| Weekend tanker strikes by both sides; traffic lowest since May | CENTCOM, IRGC claims, Kpler/trade press | Against | High | Strikes confirmed; attribution of each hull partly from belligerents |
| June 17 MOU and later stand-downs repeatedly violated | Reuters, CNN, official statements | Against | High | Confirmed |
| TSS mines reported cleared; wider mine warning remains | CENTCOM vs UKMTO/JMIC | Mixed | Medium | Disputed in scope |
| September crude flows partly recovered via escort and bypass; products still very low | Kpler, Vortexa, NYT, trade press | Mixed | Medium | Inferred; trackers disagree on level |
| Brent ~$100–102, still far above pre-war | Market reporting | Against | High | Confirmed price; premium share inferred |
| War-risk at high single-digit percent of hull or large multiples; single-voyage terms | Brokers, IUMI, trade press | Against | Medium | Confirmed direction; exact multiple varies by source and date |
| Houthis hold Bab al-Mandab; strikes on Saudi/Aramco targets including this weekend | Reuters, AFP, NYT | Against | High | Attacks confirmed; damage often disputed |
| Qatar channel still open; Trump says talks can resume | Official and wire reporting | Toward | Medium | Confirmed channel; outcome inferred |

## 6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization

1. Both sides still have a diplomatic channel and a written MOU, so a bargain is imaginable without a change of regime.
2. Partial crude recovery shows escorts, bypass pipelines, and risk-tolerant owners can move barrels. That reduces the economic pressure to escalate purely to restore supply, and it is a platform for a later volume rebound.
3. Reported mine clearance in the traffic scheme removes one physical barrier if the political regime changes.
4. US electoral timing and Gulf fiscal pressure create incentives to bank a visible reopening if Iran will trade it for sanctions or blockade relief.
5. Insurers have not permanently exited. Cover exists at a price, so the market can reprice within weeks of a real quiet period, as it did after 1988 and after shorter 2019 shocks.

## 7. Key Drivers Against Normalization

1. The political price of reopening is unmet: Iran wants sanctions and blockade relief before full opening; the US wants opening and nuclear constraints without paying that price. That deadlock is the main gate.
2. Violence is still being used as leverage. Weekend tanker strikes show neither side has retired the shipping weapon.
3. Insurance and liner behavior lag. Red Sea experience says carriers and underwriters will not treat the next announcement as durable until there are quiet weeks and renewable, cheap cover.
4. A second front is active. Houthi control of Bab al-Mandab and strikes on Saudi energy keep Gulf risk high even if Hormuz talk progresses.
5. Force posture is wartime: blockade, coastal strike capacity, and a permit claim. Drawdown is a political act, not a technical one.
6. Internal reference class: the June reopening failed within days to weeks. Base rates must be conditioned on that relapse.

Ranked: political deadlock and continued use of shipping attacks outrank mines, price, and even crude-volume recovery.

## 8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts

Probabilities that each component is in the “normal” state defined above, by horizon.

| Component | 1 week | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 1 year | 18 months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Major reduction in direct strikes, sustained | 8% | 22% | 40% | 55% | 68% | 75% |
| Safe open commercial transit (≥60/day, no permit regime) | 2% | 6% | 16% | 30% | 45% | 58% |
| Insurance normalization | 1% | 4% | 12% | 25% | 42% | 55% |
| Oil and LNG/product export recovery without escort dependence | 3% | 10% | 22% | 38% | 55% | 65% |
| Proxy restraint (Houthi/Gulf energy) | 5% | 12% | 25% | 38% | 50% | 60% |
| Force drawdown from blockade/surge | 3% | 8% | 18% | 32% | 48% | 58% |
| No new major escalation trigger in the window | 35% | 25% | 30% | 35% | 40% | 42% |

Transit, insurance, and drawdown are gating. Strike reduction can happen earlier and still leave a controlled, under-insured strait. Crude barrels can recover under escort without meeting the definition. The joint event is closer to the minimum of the gating items than to the average, with a small positive dependence: a real political deal moves several gates together.

## 9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon

### 1 week
- Probability: 1%
- Base-rate anchor: 3%
- Current-evidence adjustment: down, because weekend strikes, an explicit Iranian closure condition, and a rejected plan make a 21-day normal state impossible inside seven days.
- Core rationale: normality requires three quiet weeks already in the bank. The system is in a live exchange.
- Main gating factor: ongoing kinetic use of the strait.
- What would raise this forecast materially: nothing plausible inside seven days can meet the 21-day test.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a wider strike on Gulf hosts or ports.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 1 month
- Probability: 4%
- Base-rate anchor: 8%
- Current-evidence adjustment: down. Talks are alive, but October reopening is the low-probability branch, and insurance cannot reprice to peacetime inside a month after fresh tanker attacks.
- Core rationale: a deal could be announced. Functional normality also needs traffic, cover, and proxy quiet. The June episode showed announcement is not system reset.
- Main gating factor: political terms on blockade and sanctions.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a signed implementation deal, verified free transit above 40 per day, and no attacks for two weeks.
- What would lower this forecast materially: another tanker-strike cycle or a Houthi campaign against Saudi export terminals.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 3 months
- Probability: 12%
- Base-rate anchor: 15%
- Current-evidence adjustment: slight down. Mine clearance and partial crude flow help the physical side; deadlock, Yemen, and insurer memory hurt the commercial side.
- Core rationale: this is the first horizon where a late-2026 bargain could, if it stuck, produce a 21-day normal window by early January. Most paths still look like managed restriction.
- Main gating factor: conversion of talks into a durable opening, not another spike-and-relapse.
- What would raise this forecast materially: blockade eased, permit regime dropped, war-risk under 1 percent, transits sustainably above 40 per day.
- What would lower this forecast materially: collapse of the Qatar channel or reseeding of mines.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 6 months
- Probability: 22%
- Base-rate anchor: 28%
- Current-evidence adjustment: down. Half a year is enough for insurance to heal after a real stop, as in 1988, but the stop is not the modal path, and the Houthi front can keep Gulf premia elevated even if Hormuz is quieter.
- Core rationale: by April 2027 a deal, fatigue, or a tacit transit arrangement could have compounded. The internal base rate of failed reopenings keeps this well below even odds.
- Main gating factor: whether attacks on shipping actually stop for a full quarter.
- What would raise this forecast materially: 60-plus daily transits and renewable war cover near historical Gulf rates.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a return to general US–Iran strikes or a successful sustained attack on Saudi loading ports.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 1 year
- Probability: 38%
- Base-rate anchor: 42%
- Current-evidence adjustment: slight down. A year is long enough for a political settlement or a stable armed management that markets learn to live with. It is not long enough to assume the nuclear file, sanctions, and Yemen are resolved.
- Core rationale: the probability mass is “restrictive peace or managed corridor becomes predictable,” not “pre-2026 status quo.” Some of those outcomes still fail the definition if escorts and punitive premia remain.
- Main gating factor: replacement of wartime control arrangements by routine commercial rules.
- What would raise this forecast materially: sanctions-for-opening bargain implemented and proxy front de-escalated.
- What would lower this forecast materially: regime instability in Iran, or a decision in Washington or Tehran that closure is a permanent bargaining chip.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low-medium

### 18 months
- Probability: 52%
- Base-rate anchor: 55%
- Current-evidence adjustment: slight down. Eighteen months clears the modal length of an unresolved chokepoint crisis only if neither side still gains from keeping the strait as a weapon. That is plausible, not assured.
- Core rationale: above even odds only at this horizon, and only barely, because time allows deal, fatigue, or adaptation. The definition stays demanding: escorted crude at pre-war barrels with expensive cover would still fail.
- Main gating factor: political settlement sufficient for insurers and liners, not merely for state oil companies under escort.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a year of transit above 70 percent of baseline and war-risk inside normal Gulf bounds.
- What would lower this forecast materially: institutionalized dual control or a frozen conflict that leaves premia and permits in place.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

Long-range figures stay near 50 percent rather than above 80 percent because the operational test includes insurance, proxies, and force posture, not just the absence of missiles on a given day.

## 10. Most Likely Path

Through early 2027 the modal path is a controlled, low-throughput strait: intermittent talks, periodic strikes used as leverage, US blockade intact, selective or escorted movements, crude partially flowing by escort and bypass, products and ordinary commercial shipping lagging, war-risk remaining a transaction-by-transaction decision. Yemen stays hot enough to matter for Saudi risk. A brittle implementation deal is more likely than either a clean pre-war restoration or a total multi-year closure. Functional normality, as defined, arrives only if that deal survives long enough for underwriters and liners to treat it as routine — a step beyond the signature.

## 11. Faster Normalization Case

The stronger upside case is a narrow bargain in which Washington eases the port blockade and offers limited, reversible sanctions relief, Iran drops the permit regime and stops tanker attacks, and Gulf states plus the US keep a quiet escort only as backstop. Insurers reprice within weeks of a verified quiet period, as they did after the 1988 ceasefire. Crude and then products rebound. Houthis are persuaded or pressured to pause Saudi strikes. That path can put the system inside the definition by roughly the six-month horizon. It requires both capitals to prefer a partial deal to leverage, which weekend behavior argues against but does not rule out.

## 12. Prolonged Instability Case

The stronger downside case is a frozen weaponization: Iran keeps a claimed veto and the option to reseed mines or hit unauthorized tankers; the US keeps the blockade; each spike in talks is followed by a relapse, as in June. Houthis hold Bab al-Mandab and periodically hit Saudi energy. Insurers never leave crisis pricing. By 18 months the Gulf has a stable abnormal equilibrium — some barrels moving, normality failed. A wider strike cycle that hits Gulf ports or desalination and energy nodes would push even the 18-month probability well down.

## 13. Red-Team Critique

The forecast may understate normalization if AIS undercounts dark, state-directed, or escorted traffic and if markets will accept escort-dependent crude flow as “functional” faster than the definition allows. It may also underweight US electoral incentive to force a visible reopening before late 2026.

It may overstate normalization if the June relapse is the true regime, if Iranian domestic politics reward keeping the strait shut, and if the Houthi front is now independent enough to hold Gulf risk premia up even after a US–Iran paper deal. The 18-month figure near 50 percent is the softest number: it assumes fatigue and bargaining eventually dominate, which is a prior, not a finding. The load-bearing assumptions are that neither side wants a full return to general war, and that insurance follows a real 30–60 day quiet period rather than a political narrative.

What would prove this view wrong: sustained transits above 60 per day and war-risk under 0.5 percent inside 90 days (upside miss), or a new general strike campaign plus mine reseeding that keeps transits under 15 per day through mid-2027 (downside miss).

## 14. Critical Signals to Monitor

- Daily AIS and PortWatch commercial transits, not official “facilitated transit” counts alone.
- Whether new voyages are permit-based, escorted, or ordinary TSS traffic.
- Hull war-risk quotes as a percent of value, and whether cover returns to time policies.
- Confirmed attacks on merchant ships and mine reports from UKMTO/JMIC, separated from belligerent claims.
- Status of the US port blockade and of Iranian oil departures past enforcement.
- Product exports versus crude exports.
- Houthi attacks on Saudi loading ports and Red Sea traffic.
- Any implementation text that ties opening to sanctions or nuclear steps, and whether it survives 21 days.

## 15. Final Summary Table

| Horizon | Probability of functional normality | Confidence | Gating factor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | 1% | High | Active strikes; 21-day test cannot be met |
| 1 month | 4% | High | Political terms; insurance lag |
| 3 months | 12% | Medium | Deal must stick, unlike June |
| 6 months | 22% | Medium | A full quiet quarter for shipping attacks |
| 1 year | 38% | Low-medium | Wartime rules replaced by commercial rules |
| 18 months | 52% | Low | Settlement or fatigue sufficient for insurers and liners |

Bottom line: partial crude movement is real and should not be confused with a return to functional normality. On the definition used here, that return is very unlikely inside a month, unlikely inside six months, and only about even money by 18 months.

title: Iran War: Hormuz traffic at 3%
message:
I will ground the forecast in current reporting on the 2026 Iran conflict, Hormuz traffic, war-risk insurance, and energy flows, then build the probabilities from reference classes outward.The Persian Gulf is not near functional normality. On 3 October 2026 the disruption is in roughly day 217–218. A June memorandum produced a brief traffic rebound and then failed. Direct strikes on shipping resumed in September and continued into early October. Oil barrels have partially recovered under escort and dark transit; commercial conditions have not.

## 1. Forecast Question

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months from 3 October 2026.

## 2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”

All of the following must hold at the same time, for at least 14 consecutive days, and must not depend on ad-hoc naval escort or selective political permission as the operating system:

- Direct military activity: no state kinetic strikes on commercial vessels or Gulf energy infrastructure in the prior 14 days, and no active declared closure or toll regime enforced by force.
- Proxy activity: successful proxy strikes on Gulf shipping or energy infrastructure at or below the pre-February 2026 baseline.
- Shipping security: standard international lanes in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby Gulf of Oman usable without mine threat requiring convoy, and without a requirement to use an IRGC-designated northern corridor.
- Commercial transit: AIS-visible plus independently corroborated transits at or above 70 percent of the pre-crisis norm (about 50 or more commercial vessels per day against a baseline of roughly 74–85).
- War-risk insurance: additional war-risk premium within about 2 times the peacetime baseline, and major International Group P&I clubs restored to ordinary cover rather than cancellation or voyage-by-voyage exception.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: combined Gulf crude and LNG exports at or above 85 percent of the February 2026 baseline, without blockade waivers or selective exemptions as the binding mechanism.
- Energy-market stress: the Hormuz-specific risk premium in crude no longer the dominant price driver (illustratively under about $5–8 per barrel on a sustained basis), and freight and insurance no longer pricing the route as a war zone.
- Force posture: no active U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and no ongoing strike campaign; a residual naval presence is compatible with normality, a wartime interdiction regime is not.
- Escalation triggers: no new mine campaign, no fresh strike on critical Gulf-state energy infrastructure, and no collapse of whatever political arrangement exists into a renewed open campaign.

A ceasefire, a single strong oil-export day, or lower headline prices do not meet this definition.

## 3. Current Situation Snapshot

The war began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on 28 February 2026. Traffic collapsed within days. A memorandum in mid-June produced a short recovery: JMIC recorded 54 transits on 24 June, the high since the outbreak, and cumulative transits rose through the summer. That arrangement collapsed on 8 July. Fighting and shipping attacks resumed in early September.

As of 1–3 October:

- Live AIS monitors put visible commercial transits at roughly 3 to 6 per day, about 3–6 percent of the pre-crisis norm of about 74–85. IMF PortWatch’s lagged 7-day average was about 3 per day into late September. Some U.S.-facilitated and dark-transit counts are higher: one monitor put late-September facilitated traffic near the mid-20s per day, and Windward logged 119 transits in the week of 23–30 September, more than a third dark.
- Iran has struck commercial ships in the strait in late September and early October, including tankers transiting dark off Musandam and the Kuwait-flagged Kazimah III on 1 October. The New York Times, citing a Western security official, reported roughly 30 drone and 10 anti-ship missile launches per week against commercial ships since August, with at least four ships hit in the prior 10 days. CENTCOM has answered with strikes and described the shipping attacks as ceasefire violations.
- A U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in effect. UANI reported 125 commercial vessels redirected by 30 September.
- War-risk pricing is still extreme. Trackers cite roughly 15 times to 40 times peacetime premia; earlier in the war, seven International Group clubs cancelled Gulf war-risk cover and hull premia moved from about 0.25 percent to about 3 percent of vessel value.
- Kpler data cited by Al Jazeera put September Middle East crude exports near 16.3 million barrels per day, just under 80 percent of the February level and about 3.2 million barrels per day short. That recovery is fragile: late-September attacks and the East–West pipeline strike have already reversed confidence. LNG remains far more impaired than crude in available reporting.
- Mines, a selective Iranian permit system, Houthi pressure on the Bab el-Mandeb, and at least one reported strike on Saudi bypass infrastructure are all live second-order constraints.

Confirmed: the war is in its eighth month, a ceasefire already failed, shipping attacks and U.S. retaliation occurred in the last two weeks, and open commercial traffic is a small fraction of normal. Disputed: exact daily transit counts, because dark traffic and facilitated transits diverge sharply from AIS. Inferred: insurance, not naval presence alone, remains the binding constraint on full commercial return.

## 4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior

1. Tanker War, 1984–1988. Relevant because a state actor used limited attacks on commercial shipping to raise insurance costs without a full physical blockade. It breaks down because that campaign sat inside a longer Iran–Iraq war and ended only with the political end of the war. Partial traffic continued for years under threat. Suggests functional commercial normality only after a settlement, often 12–36 months after the political decision, not during active strikes.

2. 2019 Gulf tanker and Abqaiq attacks. Relevant as a short Gulf shipping and energy shock with an insurance spike. It breaks down because attacks were episodic, not embedded in an open U.S.–Iran war with a blockade. Traffic and premia normalized within weeks to a few months once the immediate threat receded. Suggests a 1–3 month recovery only if strikes stop and stay stopped.

3. Red Sea / Houthi campaign, late 2023 into 2025. Most useful commercial analogue. Attacks did not have to be daily to keep major liners off the route; Cape diversion and elevated war risk persisted well over a year after the peak. It breaks down because Hormuz has fewer substitutes than Suez. Suggests 6–18 months from the last credible attack to anything like insurance and liner normality, and longer if attacks recur.

4. Operation Earnest Will, 1987–1988. Relevant because escorted transit restored some flow while the threat continued. It breaks down because escort is not the definition used here. Suggests barrels can move in months while commercial normality waits on the end of the threat.

5. Black Sea grain corridor, 2022–2024. Relevant as a politically brokered, insurance-dependent reopening that repeatedly failed. Suggests intermittent openings are the base case, not durable normality, until the military facts change.

6. 1990–91 Gulf War. Weak fit. Hormuz itself stayed open. Useful only as a reminder that a short, decisive campaign can limit chokepoint damage; this war has already not taken that path.

Base-rate prior before case-specific updating, for a chokepoint war still short of settlement:

- 1 week: 3 percent
- 1 month: 7 percent
- 3 months: 15 percent
- 6 months: 28 percent
- 1 year: 42 percent
- 18 months: 55 percent

## 5. Evidence Ledger

| Evidence | Source type | Direction | Confidence | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Disruption began 28 Feb 2026; day 217–218 | Maritime trackers | Against | High | Confirmed |
| AIS-visible traffic ~3–6/day, ~3–6% of norm | PortWatch, hormuz.now, 3 Oct | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Dark and U.S.-facilitated transits materially higher than AIS | Windward, UANI | Mixed | Medium | Confirmed pattern, counts differ |
| June MoU, 54 transits on 24 June, collapse 8 July | JMIC via UANI; Alcon | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Late-Sep / 1 Oct strikes on tankers and Kazimah III | NYT, UANI, Windward | Against | High | Confirmed |
| ~30 drone and ~10 missile attacks per week since August | NYT citing Western official | Against | Medium | Reported, not fully public |
| U.S. blockade of Iranian ports ongoing; 125 ships redirected | UANI | Against | Medium | Reported |
| September crude exports ~16.3 mb/d, ~80% of February | Kpler via Al Jazeera | Toward | Medium | Reported |
| War-risk still ~15–40×; earlier P&I cancellation wave | Maritime trackers, trade press | Against | Medium | Reported, methodologies differ |
| East–West pipeline struck; Yanbu loadings interrupted | Flint, Foreign Affairs | Against | Medium | Reported |
| Houthi threat to Bab el-Mandeb renewed | Foreign Affairs, trade press | Against | Medium | Reported |
| Qatar–Iran contacts in New York, late September | Alcon | Toward | Low | Reported |
| Mines still cited as a lane constraint | Columbia CGEP | Against | Medium | Assessed |

Where counts conflict, AIS and PortWatch are treated as the lower bound on open commercial traffic, and Windward/UANI as evidence that some flow continues under escort or dark. Neither series meets the 70 percent open-lane test.

## 6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization

1. Both sides have already shown they can pause. The June window produced a real transit rebound, so the operational path exists.
2. Crude exports recovered to roughly 80 percent of pre-war in September, which shows producers and some charterers will move barrels when protection is credible.
3. A de facto hotline and limited retaliatory strikes suggest neither side currently wants uncontrolled escalation.
4. Gulf producers have bypass capacity and a commercial incentive to restore flows; Asian buyers have an incentive to receive them.
5. U.S. domestic sensitivity to fuel prices is a recurring constraint on how long Washington sustains a full closure regime.

## 7. Key Drivers Against Normalization

1. Insurance is the binding constraint. Clubs have already cancelled once. Repeated post-ceasefire attacks reset the trust clock. Kpler’s own risk note makes this explicit.
2. The political issue is unresolved. Iran links reopening to lifting the blockade; Washington links relief to Iranian behavior. Alcon judged an October reopening deal unlikely.
3. Iran retains a cheap disruption option: intermittent strikes, mines, and a permit regime. That option is being used.
4. One ceasefire has already failed. Each failure raises the evidence threshold for the next recovery.
5. Second-order theaters are active: Houthis, the Saudi bypass pipeline, and Gulf-state exposure to Iranian retaliation.
6. Dark transit and escorted convoys can move oil without restoring the commercial system this definition requires.

Ranked, insurance confidence and the absence of a durable political bargain dominate naval tactical control.

## 8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts

Probabilities that each component is true at that horizon:

| Component | 1 week | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 1 year | 18 months |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Major reduction in direct strikes | 15% | 30% | 45% | 55% | 65% | 72% |
| Sustained safe open-lane transit ≥70% | 2% | 6% | 15% | 28% | 42% | 55% |
| Insurance near peacetime | 1% | 4% | 12% | 25% | 40% | 52% |
| Oil and LNG exports ≥85% baseline | 8% | 18% | 35% | 48% | 60% | 70% |
| Proxy restraint | 25% | 35% | 45% | 55% | 62% | 68% |
| Force drawdown from blockade/strike posture | 5% | 12% | 25% | 38% | 50% | 60% |
| No new major escalation trigger | 40% | 45% | 50% | 52% | 55% | 58% |

Oil recovery leads. Insurance and open-lane transit lag. The joint event is gated by the slowest commercial components, not by the oil series.

## 9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon

Synthesis rule: functional normality requires the commercial gates (open transit and insurance) plus a quiet military baseline. Oil recovery is necessary but not sufficient. Probabilities are therefore pulled down from the oil sub-forecast toward the insurance and transit sub-forecasts, with an additional penalty for the already-failed ceasefire.

### 1 week
- Probability: 1%
- Base-rate anchor: 3 percent
- Current-evidence adjustment: down, because strikes and retaliation are current, not residual
- Core rationale: Attacks occurred in the last 10 days. Insurance is still in extreme territory. No political arrangement is in force.
- Main gating factor: active kinetic exchange
- What would raise this forecast materially: an immediate, verified mutual halt and a club statement restoring cover
- What would lower this forecast materially: a mine incident or a strike on a Gulf export terminal
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 1 month
- Probability: 4%
- Base-rate anchor: 7 percent
- Current-evidence adjustment: down, given Alcon’s judgment that an October deal is unlikely and the fresh attack cycle
- Core rationale: A tactical pause is plausible. Fourteen days of open-lane traffic plus insurance normalization is not. Charterers will not treat a one-week lull as a regime change.
- Main gating factor: insurance and lane confidence
- What would raise this forecast materially: a signed reopening arrangement plus two clean weeks and premium collapse
- What would lower this forecast materially: another tanker strike or expansion of the blockade
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 3 months
- Probability: 10%
- Base-rate anchor: 15 percent
- Current-evidence adjustment: down, because the June–July failure is the relevant within-case base rate
- Core rationale: By early January a winter political pause is possible. The Red Sea reference class says insurers and liners will still be waiting for a longer clean period. LNG and mine clearance alone can consume much of this window.
- Main gating factor: durability of any pause beyond 60 days
- What would raise this forecast materially: 45 or more days without a shipping attack and P&I restoration
- What would lower this forecast materially: renewed strikes on Gulf-state bases or a second pipeline hit
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 6 months
- Probability: 20%
- Base-rate anchor: 28 percent
- Current-evidence adjustment: down, for unresolved blockade-for-access bargaining and proxy theaters
- Core rationale: Enough time for a limited deal and a partial mine-cleared lane, but not enough to erase two failed or fragile openings unless the military threat is visibly dismantled. Escorted oil flow at high levels remains more likely than the joint definition.
- Main gating factor: political bargain that removes Iran’s incentive to tax the strait
- What would raise this forecast materially: blockade relief tied to a verified shipping halt and club re-entry
- What would lower this forecast materially: a spring escalation cycle similar to September
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 1 year
- Probability: 36%
- Base-rate anchor: 42 percent
- Current-evidence adjustment: modestly down
- Core rationale: A year is long enough for war-weariness, fuel-price politics, and a narrow deal to produce a real commercial reset. It is also long enough for another collapse. The Tanker War and Red Sea cases both say residual premia and routing changes often outlast the headlines.
- Main gating factor: whether a settlement survives its first test
- What would raise this forecast materially: six continuous months of open traffic and premia near baseline
- What would lower this forecast materially: Iranian leadership conclusion that strait pressure is the only remaining leverage
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 18 months
- Probability: 50%
- Base-rate anchor: 55 percent
- Current-evidence adjustment: slightly down
- Core rationale: By April 2028 the modal path is a damaged but functioning corridor, either after a formal arrangement or after both sides accept a managed, lower-threat status quo. The probability stays near even because structural bypass investment, dark-fleet habits, and the option to re-mine do not disappear with a ceasefire. Long-horizon certainty above 80 percent is not justified: the operational bar includes insurance and open lanes, not merely the absence of daily strikes.
- Main gating factor: whether the threat capability is constrained or merely unused
- What would raise this forecast materially: verified drawdown of coastal anti-ship systems and a full club return
- What would lower this forecast materially: a frozen conflict in which Hormuz stays a licensed waterway
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

## 10. Most Likely Path

Through late 2026, intermittent shipping attacks and limited U.S. retaliation continue. Crude moves in bursts via escorted and dark transits, somewhere in a wide band below the pre-war level, while LNG and container traffic stay impaired. Insurance remains the choke point. A fragile political arrangement is more plausible in the first half of 2027 than in October 2026. Even then, functional normality as defined here arrives only after a clean multi-month period, not on the day a memorandum is signed. The modal state at 12–18 months is partial commercial recovery with a residual risk premium, not full normality. The probability that the full definition is met by 18 months is about even.

## 11. Faster Normalization Case

A bargain in which Washington relaxes the port blockade, Iran stops permit enforcement and attacks, and Gulf states finance a mine-clearance and reinsurance bridge. The June transit spike shows the physical response can be fast. If that package held for 60 days, the 6-month probability would move toward 40 percent and the 1-year probability toward 60 percent. This case requires both sides to trade leverage they are currently using.

## 12. Prolonged Instability Case

Iran treats limited strikes and a toll regime as sustainable leverage. The United States keeps the blockade. Houthis and Iraqi militias periodically hit bypass routes. Insurers never fully return. By 18 months the corridor is a managed risk zone at 30–50 percent of former open traffic, with oil moving and normality unmet. Under that case the 18-month probability falls toward 25 percent. Foreign Affairs and Flint descriptions of a widening, no-off-ramp conflict are the skeleton of this case.

## 13. Red-Team Critique

The forecast may understate normalization if dark and facilitated traffic is already doing more commercial work than AIS implies, and if markets will accept escort-based flow as “normal” faster than this definition allows. The September crude recovery is the best evidence for that critique.

The forecast may overstate normalization if the failed June–July opening is the true base rate. Repeated attacks after a ceasefire do more damage to insurer confidence than the initial closure. A licensed strait can persist for years without looking like the Tanker War’s endpoint. The 18-month figure of 50 percent is the softest number in the set and should be revised down if another opening fails in the next quarter.

Load-bearing assumptions: Iran can still be induced to stop attacking shipping; U.S. fuel-price politics eventually cap escalation; mines are a clearance problem measured in months, not a permanent closure; proxies do not independently veto a deal.

## 14. Critical Signals to Monitor

- 14-day count of confirmed attacks on commercial vessels, from UKMTO or equivalent
- International Group club circulars on Gulf war-risk cover
- Additional premium as a percent of hull value, not just tracker multiples
- Open-lane versus northern-corridor share of transits
- U.S. blockade redirection counts
- LNG export recovery, which has lagged crude
- Any new strike on East–West or Fujairah infrastructure
- Houthi actions at Bab el-Mandeb
- Text of any arrangement linking blockade relief to shipping access

## 15. Final Summary Table

| Horizon | Probability | Confidence | Gating factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 week | 1% | High | Active strikes |
| 1 month | 4% | High | Insurance and lane trust |
| 3 months | 10% | Medium | Pause durability |
| 6 months | 20% | Medium | Political bargain |
| 1 year | 36% | Medium | Settlement survives first test |
| 18 months | 50% | Low | Threat constrained, not merely unused |

These figures are the probability that the joint operational definition is met, not the probability that oil is moving or that a ceasefire has been announced.

title: Hormuz traffic at 5%
message:
I will ground the forecast in current reporting on the 2026 Iran war, Hormuz transit, war-risk insurance, and energy flows before setting base rates and probabilities.The Persian Gulf is not near functional normality. Seven months into the war, the Strait of Hormuz is still a restricted, contested system: AIS-visible traffic is about 5 percent of the pre-crisis baseline, war-risk pricing remains an order of magnitude above peacetime, attacks were reported this week, and US–Iran talks are stalled over sequencing.

## 1. Forecast Question

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality, as defined below, by each horizon from 2 October 2026: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months.

## 2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”

Normality means all of the following have held for at least 14 consecutive days ending on the horizon date. A ceasefire, a lower oil price, or a one-week traffic spike does not qualify.

- Direct military activity: no kinetic strikes by the United States, Israel, or Iran on each other’s territory, bases, or warships, and no declared closure of Hormuz.
- Proxy activity: attacks by Hezbollah, the Houthis, or other Iran-linked groups on Gulf shipping, Gulf energy infrastructure, or US forces at or below the pre-February 2026 baseline. An isolated incident does not fail the test; a renewed pattern does.
- Shipping security: the traffic separation scheme is usable without a belligerent permit or toll as a condition of passage. The United States is not blockading non-sanctioned commercial calls at Gulf ports. Residual mine risk is not producing casualties or repeated aborts.
- Commercial transit: AIS-visible commercial crossings average at least 70 percent of the pre-crisis baseline of about 85 vessels a day (roughly 60 or more), including oil-major and mainline container operators, not only shadow-fleet or selectively tolerated hulls.
- War-risk insurance: additional hull war-risk premium at or below about 0.5 percent of hull value (about twice the pre-war 0.25 percent), with broad market capacity rather than a thin specialty facility.
- Oil and LNG continuity: combined Gulf crude, condensate, products, and LNG exports, excluding Iran’s pre-war sanctions baseline, within 15 percent of the Q4 2025 run-rate, moving on ordinary commercial cover.
- Energy-market stress: Middle East–Asia VLCC freight no longer structurally war-priced (not on the order of tens of dollars per barrel), and Brent is not being driven by an active Hormuz risk premium. A lower price alone is not sufficient.
- Force posture: routine transit does not require a combat escort surge, and Iranian fast-attack or mining forces are not actively interdicting the southern corridor.
- Escalation triggers: no new major trigger in the prior 14 days, including a leadership strike, a renewed mining campaign, an attack on Gulf-state energy infrastructure, or reimposition of either blockade.

## 3. Current Situation Snapshot

The war began on 28 February 2026 with US–Israeli strikes (Operation Epic Fury), including the killing of Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missile fire on Israel and US bases in the Gulf and, from early March, a de facto closure of Hormuz by warning, boarding, attack, and mining. The United States later blockaded Iranian ports. The result is a dual blockade, not a settled ceasefire. This is day 217 of the Hormuz crisis. <grok:render card_id="260744" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">3</argument></grok:render>

The 17 June Islamabad Memorandum aimed to suspend hostilities and restore pre-war transit volumes within 30 days after mine clearance. It broke down after Iranian attacks on commercial ships in early July and a US strike round on 7 July. The 60-day window expired in mid-August with no final agreement. Iran now asserts a permit regime through a Persian Gulf Strait Authority; Washington rejects it. <grok:render card_id="f815d8" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">32</argument></grok:render> <grok:render card_id="989918" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">16</argument></grok:render>

As of 2 October, hormuz.now rates the strait Restricted. AIS-visible commercial traffic over the past week is about 4.4 crossings a day against 84.8 before the crisis, roughly 5 percent of normal. Ships that move do so under US coordination or Iranian claim of permit control. <grok:render card_id="848af9" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">0</argument></grok:render> UK maritime monitors reported three vessels hit in the strait around 1 October. <grok:render card_id="451f6f" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">25</argument></grok:render> September included destruction of Iranian tankers and Houthi fire on Saudi targets.

Oil has partially reappeared through selective and dark transits. Kpler put oil and product flows near 13.1 million barrels a day in the week to about 27 September, against about 17.1 million before the war on its measure. Other estimates differ, including higher “facilitated” counts and lower confirmed clearances. Dark-fleet and AIS-off traffic explain much of the gap. Major operators have not returned. <grok:render card_id="7ebd9b" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">12</argument></grok:render> Brent was reported near $102 after the latest attacks. War-risk quotes in 2026 have run from about 3 percent to 10 percent of hull value, against about 0.25 percent before the war. <grok:render card_id="eb8d07" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">12</argument></grok:render> <grok:render card_id="9e213c" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">20</argument></grok:render>

Talks restarted in late September via Qatar and Pakistan. Iran’s seven-day plan would reopen the strait only after an end to hostilities, including in Lebanon, a lifted US blockade, unfrozen assets, and oil-sanctions relief, then nuclear talks. Trump rejected that proposal on 26 September. Mediators have circulated a shorter compromise. Both sides say positions remain far apart. <grok:render card_id="6cc4b9" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">23</argument></grok:render> <grok:render card_id="e35129" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">24</argument></grok:render>

Disputed or soft points: exact daily oil volumes, how many mines remain after the US claim of traffic-separation-scheme clearance in late August, and whether unnamed officials expect strikes to resume after the US midterms. Those are claims, not confirmed plans.

## 4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior

1. Tanker War, 1984–88. Relevant because it is the only modern Gulf shipping war with sustained attacks, elevated insurance, and escort operations. It breaks down because the strait was never fully closed and volumes largely continued. Commercial confidence normalized only after the August 1988 ceasefire, with a lag of months. Suggests 6–18 months after a political settlement, not after a pause in fire.

2. Red Sea / Houthi campaign, 2023–25. Relevant because insurers and liners treated an unresolved threat as structural and rerouted for more than a year despite lulls. It breaks down because Bab el-Mandeb has substitutes and Hormuz does not. Suggests 6–18 months after attacks clearly stop before blue-chip traffic and peacetime war-risk pricing return.

3. 2019 Gulf tanker and Abqaiq attacks. Relevant as a short shock to the same insurance market. It breaks down because there was no war, no mining campaign, and no blockade. Recovery in weeks to about two months once the attack pattern stopped. This is the fast-normalization ceiling, not the base case.

4. Suez closures, 1956 and 1967–75. Relevant if control of the waterway becomes a sovereignty claim rather than a wartime tactic. The 1967 closure lasted about eight years. It breaks down because Hormuz is Iranian and Omani territorial waters with a transit regime, and both Washington and the Gulf exporters have stronger incentives to force a corridor. Suggests a long right tail if the permit regime sticks.

5. 1990–91 Gulf War. Relevant for oil-market behavior after a regional war. It breaks down because Hormuz stayed open. Prices eased within months of the ceasefire; Kuwaiti production took years. Useful for energy stress, weak for chokepoint normality.

6. Operation Earnest Will, 1987–88. Relevant because escorted transit is not commercial normality. Insurance and routing normalized after the political end of the war, not when escorts began.

Outside-in prior for this definition, before case-specific updating: 1 week 3 percent; 1 month 6 percent; 3 months 12 percent; 6 months 22 percent; 1 year 40 percent; 18 months 55 percent. The prior already assumes that full closure cases last longer than raid cases, and that insurance lags any ceasefire.

## 5. Evidence Ledger

| Evidence | Source type | Impact on normality | Confidence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| War began 28 Feb 2026; Hormuz restricted since early March; day 217 | Encyclopedia synthesis of contemporary reporting | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| AIS-visible traffic ~4.4/day vs ~85 baseline, week to 2 Oct | AIS aggregator | Strongly negative | Medium-high | Confirmed as AIS-visible; dark traffic not fully captured |
| Islamabad MoU 17 June collapsed by early July; 60-day window expired mid-August | Legal/news reporting | Negative | High | Confirmed |
| Iran permit/toll claim; US rejects it and blockades Iranian ports | Official statements via news | Negative | High | Confirmed positions; legal effect disputed |
| Three vessels reported hit around 1 Oct; September tanker strikes and Houthi fire on Saudi targets | UK monitors, news | Strongly negative | Medium-high | Attacks reported; attribution sometimes disputed |
| Late-September indirect talks; Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day plan 26 Sept; mediators still active | Reuters | Mildly positive on process, negative on terms | High | Confirmed |
| Kpler oil/products ~13.1 mbd late September vs ~17.1 pre-war | Market data via news | Partial positive for barrels, not for normality | Medium | Estimate; conflicts with lower clearance figures |
| War-risk still about 3–10% of hull vs 0.25% pre-war | Broker commentary | Strongly negative | Medium | Confirmed range, not a single print |
| US claim of mine clearance in the traffic scheme by late August | Official claim | Mildly positive if true | Low-medium | Disputed in effect; remining risk remains |
| Brent near $102 after latest attacks; VLCC freight still war-priced | Market reporting | Negative | Medium | Price confirmed in reports; driver is inferred |
| Iranian crude still moving mainly dark to China under US blockade | Shipping analysts | Does not equal Gulf normality | Medium | Inferred from tracking |

Weight AIS, insurer behavior, and the absence of oil majors over higher “facilitated transit” counts. Facilitated or dark movements can move barrels without restoring a commercial system.

## 6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization

1. Mutual economic pain. Iran’s ports are blockaded; Gulf exporters and Asian buyers need the strait. That is the strongest reason a deal eventually exists.
2. A live mediator channel (Qatar, Pakistan, Oman) and an already-drafted June framework to return to.
3. Partial physical workarounds already proven: a southern corridor, some US-coordinated transits, and dark Iranian exports. The system is degraded, not destroyed.
4. US ability to suppress Iranian coastal radars and fast-attack craft, which raises the cost of a total closure.
5. Chinese interest in stable Gulf supply, visible in diplomatic support for a return to the June understanding.

## 7. Key Drivers Against Normalization

1. Sequencing deadlock. Iran wants the blockade, sanctions, assets, and Lebanon quiet before it reopens the strait. Washington wants the strait and nuclear concessions first. This is the main gate.
2. Active use of shipping as leverage. Attacks this week show the weapon has not been retired.
3. Insurance memory. Premiums at several percent of hull value keep oil majors and liners out even if a corridor is technically open.
4. Proxy network. Houthis have already hit Saudi targets during this war; a Hormuz deal need not bind them or Hezbollah.
5. Domestic incentives on both sides to look undefeated. A permit regime is now an Iranian institutional claim, not only a tactic.
6. Mine and remining risk, which can veto large-ship traffic after a paper ceasefire.
7. Reported US political calendar risk around the midterms. Unconfirmed, but consistent with the current standoff.

## 8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts

Probabilities that each component meets the 14-day test at the horizon. These are not independent. Transit, insurance, and force posture move together.

| Component | 1 week | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 1 year | 18 months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Major reduction in direct strikes | 15% | 25% | 40% | 55% | 70% | 75% |
| Sustained safe commercial transit at ≥70% baseline, majors included | 2% | 5% | 12% | 25% | 45% | 60% |
| Insurance near peacetime | 1% | 3% | 8% | 18% | 40% | 55% |
| Oil/LNG on ordinary commercial cover within 15% of baseline | 5% | 10% | 20% | 35% | 55% | 68% |
| Proxy restraint at pre-war baseline | 20% | 30% | 40% | 50% | 60% | 65% |
| Blockade lifted and no escort requirement | 3% | 8% | 15% | 28% | 48% | 60% |
| No new major escalation trigger in prior 14 days | 40% | 35% | 40% | 45% | 55% | 50% |

The binding constraints are transit, insurance, and removal of the dual blockade. Strike pauses are more likely than those three, and do not by themselves clear the definition.

## 9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon

Synthesis rule: the headline probability tracks the joint event, gated by commercial transit plus insurance plus a political arrangement that has survived 14 days. It is below the strike-pause odds and close to, but not identical with, the transit odds, because a traffic recovery without insurance or with a fresh escalation fails the definition.

### 1 week
- Probability: 2%
- Base-rate anchor: 3 percent. Even short Gulf shocks rarely clear insurance and routing inside seven days.
- Current-evidence adjustment: down slightly. Attacks were reported around 1 October, talks just failed a public test, and AIS is at 5 percent.
- Core rationale: a 14-day clean window cannot exist inside seven days unless the prior week was already normal. It was not.
- Main gating factor: active interdiction and insurance.
- What would raise this forecast materially: an immediate, verified mutual halt and a public lifting of both the permit regime and the port blockade, followed by oil-major fixtures. Still unlikely to meet the 14-day test inside a week.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a further ship strike or a announced US strike package.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 1 month
- Probability: 5%
- Base-rate anchor: 6 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: slightly down. Alcon-type assessments and Reuters both describe an October deal as unlikely; Iran’s condition set was rejected.
- Core rationale: mediators can produce a paper pause. Insurers and majors will not treat October as peacetime after this week’s attacks and seven months of broken truces.
- Main gating factor: sequencing. Iran will not reopen unconditionally while the blockade stands.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a signed return to the June MoU with blockade relief and a week of uneventful, insured transits by non-shadow tonnage.
- What would lower this forecast materially: another multi-ship attack wave or Houthi strikes on Saudi export facilities.
- Confidence in this estimate: High

### 3 months
- Probability: 10%
- Base-rate anchor: 12 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: slightly down. Three months covers the US post-midterm window and another winter of energy stress, both escalation risks.
- Core rationale: enough time for a fragile deal and a first mine-clearance pulse, not enough for insurers to reprice to 0.5 percent or for liners to rebuild networks. Container recovery after the June deal was already estimated in months, and that deal failed.
- Main gating factor: insurance and operator re-entry, even if a corridor opens.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a deal in October–November that holds, with AIS above 40 a day and war-risk under 1 percent by December.
- What would lower this forecast materially: remining, or a renewed air campaign after the US elections.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 6 months
- Probability: 20%
- Base-rate anchor: 22 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: small down. The failed June–August cycle shows that a memorandum can raise traffic briefly and still not stick.
- Core rationale: six months is the first horizon at which a real settlement, if reached in the next one to two months, could have produced a 14-day commercial normal. The probability of that settlement itself is well below half.
- Main gating factor: a durable bargain on blockade versus strait control, plus proxy quiet.
- What would raise this forecast materially: blockade lift, end of the permit regime, and no ship attacks for 60 days.
- What would lower this forecast materially: institutionalization of tolls, or a second collapse after a winter deal.
- Confidence in this estimate: Medium

### 1 year
- Probability: 38%
- Base-rate anchor: 40 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: small down. Nuclear issues, Lebanon, and the permit claim are unresolved; partial oil flow reduces the urgency that would otherwise force a faster bargain.
- Core rationale: a year is long enough for war-weariness and Asian buyer pressure to produce a working arrangement, and for insurance to follow 60–90 days of clean transit. It is not long enough to treat relapse as unlikely. The June precedent is a direct warning.
- Main gating factor: whether control of Hormuz has been converted from a wartime lever into a standing political claim.
- What would raise this forecast materially: a verified nuclear side-understanding and Gulf-state sign-off on a demilitarized transit scheme.
- What would lower this forecast materially: leadership change in Tehran toward a harder line, or a US decision to keep the port blockade as permanent sanctions enforcement.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low-medium

### 18 months
- Probability: 52%
- Base-rate anchor: 55 percent.
- Current-evidence adjustment: small down. Suez-style sovereignty disputes and Houthi-style persistent threats justify a fat right tail.
- Core rationale: by spring 2028 the modal path is a degraded peace or a managed corridor that finally meets the 14-day test. Just under half the probability mass still sits in renewed closure, a toll regime the market will not call normal, or proxy relapse. Above 80 percent would require assuming the political conflict ends cleanly. Nothing in the file supports that.
- Main gating factor: absence of a new escalation cycle, not the technical state of the waterway.
- What would raise this forecast materially: 90 days of majors, peacetime war-risk, and no proxy attacks on Gulf energy.
- What would lower this forecast materially: a frozen conflict with periodic ship strikes, which can last years.
- Confidence in this estimate: Low

## 10. Most Likely Path

Through October and into early winter, the standoff continues. The US blockade of Iranian ports stays. Iran keeps a selective permit regime and intermittent attacks on non-coordinated hulls. AIS-visible traffic remains a small fraction of normal, while some barrels move dark or under naval coordination. Brent stays war-sensitive. A mediator text in late 2026 is plausible; implementation that survives contact with Lebanon, mines, and the blockade is not the base case before year-end.

The modal 2027 path is a second, narrower arrangement: blockade eased against Iranian non-interference, a monitored corridor, war-risk still above peacetime but falling, and Gulf exports recovering in steps. Functional normality under the definition above is a late-2027 outcome if that arrangement holds, not a 2026 outcome. Proxies remain the most likely spoiler after a paper deal.

## 11. Faster Normalization Case

Washington accepts a sequenced pause: blockade eased first, strait opened under the June text, nuclear talks deferred but with a uranium freeze. Iran stops ship attacks for 45 days. Insurers cut hull war-risk under 1 percent. Oil majors return on Gulf-state cargoes. That path can clear the definition around the six-month horizon and would push the one-year probability toward 60 percent. It requires both sides to reverse stated conditions. Probability of this path inside six months is low, on the order of 15 percent.

## 12. Prolonged Instability Case

Talks fail, a post-election strike round hits Iranian coastal and naval targets, Iran remine and the Houthis hit Saudi or UAE energy sites, and the permit regime hardens into law. Insurers withdraw again. Traffic stays in the single digits to low tens, with only shadow and state-tolerated hulls. This can persist through 18 months and beyond, on the Tanker War plus Red Sea model. This path is less likely than a messy partial reopening, but it is the main reason the 18-month probability stays near a coin flip rather than a strong majority.

## 13. Red-Team Critique

The forecast may understate normalization if AIS at 5 percent is a tracking artifact and true commercial flows are already close to the higher late-summer facilitated counts. If those counts are real and majors are quietly returning, the insurance gate could open faster than the Red Sea analogue implies. It may overstate normalization if Iranian control of the strait has become a regime-survival symbol after Khamenei’s death and the loss of the June deal. In that world, 18-month odds belong closer to 30–35 percent. The load-bearing assumptions are that neither side wants an indefinite total closure, and that insurers will follow 60 days of clean water. Both are reasonable and both have already been wrong once in 2026.

## 14. Critical Signals to Monitor

- Daily AIS and JMIC transits, split by flag, operator, and laden status, not a single headline number.
- Hull war-risk quotes from Marsh or Lloyd’s syndicates, and whether oil majors fix Gulf stems.
- Any text that lifts the US port blockade before, or only after, Iranian nuclear steps.
- UKMTO and JMIC incident reports, especially mining and attacks on non-Iranian tankers.
- Houthi attacks on Saudi or UAE energy facilities.
- Israeli strikes in Lebanon tied by Tehran to the strait.
- Ballast inbound counts. Falling ballast is an early signal that owners have stopped believing a reopening.

## 15. Final Summary Table

| Horizon | Probability | Confidence | Binding gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 week | 2% | High | Cannot satisfy a 14-day test; attacks ongoing |
| 1 month | 5% | High | Talks far apart; insurance and majors absent |
| 3 months | 10% | Medium | Deal possible, commercial system not |
| 6 months | 20% | Medium | Needs a settlement that survives the June failure mode |
| 1 year | 38% | Low-medium | Political bargain, then insurance lag |
| 18 months | 52% | Low | Relapse and proxy risk still large |

Bottom line: military pauses will arrive before commercial normality. Under a definition that requires open transit, peacetime-like insurance, ordinary export cover, proxy quiet, and no fresh blockade, the probability stays in single digits through one month, about one in five at six months, and only about even at 18 months.

title: Iran War: 1% normality in 1 week
message:
I will ground the forecast in current reporting on the 2026 Iran conflict and Hormuz disruption, then build the probability estimates from reference classes and an evidence ledger.The Persian Gulf is not functionally normal on 1 October 2026, and the gap between partial energy flows and commercial normalization is the central fact in this forecast. Oil is moving. The operating system that made Hormuz routine is not.

## 1. Forecast Question

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality after the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months from 1 October 2026.

## 2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”

Normality requires all of the following to hold together for at least 14 consecutive days, with no credible near-term trigger for reversal. A ceasefire, a lower oil price, or a convoy workaround does not qualify.

- Direct military activity. No sustained US or Israeli strikes on Iranian territory, and no Iranian ballistic, cruise-missile, or large drone salvos against US, Israeli, or Gulf-state targets. Isolated harassment below a fatal, campaign threshold can be tolerated. A pause that either side can end at will does not count.
- Proxy activity. No campaign-level Houthi, Iraqi-militia, or Hezbollah attacks on shipping or regional energy infrastructure linked to this war.
- Shipping security. Joint Maritime Information Center or UKMTO threat in the Strait of Hormuz and adjacent waters no longer Severe or Critical. No systematic mine threat in the traffic separation scheme. No enforced Iranian permit, toll, or routing regime. No recurring projectile attacks on commercial ships.
- Commercial transit. AIS-visible commercial transits sustained at or above about 70 percent of the pre-war baseline. That baseline was roughly 85 to 140 vessels a day depending on the counter. The operational bar used here is about 70 vessels a day, not a handful of escorted or dark transits.
- War-risk insurance. Additional war-risk premiums back near pre-crisis levels, under about 0.5 percent of hull value, versus the crisis range of roughly 1 to 5 percent and higher quotes. Standard P&I war cover available without crisis voyage-by-voyage pricing. Joint War Committee treatment narrowed.
- Oil and LNG continuity. Hormuz crude, products, and Qatari LNG at or above about 85 percent of pre-war flows on ordinary commercial terms. Dark-fleet passages, US Navy shuttle convoys, and Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship transfers do not count as normal export continuity.
- Energy-market stress. The structural war premium largely gone. Brent is about $100, roughly 39 percent above the February 2026 baseline near $72. Freight is no longer a dominant share of the free-on-board crude price because of war risk.
- Force posture. US naval blockade of Iranian ports ended. Routine transit no longer depends on a carrier and escort surge. Iranian coastal forces not actively interdicting non-compliant traffic.
- Escalation triggers. No unresolved major trigger — nuclear brinkmanship, a new Gulf-infrastructure campaign, or a regime-survival fight — that markets and insurers treat as imminent.

## 3. Current Situation Snapshot

The war began with US and Israeli strikes on 28 February 2026. This is roughly day 216 of the Hormuz crisis. An interim understanding around 17–18 June collapsed. The 60-day Islamabad memorandum window lapsed on 17 August without a settlement. Fighting flared again in early September. By late September, announced US strikes on Iranian territory had paused for a stretch of days, but the maritime fight had not.

Confirmed or well-corroborated as of 1 October:

- AIS-visible commercial traffic is about 5 percent of normal: roughly 4.6 vessels a day over the past week against about 85 before the crisis. hormuz.now rated the strait Restricted, threat Severe, with ships crossing under US naval coordination while Iran claims control and requires permits.
- JMIC held the threat at Severe on 27 September, citing IRGC UAV overflights, surveillance, and VHF hailing, and continued to warn of mining risk. UKMTO had described traffic about 90 percent below pre-conflict levels earlier in September. CENTCOM has said designated lanes were cleared; authorities have not declared the wider waterway mine-free.
- Energy volumes and ship counts diverge. Kpler and CNN put oil and products through Hormuz near 13.1 million barrels a day in late September, just under 80 percent of a 17.1 million barrel pre-war figure. JPMorgan has described regional crude shipments near 17.5 million barrels a day, about 98 percent of pre-war, while products lagged near 58 percent. Soufan Center notes some shipping observers put mitigation closer to 50 percent. Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship transfers have run several million barrels a day. These are workarounds.
- Brent is about $98 to $100, up roughly 39 percent from the February baseline near $72.
- Diplomacy at the UN General Assembly failed to change the structure. Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day reopening proposal, which was conditioned on lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions relief. Araghchi left New York without a deal. Both sides say talks may continue. Iranian officials say they are ready to resume war. The US blockade of Iranian ports remains in place. Iran’s parliament has moved a navigation article allowing seizure of non-compliant vessels.
- Attacks on commercial ships continued into late September, including a fatal strike on the bulk carrier Cape Dao off Musandam on 23 September, attribution disputed. A reported 14 September cruise-missile strike injuring US Marines was not in the original Defense Department count.

Disputed: exact Hormuz throughput, whether Mojtaba Khamenei is alive and in effective control, and responsibility for some recent ship attacks. Belligerent claims of “control” of the strait are treated as claims, not facts.

## 4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior

The relevant class is not “wars end.” It is “chokepoint commerce returns to unescorted, insurable routine after a state with local anti-ship capability has used that chokepoint as leverage.”

- Tanker War, 1984–1988. Relevant because Iran and Iraq attacked merchant ships for years while oil still moved at a premium. It breaks down because that war was attrition between two regional states, not a US blockade plus nuclear diplomacy. It implies multi-year disruption if the political incentive to attack ships remains, with partial adaptation in months and real normalization only after the August 1988 ceasefire plus a further lag.
- 2019 Gulf attacks and Abqaiq. Relevant as an insurance and routing shock. It breaks down because there was no open war, no blockade, and no mine campaign. Premiums and behavior normalized in weeks to a few months once attacks stopped. That is an upper bound on speed, not a base case.
- Red Sea and Houthi campaign, late 2023 into 2025. Most relevant commercial analogue. Traffic diversion and elevated war-risk pricing persisted for more than a year despite pauses, because the attacker kept capability and a political reason to use it. Full route normality lagged the reduction in threat by many months. Suggests 12 to 24 months if Iranian leverage over Hormuz is unresolved.
- Kuwait liberation and northern Gulf mines, 1991. Hormuz itself stayed open. Mine clearance and insurer comfort in mined waters took months after the February ceasefire. Useful for the clearance lag, not for the politics.
- Black Sea grain corridor, 2022–2023. Naval coordination and special insurance restored partial flows within months. Full commercial normality did not return while the war continued. Direct warning against equating escorted barrels with normality.
- June–August 2026 Islamabad window. Inside case. Oil moved faster than politics. Commitments on waivers, blockade lift, and mine clearance failed before day 60. Traffic never approached baseline. This lowers the weight on the next paper deal.

Base-rate prior before case-specific updating, for this strict definition: 1 week 2 percent; 1 month 6 percent; 3 months 14 percent; 6 months 28 percent; 1 year 42 percent; 18 months 55 percent. The prior already assumes partial flows return long before functional normality.

## 5. Evidence Ledger

| Evidence | Source type | Direction | Confidence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AIS traffic about 5 percent of baseline, threat Severe | Vessel tracker, JMIC/UKMTO reporting | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Oil and products near 13 mb/d through Hormuz; regional crude estimates up to about 98 percent | Kpler, CNN, JPMorgan, officials | Supports partial adaptation, not normality | Medium | Disputed on level |
| Ship-to-ship transfers in Gulf of Oman at multi-mb/d rates | Kpler and specialist trackers | Against normality; shows workaround | Medium | Reported |
| US blockade of Iranian ports still enforced | CENTCOM, Treasury, UANI tracking | Against | High | Confirmed |
| June MoU lapsed 17 August; mine-clearance and blockade commitments not completed | Trade and policy reporting | Against near-term political fix | Medium-high | Confirmed |
| UNGA talks failed; Trump rejected seven-day plan; Iran says ready to resume war | Soufan, Al Jazeera, official statements | Against | High | Confirmed |
| JMIC Severe on 27 September; mine warning continues after lane clearance claim | JMIC, gCaptain, CENTCOM | Against | High | Confirmed, scope of clearance disputed |
| Commercial attacks into late September, including fatal Cape Dao strike | Wire and maritime reporting | Against | Medium | Confirmed events, attribution often disputed |
| Brent near $100, about 39 percent above February baseline | Market data | Against market normality | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk cover exists but at crisis premiums; earlier P&I suspensions | Marsh, IUMI, Legal500, trade press | Against | Medium | Confirmed elevated; exact current quote disputed |
| No announced ashore strikes for a stretch of late September | GlobalSecurity campaign logs | Mildly toward military pause | Medium | Reported |
| Both sides signal further talks; Qatar mediating | Soufan, official remarks | Mildly toward | Medium | Confirmed contact, not terms |
| Iran currency near 2.5 million rials per dollar; oil exports constrained by blockade | Treasury claims, Soufan | Mixed: pressure toward a deal, or toward escalation | Medium | Partially confirmed |
| US officials shift demands toward nuclear limits | Soufan | Against near-term deal | Medium | Reported official stance |

## 6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization

1. Partial physical recovery already exists. Escorted and dark flows near a large share of pre-war crude reduce the economic cost of waiting and show the route is not physically sealed.
2. Both sides are still talking, with Qatar in the channel. A transactional reopening-for-blockade deal remains available in principle.
3. Iranian economic stress is real. Currency collapse and blocked crude exports create a regime incentive to trade shipping pressure for relief.
4. US political calendar. Midterms in November 2026 raise the cost of a fresh price spike, which can favor a limited deal even without a nuclear settlement.
5. Mine-lane clearance, if it holds, removes one technical barrier. Insurers reprice faster once attacks stop than governments settle underlying disputes.
6. Gulf producers have adapted with bypass pipeline use, ship-to-ship transfers, and naval coordination, which lowers the chance of an indefinite total closure.

## 7. Key Drivers Against Normalization

1. Bargaining deadlock. Iran wants the blockade lifted before nuclear concessions. Washington, believing flows are restored, is raising the nuclear price. Each side thinks it is winning.
2. Iran still has a working coercive theory. Late-September attacks show it can still impose cost in the strait. That incentive lasts as long as the blockade lasts.
3. Insurance and flag behavior lag politics. Even after a deal, premiums, crew refusal, and schedule repair take weeks to months. The June window already demonstrated this.
4. Residual mine and projectile risk. Lane clearance is not a mine-free strait. JMIC still rates the threat Severe.
5. Proxy and horizontal risk. Iranian officials have already pointed at a Red Sea front if strikes resume.
6. Workaround success can delay a settlement. If Washington believes 80 to 95 percent of energy is moving, the urgency to pay Iran’s price falls.
7. Leadership and succession opacity in Tehran raises the chance of hardline vetoes over any compromise.

Ranked: political sequencing and Iranian retention of anti-ship capability dominate. Mines, insurance, and schedules are lags, not the root cause.

## 8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts

Probabilities that each component is in the normal state by the horizon. These are not independent. Insurance, transit, and export normality are downstream of attacks and the blockade.

| Component | 1 week | 1 month | 3 months | 6 months | 1 year | 18 months |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Major reduction in direct strikes | 35% | 45% | 55% | 62% | 70% | 74% |
| Sustained safe unescorted commercial transit | 1% | 4% | 12% | 22% | 38% | 50% |
| Insurance near pre-crisis | 1% | 3% | 10% | 20% | 36% | 48% |
| Oil and LNG on normal commercial terms | 2% | 6% | 15% | 28% | 45% | 58% |
| Proxy restraint at campaign level | 40% | 42% | 48% | 55% | 62% | 66% |
| Force drawdown, blockade ended, escorts not required | 2% | 5% | 14% | 24% | 40% | 52% |
| No new major escalation trigger in the period | 55% | 40% | 35% | 38% | 42% | 45% |

The binding constraints are unescorted transit, insurance, and force posture. Strike pauses are already more common than commercial normality and will not pull the joint outcome up.

## 9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon
