Probability of this path materializing is low but non-zero (~15–20% chance it becomes the dominant trajectory within 6 months).

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Political gap persists; intermittent strikes and vessel incidents continue; Houthi or other proxies keep residual capacity; insurance remains prohibitive; Gulf states hedge further; energy markets permanently reprice a higher Hormuz risk. Functional normality delayed beyond 18 months. This path is consistent with the Tanker War and multi-year Red Sea experience.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Possible over-estimation of longer-horizon probabilities: commercial and insurance normalization may prove stickier than historical analogies if the political conflict remains unresolved and Iran retains denial options. The operational definition is deliberately demanding; markets and shipowners may accept a “new normal” of higher risk that still fails the criteria. Possible under-estimation of near-to-medium term: mutual economic pain and US political incentives could produce a faster pause than base rates imply. Load-bearing assumptions include continued Iranian regime coherence and absence of a sudden, decisive military or political shock.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily AIS / PortWatch / UKMTO transit counts and incident reports.
- War-risk premium quotes from major brokers.
- Actual (not claimed) crude + LNG export volumes from Gulf terminals and East-West pipeline status.
- Content and durability of any new mediated proposal vs. kinetic actions.
- Houthi launch tempo and Saudi interception rates.
- US force posture statements and any change in blockade enforcement.
- Post-midterm US policy signals on Iran.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Main Gating Factor                  |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|-------------------------------------|
| 1 Week    | 2%         | High        | Insurance + sustained safe transit |
| 1 Month   | 8%         | Medium-High | Credible multi-week safety record  |
| 3 Months  | 22%        | Medium      | Durable political settlement       |
| 6 Months  | 38%        | Medium      | Insurance re-entry + no attacks    |
| 1 Year    | 52%        | Medium      | Political or military equilibrium  |
| 18 Months | 62%        | Medium-Low  | Cumulative adaptation + equilibrium|

The forecast remains calibrated to the demanding multi-domain definition. Near-term probabilities are near floor levels because commercial and insurance systems do not reset on political declarations. Longer horizons incorporate base-rate recovery tempered by the persistent political and proxy obstacles visible in current evidence.

title: Gulf normality odds hold steady
message:
**1. Forecast Question**  
Probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (from 26 September 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
All of the following must hold simultaneously for a continuous period of at least 14 days (to distinguish from temporary pauses):

- Direct military activity: No US/coalition strikes on Iranian territory or Iranian ballistic-missile/drone strikes on US/Gulf-host-state bases or territory.  
- Proxy activity: No sustained Houthi or other Iranian-aligned attacks that close or significantly disrupt Bab al-Mandeb / Red Sea commercial traffic or Saudi energy infrastructure.  
- Shipping security (Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters): No successful attacks on commercial vessels; clear, internationally recognized transit corridors free of mines or active interdiction; UKMTO/IMO advisories no longer listing the area as high-risk for kinetic attack.  
- Commercial transit levels: Daily commodity-vessel transits ≥70% of pre-war baseline (~85–90 of the ~125 large commercial vessels/day).  
- War-risk insurance: Additional war-risk premiums ≤0.5% of hull value (pre-war ~0.125–0.25%; current multiples still elevated).  
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Persian Gulf oil exports ≥18 mb/d (pre-war ~20 mb/d through Hormuz) and Qatar/UAE LNG loadings near pre-war rates, without reliance on ship-to-ship transfers as the primary workaround.  
- Energy market stress: Brent crude < $85/bbl on a sustained basis and realized 30-day volatility below the levels observed during the active phases of the war.  
- Force posture: Material drawdown or repositioning of major US naval/air assets from surge levels in the Gulf; Iranian coastal anti-shipping systems not actively reconstituted at pre-July 2026 threat density.  
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No new Iranian nuclear breakout steps, no major third-party intervention that reopens kinetic exchange, and no collapse of any interim political understanding that restarts the tanker war.

A temporary ceasefire, lower oil prices alone, or a battlefield pause without commercial/insurance recovery does **not** qualify.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 26 September 2026)**  
War day ~211. Conflict opened 28 February 2026. A June 17 MOU collapsed by early July; kinetic exchanges resumed. As of late September: multi-week pause in announced US strikes ashore and Iranian ballistic salvos against host states; limited maritime incidents continue. Hormuz commodity transits in single digits to low teens (9–18 range recently; 10-day average ~18) versus ~125 pre-war. Ship-to-ship transfers in Gulf of Oman at capacity. Saudi East-West pipeline previously disrupted and usage constrained. Brent ~$104–105/bbl. War-risk premiums remain multiples of pre-war levels (reports of 3–5%+ of hull value at peaks; still elevated). Diplomatic contacts (Witkoff/Kushner–Araghchi, Qatari mediation, Iranian 7-day road-map proposals) ongoing but no agreement; Gulf states divided on concessions. Houthi control of Yemen Red Sea coastline expands the second chokepoint. US blockade of Iranian ports continues; Iranian conditions for reopening include full blockade lift, asset release, and acceptance of Iran-Oman corridor arrangements.<grok:render card_id="2b59db" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">40</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**  
Relevant classes (with breakdowns):

1. **1980–88 Iran–Iraq Tanker War / Operation Earnest Will**: Multi-year intermittent attacks on shipping; US reflagging and escorts; commercial traffic never fully normalized until ceasefire. Partial stabilization after major US intervention took months to years; full commercial recovery lagged military pause. Suggests 6–18+ months for functional normality after major escalation ends.  
2. **2019 Gulf tanker attacks / Iran–US near-war**: Short, high-intensity interdiction period; insurance spiked; traffic recovered within weeks–months once kinetic risk subsided and diplomatic de-escalation occurred. Faster recovery possible when political will exists and damage is limited.  
3. **Houthi Red Sea campaign 2023–25**: Sustained proxy disruption of a chokepoint; traffic diversion (Cape of Good Hope); insurance elevated for >12–18 months; partial recovery only after sustained kinetic pressure + diplomacy, still incomplete. Shows proxy persistence can extend commercial abnormality well beyond kinetic peaks.  
4. **Suez Canal closures / major chokepoint disruptions (1956, 1967–75)**: Full or near-full closures lasted months to years; recovery of traffic and insurance lagged formal reopenings by weeks–months due to risk perception.  
5. **Post-ceasefire Gulf or Levant conflicts with maritime dimensions** (e.g., 2006 Lebanon, earlier Iran proxy cycles): Military pauses often preceded commercial normalization by 1–6 months; insurance and force posture lagged further.

**Base-rate prior (pre-current-evidence adjustment)**:  
- 1 week: <5%  
- 1 month: 8–12%  
- 3 months: 20–30%  
- 6 months: 35–45%  
- 1 year: 50–60%  
- 18 months: 60–70%  

These reflect that commercial/insurance recovery historically trails military pauses, and prolonged proxy or unresolved political disputes keep risk elevated.

**5. Evidence Ledger**  

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| Hormuz transits single-digit to low teens vs ~125 pre-war | Ship-tracking (Kpler/Reuters) | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| Multi-week pause in major land strikes/salvos | CENTCOM/Iran reporting, GlobalSecurity daily | Mildly positive (kinetic) | Medium-High | Confirmed for announced actions |
| Ongoing limited vessel attacks / high insurance multiples | UKMTO, insurance commentary, Reuters | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| Diplomatic contacts + Iranian road-map proposals; no deal | JINSA, Reuters, WSJ, GlobalSecurity | Mildly positive (process) | Medium | Confirmed contacts; outcome disputed |
| Houthi Red Sea coastline control expansion | Multiple reporting | Strongly negative (second chokepoint) | High | Confirmed |
| Brent ~$104–105; STS transfers at capacity | Market data, Reuters | Negative (stress) | High | Confirmed |
| Gulf states (esp. Saudi/UAE) resistance to concessions | WSJ/JINSA | Negative (political) | Medium | Reporting |
| US midterm timing / domestic incentives for de-escalation | Analysis + Trump statements | Mildly positive for short-term pause | Medium | Inferred |
| Iranian internal economic stress + nuclear file unresolved | Multiple | Mixed (pressure for deal vs hard-line) | Medium | Confirmed stress; nuclear disputed |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization** (ranked)  
1. Mutual political incentive for a transactional deal (US midterms; Iranian economic pain).  
2. Sustained kinetic pause reducing immediate risk perception.  
3. Possible limited Iran–Oman corridor arrangement accepted by enough commercial actors.  
4. Gradual insurance capacity return once incidents fall.  
5. Asian buyer pressure for restored volumes.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization** (ranked)  
1. Unresolved political fundamentals (blockade, assets, corridor sovereignty, nuclear).  
2. Insurance and risk-perception lag (historical pattern).  
3. Proxy (Houthi) autonomy and Red Sea expansion.  
4. Gulf Arab opposition to deals that legitimize Iranian control claims.  
5. Ability of either side to reconstitute anti-shipping capability quickly.  
6. Second-order market effects (STS, pipeline risk, volatility) that sustain elevated premiums.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts** (approximate probabilities of each component being largely satisfied)  

| Component | 1 wk | 1 mo | 3 mo | 6 mo | 1 yr | 18 mo |
|-----------|------|------|------|------|------|-------|
| Major reduction in direct strikes | 70% | 55% | 50% | 55% | 60% | 65% |
| Sustained safe commercial transit Hormuz | <5% | 10% | 25% | 40% | 55% | 65% |
| Meaningful insurance normalization | <5% | 8% | 20% | 35% | 50% | 60% |
| Oil/LNG export recovery | <5% | 12% | 30% | 45% | 60% | 70% |
| Proxy restraint | 20% | 25% | 30% | 40% | 50% | 55% |
| Force drawdown | <5% | 10% | 20% | 35% | 50% | 60% |
| No new major escalation trigger | 60% | 45% | 40% | 45% | 50% | 55% |

Gating factors are safe transit + insurance + export recovery; kinetic pause alone is insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 2%  
- Base-rate anchor: <5%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly lower (transits and insurance still extreme; no deal).  
- Core rationale: Operational definition requires multi-domain recovery; none of the commercial/insurance thresholds are near.  
- Main gating factor: Commercial transit and insurance.  
- What would raise: Sudden verified full corridor opening + insurance capacity announcement.  
- What would lower: New vessel attack or strike resumption.  
- Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: 8–12%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slightly lower (diplomacy present but Gulf resistance and Houthi factor).  
- Core rationale: Even an aggressive deal would leave insurance and risk perception lagging; transit recovery historically slow.  
- Main gating factor: Verified safe transit + initial insurance easing.  
- What would raise: Signed interim arrangement + 2+ weeks zero incidents + measurable transit jump.  
- What would lower: Breakdown of talks or proxy escalation.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: 20–30%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly lower (proxy second front + political gaps).  
- Core rationale: Possible transactional deal around midterms, but commercial/insurance normalization and proxy restraint remain incomplete.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance + sustained transit without incident.  
- What would raise: Durable ceasefire + observable force posture change + insurance rates falling toward 1%.  
- What would lower: Resumed tanker war or Red Sea closure.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: 35–45%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
- Core rationale: Time allows for deal + gradual commercial recovery if kinetic risk stays low; historical lag still material.  
- Main gating factor: Political settlement durability + proxy behavior.  
- What would raise: Verified multi-month zero-incident period + export volumes recovering.  
- What would lower: New nuclear steps or major proxy campaign.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: 50–60%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slightly lower (second chokepoint risk).  
- Core rationale: Longer horizon allows political resolution or mutual exhaustion; still material chance of prolonged low-level disruption.  
- Main gating factor: Absence of re-escalation + insurance market reset.  
- What would raise: Formal political understanding + sustained high transit volumes.  
- What would lower: Entrenched dual-chokepoint contest or sanctions spiral.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 62%  
- Base-rate anchor: 60–70%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly lower.  
- Core rationale: Most historical chokepoint disruptions eventually normalize, but residual proxy and political issues keep probability well below certainty.  
- Main gating factor: Structural political settlement vs frozen conflict.  
- What would raise: Comprehensive deal including nuclear/proxy elements.  
- What would lower: Regime instability or renewed great-power proxy contest.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low (long horizon)

**10. Most Likely Path**  
Continued low-level maritime friction and elevated insurance through late 2026; possible limited transactional arrangement around or after US midterms that restores partial transit (40–60% of pre-war) by early–mid 2027; full functional normality (per definition) more likely only in H2 2027 or later if proxy and political issues are managed. Oil prices ease gradually but volatility remains elevated until insurance normalizes.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**  
Decisive US–Iran understanding that includes blockade lift, corridor rules acceptable to commercial operators, and credible proxy restraint signals. Transit jumps within weeks; insurers rapidly expand capacity. Probability of this path ~15–20% by 6 months.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**  
Talks fail; intermittent attacks resume; Houthi Red Sea control hardens; Gulf states harden against any Iranian legitimization of control claims. Dual-chokepoint disruption persists into 2027–28. Probability of this path ~30–35% at 18-month horizon.

**13. Red-Team Critique**  
Possible over-estimation of normalization: Insurance and risk-perception lags have been deeper and longer in recent chokepoint cases than pure military timelines suggest; Houthi autonomy may be higher than modeled; Gulf Arab veto power on deals may be stronger.  
Possible under-estimation: Mutual economic pain + US domestic calendar could produce a faster transactional deal than reference classes imply; Asian demand pressure could force commercial actors to accept higher residual risk faster than expected.  
Load-bearing assumptions: Kinetic pause remains fragile; political fundamentals are not easily bridged; insurance reacts with multi-month lag.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**  
- Daily Hormuz transit counts and AIS patterns (Kpler/UKMTO).  
- War-risk premium quotes from major brokers.  
- Any formal corridor agreement text and commercial uptake.  
- Houthi Red Sea incident rate and Bab al-Mandeb transit data.  
- Brent term structure and realized volatility.  
- Announced force posture changes or new strike packages.  
- Content of any next US–Iran or GCC–Iran meeting.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Main Gating Factor              |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|---------------------------------|
| 1 Week    | 2%          | High         | Transit + insurance             |
| 1 Month   | 8%          | Medium-High  | Safe transit + initial insurance|
| 3 Months  | 22%         | Medium       | Insurance + sustained transit   |
| 6 Months  | 38%         | Medium       | Political durability + proxies  |
| 1 Year    | 52%         | Medium       | Re-escalation absence + insurance reset |
| 18 Months | 62%         | Medium-Low   | Structural settlement vs frozen conflict |

The forecast remains deliberately conservative on short horizons because the operational definition is demanding and historical commercial recovery consistently lags military pauses. Longer-horizon probabilities rise with time for political resolution but stay well below levels that would imply high confidence in full multi-domain normality.

title: Gulf normality forecast updated
message:
**1. Forecast Question**  
Probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War (onset ~28 February 2026) by horizons of 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months from 25 September 2026.

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
All of the following must hold concurrently and sustainably (not a temporary pause or partial recovery):

- Direct military activity: No sustained direct strikes by major belligerents (US/coalition/Israel vs. Iran) on each other’s territory, forces, or critical infrastructure in/around the Gulf for a sustained period; no active large-scale maritime interdiction campaign by either side targeting the other’s commercial or military assets as primary policy.
- Proxy activity: Material reduction in proxy attacks (Houthis and others) on commercial shipping, energy infrastructure, or Gulf state assets linked to the main conflict; no sustained proxy campaign that keeps insurance or routing elevated.
- Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters: AIS-visible commercial transit volumes recovering to ≥70–80% of pre-war baseline (~85–125 large commercial vessels/day depending on source); absence of repeated vessel strikes, mining threats, or enforced alternate corridors that force dark sailing or major diversions; JMIC or equivalent threat rating not at “Severe.”
- Commercial transit levels: Sustained recovery in energy and non-energy cargo movements through Hormuz without systemic backlog of hundreds of vessels or widespread carrier suspensions/reroutes via Cape.
- War-risk insurance conditions: Hull war-risk premiums for Hormuz transits returning to ≤0.5–1% of hull value (or clear multi-week trend toward pre-war ~0.1–0.25% levels) with broad market capacity and removal or narrowing of Joint War Committee listed-area designations; cargo war-risk not remaining prohibitively elevated.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf (including Saudi, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Iraq, and residual Iranian) seaborne oil/LNG exports recovering toward pre-war volumes without reliance on high-risk escorted or shadow fleets as the dominant mode; no sustained pipeline or terminal outages that keep effective export capacity materially impaired.
- Energy market stress and volatility: Brent (and related benchmarks) no longer carrying a large persistent Gulf/Hormuz risk premium relative to fundamentals; reduced day-to-day volatility driven by daily transit counts or attack reports; physical differentials and freight rates normalizing.
- Force posture of major actors: No major new forward deployments or escalatory force movements that signal imminent large-scale resumption; observable drawdown or stabilization of US/coalition maritime presence from peak wartime levels and Iranian coastal/anti-access posture from peak disruption mode.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No new nuclear threshold events, major third-party interventions, or irreversible territorial/control claims over the strait that would reset commercial risk pricing.

A temporary ceasefire, partial reopening under escort, lower oil prices from demand destruction or non-Gulf supply, or a battlefield pause without commercial normalization does **not** meet the definition.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of ~25 September 2026, ~Day 209–210)**  
War began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran ~28 February 2026. Multiple ceasefires/MOUs (notably April and the June Islamabad MOU) collapsed. Direct strikes on Iranian territory have been paused for multiple consecutive operational periods (mid-to-late September reports of 15+ days without Iranian ballistic launches at host states and longer without certain drone attacks), but the US naval blockade/interception campaign continues, Iranian conditions for reopening remain unmet, and sporadic vessel incidents persist.<grok:render card_id="20b13e" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">4</argument></grok:render>

Hormuz commercial transits remain severely depressed: recent Kpler/Reuters figures show single-digit to low-teen daily AIS-visible commodity vessel transits (e.g., 9 on 24 September, 10-day averages ~15–18) versus pre-war ~85–125. Hundreds of vessels remain delayed or holding; dark sailing continues. US claims of higher oil flow percentages exist but are not fully reconciled to independent transit datasets.<grok:render card_id="ba0bd1" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">45</argument></grok:render>

War-risk insurance remains elevated (reports ranging ~1.5% to ~5% of hull value for exposed voyages versus pre-war ~0.1–0.25%; multiples of 15x or higher still cited). Claims from vessel casualties are substantial (~$1.5–2bn range reported).<grok:render card_id="241783" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">55</argument></grok:render>

Brent has traded in the high $90s to ~$106 range recently, with persistent risk premium and volatility tied to diplomacy and attack reports. Houthi activity and pipeline/infrastructure strikes have complicated alternative routes. Diplomatic activity is elevated (Iranian written road map, deadlines of days, UNGA exchanges, mediator contacts), but core gaps (blockade, nuclear file, sequencing of reopening) remain. Proxy and secondary fronts (Yemen/Red Sea) are active.<grok:render card_id="42331a" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">65</argument></grok:render>

Evidence base is mixed: high-frequency shipping and price data are relatively hard; attribution of some vessel attacks and exact flow recovery percentages contain disputes between official claims and independent trackers.

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**  
Relevant classes (with caveats):

- **Tanker War (Iran-Iraq, 1980s, especially 1984–88 peak)**: Prolonged attacks on shipping in the Gulf/Hormuz approaches. Commercial traffic adapted (escorts, flags of convenience, higher premiums) but never fully normalized until the broader war ended. Partial adaptation occurred within months; functional commercial normality required years and the 1988 ceasefire. Breaks down because it was a bilateral conventional war without today’s precision weapons, globalized insurance markets, or LNG dependence.
- **2019 Gulf tanker attacks + Abqaiq/Khurais (Iran-linked)**: Short, sharp disruptions. Shipping and insurance normalized within weeks to a few months once attacks stopped and deterrence held. Suggests rapid partial recovery possible if kinetic activity ceases cleanly. Breaks down: limited scale, no sustained blockade or multi-month war.
- **Red Sea/Houthi campaign (2023–ongoing, intensified 2024–25)**: Sustained proxy attacks on shipping. Major carriers rerouted for many months; insurance elevated; partial traffic recovery only with sustained naval presence and reduced attack success. Full commercial normality still incomplete years later in some metrics. Highly relevant for proxy/insurance lag; differs in scale (Hormuz is higher-value energy artery) and state involvement.
- **Suez closures (1956, 1967–75)**: Full closures lasted months to years; traffic recovered post-reopening but with permanent route diversification and political residual risk. Suggests multi-month lag even after political resolution.
- **Post-Gulf War I (1991) and limited Iran-Israel exchanges (e.g., 2024)**: Relatively rapid shipping/energy market recovery once major combat ended, but residual insurance and posture effects lingered. Limited by lower duration/intensity than current case.
- **Broader chokepoint disruptions (e.g., Black Sea grain after 2022)**: Partial corridors and insurance workarounds within months; full pre-disruption normality often took 1–2+ years or never fully returned under continued risk.

Base-rate prior (before case-specific updating; approximate probabilities of meeting a demanding multi-domain normality standard):  
- 1 week: <5%  
- 1 month: 5–15%  
- 3 months: 15–30%  
- 6 months: 25–45%  
- 1 year: 40–60%  
- 18 months: 50–70%  

These reflect historical lags between kinetic pauses and commercial/insurance normalization, plus the frequency of incomplete or reversed stabilizations in Gulf/proxy cases.

**5. Evidence Ledger** (selected high-signal items)

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| Extremely low AIS-visible Hormuz transits (single digits–low teens vs. 85–125 pre-war) | Ship-tracking (Kpler, Reuters, others) | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Elevated war-risk premiums (multiples of pre-war; ~1.5–5% hull still reported) | Broker/insurer reporting, market summaries | Strongly against | Medium-High | Confirmed range; exact quotes vary |
| Recent vessel incidents (e.g., strikes/casualties in Sept) | UKMTO, media, official | Against | Medium | Confirmed incidents; attribution sometimes disputed |
| Prolonged pause in major Iranian ballistic/drone salvos at host states | Military reporting, CENTCOM silence patterns | Toward (military component) | Medium | Observed; sustainability unproven |
| Ongoing US blockade/interception + Iranian conditions/road map with short deadlines | Official statements, mediator reporting | Mixed (diplomacy up; gaps large) | Medium | Confirmed proposals; acceptance unclear |
| Houthi/pipeline activity complicating alternatives | Regional reporting | Against | Medium-High | Confirmed |
| Oil prices ~$100–106 with risk premium | Market data | Against (stress remains) | High | Confirmed |
| Claims of higher assisted oil flows vs. low independent transit counts | US officials vs. trackers | Mixed/disputed | Medium | Disputed interpretation |
| Large vessel backlog / carrier suspensions | IMO, carrier advisories, trackers | Against | High | Confirmed |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**  
Ranked roughly by importance: (1) Durable political/military settlement or sustained de facto pause that removes the blockade and Iranian interdiction threat; (2) Sustained absence of vessel attacks allowing insurance repricing and carrier return; (3) Demonstrated safe transit volume recovery that rebuilds commercial confidence; (4) Gulf state mediation and hedging that reduces secondary fronts; (5) Market adaptation (alternative routes, non-Gulf supply) that lowers the cost of residual risk.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**  
Ranked: (1) Core unresolved issues (blockade sequencing, nuclear file, Iranian control claims over the strait); (2) Insurance and commercial lag even after kinetic pauses (historical pattern); (3) Proxy autonomy and secondary fronts (Houthis, others); (4) Mutual incentives to maintain pressure (Iran leverage via strait; US/coalition sanctions/blockade leverage); (5) Residual force posture and risk of miscalculation or spoilers; (6) Physical damage, backlog, and crew/owner risk aversion.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts** (approximate probabilities of meaningful progress on each component by horizon; these are building blocks, not mechanical averages)

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w ~40–50%; 1m ~55–65%; 3m ~65–75%; 6m+ higher but with relapse risk.
- Sustained safe commercial transit (volume + security): 1w <10%; 1m ~15–25%; 3m ~30–45%; 6m ~45–60%; 1y ~55–70%; 18m ~60–75%.
- Meaningful insurance normalization: lags transit security; 1w/1m very low; 3m ~20–35%; 6m ~40–55%; longer higher but sticky.
- Oil/LNG export recovery (volume + continuity): partially decoupled via alternatives but still constrained; similar lag to transit, somewhat faster for non-Iranian Gulf volumes.
- Proxy restraint: lower and more variable; meaningful sustained restraint lower probability than direct-strike pause.
- Force drawdown / no new major escalation trigger: moderate near-term (pause exists), declining certainty at longer horizons without political settlement.

Gating factors are primarily shipping security + insurance + absence of new triggers; military pause alone is insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 3%  
- Base-rate anchor: <5%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly lower; low transits, elevated insurance, active diplomacy but short deadlines and gaps.  
- Core rationale: Even a sudden deal cannot unwind backlog, insurance, and confidence in days.  
- Main gating factor: Commercial/insurance lag.  
- What would raise: Immediate verified deal + rapid transit surge + insurance capacity announcement.  
- What would lower: New vessel attacks or failed deadline leading to resumed strikes.  
- Confidence: High (near-term data dense).

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 12%  
- Base-rate anchor: 5–15%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Near base; diplomacy active but structural gaps large; military pause exists but untested.  
- Core rationale: Possible if road map accepted and held, but historical commercial lag and proxy risk remain.  
- Main gating factor: Conversion of any political pause into sustained safe transit + insurance response.  
- What would raise: Verified multi-week incident-free high-volume transit + premium compression.  
- What would lower: Breakdown of talks, renewed vessel campaign, or proxy surge.  
- Confidence: Medium-High.

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 28%  
- Base-rate anchor: 15–30%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Near/slightly above base if current pause and diplomacy continue; still constrained by insurance and proxies.  
- Core rationale: Window long enough for partial commercial recovery if kinetic activity stays low, but full multi-domain normality remains demanding.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance market response and carrier confidence after sustained safe passage.  
- What would raise: Formal settlement + Joint War Committee de-listing progress + volume recovery to 50%+.  
- What would lower: Relapse into vessel attacks or major new escalation.  
- Confidence: Medium.

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 42%  
- Base-rate anchor: 25–45%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight upward if de facto pause holds; still below 50% because of residual risk and historical incomplete recoveries.  
- Core rationale: Time allows adaptation and partial normalization, but unresolved political issues and proxy dynamics keep full functional normality below even odds.  
- Main gating factor: Durability of any settlement against spoilers and secondary fronts.  
- What would raise: Comprehensive political agreement + sustained high transit + clear insurance normalization.  
- What would lower: Prolonged stalemate with intermittent attacks or expanded proxy activity.  
- Confidence: Medium.

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 55%  
- Base-rate anchor: 40–60%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Near base; long enough for markets to adapt even under residual risk, but definition remains strict.  
- Core rationale: Cumulative pressure for settlement or durable adaptation rises; still material chance of prolonged managed instability.  
- Main gating factor: Whether a political settlement or stable deterrence equilibrium emerges.  
- What would raise: Verified durable settlement + multi-quarter commercial recovery.  
- What would lower: Entrenched new status quo of controlled disruption or major escalation.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low (longer horizon).

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 62%  
- Base-rate anchor: 50–70%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly conservative relative to upper base given severity and multi-domain definition.  
- Core rationale: Base rates favor eventual stabilization or adaptation; full “functional normality” as defined still faces residual Gulf risk and potential incomplete political resolution.  
- Main gating factor: Long-term political settlement vs. frozen conflict with elevated baseline risk.  
- What would raise: Clear end to hostilities + structural commercial recovery.  
- What would lower: Transformation into longer frozen conflict with permanent insurance/posture premium.  
- Confidence: Low-Medium.

**10. Most Likely Path**  
Continued diplomatic engagement with intermittent progress and setbacks. Military activity remains lower than peak but with residual vessel incidents and proxy actions. Gradual, uneven recovery in non-Iranian Gulf exports and some escorted or alternative-route traffic. Insurance and full commercial confidence lag. Partial normalization of volumes by 3–6 months is plausible under continued pause; full multi-domain functional normality more likely only if a durable political arrangement solidifies in the 6–18 month window. Residual elevated risk persists longer.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**  
Rapid acceptance of a sequenced deal (ceasefire + phased reopening + talks), sustained incident-free transit for weeks, insurance capacity floods back, carriers resume, and proxies stand down. Could push 3-month probability toward 45–50% and 6-month toward 60%+. Requires both sides prioritizing economic relief over leverage.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**  
Talks stall or produce only temporary pauses; intermittent vessel attacks and proxy campaigns continue; insurance stays elevated; carriers maintain heavy diversions; secondary fronts expand. Normalization probabilities compress across horizons (e.g., 1-year closer to 35–40%). Supported by mutual leverage incentives and historical proxy stickiness.

**13. Red-Team Critique**  
Possible overestimation of normalization: The definition is deliberately strict; commercial and insurance markets have shown multi-month lags even after kinetic pauses (Red Sea precedent); Iranian incentives to retain strait leverage and proxy autonomy may prevent clean resolution; US domestic/political timelines could produce pressure for incomplete deals that fail.  
Possible underestimation: Economic pain (oil, insurance, Gulf state costs, Iranian isolation) is high and rising; adaptation (pipelines, non-Gulf supply, dark fleets) already occurring; a single durable deal could unlock faster commercial recovery than base rates imply because global energy demand and Asian buyers create strong pull.  
Load-bearing assumptions: That commercial normality requires more than a military pause; that proxy restraint is harder than direct-strike restraint; that insurance responds with lag to observed security rather than announcements.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**  
- Daily/ weekly AIS-visible and estimated total Hormuz transit volumes (Kpler, MarineTraffic, PortWatch equivalents).  
- War-risk premium quotes and Joint War Committee listed-area changes.  
- Frequency and attribution of vessel incidents (UKMTO, JMIC).  
- Concrete progress or breakdown on Iranian conditions / US blockade sequencing.  
- Houthi and other proxy attack rates on shipping/energy.  
- Independent vs. official oil/LNG flow estimates out of the Gulf.  
- Force posture changes (new deployments or announced drawdowns).  
- Physical market signals (freight, differentials, backlog clearance).

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence     | Primary Rationale Summary |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|---------------------------|
| 1 Week   | 3%         | High          | Commercial/insurance lag insurmountable in days |
| 1 Month  | 12%        | Medium-High   | Possible with rapid deal, but historical lag and gaps large |
| 3 Months | 28%        | Medium        | Window for partial recovery if pause holds; full normality still hard |
| 6 Months | 42%        | Medium        | Adaptation possible; unresolved politics and proxies constrain |
| 1 Year   | 55%        | Medium-Low    | Base rates favor eventual stabilization under strict definition |
| 18 Months| 62%        | Low-Medium    | Longer adaptation window; residual risk still material |

Probabilities are calibrated to the strict operational definition and current evidence of low transits, elevated insurance, and incomplete diplomacy. They treat military pauses as necessary but far from sufficient.

title: Gulf normality odds rise to 62%
message:
**1. Forecast Question**  
Probability that the Persian Gulf returns to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War (begun ~28 February 2026), by horizons of 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (from 24 September 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
Functional normality requires simultaneous satisfaction of these observable, multi-domain thresholds for a sustained period (not a single-day snapshot or temporary pause):

- Direct military activity: No sustained US/Iran or major-party kinetic exchanges (strikes on territory, naval assets, or commercial shipping) beyond isolated incidents that are rapidly contained and do not trigger retaliation cycles. No active mining or systematic interdiction.
- Proxy activity: No significant activation or sustained attacks by Iranian-aligned proxies (Houthis, Hezbollah remnants, Iraqi militias, etc.) targeting Gulf energy infrastructure, shipping, or US/partner forces that materially disrupt operations.
- Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters: Commercial vessels transit freely on internationally recognized routes without mandatory Iranian coordination/permits, without routine projectile/drone/mine threats, and without routine US Navy escort or redirection requirements. AIS visibility and normal navigational profiles resume.
- Commercial transit levels: Daily transits of commercial vessels recover to ≥70–80% of pre-war baseline (~100–130 vessels/day range; sources vary on exact pre-war average but consistently indicate severe current collapse to single digits or low teens). Sustained multi-week averages, not spikes.
- War-risk insurance conditions: Hull war-risk premiums for Hormuz transit fall to ≤0.5–1% of hull value (vs. current elevated levels of ~5% or higher in many reports; pre-war ~0.15–0.25%). Cover widely available without special facilities or prohibitive deductibles; cargo war risk normalizes.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf crude/LNG exports via Hormuz recover to ≥80% of pre-war volumes (~20 mbpd oil equivalent range pre-war; current flows highly constrained, with Iranian exports restricted by blockade and others using escorts/STS/bypass where possible). Continuous terminal operations without major backlog or dark-fleet dominance as the primary mode.
- Energy market stress and volatility: Brent crude and related products show no persistent war-risk premium exceeding $10–15/bbl above non-Gulf fundamentals; realized volatility returns toward pre-war norms without repeated $10+ daily swings driven by Hormuz incidents.
- Force posture of major actors: Meaningful de-escalation in US/partner forward presence dedicated to Hormuz escort/blockade and Iranian coastal force posture (IRGCN small boats, anti-ship missiles, radar). No large-scale ongoing blockade or counter-blockade.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No unresolved territorial claims over strait management, no active sanctions re-imposition cycles tied to maritime control, and no credible threats of closure or toll regimes that deter commercial operators.

A temporary ceasefire, lower oil prices from demand weakness, or a battlefield pause alone does **not** meet the standard. Commercial and insurance normalization lag military pauses and are gating.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 24 September 2026)**  
War day ~208. June 2026 US-Iran MOU (Islamabad) briefly enabled partial recovery (daily transits peaked in the 40–70 range briefly; some evacuation and oil movement). It collapsed amid mutual accusations of violations, Iranian assertions of strait control, and resumed attacks. US naval blockade of Iranian ports remains active. Recent data (Windward, Kpler/PortWatch-linked, UKMTO, JMIC): daily AIS-visible/confirmed transits in single digits to low teens (e.g., ~11 on 23 Sep; ~3/day 7-day averages in some trackers; far below pre-war). Attacks on commercial vessels continue (projectile strike on cargo vessel 23 Sep causing fire/casualties; earlier September tanker exchanges). Oil flows constrained; Saudi East-West pipeline has faced disruptions; Iranian shadow-fleet/STS activity persists under pressure. Brent trading ~$100–105 range (elevated with risk premium). War-risk premiums remain multiples of pre-war levels (reports of ~5% of hull value common; claims already in the $1.5–2bn+ range). Force posture remains high; proxies intermittently active. No durable transit settlement. Evidence base is solid on maritime metrics from multiple trackers but contested on exact attribution of every incident and precise export volumes (dark fleet complicates counts).<grok:render card_id="6aa6e5" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">6</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**  
Relevant classes (Gulf/chokepoint/maritime disruption/regional war):

- 1980–88 Tanker War (Iran-Iraq): Shipping continued under risk with escorts/convoys; full commercial/insurance normalization lagged formal ceasefire by many months to years. Partial functional recovery of volumes took 6–18+ months post-ceasefire amid residual mining/risk. Breaks down: bilateral conventional war, less great-power direct involvement, no modern drone/missile density.
- 2019 Gulf tanker attacks / Abqaiq-Khurais: Temporary spike in risk and premiums; shipping largely continued; normalization of insurance/risk perception within weeks to a few months after de-escalation. Breaks down: limited duration/scope, no full-scale war or blockade.
- Houthi Red Sea campaign (2023–ongoing into 2026 context): Partial diversion and elevated premiums persist for extended periods even after intensity drops; full commercial return incomplete for 12–24+ months in high-threat phases. Breaks down: asymmetric proxy, different geography (Bab el-Mandeb), less direct state-on-state naval contest.
- Post-1991 Gulf War / post-2003 Iraq maritime recovery: Commercial shipping recovered relatively quickly once major combat ended and mines cleared, but residual risk and force posture lingered. Breaks down: coalition victory and regime change dynamics differ.
- Broader chokepoint disruptions (Suez 1956/1967/2021; historical Hormuz threats): Full volume recovery typically 1–6 months after clear security restoration; insurance lags physical security by weeks to months.

Base-rate prior (pre-current-evidence adjustment, weighted toward longer maritime/insurance lags and persistent Iranian leverage incentives):  
1 week: ~2–5%  
1 month: ~8–12%  
3 months: ~20–30%  
6 months: ~35–45%  
1 year: ~50–60%  
18 months: ~60–70%  

These reflect that physical passage often resumes before commercial confidence, insurance, and export continuity fully normalize. Current case is more severe and politicized than 2019 but less total-war than 1980s.

**5. Evidence Ledger**  
(Selected high-impact items; direction relative to normalization probability.)

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|-----------|------------|--------|
| Daily commercial transits ~3–11 vs pre-war ~100+ | Vessel trackers (Windward, Kpler/PortWatch-linked, AIS) | Strong against | High | Confirmed |
| Continued projectile/drone strikes on commercial vessels (incl. 23 Sep) | UKMTO, CENTCOM, media | Strong against | High | Confirmed incidents; attribution sometimes disputed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports active; Iranian oil flows constrained | Trackers, UANI, reporting | Against | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk premiums still elevated (~5% hull value range in recent commentary; claims $1.5–2bn+) | Insurance market reports, brokers | Strong against | Medium-High | Confirmed elevated; exact quotes vary |
| June MOU collapsed; no durable transit settlement | Official statements, ISW/Critical Threats, media | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Brief June–July partial recovery then reverse | Kpler, NYT, Windward | Neutral/illustrates fragility | High | Confirmed |
| Oil prices ~$100+ with risk component | Market data | Against (stress) | High | Confirmed |
| Iranian insistence on strait management/control as strategic objective | Iranian statements, ISW analysis | Against | High | Confirmed intent |
| US facilitation of limited escorted/coordinated transits | CENTCOM/JMIC | Mild toward (keeps some flow) | High | Confirmed |
| Proxy/Houthi and pipeline disruptions intermittent | Reporting | Against | Medium | Confirmed incidents |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization** (ranked)  
1. Durable political settlement removing Iranian incentive/ability to contest Hormuz control and US incentive for blockade.  
2. Sustained absence of attacks for multiple weeks, enabling insurer and operator confidence.  
3. Clearance of residual mines/threats + verified free transit routes without permits.  
4. Economic pressure on Iran (and oil-importing states) creating mutual interest in volume recovery.  
5. Third-party mediation (Oman, Qatar, others) producing enforceable corridor rules.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization** (ranked)  
1. Iranian strategic view of Hormuz control as core post-war leverage and deterrent; resistance to unconditional free transit.  
2. Mutual escalation cycles (attacks on shipping ↔ retaliatory strikes on assets/tankers).  
3. High war-risk insurance and operator risk aversion that persist even after kinetic pauses.  
4. US blockade and sanctions linkage to maritime behavior.  
5. Proxy residual capacity and Gulf state security dilemmas.  
6. Political timelines (US midterms, Iranian internal consolidation) that reward posturing over settlement.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts** (approximate probabilities of each major component holding by horizon; gating noted)  

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 10%; 1m 25%; 3m 45%; 6m 60%; 1y 70%; 18m 75%.  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (no routine threats/escorts required): 1w 5%; 1m 15%; 3m 35%; 6m 50%; 1y 65%; 18m 70%. (Gating for most others.)  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤1% range, broad availability): 1w <5%; 1m 10%; 3m 25%; 6m 40%; 1y 55%; 18m 65%. (Lags physical security.)  
- Oil/LNG export recovery ≥80% pre-war via normal channels: 1w 5%; 1m 15%; 3m 30%; 6m 45%; 1y 60%; 18m 70%.  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 30%; 1m 40%; 3m 55%; 6m 65%; 1y 70%; 18m 75%.  
- Force drawdown/meaningful de-escalation of dedicated postures: 1w 5%; 1m 15%; 3m 30%; 6m 45%; 1y 55%; 18m 65%.  
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 40%; 1m 35%; 3m 40%; 6m 45%; 1y 50%; 18m 55% (cumulative risk rises then plateaus).  

Synthesis is not arithmetic average. Safe transit + insurance + export continuity are the primary commercial gating factors; military pause is necessary but insufficient. Political settlement is the highest-leverage upstream driver.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**  

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 3%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~2–5%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (active recent attacks, blockade, low transits).  
- Core rationale: No pathway exists for multi-domain normalization in days. Even a sudden ceasefire would leave insurance, operator behavior, and residual threats unresolved.  
- Main gating factor: Ongoing kinetic risk and operator/insurer confidence.  
- What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate verified mutual stand-down + public joint transit protocol + insurer rate cuts.  
- What would lower this forecast materially: Further attacks or formal re-declaration of closure.  
- Confidence in this estimate: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~8–12%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward.  
- Core rationale: Possible for kinetic pause and limited transit uptick, but insurance lag, Iranian control claims, and blockade make full functional recovery improbable. Historical chokepoint recoveries rarely compress this tightly after multi-month war.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance and commercial confidence.  
- What would raise: Durable MOU revival with enforceable free-transit language and verified demining/escort drawdown.  
- What would lower: Renewed tanker/port strikes or proxy activation.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~20–30%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward (persistent Iranian strategic interest + fragile prior MOU).  
- Core rationale: Window for mediated corridor agreement and partial volume recovery exists if both sides prioritize economics over leverage. Still requires overcoming insurance inertia and residual force posture.  
- Main gating factor: Political settlement on strait management.  
- What would raise: Successful third-party mediation producing operational free-transit rules accepted by operators/insurers.  
- What would lower: Escalation cycle or formal Iranian toll/permit regime.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~35–45%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight downward.  
- Core rationale: Time allows for fatigue, economic pressure, and technical demining/arrangements. Reference classes (Tanker War lag, Red Sea persistence) support meaningful chance of partial-to-functional recovery, but Iranian leverage incentives and US political calendar create drag.  
- Main gating factor: Whether a settlement removes the control contest.  
- What would raise: Clear mutual economic incentives + verified sustained low-incident period feeding insurer competition.  
- What would lower: Prolonged low-intensity contest or new sanctions/blockade tightening.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~50–60%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward for political stickiness.  
- Core rationale: Longer horizon favors eventual volume and insurance recovery once major combat utility declines, consistent with historical maritime disruption patterns. Full multi-domain normality still requires political resolution of Hormuz status; otherwise a managed, higher-risk equilibrium can persist.  
- Main gating factor: Enduring political settlement vs. managed instability.  
- What would raise: Regime or leadership incentives shifting decisively toward economic reintegration.  
- What would lower: Entrenched Iranian control narrative + sustained US enforcement posture.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 62%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~60–70%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward.  
- Core rationale: Base rates and economic gravity support eventual functional recovery in most comparable cases, but the operational definition remains demanding (insurance, free transit without political conditionality, export continuity). Residual risk of prolonged contest keeps the number below higher certainty.  
- Main gating factor: Whether the strategic contest over the strait is resolved or merely managed.  
- What would raise: Comprehensive deal covering nuclear, sanctions, and navigation with verification.  
- What would lower: Permanent shift to dual-corridor/permission-based regime accepted as new normal.  
- Confidence: Medium (long-horizon uncertainty rises)  

**10. Most Likely Path**  
Intermittent low-to-moderate intensity contest continues for months: limited escorted/coordinated transits, elevated but not prohibitive insurance for some operators, partial oil flows via STS/bypass/escorts, occasional attacks, and diplomatic cycles that produce temporary pauses without durable free-transit rules. Gradual volume recovery toward 40–60% of pre-war by 6–12 months if major escalation is avoided; full multi-domain normality only if a settlement removes the control incentive. Oil markets remain intermittently stressed.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**  
A new mediated agreement (Oman/Qatar/China facilitation) produces enforceable free-transit rules, rapid demining, insurer rate compression via competition/special facilities, and mutual blockade/sanctions relief. Kinetic incidents drop to near-zero for 4–6 weeks. Probability mass shifts upward most at 3–6 month horizons (could reach 40–50% at 3 months under this path).

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**  
Iran prioritizes permanent management rights; US maintains blockade and retaliatory tanker strikes; proxies remain active; insurance stays elevated; operators largely avoid or demand heavy escorts. New normal of low-double-digit daily transits and persistent risk premium. Long-horizon probabilities compress (1-year ~30–40%).

**13. Red-Team Critique**  
Possible overestimation of normalization: Underweights Iranian regime survival incentive to retain Hormuz as permanent deterrent/leverage after wartime losses; underweights how insurance markets and charterers reprice permanently after multi-month disruption and $2bn+ claims. Possible underestimation: Underweights pure economic gravity (Gulf exporters + Asian importers + tanker owners) and historical pattern that chokepoints eventually clear once combat utility falls. Load-bearing assumptions include continued Iranian capacity to contest and continued US willingness to enforce. Strongest falsifier for current view would be a verified multi-week attack-free period accompanied by insurer rate cuts and volume surge without political settlement.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**  
- Daily/weekly transit counts and corridor usage (AIS + satellite trackers).  
- UKMTO/JMIC incident frequency and severity.  
- War-risk premium quotes from major brokers (Marsh, etc.).  
- Iranian and US official language on strait administration vs. free navigation.  
- Blockade enforcement metrics and Iranian export volumes.  
- Any new mediated text on transit rules.  
- Proxy attack tempo on energy infrastructure.  
- Brent risk-premium decomposition and volatility.

**15. Final Summary Table**  

Horizon | Probability | Confidence  
---|---|---  
1 week | 3% | High  
1 month | 8% | Medium-High  
3 months | 22% | Medium  
6 months | 38% | Medium  
1 year | 52% | Medium  
18 months | 62% | Medium  

The forecast is decision-grade for risk planning: short horizons are near-certain non-normalization; medium horizons remain against; longer horizons approach even odds only because economic pressure eventually dominates in most reference classes, not because current evidence points to imminent resolution.

title: Gulf normality odds rise to 58%
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each horizon: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months (as of 23 September 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

Functional normality requires simultaneous satisfaction of all the following observable thresholds for a sustained period (minimum 14 consecutive days without material breach):

- Direct military activity: No major state-on-state missile, drone, or naval strikes between Iran and the US/Israel/coalition forces targeting bases, energy infrastructure, or naval assets in the Gulf region. Isolated intercepts or single small-boat incidents do not count as breach if contained.
- Proxy activity: No sustained proxy campaigns (Houthis, Iraqi militias, Hezbollah-linked) producing damage to commercial shipping, energy infrastructure, or GCC territory at a rate exceeding one successful strike per week on average.
- Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters: Commercial transit free of kinetic attacks, mining threats, or coercive boarding/interception requiring naval escort as the default. US/coalition facilitation of transit falls below 20% of total volume.
- Commercial transit levels: Daily two-way commercial vessel transits (AIS/satellite-tracked, IMF PortWatch or equivalent) average ≥60% of pre-war baseline (~50–55+ vessels/day vs. ~85–90 pre-war). Sustained for 14 days.
- War-risk insurance conditions: Hull war-risk premiums for standard VLCC/Suezmax Hormuz transit ≤0.5% of hull value (vs. current ~1.5% / 15× peacetime; pre-war ~0.1%). Capacity freely available without special government facilities.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Combined crude + condensate + LNG loadings from Persian Gulf terminals (ex-Iran under blockade if still in force) recover to ≥85% of pre-war volumes on a 30-day average, with no force-majeure declarations by major exporters (Saudi, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Iraq).
- Energy market stress and volatility: Brent 30-day realized volatility ≤25% annualized and no sustained risk premium >$10/bbl attributable to Hormuz closure risk (current Brent ~$95–100 range with elevated risk pricing).
- Force posture of major actors: Material reduction in surge deployments (carrier groups, additional Patriot/THAAD batteries, IRGC naval concentration) relative to peak war levels; no new permanent forward basing announced as wartime necessity.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No nuclear threshold crossing, no large-scale mining of the strait, no direct attack on a major LNG train or desalination plant, and no formal declaration of closed strait by either side.

A temporary ceasefire, partial transit recovery under escort, or oil-price decline alone does not meet the definition. Commercial and insurance normalization are gating factors; military pause is necessary but insufficient.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 22–23 September 2026)**

War day ~207. Joint US-Israeli strikes began 28 February 2026. June 17 Islamabad MOU (60-day negotiating window to end war and reopen Hormuz) expired without durable settlement. Intermittent kinetic exchanges continue: US maintains naval blockade of Iranian ports (claimed 100% effective, >110 vessels turned back); Iran asserts control over Hormuz transit and has conducted attacks on commercial vessels (recent UKMTO reports of strikes 21 September). Iranian fire against GCC host states has paused ~13–17 days; US/coalition strikes ashore paused ~15 periods. 

Transit: Independent trackers (IMF PortWatch, Kpler, AIS) show 7-day averages of ~3 vessels/day (~3–4% of pre-war ~74–85/day). CENTCOM claims higher facilitated volumes and “six-month high” flows in barrel terms via rerouting/escort, but commercial hull counts remain severely suppressed. Saudi East-West pipeline restarted at reduced rate after drone-forced closure. War-risk premiums ~15× peacetime (~1.5% hull value). Brent ~$95–100 after recent 9% multi-session decline; still carries significant risk premium. Iranian conditions for reopening include end to blockade, release of frozen funds, end to attacks on proxies, and formal US diplomatic announcement. UNGA diplomacy active (Pezeshkian address 23 September; possible sideline contact). US midterms 3 November. Proxy activity (Houthis) continues against Saudi targets and Red Sea routes. Evidence base is mixed on exact volumes (CENTCOM vs. commercial trackers); commercial and insurance data weighted more heavily for normality assessment.

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant classes (selected for Gulf/chokepoint/maritime disruption and regional war duration):

1. Iran-Iraq Tanker War (1984–1988 phase): Multi-year attacks on shipping; strait never fully closed but risk elevated for years. Stabilization required war end + years of residual risk. Suggests functional commercial normality takes 1–3+ years post-major fighting.
2. 2019 Gulf shipping crisis (tanker attacks, mine incidents): ~4–5 months of elevated risk; insurance and transit largely normalized within 3–6 months of de-escalation after US response and diplomatic signaling. Breaks down because scale was far smaller (no full war, no blockade, limited infrastructure damage).
3. Red Sea/Houthi disruption (2023–ongoing): Partial closure effects; insurance elevated for >12–18 months even after partial de-escalation; commercial avoidance persists. Suggests insurance and voluntary transit lag military pause by 6–18 months.
4. 1990–91 Gulf War energy disruption: Oil spike and regional risk resolved in months after decisive military outcome and ceasefire; commercial flows recovered rapidly once Kuwait liberated and risk premium collapsed. Breaks down because clear victory and rapid coalition dominance.
5. Post-ceasefire chokepoint recoveries (e.g., Suez 1956/1967/1973 analogs, limited mine-clearance cases): Physical reopening often weeks; full commercial/insurance confidence 3–12 months. Mine clearance alone historically 40–50+ days in contested waters.
6. Broader post-major Middle East wars (1973, 1980–88 residual, 2003 Iraq): Energy market stress often persists 6–24 months after kinetic peak due to infrastructure damage, force posture, and residual proxy risk.

Base-rate prior (pre-current-evidence, timeline probability of meeting the full operational definition):  
- 1 week: 1–3%  
- 1 month: 5–10%  
- 3 months: 15–25%  
- 6 months: 30–40%  
- 1 year: 45–55%  
- 18 months: 55–65%  

These reflect that commercial/insurance lag military pause, historical Gulf disruptions rarely normalize fully inside 6 months, and multi-year residual risk is common without decisive settlement.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| Transit ~3 vessels/day (7-day avg), ~3% baseline | IMF PortWatch / AIS trackers | Strong against | High | Confirmed |
| CENTCOM claims higher facilitated barrel flows / 1bn+ barrels assisted | US military statements | Mild toward (partial functionality) | Medium | Confirmed claims; volumes disputed vs commercial trackers |
| War-risk ~15× / ~1.5% hull | Broker / Lloyd’s-derived monitors | Strong against | High | Confirmed range |
| Recent commercial vessel strikes (21 Sep) | UKMTO | Against | High | Confirmed reports |
| Iranian 7-day reopening offer conditional on US easing blockade/pressure | Iranian official to Reuters | Conditional toward | Medium | Confirmed statement; intent/credibility disputed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports ongoing, claimed 100% effective | CENTCOM | Against (maintains leverage/conflict) | High | Confirmed |
| Pause in Iranian strikes on GCC hosts (~13–17 days) and US ashore strikes (~15 periods) | Multiple trackers / statements | Mild toward | Medium | Confirmed pause; durability unproven |
| Saudi East-West pipeline reduced restart after drone attacks | Saudi / Reuters | Mild toward (bypass capacity) | Medium | Confirmed restart; rate and durability partial |
| Brent ~$95–100 with recent decline but elevated risk premium | Market data | Neutral-mild against | High | Confirmed |
| UNGA diplomacy active; possible contact window | Official statements | Mild toward | Medium | Confirmed presence; outcomes unknown |
| Proxy (Houthi) activity vs Saudi/Red Sea continues | Multiple reports | Against | High | Confirmed |
| MOU expired without settlement; war of attrition framing | Multiple analyses / statements | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Infrastructure damage (energy facilities, possible mines) | IEA / industry estimates from earlier phases | Against (recovery lag) | Medium | Confirmed damage; current mine status inferred |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

Ranked by importance:  
1. Diplomatic breakthrough at/around UNGA producing credible, mutual de-escalation (end blockade + Iranian transit restraint).  
2. Sustained kinetic pause (>30–60 days) reducing perceived attack probability.  
3. Insurance market response to demonstrated safety (capacity return, rate compression).  
4. Clearance of any residual mines/threats and backlog clearance producing visible transit recovery.  
5. US domestic political calendar (midterms) incentivizing de-escalation if costs rise.  
6. GCC economic pressure for reopening and energy revenue restoration.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

Ranked by importance:  
1. Structural disagreement over Hormuz control, blockade, frozen assets, and proxy wars (Iran views control as strategic gain; US rejects tolls/control).  
2. Residual attack capability and demonstrated willingness (Iran asymmetric tools; US strike capacity).  
3. Insurance and shipowner risk aversion lagging any political pause (historical pattern).  
4. Proxy autonomy and activation risk (Houthis already active).  
5. Infrastructure repair timelines and force-posture inertia.  
6. Domestic hardline audiences on both sides punishing compromise.  
7. Potential for new triggers (nuclear file, major infrastructure hit, election-driven escalation).

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities of each major component reaching “normalized” threshold by horizon (independent estimates, then conditioned):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 15%, 1m 35%, 3m 55%, 6m 70%, 1y 80%, 18m 85%.  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥60% baseline, low escort): 1w 5%, 1m 15%, 3m 30%, 6m 45%, 1y 60%, 18m 70%.  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤0.5%): 1w 2%, 1m 10%, 3m 25%, 6m 40%, 1y 55%, 18m 65%.  
- Oil/LNG export recovery (≥85%): 1w 10%, 1m 25%, 3m 40%, 6m 55%, 1y 70%, 18m 80%.  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 20%, 1m 30%, 3m 45%, 6m 55%, 1y 65%, 18m 70%.  
- Force drawdown: 1w 5%, 1m 15%, 3m 30%, 6m 45%, 1y 60%, 18m 70%.  
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 70%, 1m 55%, 3m 45%, 6m 40%, 1y 35%, 18m 30% (declining as time for triggers expands).

Gating factors are transit + insurance + absence of new triggers; military pause is necessary but not sufficient. Joint probability is lower than the weakest critical component due to dependence and residual risk.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 2%  
- Base-rate anchor: 1–3%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (active recent strikes, no deal yet, transit near zero).  
- Core rationale: Even a dramatic UNGA announcement cannot clear mines, restore insurance, clear backlog, or demonstrate 14-day safety in seven days.  
- Main gating factor: Physical and commercial logistics cannot compress to one week.  
- What would raise: Immediate mutual stand-down + rapid mine-clearance declaration + emergency insurance facility.  
- What would lower: Any new strike or rejection of Iranian offer.  
- Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: 5–10%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward (attrition pattern, conditional offers only).  
- Core rationale: Possible kinetic pause and initial transit rebound if diplomacy succeeds, but insurance lag, backlog, and verification period make full definition improbable.  
- Main gating factor: Demonstrated multi-week safety + insurance response.  
- What would raise: Signed framework ending blockade + Iranian transit commitment + 3+ weeks zero attacks.  
- What would lower: Continued vessel strikes or midterms-driven escalation rhetoric.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 18%  
- Base-rate anchor: 15–25%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward (expired MOU, structural issues on control/blockade).  
- Core rationale: Window for post-midterms deal and initial recovery, but historical lag in commercial confidence and proxy risk keep probability modest.  
- Main gating factor: Durable political settlement + insurance normalization.  
- What would raise: Verifiable ceasefire + transit recovery to 40%+ sustained + rate compression.  
- What would lower: Renewed large-scale strikes or major proxy campaign.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 32%  
- Base-rate anchor: 30–40%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight downward.  
- Core rationale: Sufficient time for diplomacy, clearance, and market response if political will exists; still constrained by residual risk and historical Gulf patterns.  
- Main gating factor: Absence of new triggers + sustained commercial volumes.  
- What would raise: Clear post-election settlement and 90+ days of safe transit.  
- What would lower: Attrition continues or nuclear file re-escalates.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 48%  
- Base-rate anchor: 45–55%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
- Core rationale: Base rates and recovery timelines support roughly even odds once political settlement window and repair cycles complete; residual proxy and insurance lag prevent higher.  
- Main gating factor: Long-term political settlement durability.  
- What would raise: Formal peace framework + force posture reduction + insurance back near peacetime.  
- What would lower: Protracted low-level conflict or new regional war expansion.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 58%  
- Base-rate anchor: 55–65%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
- Core rationale: Longer horizon allows for eventual exhaustion, new leadership dynamics, or negotiated off-ramps; still well below high confidence because of structural Hormuz leverage incentives and historical multi-year residual risk.  
- Main gating factor: Enduring absence of escalation triggers and market confidence restoration.  
- What would raise: Durable regional security architecture replacing pure coercion.  
- What would lower: Entrenched Iranian control claims or repeated proxy activation.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low (long-horizon uncertainty rises)

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued low-to-medium intensity attrition through US midterms. Conditional diplomacy produces intermittent pauses and partial transit recoveries under escort, but full commercial/insurance normalization lags. Oil flows partially recover via bypasses and escorted routes; risk premium persists. Functional normality most probable in the 12–18 month window if a post-election settlement emerges; otherwise residual elevated risk continues.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Credible UNGA or post-midterms deal ends blockade, commits Iran to free transit without tolls, and produces 60+ days of zero attacks. Mine clearance accelerates, insurance capacity returns rapidly, backlog clears, and volumes reach 60%+ within 2–3 months. Probability of this path ~15–20%. Would raise short- and medium-horizon forecasts materially.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

No durable deal; Iran retains Hormuz leverage; proxies remain active; US maintains blockade and periodic strikes. Transit stays suppressed, insurance elevated, infrastructure repair delayed. Functional normality deferred beyond 18 months. Probability of this path ~30–40%. Consistent with Tanker War residual patterns.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Overestimation risk: Treating recent kinetic pauses as durable; under-weighting Iranian strategic interest in Hormuz control as wartime gain; assuming insurance markets respond linearly to political signals (they historically lag and require demonstrated loss-free periods). Underestimation risk: Under-weighting US domestic cost pressures and GCC economic urgency that could force faster compromise; possible rapid mine-clearance and escorted recovery producing de-facto commercial normality faster than pure base rates. Load-bearing assumptions: that commercial transit + insurance are true gating factors (correct per definition) and that no decisive military outcome occurs (consistent with current attrition). Strongest contrary evidence would be rapid, verified transit recovery to 50%+ with simultaneous rate collapse without a formal deal.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily/weekly AIS and PortWatch transit counts and CENTCOM facilitation share.  
- Broker-quoted war-risk rates and capacity availability.  
- Any formal US response to the Iranian 7-day offer or UNGA contact outcomes.  
- Duration of current kinetic pauses and any new vessel or infrastructure strikes.  
- Saudi/UAE/Qatar loading and force-majeure status.  
- Houthi/Red Sea activity intensity.  
- Post-midterms US policy statements and Iranian domestic signaling.  
- Mine-clearance announcements or satellite evidence of residual threats.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Key Rationale Summary |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|-----------------------|
| 1 week   | 2%         | High        | Logistics and verification impossible |
| 1 month  | 8%         | Medium-High | Possible pause; commercial lag dominates |
| 3 months | 18%        | Medium      | Diplomacy window; residual risk high |
| 6 months | 32%        | Medium      | Time for settlement + market response |
| 1 year   | 48%        | Medium      | Base-rate recovery window |
| 18 months| 58%        | Medium-Low  | Event exhaustion or architecture possible; structural risks remain |

Probabilities are internally consistent with gating components and historical lags between military pause and commercial normality. They remain decision-grade for risk, shipping, and energy planning: short-horizon risk of disruption remains very high; meaningful normalization is a 2027 story under base case.

title: Iran War: Gulf normality 62% by 18m
message:
**1. Forecast Question**  
Probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War, by horizons of 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (as of 22 September 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
Functional normality requires concurrent, observable conditions across domains for a sustained period (not a single-day snapshot or temporary pause):

- Direct military activity: No sustained reciprocal kinetic strikes by major state actors (US/coalition and Iran) on each other’s forces, bases, energy infrastructure, or territory in the Gulf theater; residual low-level incidents do not reverse trend.
- Proxy activity: Meaningful restraint by Iranian-aligned proxies (notably Houthis) such that they do not systematically close or heavily attrit alternative routes (Red Sea/Bab el-Mandeb) or strike Gulf energy nodes at scale.
- Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters: AIS-visible commercial transits recover to ≥70–80% of pre-war baseline (~100–125 large commercial vessels/day pre-February 2026); mines cleared and not routinely re-laid; attacks on commercial vessels rare and not systemic.
- Commercial transit levels: Regular, unescorted or lightly escorted traffic by major Western, Asian, and regional operators without widespread dark running or avoidance.
- War-risk insurance conditions: Hull war-risk premiums for Hormuz transits fall to ≤0.5–1% of hull value (from current elevated multiples of 15–40× peacetime ~0.1–0.25%) and capacity is broadly available without special government backstops dominating.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Combined Gulf (ex-Iran where sanctioned) crude + products + LNG flows recover to ≥80–85% of pre-war levels through Hormuz or fully equivalent secure alternatives; Iranian exports (if any) move under predictable rules rather than shadow-fleet improvisation.
- Energy market stress and volatility: Brent risk premium attributable to Gulf disruption compresses materially (current ~$100–101 vs ~$72 pre-crisis baseline implies substantial residual premium); volatility normalizes toward pre-war ranges.
- Force posture of major actors: US/coalition naval posture shifts from high-tempo blockade/escort/interdiction to routine presence; Iranian forces cease systematic interdiction or toll regimes.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No significant new mining campaigns, massed anti-ship strikes, base attacks, or nuclear-related escalations that re-freeze traffic/insurance.

A temporary ceasefire, partial escorted traffic, lower oil prices alone, or battlefield pause does not qualify. Commercial and insurance normalization lag military de-escalation and are gating.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot** (as of ~22 September 2026)  
War began ~28 February 2026 with US-Israeli strikes. A June Islamabad MOU produced a partial, fragile reopening and evacuation efforts; it collapsed amid tit-for-tat strikes in late June/July. Subsequent cycles of escalation and pauses have occurred. As of mid-to-late September: a multi-day “fire pause” on ballistic/drone attacks against host states exists (roughly 10+ days by 19 September reporting), but maritime incidents, claims of attacks on vessels, Iranian assertions of control/restricted zones/tolls, and US blockade/redirection activity continue.<grok:render card_id="513e04" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">40</argument></grok:render>

Visible commodity-vessel transits through Hormuz remain a small fraction of pre-war (single digits to low teens on many recent days vs ~100–125 baseline; some datasets show weekend totals of ~12–17). Dark running, escorts, and ship-to-ship transfers (e.g., Saudi volumes via Oman routes) partially compensate. Saudi crude movements through/near the strait have risen from August lows but remain well below pre-war. War-risk premiums remain elevated (reports of ~1.5% to ~5% of hull value, multiples of 15–40× peacetime; claims totals already $1.5–2bn+). Brent trades ~$100–101 (elevated ~40% vs ~$72 pre-crisis). Iranian economy shows severe stress; US/coalition force posture remains elevated; proxy activity (Houthis) adds pressure on Red Sea routes. No durable political settlement or recognized free-navigation regime exists. Evidence base is imperfect (conflicting transit/throughput claims between AIS, satellite, official statements).<grok:render card_id="02cc72" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">42</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**  
Relevant classes (Gulf/chokepoint/maritime disruption + limited regional wars):
