• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (active incidents, low traffic, no deal).  
• Core rationale: Zero evidence of the multi-domain package required; traffic and incidents still adverse.  
• Main gating factor: Immediate cessation of attacks + insurance restart (neither occurring).  
• What would raise: Verified multi-day zero-incident window + major insurer reinstatement announcement.  
• What would lower: New vessel strikes or pipeline attacks.  
• Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
• Probability: 8%  
• Base-rate anchor: 5–10%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight downward.  
• Core rationale: Possible temporary restraint around UNGA/midterms rhetoric, but commercial/insurance lag and control dispute remain unresolved.  
• Main gating factor: Credible transit regime agreement + insurer response.  
• What would raise: Signed interim transit protocol with monitoring + rapid traffic rebound.  
• What would lower: Renewal of tit-for-tat vessel/infrastructure attacks.  
• Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
• Probability: 22%  
• Base-rate anchor: 15–25%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight upward from diplomatic signals, still constrained by history of collapsed MOUs.  
• Core rationale: Time for negotiation windows and exhaustion effects, but historical lag and unresolved sovereignty claims over the strait keep probability modest.  
• Main gating factor: Durable (not temporary) de-escalation that insurers and charterers believe.  
• What would raise: Monitored ceasefire + volume recovery past 50% of baseline sustained.  
• What would lower: Major new infrastructure attack or Houthi expansion that re-closes workarounds.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
• Probability: 38%  
• Base-rate anchor: 30–40%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mild upward (political calendars, mutual economic pain).  
• Core rationale: Higher chance of a political settlement or enforced restraint, yet commercial normalization still requires insurer and operator confidence that historically trails military pauses.  
• Main gating factor: Insurance market and charterer behavior after any deal.  
• What would raise: Verified high transit volumes + premium collapse for ≥30 days.  
• What would lower: Breakdown of any interim deal into renewed shipping attacks.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
• Probability: 55%  
• Base-rate anchor: 45–55%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mild upward.  
• Core rationale: Cumulative exhaustion, alternative supply adaptations, and political incentives raise odds of a workable (if imperfect) status quo that meets most definition elements; residual risk remains from unresolved control claims.  
• Main gating factor: Whether any settlement produces sustained commercial confidence rather than managed instability.  
• What would raise: Formal transit agreement with third-party monitoring + sustained 70%+ volumes.  
• What would lower: Regime instability inside Iran or major US policy reversal that re-escalates.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
• Probability: 65%  
• Base-rate anchor: 55–65%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mild upward.  
• Core rationale: Longer horizon allows structural adaptation and political change, but full multi-domain normality is still not the modal outcome while core disputes over Hormuz governance persist.  
• Main gating factor: Long-term governance arrangement for the strait and proxy restraint.  
• What would raise: Comprehensive settlement that includes energy and security tracks.  
• What would lower: Protracted low-intensity conflict that keeps insurance and volumes structurally impaired.  
• Confidence: Medium-Low (long horizon)

**10. Most Likely Path**  
Managed instability / “no war, no peace” for several more months: intermittent low-level maritime and proxy incidents, partial traffic recovery under escort or dark sailing, elevated but fluctuating oil prices, and repeated diplomatic attempts that produce temporary pauses rather than the full operational package. Gradual improvement in volumes and insurance only after a more durable political arrangement, most likely post-US midterms or after further mutual attrition.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**  
Decisive mutual restraint triggered by economic pain + political calendars, producing a monitored interim transit regime within 1–3 months that insurers rapidly price in. Traffic rebounds toward 70%+, premiums fall, and proxy activity is contained. Requires both sides to prioritize revenue and domestic politics over maximalist control claims.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**  
Unresolved dispute over Hormuz rules + residual capabilities keep the strait commercially impaired for 12–18+ months. Periodic attacks, Houthi pressure on the Red Sea, and insurance aversion maintain a structural risk premium. Gulf states hedge further; energy markets adapt via longer routes and stock management rather than full Hormuz recovery.

**13. Red-Team Critique**  
Possible overestimation of normalization: Historical chokepoint recoveries often take longer than expected once insurance and charterer confidence are damaged; current mutual claims of control create a harder coordination problem than pure tanker-war episodes. Possible underestimation: Mutual economic incentives and US political calendar could produce faster tactical de-escalation than base rates imply; adaptive workarounds (STS transfers, pipelines, dark fleets) already blunt some pressure. Load-bearing assumptions include continued Iranian capacity to threaten shipping and continued insurer risk aversion. The forecast could be wrong if a sudden comprehensive deal materializes or if one side suffers a decisive military/political collapse.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**  
- Daily AIS + satellite transit counts and incident reports (UKMTO/JMIC).  
- War-risk premium quotes and major insurer/P&I club statements.  
- Actual crude/LNG loading and export volumes from GCC terminals (vs STS workarounds).  
- Diplomatic texts or verified interim protocols on transit rules.  
- Houthi activity and Saudi pipeline status.  
- Force posture changes (blockade intensity, Iranian “prohibited zone” enforcement).  
- Oil price risk premia relative to non-Gulf benchmarks.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Key Constraint                  |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|---------------------------------|
| 1 week    | 3%         | High        | Active incidents + zero deal   |
| 1 month   | 8%         | Medium-High | Insurance + control dispute    |
| 3 months  | 22%        | Medium      | Durable vs temporary restraint |
| 6 months  | 38%        | Medium      | Commercial confidence lag      |
| 1 year    | 55%        | Medium      | Governance of the strait       |
| 18 months | 65%        | Medium-Low  | Structural political settlement|

Probabilities are calibrated to the demanding multi-domain definition and remain modest at short horizons because commercial and insurance recovery historically trails military pauses. Longer horizons incorporate exhaustion and adaptation but stay below high certainty given unresolved core disputes.

title: Iran War: 3% 1-week normality
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by the horizons of 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (from 17 September 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

“Return to functional normality” requires simultaneous satisfaction of all of the following observable conditions for a sustained period (not a single-day snapshot or temporary pause):

- Direct military activity: No sustained US–Iran or coalition–Iran kinetic exchanges (strikes on military targets, coastal infrastructure, or vessels) at a rate exceeding sporadic, isolated incidents that are contained without reciprocal escalation.
- Proxy activity: Material restraint by Iran-aligned proxies (Houthis, Iraqi militias, Hezbollah remnants) such that attacks on Gulf shipping, energy infrastructure, or partner states do not produce new closures or major insurance spikes.
- Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters: Free, unrestricted commercial transit without requirement for Iranian permits/tolls, mandatory IRGC coordination, or exclusive reliance on Iranian-controlled northern routes; no active mining, systematic drone/missile attacks on merchant vessels, or effective exclusion zones that force dark transits or escorts as the dominant mode.
- Commercial transit levels: Daily two-way vessel transits averaging ≥70–80% of pre-war baseline (~85 vessels/day per IMF PortWatch/Kpler-type trackers) for at least 14 consecutive days, with a representative mix of tankers, bulk, and container vessels from diverse flags (not dominated by Iranian/Chinese/shadow-fleet traffic).
- War-risk insurance conditions: Hull war-risk premiums for Hormuz transit at ≤2–3× pre-war baseline (pre-war ~0.1–0.25% of hull value) and readily available from major underwriters without mass cancellations or capacity rationing; cargo war-risk cover similarly normalized.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf producers (Saudi, UAE, Kuwait, Iraq, Qatar) exporting at ≥85–90% of pre-war volumes via Hormuz or viable bypasses without sustained force majeure; Iranian exports no longer subject to active US naval blockade that prevents meaningful loadings from reaching buyers.
- Energy market stress and volatility: Brent crude no longer reflecting a persistent Hormuz risk premium that keeps prices structurally elevated and volatile solely due to chokepoint insecurity (distinct from broader macro factors); no repeated spikes triggered by single transit incidents.
- Force posture of major actors: Material drawdown or stabilization of elevated US/coalition naval and air presence in the Gulf/Hormuz approaches to levels consistent with routine presence rather than active blockade/escort operations; Iranian coastal forces not in continuous high-alert interdiction posture.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No new leadership assassinations, large-scale attacks on energy terminals/pipelines, formal re-declaration of closure, or introduction of new toll/permit regimes that reset commercial confidence.

A temporary ceasefire, partial traffic recovery under escort, lower oil prices from demand destruction, or battlefield pause alone does **not** meet the definition. Commercial and insurance normalization are gating factors; military de-escalation is necessary but insufficient.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 17 September 2026)**

War day ~201 (outbreak ~28 February 2026). A June 17 US–Iran MOU briefly allowed partial traffic recovery (peaks near half of pre-war in late June) before collapsing in early July with renewed Iranian attacks on shipping, US retaliatory strikes, and reimposition of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports. Traffic remains severely degraded: IMF PortWatch and Kpler-type data show single-digit daily commodity vessel transits (recent figures 3–9 vessels; ~5–9% of ~85/day pre-war baseline). War-risk premiums remain elevated (reports of 15× baseline or higher earlier peaks of 3–10% of hull value). Iranian crude exports are heavily constrained by the blockade (loadings far below pre-war ~1.7–2 mbpd; floating storage depleting). Tit-for-tat strikes continue (US on Iranian coastal/missile/drone assets and tankers; Iran/proxies on shipping, bases in Bahrain/Kuwait/Jordan, and recently Saudi East-West pipeline plus Houthi advances affecting Bab el-Mandeb). US claims of higher protected flows conflict with independent trackers. Diplomatic signals exist (Trump statements on possible end/talks; Iranian rejection of talks without conditions) but no durable agreement. Midterm elections (~7 weeks away) add political pressure. Energy markets remain stressed (Brent elevated).<grok:render card_id="ffe874" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">7</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="c1f1f7" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">38</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="0516b6" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">56</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant historical reference classes (3–6):

1. **Iran–Iraq Tanker War (1984–1988)**: Prolonged anti-shipping campaign in Gulf/Hormuz approaches with Western naval escorts (Operation Earnest Will). Relevant because of Iranian asymmetric tactics, insurance spikes, and chokepoint focus. Breaks down because it was bilateral Iran–Iraq with less direct great-power kinetic involvement and no full formal “closure.” Suggests multi-year partial disruption with gradual commercial recovery only after major political settlement (years, not months).

2. **2019 Gulf shipping crisis (tanker attacks, seizures, limited mining threats)**: Short, intense insurance and transit disruption after attacks attributed to Iran. Relevant for insurance pricing dynamics and rapid commercial caution. Breaks down because no full-scale war or sustained blockade. Suggests 3–6 months for meaningful insurance/traffic recovery once kinetic incidents stop.

3. **Red Sea/Houthi disruption (late 2023–ongoing into 2026 context)**: Proxy attacks on shipping leading to major rerouting, insurance hikes, and partial recovery only after sustained restraint + naval presence. Relevant for proxy persistence and commercial lag behind military pauses. Breaks down because alternative routes (Cape) exist and volume is lower than Hormuz energy flows. Suggests 6–18 months for functional normalization even after de-escalation signals.

4. **1990–91 Gulf War / post-Kuwait invasion energy recovery**: Major supply disruption followed by relatively rapid physical recovery once combat ended, but insurance and commercial confidence lagged. Relevant for scale of energy impact. Breaks down because clear battlefield victory and no sustained Iranian control claims over the strait.

5. **Post-ceasefire commercial reopening lags in other chokepoints (Suez 1956/1973 analogs, limited modern data)**: Political agreements often precede insurance and operator confidence by weeks to many months.

Base-rate prior (pre-current-evidence adjustment, averaged across classes weighted toward prolonged asymmetric Gulf cases): Probability of functional normality (per definition) by horizon roughly 1 week <5%; 1 month 8–12%; 3 months 20–30%; 6 months 35–45%; 1 year 50–60%; 18 months 60–70%. These reflect that military pauses occur faster than insurance/commercial normalization, and full multi-domain recovery historically lags political announcements by months to years.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Confirmed / disputed / inferred |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|---------------------------------|
| Daily commodity transits ~3–9 vessels (~5–9% of pre-war) | Ship-tracking (Kpler, IMF PortWatch, Windward) | Strong against | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk premiums still multiples of baseline (reports 15× or higher peaks earlier) | Broker/insurer commentary, market reports | Strong against | Medium-High | Confirmed (exact multiple varies by report) |
| US naval blockade active on Iranian ports; Iranian loadings/exports sharply reduced | US statements, tracker data (Kpler/Vortexa) | Against (Iran side); mixed for overall Gulf flows | High | Confirmed |
| Ongoing tit-for-tat strikes (US on Iranian coastal/missile assets & tankers; Iran on shipping/bases) | CENTCOM, IRGC claims, UKMTO, media | Strong against | High | Confirmed (attribution of some incidents disputed) |
| June MOU collapse after brief traffic recovery | Primary (Trump declaration), contemporaneous reporting | Against (demonstrates fragility) | High | Confirmed |
| Houthi advances, Saudi pipeline attack, Red Sea pressure | Reporting, Saudi statements | Against (proxy spillover) | High | Confirmed |
| Trump signals openness to deal / “hopefully toward end”; Iranian conditions unmet | Public statements | Mildly toward (diplomatic channel) | Medium | Confirmed statements; intentions inferred |
| Claims of higher protected US-escorted flows vs independent low transit counts | Official vs trackers | Mixed/disputed | Medium | Disputed |
| Depleted US munitions stocks, political midterm pressure | Reporting, CBO/IG figures | Mildly toward (incentive for off-ramp) | Medium | Partially confirmed |
| Iranian insistence on long-term control/tolls over strait | Iranian official statements | Strong against | High | Confirmed |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

Ranked by importance:
1. Durable political settlement removing Iranian toll/permit claims and US blockade.
2. Sustained absence of kinetic attacks on shipping for weeks, allowing insurance capacity and premiums to ease.
3. Midterm political pressure on US side + Iranian economic pain from blocked exports creating mutual incentive for off-ramp.
4. Successful demining + protected corridor becoming routine enough for major operators to return.
5. Proxy restraint (especially Houthis) to prevent secondary chokepoint shocks.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

Ranked by importance:
1. Iranian strategic insistence on permanent management/control of Hormuz as leverage (repeated official statements).
2. Insurance market stickiness: premiums rise fast, fall slowly; single incident resets confidence.
3. Proxy autonomy and spillover (Houthis, others) independent of central Iranian restraint.
4. Mutual escalation dynamics and depleted inventories making “mowing the lawn” the default.
5. Commercial operator caution and vessel repositioning lags even after political signals.
6. Domestic Iranian hardliner influence that previously undermined the June MOU.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities of major sub-components holding by horizon (these are inputs, not mechanical averages):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w ~15%; 1m ~30%; 3m ~45%; 6m ~55%; 1y ~65%; 18m ~70%.
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥70% baseline without heavy escort/dark dominance): 1w <5%; 1m ~10%; 3m ~25%; 6m ~40%; 1y ~55%; 18m ~65%.
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤2–3× baseline, available capacity): 1w <5%; 1m ~8%; 3m ~20%; 6m ~35%; 1y ~50%; 18m ~60%.
- Oil/LNG export recovery (≥85% regional pre-war continuity): 1w ~10%; 1m ~20%; 3m ~35%; 6m ~50%; 1y ~65%; 18m ~75%.
- Proxy restraint: 1w ~20%; 1m ~30%; 3m ~40%; 6m ~50%; 1y ~55%; 18m ~60%.
- Force drawdown/stabilization: 1w <10%; 1m ~15%; 3m ~30%; 6m ~45%; 1y ~55%; 18m ~65%.
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w ~60%; 1m ~45%; 3m ~40%; 6m ~45%; 1y ~50%; 18m ~55%.

Gating factors are shipping security + insurance + commercial transit levels. Military reduction alone is insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 3%  
- Base-rate anchor: <5%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Down (active strikes, single-digit traffic, elevated premiums)  
- Core rationale: No pathway exists for multi-domain normalization in days; backlog, insurance, and confidence cannot clear.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance and operator willingness.  
- What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate comprehensive ceasefire + verified zero attacks + major underwriter announcements of rate cuts.  
- What would lower this forecast materially: Further successful attacks on shipping or bases.  
- Confidence in this estimate: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~10%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly down (fragility of prior MOU, ongoing kinetic cycle, proxy activity)  
- Core rationale: Even an optimistic diplomatic breakthrough would face weeks of demining, vessel repositioning, and insurance lag. Historical commercial recovery trails politics.  
- Main gating factor: Sustained safe transit without incidents.  
- What would raise: Verified durable deal removing toll claims + 2+ weeks zero shipping attacks + premium cuts.  
- What would lower: Renewed large-scale exchanges or Houthi escalation closing secondary routes.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~25%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly down (Iranian control insistence + insurance stickiness)  
- Core rationale: Possible if midterms produce political pressure for off-ramp and both sides accept a monitored corridor, but commercial/insurance normalization remains the bottleneck.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance capacity return + operator confidence.  
- What would raise: Binding agreement + sustained low incident rate + measured traffic recovery to >50%.  
- What would lower: Hardliner sabotage of any deal or major energy infrastructure strike.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~40%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slightly down  
- Core rationale: Reference classes show partial stabilization possible within half a year after major political shift, but full functional normality (especially insurance and unrestricted transit) is still demanding.  
- Main gating factor: Removal of Iranian long-term control claims + commercial volume recovery.  
- What would raise: Clear post-midterm settlement + proxy de-escalation + traffic consistently >60%.  
- What would lower: Prolonged low-intensity war of attrition or new toll regime.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~55%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly down (persistence risk from Iranian strategy and proxies)  
- Core rationale: Cumulative economic pain and political fatigue raise odds of settlement, but definition requires commercial/insurance recovery that historically lags. Overconfidence risk is high at this horizon.  
- Main gating factor: Durable multi-party acceptance of free navigation without Iranian administrative control.  
- What would raise: Formal treaty-like arrangement + sustained >70% traffic + normalized premiums.  
- What would lower: Entrenched Iranian control claims or repeated proxy disruptions.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 62%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~65%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slightly down  
- Core rationale: Longer horizon allows more political cycles and economic pressure to force accommodation, yet full multi-domain normality remains non-automatic given reference-class duration of asymmetric Gulf disruptions.  
- Main gating factor: Same as 1-year plus absence of new triggers.  
- What would raise: Verified long-term security arrangement + full commercial return.  
- What would lower: Regime hardening around Hormuz leverage as permanent doctrine.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low  

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued low-to-medium intensity exchanges and constrained traffic through the US midterms. Post-election political incentives produce another negotiated pause or limited corridor arrangement in late 2026/early 2027. Traffic recovers partially under escort or monitored routes over subsequent months, but insurance remains elevated and full unrestricted commercial normality is delayed into mid-to-late 2027. Iranian control claims are fudged rather than fully abandoned. Proxy activity continues at lower intensity. Functional normality per the strict definition is more likely after 12 months than before, but remains incomplete.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Decisive post-midterm deal that explicitly guarantees free navigation without Iranian permits/tolls, verified demining, rapid underwriter capacity return, and credible proxy restraint. Traffic recovers to 60%+ within 6–8 weeks of the deal and insurance falls toward 2–3× baseline. Probability of this path is low (~15–20% conditional on a deal occurring) because of demonstrated fragility of the June MOU and Iranian strategic view of the strait.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Iran treats Hormuz management as non-negotiable core interest; hardliners block meaningful concessions; proxies keep secondary pressure; insurance markets stay risk-averse after repeated incidents; US maintains blockade and periodic strikes (“mow the lawn”). Traffic remains <30% for an extended period. This path is consistent with Tanker War duration and current Iranian statements. Probability elevated relative to base rate because of the control doctrine.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Strongest case I may be overestimating normalization: Insurance stickiness and commercial caution are under-weighted; a political deal does not automatically restore operator confidence (Red Sea precedent). Iranian domestic politics may lock in the control claim more firmly than economic pain suggests.  
Strongest case I may be underestimating: Mutual exhaustion + midterm pressure + Chinese interest in stable energy flows could produce a faster practical corridor arrangement than pure reference classes imply. Official claims of higher protected flows, if sustained and verified, would raise shorter-horizon probabilities.  
Load-bearing assumptions: That commercial/insurance metrics are true gating factors (they are); that Iranian control claims are sticky (supported by repeated statements); that no catastrophic escalation or sudden regime change intervenes (base case).

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily/weekly independent transit counts (Kpler, PortWatch, Windward) vs official claims.  
- War-risk premium quotes from major brokers and Joint War Committee listed-area status.  
- Concrete diplomatic text (not rhetoric) on navigation rights and absence of tolls/permits.  
- Attribution and frequency of attacks on merchant vessels.  
- Iranian export loadings that successfully clear any blockade line.  
- Proxy behavior (especially Houthi) and Saudi pipeline status.  
- US force posture changes and munitions/readiness indicators.  
- Post-midterm political statements and any new MOU language.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Primary gating factor              |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|------------------------------------|
| 1 week    | 3%          | High         | Insurance + operator willingness   |
| 1 month   | 8%          | Medium-High  | Sustained safe transit             |
| 3 months  | 22%         | Medium       | Insurance + commercial volume      |
| 6 months  | 38%         | Medium       | Removal of control claims          |
| 1 year    | 52%         | Medium-Low   | Durable free-navigation acceptance |
| 18 months | 62%         | Medium-Low   | Same + no new triggers             |

The forecast is calibrated to the demanding operational definition. Shorter horizons are near-zero because multi-domain recovery cannot occur in days or a few weeks under current conditions. Longer horizons rise with political and economic pressure but remain well below certainty because historical chokepoint and asymmetric Gulf cases show commercial and insurance normalization lagging military or diplomatic pauses by many months.

title: Gulf normality odds rise to 63%
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War (began 28 February 2026) by these horizons: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months. Current date is 16 September 2026 (~Day 200).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

A multi-domain, observable state lasting at least 30 consecutive days in which:

- Direct military activity: No kinetic exchanges between major state actors (US/Israel–Iran) involving strikes on Iranian territory, US/allied bases in the Gulf, or Iranian coastal/missile infrastructure at a rate exceeding pre-war baseline harassment. No sustained naval combat or blockade enforcement actions beyond routine presence.
- Proxy activity: No sustained attacks by Iran-aligned groups (Houthis, residual Hezbollah, Iraqi militias) on Gulf shipping, energy infrastructure, or Saudi/UAE targets that materially disrupt operations.
- Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters: Free, unimpeded transit passage without Iranian “permission” regimes, mine threats requiring active clearance, or regular anti-ship attacks. AIS-visible commercial transits average ≥70–80% of pre-war baseline (~85–130 vessels/day depending on source; use ~100 as midpoint).
- Commercial transit levels: Sustained two-way commercial traffic (tankers, LNG, dry bulk, containers) at ≥70% of pre-war volumes without reliance on dark transits, shuttle STS transfers as primary mode, or systemic avoidance by major Western/Asian owners.
- War-risk insurance conditions: Additional war-risk premiums for Hormuz/Gulf voyages ≤2–3× pre-war baseline (pre-war ~0.1–0.25% of hull value; current multiples 15–40× reported). Lloyd’s Joint War Committee listing risk reduced or premiums competitive enough that most major operators resume regular scheduling.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Persian Gulf crude + products + LNG exports sustained at ≥85–90% of pre-war levels (~21–23 mb/d crude/products equivalent + Qatar LNG) without force majeure declarations, pipeline shutdowns as primary workaround, or floating storage backlogs as structural feature. Iranian exports not zeroed by blockade.
- Energy market stress and volatility: Brent volatility and risk premium no longer dominated by Hormuz-specific risk; prices and spreads reflect global balances rather than chokepoint disruption (current Brent ~$105–108 with elevated diesel cracks).
- Force posture of major actors: No active US naval blockade of Iranian ports; Iranian forces not enforcing a transit regime or mining lanes; US/allied force levels and alert status consistent with post-conflict residual presence rather than combat operations.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No IAEA referral outcomes, leadership succession crises, or proxy territorial gains that restart tit-for-tat cycles.

Temporary ceasefires, price drops from demand destruction, or battlefield pauses without commercial recovery do **not** count. Partial recovery via bypass pipelines (East-West, Habshan-Fujairah) alone is insufficient.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of ~15–16 September 2026)**

War ongoing ~200 days. Initial US-Israeli strikes (28 Feb) killed Khamenei; Iranian missile/drone responses hit Gulf bases; effective Hormuz closure followed. April ceasefire collapsed; June Islamabad MOU (60-day talks window) produced brief partial reopening then collapsed amid ship attacks and US responses. Current phase: intermittent tit-for-tat (US strikes on Iranian tankers/coastal targets; Iranian attempts on US ships and commercial vessels); US maintains effective pressure/blockade elements; Iran asserts control claims.<grok:render card_id="d2ead6" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">1</argument></grok:render>

Hormuz AIS/commodity transits: single digits to low teens daily (e.g., 4 on 15 Sep; 7-day averages ~5 or ~3–18 depending on source; ~5–10% of pre-war ~85–130). Some dark/Iranian-route traffic; no VLCC/LNG dominance.<grok:render card_id="23d1c0" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">40</argument></grok:render>

Gulf oil exports: estimates ~15–16 mb/d (roughly two-thirds pre-war ~23 mb/d), via Hormuz dark/partial, Saudi East-West (recently disrupted by drone), UAE Fujairah, STS. Iranian loadings/exports collapsed (hundreds of kb/d or near zero under pressure). LNG disrupted earlier.<grok:render card_id="9048fb" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">8</argument></grok:render>

Insurance: war-risk multiples ~15–40× peacetime; voyage costs for VLCC still multi-million dollars; claims cumulative high.<grok:render card_id="0769fb" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">50</argument></grok:render>

Diplomacy: GCC-Iran talks postponed; Trump signals openness but Iran conditions unmet; munitions strain reported; Houthi gains at Bab el-Mandeb add second chokepoint pressure. Oil ~$105–108 Brent; elevated product cracks and US diesel prices. No durable settlement.<grok:render card_id="dc39d9" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">6</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant classes (3–6):

1. **1984–1988 Tanker War (Iran-Iraq)**: Systematic attacks on shipping in Gulf; ~500 vessels hit; US reflagging/escorts (Earnest Will); mines. Shipping never fully stopped but risk elevated for years. Normalization of commercial behavior and insurance took the 1988 ceasefire + demining + time (months to 1–2 years post-ceasefire for confidence). Relevance: same geography, IRGC tactics, oil chokepoint. Breaks down: bilateral attrition war without nuclear dimension, superpower patronage of one side, no full “closure” claim or modern precision munitions/proxies. Timeline suggestion: partial stabilization 6–18 months after decisive ceasefire.

2. **2023–2025 Red Sea/Houthi disruptions**: Sustained attacks; traffic collapse via Suez/Bab el-Mandeb; insurance spikes; partial recovery with escorts/diplomacy but elevated risk persisted >12–18 months. Relevance: Iran-linked proxies, insurance/shipping behavior, chokepoint. Breaks down: less central to global oil, no direct state-on-state war with US. Timeline: meaningful commercial recovery 6–12+ months after peak intensity drop.

3. **Post-1991 Gulf War / Kuwait liberation maritime recovery**: Rapid physical reopening after decisive coalition victory, but residual mines, insurance caution, and force posture adjustments lasted months. Relevance: Gulf energy infrastructure + US-led ops. Breaks down: clear military victory vs. current inconclusive attrition.

4. **2019–2020 Gulf tanker attacks / Abqaiq**: Limited Iranian/proxy attacks; short insurance spike and traffic caution; rapid de-escalation after US response/diplomacy. Relevance: recent IRGC maritime playbook. Breaks down: far smaller scale, no multi-month war or leadership decapitation.

5. **Broader post-major-war maritime chokepoint recovery** (e.g., post-Suez 1956/1967/1973 patterns, Black Sea post-2022 partial): Commercial confidence lags physical access by 3–12 months; insurance and owner risk appetite slower than naval claims of “open.”

**Base-rate prior (pre-current-evidence adjustment, approximate cumulative probability of meeting full operational definition by horizon, assuming inconclusive war continues without decisive victory or collapse):**  
1 week: ~1–3%; 1 month: ~5–10%; 3 months: ~15–25%; 6 months: ~30–45%; 1 year: ~45–60%; 18 months: ~55–70%.  
(Derived from Tanker War/Red Sea lag of commercial normalization after intensity drop; higher for longer horizons as attrition and economic pain create incentives, lower near-term due to demonstrated fragility of MOUs.)

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| War ongoing ~200 days; intermittent kinetic exchanges (ship attacks, coastal strikes) | Military reporting (CENTCOM, IRGC claims, UKMTO), daily trackers | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Hormuz commodity/AIS transits single digits–low teens (~5–10% pre-war) | Ship-tracking (Kpler, Reuters, IMF PortWatch proxies, Windward) | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Gulf oil exports ~15–16 mb/d (~2/3 pre-war); Iranian near-collapse | Goldman, Vortexa, Kpler, trackers | Against (partial recovery via bypasses insufficient) | Medium-High | Confirmed range |
| War-risk premiums 15–40× peacetime; multi-$M per VLCC voyage | Broker/insurer commentary, Lloyd’s-linked trackers | Strongly against | Medium-High | Confirmed elevated; exact multiple varies |
| June MOU produced brief partial reopening then collapse on ship attacks | Diplomatic reporting, contemporaneous tracking | Against (fragility demonstrated) | High | Confirmed |
| Recent East-West pipeline disruption; Houthi Bab el-Mandeb gains | Regional reporting, Saudi statements | Against (second-order cascade) | Medium | Confirmed disruption; Houthi control claims |
| Diplomatic talks postponed; conditions mismatch; munitions strain | Official statements, think-tank/monitor | Mildly against near-term | Medium | Confirmed postponements |
| Some dark/Iranian-route traffic and UAE recovery via Fujairah | Trackers | Mildly toward (workarounds exist) | Medium | Confirmed partial |
| No resumed enrichment confirmed; IAEA access issues | IAEA/DNI statements | Neutral to mildly against (nuclear file unresolved) | Medium | Confirmed access barriers |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization** (ranked)

1. Economic pain on all sides (Iran oil revenue collapse; Gulf states export losses; US inflation/diesel; global buyer pressure) creating incentives for durable deal.  
2. US political calendar (midterms) and munitions costs potentially favoring de-escalation.  
3. Bypass infrastructure and dark shipping already limiting worst-case supply loss.  
4. Prior MOU precedent showing both sides can pause when costs high.  
5. China/India/Asia demand for volume over pure risk aversion.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization** (ranked)

1. Core unresolved issues (nuclear stockpile, Hormuz control claims, leadership legitimacy post-Khamenei, proxy networks).  
2. Demonstrated MOU fragility and mutual distrust; hardliner sabotage risk.  
3. Second-order cascades (Houthi expansion, pipeline vulnerability, insurance inertia).  
4. Force posture lock-in (US blockade elements vs. Iranian coastal/missile residual capability).  
5. Commercial risk aversion lags military claims of control (owners/insurers require sustained quiet).  
6. No decisive military outcome; attrition favors prolonged contestation of the strait.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities of key components holding for sufficient duration to support overall normality (independent estimates, then gated):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w ~5–10%; 1m ~15–25%; 3m ~35–50%; 6m ~50–65%; 1y ~60–75%; 18m ~70–80%.  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥70% volumes): 1w <5%; 1m ~10%; 3m ~25–35%; 6m ~40–55%; 1y ~55–70%; 18m ~65–75%.  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤2–3×): lags transit by 1–3 months; lower than transit probs by ~10–20 pts near-term.  
- Oil/LNG export recovery to ≥85–90%: similar to transit but slightly higher due to bypasses (current ~2/3 already).  
- Proxy restraint: lower than direct strikes due to Houthi autonomy (especially 3–12m).  
- Force drawdown / no blockade: tightly coupled to deal; low near-term.  
- No new major escalation trigger: ~60–70% short horizons declining modestly with time as new risks (succession, IAEA, Yemen) accumulate.

Gating factors: commercial transit + insurance are the binding constraints after any kinetic pause. Military pause alone is insufficient (June example).

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 2%  
- Base-rate anchor: 1–3%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Negligible upward; active single-digit traffic, recent attacks, postponed talks.  
- Core rationale: Physical and commercial conditions nowhere near definition; no pathway for 30-day sustained normality starting now.  
- Main gating factor: Immediate kinetic and traffic levels.  
- What would raise: Unexpected comprehensive ceasefire + rapid demining + insurer statements (still low probability of meeting full def).  
- What would lower: Further ship attacks or pipeline hits (already near floor).  
- Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: 5–10%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward from demonstrated MOU fragility and Houthi expansion.  
- Core rationale: Even a new pause would leave traffic, insurance, and force posture unrecovered within 30 days.  
- Main gating factor: Sustained safe transit + insurance response.  
- What would raise: Verified durable ceasefire + surge in escorted traffic + premium compression.  
- What would lower: Renewed tanker strikes or East-West outage extension.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: 15–25%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward (attrition entrenched; second chokepoint).  
- Core rationale: Possible if deal reached and held 6–8 weeks with demining/escorts; still requires commercial confidence rebuild.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance + owner willingness after kinetic quiet.  
- What would raise: Signed comprehensive settlement with verification + observed traffic ramp.  
- What would lower: Hardliner sabotage or proxy territorial gains.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: 30–45%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (nuclear/Hormuz sovereignty gaps large).  
- Core rationale: Economic pressure + political calendars raise chance of functional arrangement; commercial lag remains.  
- Main gating factor: Durable absence of escalation triggers + export continuity.  
- What would raise: Verified Iranian restraint on proxies + premium normalization + export data ≥85%.  
- What would lower: Leadership crisis in Iran or major US munitions shortfall forcing posture change that invites probing.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: 45–60%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight downward (prolonged inconclusive wars tend to entrench contested norms).  
- Core rationale: Base rates from Tanker War/Red Sea support gradual commercial recovery if intensity drops; unresolved core issues keep probability from rising higher.  
- Main gating factor: Force posture normalization and insurance.  
- What would raise: Formal settlement + sustained traffic data + reduced JWC risk.  
- What would lower: Expanded proxy campaigns or new nuclear crisis.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 63%  
- Base-rate anchor: 55–70%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
- Core rationale: Long-horizon attrition and global economic costs favor some functional accommodation short of full political resolution; definition remains demanding so not higher.  
- Main gating factor: Absence of major new triggers over extended period.  
- What would raise: Structural bypass expansion + durable quiet + market de-risking.  
- What would lower: Regime instability or great-power entanglement deepening contestation.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low (long horizon inherent uncertainty)  

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued low-to-medium intensity contestation of the strait with intermittent pauses. Partial commercial recovery via bypasses, dark shipping, and selective risk-tolerant operators keeps Gulf exports in the 60–80% range. Full functional normality (per definition) remains elusive until a more durable political-military arrangement addresses Hormuz control claims and residual capabilities. Insurance and owner risk appetite recover slowly even after kinetic quiet. Probability rises with time mainly because prolonged pain increases deal incentives, not because resolution is inevitable.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

A comprehensive package (nuclear limits, Hormuz transit protocol with verification, proxy restraint mechanisms, sanctions relief elements) brokered under economic/political pressure, held for 60+ days with rapid demining/escorts and insurer response. Traffic and premiums normalize within 2–4 months of signing. Probability of this path: low-to-moderate (15–25% within 6 months).

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

MOUs repeatedly fail; Iran maintains residual anti-access capability and proxy leverage; US maintains pressure; Houthi/Bab el-Mandeb linkage persists; insurance stays elevated; commercial traffic structurally lower. Gulf states deepen hedging. Normality deferred beyond 18 months. Credible given current evidence of fragility.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Overestimation risk: Commercial lag may be longer than modeled (owners remember June collapse); second-order effects (Yemen, diesel markets, munitions) create more escalation triggers than assumed; base rates from Tanker War underweight modern precision and information effects. Underestimation risk: Economic costs (Iran revenue, US political, Asian demand) could force faster accommodation than historical inconclusive wars; bypass infrastructure already softens the worst case, reducing incentives for total contestation. Load-bearing assumptions: commercial/insurance behavior remains risk-averse; no sudden decisive military or political collapse on either side. Strongest critique of own numbers: 6–18 month figures may still be too high given the operational definition’s stringency and the demonstrated ability of hardliners to spoil.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily/weekly AIS and commodity transit counts through Hormuz (threshold ≥60–70 sustained).  
- War-risk premium quotes and JWC listing status.  
- Verified cessation of anti-ship and coastal strikes for ≥30 days.  
- East-West and other bypass operational status.  
- Iranian export loadings vs. blockade effectiveness.  
- Diplomatic track progress (conditions lists, verification mechanisms).  
- Houthi activity and Bab el-Mandeb traffic.  
- Force posture statements and munitions reporting.  
- IAEA access and nuclear stockpile developments.

**15. Final Summary Table**

Horizon | Probability | Confidence  
---|---|---  
1 week | 2% | High  
1 month | 8% | Medium-High  
3 months | 22% | Medium  
6 months | 38% | Medium  
1 year | 52% | Medium  
18 months | 63% | Medium-Low  

The forecast is calibrated to a demanding multi-domain definition. Near-term probabilities are low because current traffic, insurance, and kinetic conditions are far from the standard and recent pauses have not produced commercial recovery. Longer horizons rise with base rates from comparable disruptions but remain well below certainty because core political-military issues are unresolved and commercial confidence is sticky.

title: Gulf normality odds rise to 62%
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (from 15 September 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

Functional normality requires simultaneous satisfaction of all the following observable conditions for a sustained period (not a single-day snapshot or temporary lull):

- Direct military activity: No sustained US/Iran or Iran/Gulf-state kinetic exchanges targeting military or dual-use coastal/maritime assets; no active mining or anti-ship campaigns in the Strait of Hormuz (SoH) or approaches.
- Proxy activity: No significant Iran-aligned proxy attacks (Houthis, Iraqi militias, etc.) on Gulf energy infrastructure, shipping, or US/partner bases that materially affect transit or export confidence.
- Shipping security: Commercial vessels can transit SoH and nearby waters without military escort as the default; attack/incident rate on commercial shipping returns to near pre-February 2026 baseline (<1 confirmed kinetic incident per month on average).
- Commercial transit levels: Daily two-way commercial vessel transits through SoH sustain at ≥70–80% of pre-war baseline (~85–100+ vessels/day per IMF PortWatch/Kpler-type tracking), including meaningful tanker and LNG volumes, for at least 2 consecutive weeks.
- War-risk insurance: Additional war-risk premiums for SoH/Gulf transit fall to ≤2–3× pre-war levels (pre-war ~0.1–0.25% of hull value; current ~1.5%+ or 10–15×+ multiples) and remain available without widespread exclusions or capacity withdrawal.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf producers (Saudi, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Iraq, residual Iran) restore aggregate crude + condensate + LNG flows through or around SoH to ≥85% of pre-war levels without reliance on emergency pipeline surges or dark fleet dominance; no major terminal or pipeline outages from conflict.
- Energy market stress: Brent crude and related benchmarks no longer embed a large, persistent conflict risk premium driven by Hormuz/Gulf insecurity (prices and volatility consistent with non-conflict fundamentals); no sustained $20+/bbl war premium.
- Force posture: Major actors (US, Iran, Gulf states) have drawn down from wartime forward posture to levels consistent with routine presence or post-conflict stabilization (no dual-carrier sustained presence oriented on Iran, no active large-scale blockade enforcement as primary mission).
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No new mine-laying campaigns, large-scale attacks on energy infrastructure, or formal assertions of exclusive Iranian administrative control that re-close commercial access.

A temporary ceasefire, lower oil prices from demand destruction, or escorted “facilitated” transits do **not** count. Battlefield pauses without commercial and insurance normalization do **not** count.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 15 September 2026)**

War ongoing ~199 days since ~28 February 2026 outbreak. SoH commercially closed/severely restricted: IMF PortWatch-style data show ~3–6 commercial transits/day (7-day averages ~3–4% of pre-war ~74–100+ baseline); many days near zero tankers. US-facilitated/escorted movements occur but do not restore normal commercial traffic.<grok:render card_id="401d46" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">40</argument></grok:render>

Recent kinetic activity (early–mid September): US strikes on Iranian tankers and coastal assets; Iranian claims of attacks on US vessels and commercial shipping (some disputed); vessel hit near Hengam; Saudi East-West pipeline struck (drones from Iraq claimed) and shut as precaution; Houthi advances including Perim Island / Bab el-Mandeb area. Diplomatic track stalled (Oman-hosted GCC-Iran meeting postponed 14 September).<grok:render card_id="dae8b8" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">31</argument></grok:render>

Brent ~$105–108/bbl (elevated with conflict premium). War-risk insurance remains elevated (reports of ~1.5% of hull value / 10–15×+ multiples; earlier peaks higher; adds several dollars per barrel). Iranian crude continues via shadow fleet/China routes at reduced levels; broader Gulf export recovery incomplete due to security, insurance, and bypass constraints. US maintains elevated naval presence (carrier groups oriented on the theater); Iran continues efforts to assert administrative control over SoH.<grok:render card_id="364375" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">45</argument></grok:render>

Evidence base is solid on traffic, prices, and high-level kinetic patterns from multiple trackers (Kpler, IMF PortWatch derivatives, UKMTO/JMIC, CENTCOM statements, insurer commentary) but thinner and more disputed on exact attribution of some vessel hits and internal Iranian decision-making.

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant classes (3–6):

1. **Iran-Iraq “Tanker War” phase (1984–1988)**: Prolonged attacks on shipping in Gulf/SoH approaches. Traffic never fully normalized until war end; insurance elevated for years; recovery of commercial confidence took months after ceasefire. Suggests multi-month to multi-year commercial lag after kinetic reduction. Breaks down: lower intensity, no full-scale great-power involvement, different insurance market.

2. **1990–91 Gulf War / Kuwait invasion aftermath**: Rapid coalition military victory; SoH/Gulf shipping recovered within weeks–months once combat ended and mines cleared, but insurance and residual risk lingered. Suggests 1–3 months for transit recovery post-decisive outcome, longer for full insurance/posture normalization. Breaks down: clear conventional victory and regime change in Kuwait; Iran not the primary antagonist controlling the littoral.

3. **Houthi Red Sea / Bab el-Mandeb campaign (2023–2025+)**: Persistent low-cost attacks caused sustained traffic collapse, insurance spikes, and re-routing despite intermittent pauses. Normalization incomplete years later without full proxy restraint. Suggests months-to-years for insurance and commercial recovery even after major reduction in attacks. Highly relevant to proxy dimension and insurance lag.

4. **Iran nuclear deal / JCPOA period and prior Hormuz threats (2011–12, 2018–19)**: Threats and limited seizures produced short spikes in risk premium and some traffic caution; rapid partial recovery when threats subsided. Suggests weeks for partial transit recovery if pure signaling. Breaks down: no sustained multi-month kinetic war or closure.

5. **Post-conflict maritime recovery after major wars (Falklands, broader post-WWII chokepoint reopenings)**: Physical clearance (mines) + political settlement required; commercial/insurance normalization lagged military pause by 3–12+ months.

Base-rate prior (pre-current-evidence adjustment, treating this as a high-intensity, multi-month interstate + proxy conflict with chokepoint control contest):

- 1 week: ~2–5%
- 1 month: ~8–12%
- 3 months: ~20–30%
- 6 months: ~35–45%
- 1 year: ~50–60%
- 18 months: ~60–70%

These are already lower than pure “ceasefire then reopen” cases because of the demanding multi-domain definition and the historical lag between kinetic reduction and commercial/insurance recovery.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| SoH traffic ~3–6 vessels/day vs ~85–100+ pre-war | Vessel tracking (IMF PortWatch derivatives, Kpler, commercial monitors) | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk premiums still 10–15×+ (or ~1.5% hull) | Insurer/broker commentary, market reports | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed (ranges vary) |
| Brent ~$105–108 with conflict premium | Market data | Negative | High | Confirmed |
| Recent US–Iran tanker/coastal strikes + claimed vessel hits (early Sep) | CENTCOM, IRGC claims, UKMTO, trackers | Strongly negative | Medium–High | Mostly confirmed (some attribution disputed) |
| Saudi East-West pipeline hit/shut; Houthi Perim/Bab el-Mandeb gains | Saudi statements, reporting, satellite | Strongly negative (second-order) | High | Confirmed |
| Oman-hosted GCC–Iran talks postponed | Official statements | Negative | High | Confirmed |
| US elevated carrier/naval posture sustained | Reporting on deployments | Negative for posture criterion | Medium–High | Confirmed |
| Iranian residual export via shadow fleet | Trackers | Mildly positive for continuity but not normality | Medium | Confirmed |
| Prior June MOU produced temporary traffic rebound then collapse | Contemporary reporting | Shows fragility | High | Confirmed |
| US claims of “control” / facilitated transits | Official statements | Overstated relative to commercial data | Medium | Claim vs. data mismatch |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

Ranked by importance:
1. Sustained mutual interest in ending economic pain (oil prices, Iranian revenue, US midterm/political costs) leading to durable political settlement that removes Iranian incentive to contest SoH control.
2. Effective degradation of Iranian anti-ship/mine/coastal surveillance capability reducing ability to enforce restrictions.
3. Gulf-state alignment against Iranian administrative claims + Omani mediation success.
4. Insurer capacity return once attack rates drop for several consecutive weeks.
5. Bypass infrastructure recovery (pipelines) buying time and reducing leverage of pure Hormuz control.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

Ranked by importance:
1. Iranian regime view of SoH control as core residual leverage and survival asset post-leadership changes and attrition; refusal to accept pre-war status quo.
2. Low-cost asymmetric tools (drones, mines, proxies) that allow persistent disruption even under pressure.
3. Insurance and commercial confidence lag: underwriters and owners require multi-week clean record + political clarity, not just military pause.
4. Second-order expansion (Houthi Bab el-Mandeb, Iraqi militia pipeline attacks) creating multi-chokepoint stress.
5. Domestic political incentives on both sides (US midterms, Iranian hardliner consolidation) that reward visible toughness over quiet normalization.
6. Residual mining, dark fleet dynamics, and disputed route schemes that keep risk elevated.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities that each major component reaches “normal” threshold by horizon (these are intermediate judgments):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w ~5%, 1m ~15%, 3m ~40%, 6m ~55%, 1y ~70%, 18m ~75%.
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥70–80% baseline, unescorted default): 1w <5%, 1m ~10%, 3m ~25%, 6m ~40%, 1y ~55%, 18m ~65%.
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤2–3×): 1w <5%, 1m ~8%, 3m ~20%, 6m ~35%, 1y ~50%, 18m ~60%.
- Oil/LNG export recovery (≥85% aggregate continuity): 1w ~10%, 1m ~20%, 3m ~35%, 6m ~50%, 1y ~65%, 18m ~75%.
- Proxy restraint: 1w ~10%, 1m ~20%, 3m ~35%, 6m ~45%, 1y ~55%, 18m ~60%.
- Force drawdown: 1w <5%, 1m ~10%, 3m ~25%, 6m ~40%, 1y ~55%, 18m ~65%.
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w ~40%, 1m ~35%, 3m ~40%, 6m ~45%, 1y ~50%, 18m ~55% (persistent risk).

Gating factors are commercial transit + insurance + absence of new triggers. Military pause alone is insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
• Probability: 3%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~2–5%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (active recent strikes, pipeline hit, talks postponed, traffic still single digits).  
• Core rationale: Zero pathway to multi-domain normality in 7 days given current kinetic tempo and commercial freeze.  
• Main gating factor: Ongoing direct and second-order attacks.  
• What would raise this forecast materially: Immediate comprehensive ceasefire + verified mine clearance start + insurer statements of rapid premium cuts.  
• What would lower this forecast materially: Further large-scale tanker or base strikes.  
• Confidence in this estimate: High  

**1 Month**  
• Probability: 8%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~8–12%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward (fragility of prior MOU, expanded proxy/pipeline risk).  
• Core rationale: Even a rapid political pause would leave insurance, traffic recovery, and posture lagging; historical chokepoint cases rarely normalize commercially in <30 days after high-intensity phase.  
• Main gating factor: Insurance + sustained unescorted traffic.  
• What would raise: Durable political deal removing Iranian control claims + 2+ weeks zero incidents.  
• What would lower: Continued tit-for-tat or new proxy infrastructure attacks.  
• Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
• Probability: 22%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~20–30%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward (multi-chokepoint stress, Iranian leverage logic intact).  
• Core rationale: Possible if decisive political settlement + capability degradation occurs early in the window; still requires commercial confidence to rebuild.  
• Main gating factor: Political settlement that ends the control contest + clean transit record.  
• What would raise: Verified Iranian acceptance of unrestricted navigation + rapid traffic rebound to 50%+.  
• What would lower: Stalemate continuing into Q4 2026 with elevated insurance.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
• Probability: 38%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~35–45%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight downward.  
• Core rationale: More realistic window for both military reduction and the slower insurance/commercial catch-up; still well below 50% because Iranian residual leverage and proxy tools remain.  
• Main gating factor: Combination of settlement durability and insurer re-entry.  
• What would raise: Sustained low incident rate + Gulf-state buy-in to a stable regime.  
• What would lower: Hardliner consolidation in Tehran or US political incentives for continued pressure.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
• Probability: 52%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~50–60%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
• Core rationale: Time allows for either a negotiated end or sufficient attrition of Iranian maritime denial tools; commercial recovery becomes more probable once kinetic activity falls. Long-horizon uncertainty remains high.  
• Main gating factor: Whether a stable political equilibrium replaces the current control contest.  
• What would raise: Clear post-conflict security architecture accepted by major actors.  
• What would lower: Frozen conflict with intermittent disruption becoming the new normal.  
• Confidence: Medium-Low  

**18 Months**  
• Probability: 62%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~60–70%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (risk of protracted low-intensity contest).  
• Core rationale: Majority chance that some form of functional (if imperfect) normality returns, but the demanding definition and historical lag for insurance/commercial confidence keep it from higher levels. Residual risk of incomplete recovery or recurrent flare-ups remains material.  
• Main gating factor: Long-term Iranian strategic choice on leverage vs. economic recovery.  
• What would raise: Regime adaptation toward revenue prioritization + successful mine clearance and route normalization.  
• What would lower: Entrenchment of Iranian administrative claims or multi-year proxy campaign.  
• Confidence: Medium-Low  

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued low-to-medium intensity contest through late 2026 into early 2027, with intermittent pauses, facilitated/escorted traffic, elevated insurance, and partial bypass utilization. Gradual erosion of Iranian denial capacity and mutual economic pain produce a political arrangement by mid-to-late 2027 that allows commercial recovery, but full multi-domain normality (especially insurance and posture) lags the political announcement by months. Traffic and exports recover faster than insurance and force posture.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Decisive political settlement in the next 4–8 weeks that explicitly restores unrestricted navigation, combined with rapid, verified degradation of Iranian coastal anti-ship systems and a clean multi-week incident record. Insurers respond within 4–6 weeks; traffic rebounds to 60%+ by 3 months. Probability of this path is low (~15–20% conditional on early settlement).

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Iran prioritizes SoH leverage indefinitely; proxies expand attacks on pipelines and secondary chokepoints; insurance market structurally reprices Gulf risk higher; US maintains elevated posture through 2027. Traffic remains <30–40% of baseline for 12+ months. This path is plausible (~25–30%).

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Possible overestimation of normalization: The definition is deliberately demanding; historical tanker-war and Red Sea cases show commercial/insurance recovery can lag kinetic reduction by years. Iranian internal logic may treat SoH control as non-negotiable after leadership attrition. Underestimation risk: Mutual economic damage and US political calendar could force a faster settlement than base rates suggest; capability degradation may be more effective than visible. Load-bearing assumptions include continued Iranian regime coherence and the persistence of asymmetric tools. Evidence would falsify the forecast if traffic sustains >60 vessels/day with premiums <3× for 3+ consecutive weeks without a political deal, or if a deal produces immediate commercial recovery contrary to historical lag.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily/weekly SoH transit counts (IMF PortWatch, Kpler, commercial AIS) and tanker vs. non-tanker mix.
- War-risk premium quotes and Joint War Committee listed-area status.
- Confirmed commercial vessel attack rate (UKMTO/JMIC).
- Status of Saudi East-West and other bypass pipelines.
- Concrete language in any US–Iran or Iran–Oman/GCC text on “administration” or “unrestricted navigation.”
- US carrier and mine-countermeasure posture announcements.
- Iranian export volumes via shadow vs. conventional routes and Kharg activity.
- Houthi and Iraqi militia activity against energy infrastructure.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Dominant Constraint                  |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|--------------------------------------|
| 1 Week    | 3%          | High         | Active kinetic + commercial freeze  |
| 1 Month   | 8%          | Medium-High  | Insurance + traffic lag             |
| 3 Months  | 22%         | Medium       | Political settlement durability     |
| 6 Months  | 38%         | Medium       | Multi-domain catch-up               |
| 1 Year    | 52%         | Medium-Low   | Long-term equilibrium               |
| 18 Months | 62%         | Medium-Low   | Residual leverage vs. recovery      |

The forecast is deliberately conservative relative to any single “ceasefire tomorrow” narrative because the operational definition requires commercial, insurance, and posture normalization, not merely a reduction in headlines.

title: Gulf normality prob: 2%
