**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization** (ranked)

1. Mutual exhaustion + economic pressure (Iran inflation/sanctions; US domestic/energy costs) producing a durable deal that includes credible Hormuz security guarantees.  
2. Sustained US (or coalition) naval dominance that raises Iranian attack costs enough for commercial confidence without permanent blockade.  
3. Insurer capacity return and premium compression after 4–8+ weeks of zero kinetic incidents.  
4. Gulf state mediation (Oman) producing workable transit protocols without Iranian exclusive control.  
5. Strategic petroleum releases and alternative supply adaptation reducing market urgency.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization** (ranked)

1. Iranian strategic preference for Hormuz leverage as residual deterrent and bargaining chip post-war damage.  
2. Insurance market structural caution and capacity limits—premiums and availability lag kinetic reality by months.  
3. Tit-for-tat escalation traps and MoU fragility demonstrated in June–July.  
4. Proxy residual capacity (Houthis) and dark-fleet dynamics that keep risk elevated.  
5. Domestic politics on both sides (US election-cycle optics; Iranian hardliner/IRGC influence) that punish concessions.  
6. Physical residual threats (mines, coastal missiles/drones) requiring sustained clearance and deterrence.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts** (approximate conditional probabilities of each component holding by horizon; gating factors noted)

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 10%, 1m 25%, 3m 45%, 6m 60%, 1y 70%, 18m 75%.  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥70–80% baseline): 1w <5%, 1m 10%, 3m 25%, 6m 40%, 1y 55%, 18m 65%. (Gating)  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤1.5%): 1w <5%, 1m 8%, 3m 20%, 6m 35%, 1y 50%, 18m 60%. (Gating)  
- Oil/LNG export recovery: tracks transit closely but lags 2–4 weeks.  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 30%, 1m 40%, 3m 55%, 6m 65%, 1y 70%, 18m 75%.  
- Force drawdown / end of blockade: slower; 1w <5%, 1m 10%, 3m 25%, 6m 40%, 1y 55%, 18m 65%.  
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 60%, 1m 45%, 3m 40%, 6m 45%, 1y 50%, 18m 55% (declining then stabilizing).

Transit + insurance are the primary gates; military pause alone is insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
• Probability: 2%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~1–3%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (active single-digit traffic, high premiums, no talks)  
• Core rationale: Zero evidence of the multi-domain conditions; even a sudden deal cannot produce commercial volumes or insurance reset in days.  
• Main gating factor: Insurance and owner risk aversion.  
• What would raise: Immediate verified zero-incident corridor + major premium cut announcement.  
• What would lower: Further vessel attack or seizure.  
• Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
• Probability: 8%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~5–10%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral-to-slight downward  
• Core rationale: A new MoU is possible under economic pressure, but June precedent shows fragility; commercial metrics require sustained quiet that is not yet visible.  
• Main gating factor: Credible, verified security producing insurer response.  
• What would raise: Signed durable deal + 3+ weeks zero incidents + traffic >40/day.  
• What would lower: Renewed strikes or formal Iranian exclusive-control enforcement.  
• Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
• Probability: 22%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~15–25%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (leverage incentives + demonstrated collapse risk)  
• Core rationale: Reference classes allow partial recovery; current stalemate and Iranian Hormuz priority reduce odds. Transit/insurance still lag any kinetic pause.  
• Main gating factor: Insurance normalization after sustained security.  
• What would raise: Clear US-Iran security protocol + traffic sustained >70 + premiums <3%.  
• What would lower: Proxy expansion or major infrastructure strike.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
• Probability: 38%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~30–40%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral  
• Core rationale: Economic exhaustion increases deal probability; still requires overcoming Iranian residual leverage preference and insurance lag.  
• Main gating factor: Combination of deal durability and commercial confidence.  
• What would raise: Verified force posture reduction + export volumes recovering.  
• What would lower: Prolonged blockade + continued dark/Iran-only flows.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
• Probability: 55%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~45–60%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral  
• Core rationale: Longer horizon allows multiple de-escalation windows and adaptation; base rates and exhaustion support majority but not high probability given structural issues.  
• Main gating factor: Whether a post-war equilibrium accepts some residual Iranian influence or fully restores open transit.  
• What would raise: Regime or leadership shift reducing IRGC Hormuz priority; sustained low premiums.  
• What would lower: Frozen conflict with permanent elevated risk premium.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
• Probability: 65%  
• Base-rate anchor: ~55–70%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral-to-slight upward (time for institutional adaptation)  
• Core rationale: Most reference classes show eventual commercial recovery; however, full multi-domain normality (including insurance and force posture) remains demanding. Exceeding 70–80% would require stronger evidence of Iranian willingness to surrender leverage.  
• Main gating factor: Long-term security architecture and insurer memory.  
• What would raise: Durable great-power or regional security guarantee.  
• What would lower: Recurrent low-level attacks becoming the new normal.  
• Confidence: Medium-Low (long-horizon uncertainty)

**10. Most Likely Path**

Stalemate persists through autumn 2026 with sporadic incidents, single-digit to low-double-digit traffic, and elevated premiums. Economic pressure produces another limited understanding in late 2026/early 2027 that allows gradual traffic recovery under escorts or protocols. Insurance lags by 1–3 months. Full functional normality (all domains) arrives, if at all, in the 9–18-month window after a more durable arrangement, with residual risk premium higher than 2025 baseline.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Decisive US military degradation of Iranian coastal capabilities + Iranian economic collapse forcing acceptance of open transit without exclusive control. Traffic recovers to 80%+ within 6–8 weeks of a new deal; premiums fall below 2% inside 3 months. Probability of this path: ~15–20%.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Iran prioritizes Hormuz leverage indefinitely; low-level attacks and seizures continue; insurers permanently reprice the Gulf; US maintains blockade or high posture; proxies expand. Traffic stays <30% of baseline for 12+ months. Probability of this path: ~25–30%.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Overestimation risk: Under-weighting Iranian domestic hardliner strength and the demonstrated June collapse; insurance markets may stay elevated longer than historical analogies due to modern capacity concentration and ESG/owner pressures.  
Underestimation risk: Under-weighting speed of commercial adaptation once kinetic risk falls (tankers moved quickly in prior Gulf crises) and the depth of mutual economic pain.  
Load-bearing assumptions: (1) Iranian regime values Hormuz control highly enough to delay deals; (2) insurers require multi-week clean record; (3) no sudden regime-threatening internal Iranian shock. Evidence that would prove the forecast wrong: sustained >80 transits + premiums <1.5% for 30 consecutive days without a new deal, or a verified comprehensive security agreement producing immediate traffic surge.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily Kpler/Windward/AIS transit counts and composition (VLCC/LNG share, route used).  
- Broker-reported war-risk quotes and Lloyd’s JWC listed-area status.  
- CENTCOM blockade metrics and Iranian seizure/attack claims.  
- Official statements on talks (Oman channel especially) and any new MoU text.  
- Brent term structure and physical differentials for Gulf grades.  
- Gulf state (UAE/Saudi/Oman) diplomatic and insurance-related moves.  
- Residual Iranian missile/drone launch rates and US strike cadence.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Primary Gate                  |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|-------------------------------|
| 1 week    | 2%          | High         | Insurance + owner aversion    |
| 1 month   | 8%          | Medium-High  | Credible security + deal      |
| 3 months  | 22%         | Medium       | Sustained transit + premiums  |
| 6 months  | 38%         | Medium       | Deal durability + commercial  |
| 1 year    | 55%         | Medium       | Equilibrium security design   |
| 18 months | 65%         | Medium-Low   | Long-term risk architecture   |

The forecast is deliberately conservative on short horizons because commercial normality is a higher bar than military pause. Long-horizon probabilities remain well below certainty because the operational definition is demanding and Iranian leverage incentives are structural.

title: Gulf normality odds rise to 62%
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by the horizons of 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (from 21 August 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

“Return to functional normality” requires simultaneous satisfaction of all the following observable conditions for a sustained period (not a single day or temporary pause):

- Direct military activity: No US/Israeli/Iranian kinetic strikes on military, nuclear, energy, or shipping-related targets inside Iran, Gulf states, or the maritime domain for ≥14 consecutive days; no major new force deployments or alerts indicating imminent large-scale operations.
- Proxy activity: Houthis, Iraqi militias, Hezbollah, and other Iran-aligned groups show no sustained attacks on commercial shipping, energy infrastructure, or US/partner forces beyond pre-war baseline levels.
- Shipping security (Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters): Zero confirmed projectile/mine/boarding incidents against commercial vessels for ≥21 consecutive days; UKMTO/JMIA risk assessments at “moderate” or lower; no active minefields or enforced Iranian “controlled routes” with fees or mandatory coordination.
- Commercial transit levels: Daily vessel transits through Hormuz ≥80% of pre-war average (~110–130+ ships/day, including VLCCs and LNG carriers), sustained for ≥14 days, with AIS data and Kpler/equivalent trackers confirming normal routing (not exclusively dark or Iranian-coast hugging under coercion).
- War-risk insurance: Hull war-risk premiums ≤2–3% (pre-war range or modestly elevated), with major insurers and P&I clubs offering coverage without prohibitive exclusions or surcharges that effectively price out most operators.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf producers (Saudi, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Iraq, Iran if relevant) exporting at ≥90% of pre-war volumes via Hormuz or confirmed alternative routes without material diversion or stockpile buildup; no widespread port/refinery shutdowns due to security.
- Energy market stress and volatility: Brent crude sustained below $80 (or within 10% of contemporaneous non-Gulf-driven fundamentals) without Hormuz-risk premium dominating; implied volatility and crack spreads not indicating acute supply-fear regime.
- Force posture of major actors: US CENTCOM and partner naval/air assets reduced from wartime surge levels toward pre-February 2026 posture; Iranian IRGC Navy and coastal missile/drone forces not in heightened alert or actively interdicting traffic.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No leadership assassinations, nuclear breakout signals, large-scale proxy offensives, or formal declarations that reopen the conflict cycle.

A temporary ceasefire, partial traffic recovery under escort, lower oil prices from demand destruction, or battlefield pause alone does **not** meet the definition. All domains must be concurrently functional and commercially viable without continuous military escort or coercion.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 21 August 2026)**

War began ~28 February 2026 with US-Israeli strikes (including killing of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei). Cumulative Iranian deaths estimated 3,500–6,000+. Multiple failed or partial ceasefires (April, June MOU signed 17 June and declared over by early July). Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to normal commercial traffic since late February; current daily transits typically 1–7 ships (Kpler data), versus ~130–140 pre-war. No VLCCs/LNG carriers in recent windows. War-risk premiums 7.5–10%+ of hull value (vs 1–3% pre-war). Recent incidents include fatal projectile strike on *Minoan Dignity* (18 Aug, chief engineer killed), Iranian seizure of Emirati tanker, US blockade enforcement (64+ vessels redirected, 3 disabled, 2 boarded). US/Israeli strikes on Iranian territory paused ~21 consecutive nights; Iranian missile/drone attacks on Gulf states and shipping continue at lower intensity. June MOU expired mid-August; Trump announced “economic D-Day”/maximum pressure, no active talks. UAE imposed full trade/financial embargo on Iran. Brent ~$91–92. Iran demands recognition of control over Hormuz, blockade lift, sanctions relief, compensation, US withdrawal. Nuclear facilities heavily damaged but residual capabilities and stockpile status disputed. Proxy activity (Houthis) continues at elevated levels.<grok:render card_id="c19e00" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">6</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="2ee4ce" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">2</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="10fa67" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">11</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant reference classes (selected for chokepoint disruption + regional great-power/proxy war elements):

1. **Tanker War phase of Iran-Iraq War (1984–1988)**: Prolonged attacks on shipping in Gulf/Hormuz. Traffic never fully normalized until ceasefire; insurance remained elevated; functional commercial normality took 1–3 years post-ceasefire with residual risk. Relevant for asymmetric maritime interdiction. Breaks down: no superpower direct combatant role at this intensity; oil market structure different.
2. **1990–1991 Gulf War (Iraq invasion of Kuwait + Desert Storm)**: Rapid coalition victory, but shipping/insurance normalization lagged 6–18 months due to mines, residual threats, and political uncertainty. Relevant for rapid kinetic resolution followed by slow commercial recovery. Breaks down: clear territorial aggressor defeat; no enduring Iranian-style regime survival with residual missile/proxy capacity.
3. **Houthi Red Sea campaign (2023–ongoing as of 2026 baseline)**: Persistent low-level attacks forced major rerouting, insurance spikes, and incomplete recovery even after months of US/UK strikes. Normalization still incomplete after 2+ years. Relevant for proxy persistence and insurance stickiness. Breaks down: secondary chokepoint; less direct state-on-state intensity.
4. **Suez Canal closures (1956, 1967–1975)**: Political/military closures lasted months to years; full commercial normality required political settlement + demining/clearance. Relevant for chokepoint political control disputes. Breaks down: narrower waterway, different actors.
5. **Post-2003 Iraq + residual Gulf maritime risk periods**: Insurance and transit recovered over 12–24 months after major combat, with persistent elevated premiums during instability spikes.
6. **2024–2025 limited Iran-Israel exchanges + prior Hormuz threats**: Short spikes resolved in weeks, but never reached full multi-domain war intensity.

Base-rate prior (probability of meeting the full multi-domain definition, before case-specific updates):

- 1 week: 1–3%
- 1 month: 5–10%
- 3 months: 15–25%
- 6 months: 30–40%
- 1 year: 45–55%
- 18 months: 55–65%

These reflect that pure military pauses occur faster than insurance, transit volume, and force-posture normalization. Historical chokepoint recoveries under residual hostility typically require 6–24 months for commercial functionality.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| Hormuz daily transits 1–7 ships (vs ~130–140 pre-war); no sustained VLCC/LNG flow | Kpler, Reuters, maritime trackers | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk premiums 7.5–10%+ hull value | Insurer/broker commentary, maritime reports | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| Fatal ship strike (*Minoan Dignity*) + recent seizures/attacks mid-Aug | UKMTO, INTERCARGO, Windward, CENTCOM | Against | High | Confirmed |
| US blockade of Iranian ports still enforced; 64+ vessels redirected | CENTCOM statements | Against (sustains confrontation) | High | Confirmed |
| June MOU expired; Trump “economic D-Day,” no talks scheduled | Presidential statements, reporting | Against near-term deal | High | Confirmed |
| UAE full trade/financial embargo on Iran | UAE government | Against (raises stakes) | High | Confirmed |
| ~21-night pause in US/Israeli strikes on Iranian territory | CENTCOM/reporting absence | Mildly toward (tactical de-escalation) | Medium | Confirmed (absence) |
| Iranian residual missile/drone capability + demands for Hormuz control/recognition | Iranian statements, ISW, JINSA | Strongly against | High | Confirmed (capability) / Disputed (scale) |
| Nuclear facilities heavily damaged; stockpile status unclear | IAEA assessments, reporting | Neutral-to-against (uncertainty) | Medium | Partially confirmed / Disputed |
| Brent ~$91–92 with Hormuz premium | Market data | Against (stress persists) | High | Confirmed |
| Proxy (Houthi) attacks continuing | Maritime/security reports | Against | Medium | Confirmed |
| Oman channel talks on routes (technical only) | Iranian/Omani statements | Mildly toward (limited dialogue) | Low-Medium | Confirmed but narrow |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization** (ranked)

1. Mutual economic exhaustion and US domestic political pressure for lower energy prices (highest weight).
2. Sustained pause in direct strikes creating space for third-party mediation (Oman/Qatar).
3. Iranian recognition that maximalist Hormuz-control demands are unsustainable under prolonged blockade + secondary sanctions.
4. Gulf Arab states’ preference for commercial recovery over prolonged confrontation.
5. Residual US military superiority enabling credible deterrence without continuous kinetic action.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization** (ranked)

1. Iranian regime survival imperative and insistence on formal recognition of Hormuz authority/control (highest weight; existential for residual power projection).
2. Stickiness of war-risk insurance and shipper risk aversion (once elevated, slow to reprice even after kinetic pause).
3. US political commitment to “maximum pressure” and refusal of Iranian core demands (blockade lift, sanctions relief, compensation).
4. Proxy autonomy and residual Iranian missile/drone stocks enabling low-cost disruption.
5. Absence of a comprehensive political settlement addressing nuclear, regional, and maritime issues simultaneously.
6. Cumulative damage, leadership changes inside Iran, and mutual distrust after multiple collapsed understandings.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities that each component meets the operational threshold by horizon (independent estimates, then conditional synthesis):

- Major reduction in direct strikes (≥14-day quiet): 1w 25%, 1m 45%, 3m 60%, 6m 70%, 1y 75%, 18m 80%
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥80% volume, no incidents ≥21 days): 1w <5%, 1m 10%, 3m 25%, 6m 40%, 1y 55%, 18m 65%
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤2–3%): 1w <5%, 1m 8%, 3m 20%, 6m 35%, 1y 50%, 18m 60%
- Oil/LNG export recovery (≥90% volumes): 1w 10%, 1m 20%, 3m 35%, 6m 50%, 1y 65%, 18m 70%
- Proxy restraint: 1w 15%, 1m 30%, 3m 45%, 6m 55%, 1y 60%, 18m 65%
- Force drawdown toward pre-war posture: 1w <5%, 1m 10%, 3m 25%, 6m 40%, 1y 55%, 18m 65%
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 60%, 1m 50%, 3m 45%, 6m 40%, 1y 35%, 18m 30% (declining as time horizon lengthens due to more opportunity for triggers)

Gating factors are insurance + sustained safe high-volume transit + absence of new triggers. Direct-strike reduction is necessary but far from sufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 2%  
- Base-rate anchor: 1–3%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Near-zero given ongoing low traffic, high premiums, recent fatal incident, expired MOU, economic escalation rhetoric.  
- Core rationale: Impossible to achieve multi-domain commercial normality in 7 days from current severely degraded state.  
- Main gating factor: Shipping volume + insurance.  
- What would raise: Immediate comprehensive deal + verified mine clearance + insurer statements of coverage restoration.  
- What would lower: Any new ship strike or major kinetic exchange.  
- Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: 5–10%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight upward for strike pause; downward for maximalist Iranian demands and insurance stickiness.  
- Core rationale: Possible only under rapid, comprehensive political breakthrough that simultaneously resolves blockade, Hormuz control claims, and sanctions—historically rare.  
- Main gating factor: Political deal that unlocks insurance and shipper confidence.  
- What would raise: Verified Oman-brokered technical + political package accepted by both sides with immediate traffic surge.  
- What would lower: Renewed Iranian attacks or US secondary-sanctions enforcement that freezes remaining dark fleet activity.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: 15–25%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Modest upward for mutual fatigue; downward for absence of talks and residual Iranian capabilities.  
- Core rationale: Window for mediated interim arrangement exists, but full multi-domain threshold (especially insurance and force posture) remains demanding.  
- Main gating factor: Sustained safe transit volume + insurance repricing.  
- What would raise: Formal interim security mechanism + measured US force posture reduction + clear Iranian restraint.  
- What would lower: Leadership hardline shift in Tehran or major proxy escalation.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: 30–40%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Balanced; economic pressure may force compromise, but distrust and maximalist positions persist.  
- Core rationale: Historical chokepoint recoveries often begin to materialize in this window if kinetic activity stays low, but residual risk frequently prevents full insurance/volume recovery.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance market confidence + political durability of any arrangement.  
- What would raise: Durable de-escalation + visible Gulf Arab-Iran economic re-engagement.  
- What would lower: Iranian nuclear reconstitution signals or US domestic political shift hardening pressure.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: 45–55%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight upward for long-term economic incentives; downward for structural Iranian control claims.  
- Core rationale: Cumulative costs raise probability of pragmatic accommodation, yet the operational definition remains strict; partial normality more likely than full.  
- Main gating factor: Comprehensive (even if imperfect) political settlement covering maritime regime.  
- What would raise: Regime-internal pragmatism or external great-power pressure for settlement.  
- What would lower: Successful Iranian adaptation to sanctions + sustained low-cost disruption capability.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 62%  
- Base-rate anchor: 55–65%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Modest upward for attrition effects; residual uncertainty from unresolved nuclear and regional issues.  
- Core rationale: Long enough for adaptive commercial work-arounds and political exhaustion to dominate, but full multi-domain threshold still requires explicit political resolution of Hormuz status—historically slow.  
- Main gating factor: Enduring political settlement vs. managed low-level conflict.  
- What would raise: Clear Iranian strategic recalculation or US policy shift toward containment over maximum pressure.  
- What would lower: New escalation cycle triggered by nuclear or proxy developments.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low (long-horizon uncertainty)  

**10. Most Likely Path**

Protracted “no war, no peace.” Intermittent low-level Iranian interdiction or proxy actions keep insurance elevated and volumes suppressed. Occasional tactical pauses and limited technical arrangements (Oman channel) produce partial traffic recovery under high risk premiums. Full multi-domain normality remains elusive until a broader political package addresses Iranian residual capabilities, sanctions, and maritime regime. Energy markets adapt via alternative supply and demand destruction; Gulf states invest in redundancy. Probability mass concentrates on partial recovery by 6–12 months without crossing the strict operational threshold until closer to 18 months.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Decisive Iranian economic collapse or leadership pragmatism leads to acceptance of free navigation + limited sanctions relief within 1–3 months. Rapid mine clearance, insurer confidence restoration, and US force drawdown follow. Requires Iranian abandonment of maximalist Hormuz-control claims—low but non-zero probability under extreme pressure.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Iran successfully adapts to sanctions, retains sufficient missile/drone/proxy capacity for intermittent disruption, and extracts de-facto recognition of influence over Hormuz. US maintains blockade and secondary sanctions indefinitely. Insurance and shipper behavior lock in elevated risk pricing for 18+ months. Nuclear ambiguity or proxy expansion provides recurring triggers.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Possible overestimation of normalization: The operational definition is deliberately strict; historical insurance and commercial confidence recoveries after multi-month closures with residual hostility are slower than kinetic pauses. Iranian regime survival incentives and US political commitment to maximum pressure may lock the system into managed conflict longer than attrition models suggest. Possible underestimation: Markets and shippers are adaptive; dark fleet + alternative routes + eventual fatigue could produce functional (if imperfect) normality faster than pure political analysis implies. Load-bearing assumption at risk: that Iranian maximalist demands are non-negotiable under prolonged economic isolation.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily Hormuz transit counts (Kpler/AIS) and composition (VLCC/LNG presence).  
- War-risk premium quotes from major brokers.  
- Official statements on talks (Oman, Qatar, direct).  
- CENTCOM blockade enforcement metrics and any force posture changes.  
- Iranian domestic economic indicators and leadership rhetoric on Hormuz.  
- Proxy attack frequency and targeting.  
- Brent price and implied volatility relative to non-Gulf fundamentals.  
- Any verified mine-clearance or joint maritime security mechanism announcements.

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Core Constraint                  |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|----------------------------------|
| 1 Week    | 2%         | High        | Impossible from current baseline |
| 1 Month   | 8%         | Medium-High | Political breakthrough required  |
| 3 Months  | 22%        | Medium      | Insurance + volume gating        |
| 6 Months  | 38%        | Medium      | Durability of any arrangement    |
| 1 Year    | 52%        | Medium      | Comprehensive political package  |
| 18 Months | 62%        | Medium-Low  | Structural resolution vs. managed conflict |

The forecast is calibrated to the demanding multi-domain definition. Partial commercial recovery is more probable than full functional normality at every horizon.

Probability that the Persian Gulf returns to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War, by horizons: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months (as of 20 August 2026).

Functional normality requires simultaneous satisfaction of all the following observable conditions for a sustained period (not a single-day snapshot):

- Direct military activity: No kinetic exchanges (missile/drone/naval strikes) between Iran/US/Israel/Gulf states inside the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, or immediately adjacent waters for ≥30 consecutive days.
- Proxy activity: No significant proxy attacks on commercial shipping or energy infrastructure attributable to Iranian-aligned groups (Houthis, Iraqi militias, etc.) affecting Gulf transit routes.

A temporary ceasefire, isolated price drop, or partial traffic rebound does not meet the definition. All domains must be simultaneously functional.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (20 August 2026)**  
War day ~173–174 since 28 February US-Israeli strikes. June 17 US-Iran MOU (60-day framework for Hormuz reopening and negotiations) expired 17 August without extension or final deal. Trump administration states no talks scheduled; Iran demands full implementation of its interpretation of MOU terms (including recognition of control/administration of the strait) before reopening.  

Strait traffic is at ~1% of pre-war levels (single-digit daily commodity crossings vs. ~73–140 baseline; IMF PortWatch/Kpler data). War-risk insurance multiples reported at ~40× normal. Recent incidents include projectile strikes on vessels (e.g., *Minoan Dignity* with crew casualty), at least one seizure (*AMARA*), and continued US redirection/boarding of vessels attempting Iranian port access. Evidence base is multi-source (ISW, Kpler, Windward, Reuters, JINSA, straits.live, official statements) but contains disputed claims on exact control, missile attribution, and negotiation status.<grok:render card_id="0fce24" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">35</argument></grok:render>

Breaks down because current episode involves near-total effective closure and explicit sovereignty claims. Timeline signal: 6–18+ months post-ceasefire for functional shipping recovery.  
2. Suez Canal closures (1956 ~5 months; 1967–75 8 years): Political/military closure required clearance of mines/wrecks plus political settlement. 1967–75 reopening after disengagement took years for full traffic confidence. Breaks down (different geography, less energy concentration). Timeline: months to years after political deal.  
3. 2019 Gulf of Oman attacks / tanker seizures: Brief spikes in risk premiums (×10); traffic maintained; rapid partial recovery once kinetic activity subsided. Breaks down (far smaller scale). Timeline: weeks to 2–3 months.  
4. Red Sea/Houthi disruption (2023–ongoing): Sustained attacks; partial rerouting; insurance elevated; incomplete normalization years later despite diplomacy. Breaks down (alternative Cape route available). Timeline: multi-year residual risk.  
5. Ever Given Suez blockage (2021, 6 days): Physical clearance → traffic resumed in days; backlog clearance weeks. Breaks down (non-conflict). Timeline: days–weeks.  
6. Post-1991 Gulf War / Earnest Will residual: Naval presence and risk premium persisted after major combat; commercial patterns adjusted over 6–12+ months.

Base-rate prior (pre-current-evidence, averaged and adjusted for scale of current near-closure + sovereignty dispute):  
- 1 week: <5%  
- 1 month: 8–12%  
- 3 months: 20–25%  
- 6 months: 35–40%  
- 1 year: 50–55%  
- 18 months: 60–65%  

These reflect that military pauses historically precede commercial/insurance normalization by months, and sovereignty disputes prolong the gap.

**5. Evidence Ledger**  

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| MOU expired 17 Aug; no talks scheduled | Official US statements, Iranian officials, Reuters/JINSA | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| Daily Hormuz commodity crossings single digits (~1% baseline) | Kpler, IMF PortWatch, straits.live | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk insurance ~40× normal | Trade press / straits.live estimates | Strongly negative | Medium-High | Inferred from reporting |
| Recent vessel strikes/seizure (Aug 17–18) | UKMTO, Windward, Reuters | Negative | High | Confirmed |
| Brent ~$91–93 (elevated risk premium) | Market data | Negative | High | Confirmed |
| Bypass pipelines high utilization but incomplete substitute | Industry reports | Mildly positive (mitigation) | Medium | Confirmed |
| Sporadic kinetic pause in some windows; no major new US strikes inside Iran recently | CENTCOM/ISW | Mildly positive (short-term) | Medium | Confirmed/Disputed attribution |
| Iranian public claims of exclusive control/toll rights | Iranian officials | Strongly negative | High | Confirmed claims |
| UAE economic cutoff of Iran | UAE statements | Negative (regional) | High | Confirmed |
| Proxy (Houthi) Red Sea activity continues | Multiple | Negative | High | Confirmed |
| Partial traffic rebound during earlier MOU window then collapse | Kpler historical | Shows fragility | High | Confirmed |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization** (ranked)  
1. Economic pain on all parties (Iran sanctions/blockade costs; Gulf export losses; global inflation/energy stress) creating mutual incentive for deal.  
2. Availability of partial bypasses and stock draws that limit immediate catastrophic pressure.  
3. Historical precedent that prolonged chokepoint disruption eventually produces mediated technical arrangements (Oman channel talks).  
4. US domestic and midterm political calendar potentially favoring de-escalation optics.  
5. Chinese commercial interest in stable flows (though currently risk-averse).

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization** (ranked)  
1. Core sovereignty dispute over Hormuz administration/tolls/control (Iran maximalist; US/GCC rejection).  
2. IRGC institutional interest in retaining leverage tool; hardline vs. pragmatic factional split.  
3. Insurance and commercial risk aversion: once elevated, premiums and routing decisions lag kinetic pauses by months.  
4. Proxy residual capacity and Red Sea linkage.  
5. Mutual credibility problems after repeated MOU/ceasefire collapses.  
6. Elevated force postures and easy re-escalation triggers (missile incidents, seizures).

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts** (probabilities of each component holding by horizon; approximate, conditional on no major new war expansion)  

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 15%; 1m 30%; 3m 45%; 6m 55%; 1y 65%; 18m 70%  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥80% baseline): 1w 2%; 1m 8%; 3m 20%; 6m 35%; 1y 50%; 18m 60%  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤3×): 1w 1%; 1m 5%; 3m 15%; 6m 30%; 1y 45%; 18m 55%  
- Oil/LNG export recovery (≥85–90%): 1w 5%; 1m 15%; 3m 30%; 6m 45%; 1y 60%; 18m 70%  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 20%; 1m 35%; 3m 45%; 6m 55%; 1y 60%; 18m 65%  
- Force posture drawdown: 1w 5%; 1m 15%; 3m 30%; 6m 40%; 1y 55%; 18m 60%  
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 40%; 1m 35%; 3m 40%; 6m 45%; 1y 50%; 18m 55%  

Gating factors are insurance + sustained safe transit + sovereignty resolution. These are slower than kinetic pauses.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 2%  
- Base-rate anchor: <5%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Down (expired MOU, single-digit traffic, fresh incidents, no talks)  
- Core rationale: Zero realistic path to simultaneous multi-domain normalization in 7 days.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance and commercial confidence.  
- What would raise: Sudden comprehensive political deal + immediate verified mine clearance + insurance market reaction.  
- What would lower: Further seizures or strikes (already near floor).  
- Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: 8–12%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight down (stalemate signals stronger than mid-June partial reopen).  
- Core rationale: Possible kinetic pause, but commercial/insurance lag and sovereignty dispute prevent functional normality.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance normalization and sustained transit volume.  
- What would raise: Verified Iran-Oman technical corridor deal accepted by US/insurers + sustained zero incidents.  
- What would lower: New kinetic cycle or formal Iranian toll enforcement.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: 20–25%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight down.  
- Core rationale: Historical pauses produce partial traffic recovery, but full multi-domain bar (insurance + volume + posture) rarely clears inside one quarter after major sovereignty conflict.  
- Main gating factor: Political resolution of Hormuz administration.  
- What would raise: Mediated package linking nuclear restraints, sanctions relief, and neutral technical management of strait.  
- What would lower: IRGC offensive posture implementation or major proxy activation.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: 35–40%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
- Core rationale: Economic incentives accumulate; technical arrangements become more feasible; residual risk remains material.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance market and commercial operator confidence.  
- What would raise: Sustained 60+ day zero-incident period + major underwriter re-entry + volume recovery >60%.  
- What would lower: Leadership change or nuclear escalation trigger.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: 50–55%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
- Core rationale: Base rates from Tanker War and prolonged chokepoint cases support roughly even odds of functional (not perfect) normalization once economic costs dominate. Sovereignty residual and insurance lag keep it from higher.  
- Main gating factor: Durable political settlement or de-facto acceptance of managed corridor.  
- What would raise: Clear US-Iran framework with verification mechanisms and GCC buy-in.  
- What would lower: Prolonged low-intensity interdiction campaign or new regional war front.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 62%  
- Base-rate anchor: 60–65%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight down (current maximalist positions and institutional interests).  
- Core rationale: Longer horizon allows adaptation, stock rebuilding, and eventual bargaining space, but complete multi-domain return remains demanding given residual proxy capacity and trust deficit. Exceeding 80% would require stronger evidence of institutional change than currently exists.  
- Main gating factor: Absence of renewed major escalation + insurance normalization.  
- What would raise: Verifiable demilitarization of interdiction capabilities or broad regional security architecture.  
- What would lower: Entrenchment of dual-control or fee regimes rejected by insurers/operators.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low (long-horizon uncertainty rises)

**10. Most Likely Path**  
Continued stalemate with intermittent kinetic incidents and low single-digit-to-low-double-digit traffic for 1–3 months. Eventual mediated technical corridor arrangement (Oman-centric) emerges under economic pressure, producing partial volume recovery by 6 months. Insurance and full commercial confidence lag into the 9–18 month window. Residual risk premium and elevated force posture persist beyond full “normality.” Oil markets clear via bypasses + non-Gulf supply more than via full Hormuz restoration.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**  
Probability mass shifts left if a comprehensive package (sanctions relief + verified Iranian restraint on interdiction + neutral traffic management + US blockade lift) is reached within weeks, followed by rapid mine clearance and major insurer re-entry. Historical analogue: rapid post-ceasefire traffic rebound in limited prior Gulf episodes. Requires simultaneous political and commercial confidence restoration.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**  
Iran consolidates de-facto control claims; US maintains blockade/sanctions; low-level interdiction and seizures continue; proxies expand Red Sea pressure. Traffic remains structurally suppressed; insurance stays elevated; Gulf states accelerate permanent bypass infrastructure. Normalization delayed beyond 18 months or becomes “new normal” of managed high-risk corridor. Analogue: multi-year Red Sea residual or 1967–75 Suez duration.

**13. Red-Team Critique**  
Overestimation risk: Base rates from Tanker War may be too optimistic because the current episode features near-total effective closure + explicit sovereignty maximalism + post-leadership-strike Iranian internal dynamics not present in 1980s. Commercial/insurance recovery could be slower than kinetic history suggests. Underestimation risk: Global economic costs (inflation, Asian buyer pressure, US political calendar) may force faster pragmatic technical deals than sovereignty rhetoric implies. Load-bearing assumptions: (1) no sudden leadership collapse or nuclear breakout that resets incentives; (2) Chinese commercial caution continues; (3) definition’s multi-domain simultaneity remains the right bar.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**  
- Daily Kpler/IMF PortWatch transit counts and route choice (northern vs. southern corridor).  
- War-risk premium quotes from major underwriters/brokers.  
- Official US/Iran/Oman statements on corridor management and any fee language.  
- UKMTO incident frequency and severity.  
- CENTCOM/IRGC force posture announcements and any new blockade/sanction actions.  
- Brent–non-Gulf differential and floating storage levels.  
- Proxy attack tempo (Houthi especially).  
- Any verified mine-clearance activity or joint coordination center establishment.

**15. Final Summary Table**  

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Main Gating Factor                  |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|-------------------------------------|
| 1 Week    | 2%          | High         | Insurance & commercial confidence   |
| 1 Month   | 8%          | Medium-High  | Insurance + sustained transit       |
| 3 Months  | 22%         | Medium       | Political resolution of administration |
| 6 Months  | 38%         | Medium       | Insurance market re-entry           |
| 1 Year    | 52%         | Medium       | Durable political/technical settlement |
| 18 Months | 62%         | Medium-Low   | Residual risk & posture drawdown    |

Probabilities are calibrated to the strict multi-domain definition and current evidence of stalemate after MOU collapse. They are internally consistent with sub-component gating logic and historical recovery lags between kinetic pauses and commercial normality.

title: Iran War: Gulf normality forecast
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War (began ~28 February 2026) by each horizon: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months (from ~19 August 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

Observable, multi-domain standard (all must hold simultaneously for a sustained period, not a single-day snapshot):

- Direct military activity: No sustained kinetic exchanges between Iran and US/Israel/Gulf states involving ballistic missiles, drones, or major airstrikes on territory or bases in the Gulf region for ≥14 consecutive days; residual low-level incidents below the threshold that triggers automatic retaliation cycles.
- Proxy activity: No significant activation or escalation by Iran-aligned groups (Houthis, Hezbollah remnants, Iraqi/Syrian militias) that materially disrupts Gulf shipping, energy infrastructure, or US/partner forces.
- Shipping security (Strait of Hormuz and approaches): Commercial vessels transit without systematic attacks, boardings, mine threats, or IRGC “coordination” mandates that effectively control access; UKMTO/JMICS threat level reduced from extreme/high.
- Commercial transit levels: Daily vessel crossings through Hormuz recover to ≥70–80% of pre-war baseline (~130–140 ships/day → ≥90–110), sustained for ≥14 days, with AIS-visible traffic and no large backlog of stranded vessels.
- War-risk insurance: Premiums fall from current extremes (reported ~7.5–10% of hull value or multiples of 20–40× peacetime) to ≤2–3× pre-war levels for standard commercial coverage, enabling normal underwriting.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf producers (Saudi, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Iraq) and residual Iranian volumes restore seaborne exports via Hormuz (or fully viable alternatives at scale) without force majeure declarations; Qatar LNG and major crude loadings resume near pre-war rates.
- Energy market stress/volatility: Brent and related benchmarks stabilize without sustained war-risk premium of $10–20+/bbl; volatility returns toward historical Gulf norms (not crisis spikes above $90+ driven by Hormuz risk).
- Force posture of major actors: No major new deployments or escalatory repositioning; US CENTCOM posture remains defensive/enforcement rather than active campaign; Iranian coastal and IRGC naval posture not in active interdiction mode.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No nuclear-related moves, mass casualty incidents on commercial shipping, or political shocks that reopen full hostilities.

A temporary ceasefire, partial traffic recovery under Iranian administrative control, or oil price drop from demand destruction alone does **not** meet this standard. Commercial and insurance normalization are gating factors beyond pure military pause.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of ~19 August 2026)**

War day ~172–173. US/Israel strikes began 28 February 2026, killing senior Iranian leadership including Khamenei. Iran responded with large-scale missile/drone attacks on Gulf states, US bases, and shipping. Hormuz effectively closed or near-zero for prolonged periods; traffic currently single-digit daily crossings vs. ~130–140 pre-war (≈1% baseline per multiple trackers). US naval blockade of Iranian ports in force. June 17 Islamabad MOU created a 60-day negotiating window that expired 17 August with no deal and talks never substantively beginning on nuclear/sanctions/Hormuz package. Iran-Oman track on route mechanisms continues but is contested by the US (Trump has threatened action against Oman). Recent projectile strike on a vessel (UKMTO, ~18 August) caused a crew casualty. War-risk premiums remain extreme. Brent recently closed above $90. US has paused major strikes inside Iran for extended periods but maintains blockade and readiness. Iranian leadership shows hardline consolidation (IRGC influence) alongside pragmatic economic pressure. Proxies (Houthis) have activated in Bab el-Mandeb. Gulf states damaged early, seeking de-escalation but rejecting Iranian sovereignty claims over the strait. Evidence base is reasonably dense from ISW, GlobalSecurity daily updates, Reuters/Kpler shipping data, UKMTO, and official statements, though belligerent claims require discounting.<grok:render card_id="a85192" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">2</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="41d610" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">5</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="f0f484" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">15</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="6007ab" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">20</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant classes (3–6):

1. **Tanker War / Iran-Iraq War maritime phase (1980–88, especially 1984–88)**: Sustained attacks on shipping in the Gulf. Traffic never fully stopped but was severely disrupted for years; insurance soared; US reflagging and escorts eventually stabilized but full commercial normality lagged military de-escalation by months–years. Suggests multi-year partial disruption possible; functional recovery after major external intervention or war end took 6–18+ months post-peak intensity.
2. **1990–91 Gulf War / Iraq invasion of Kuwait and aftermath**: Rapid military resolution (weeks of intense fighting), but residual mines, insurance, and confidence issues delayed full shipping recovery. Post-ceasefire commercial normalization in the northern Gulf took weeks to a few months once major kinetic risk ended.
3. **Red Sea / Houthi disruption (2023–ongoing into 2026 context)**: Prolonged asymmetric attacks on commercial shipping. Traffic diverted around Africa for extended periods; insurance elevated; partial recovery only with sustained naval protection and reduced attacks. Shows that even without full closure, commercial/insurance normality can lag kinetic reduction by many months.
4. **Strait of Hormuz crises / Iranian threats and limited seizures (multiple, including 2019)**: Short-lived spikes; traffic recovered within days–weeks once acute threat subsided, because underlying state capacity and insurer confidence remained intact. Breaks down here because the 2026 case involves sustained near-closure, regime survival after leadership decapitation, and mutual blockade/interdiction.
5. **Post-ceasefire Gulf or Levantine commercial recovery (e.g., after 2006 Lebanon or earlier tanker phases)**: Military pause often precedes commercial recovery by 1–6 months due to insurer caution, charterer risk aversion, and residual proxy risk.
6. **Broader chokepoint disruptions (Suez 2021 blockage analog limited; more usefully prolonged asymmetric maritime campaigns)**: Commercial actors require sustained low-risk signals, not just declarations.

Base-rate prior (pre-current-evidence adjustment, for meeting the full operational definition):  
- 1 week: 1–3%  
- 1 month: 5–10%  
- 3 months: 15–25%  
- 6 months: 30–45%  
- 1 year: 45–60%  
- 18 months: 55–70%  

These reflect historical lag between military de-escalation and commercial/insurance recovery in Gulf/maritime conflicts, plus the high bar of the multi-domain definition. The current war’s intensity, mutual blockades, and leadership changes pull the prior downward relative to short-crisis cases.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

| Evidence item | Source type | Direction on normalization | Confidence | Status |
|---------------|-------------|----------------------------|------------|--------|
| Hormuz traffic ~1% / single-digit daily crossings; ~270 stranded vessels | Shipping data (Kpler, trackers), Reuters, specialized monitors | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| War-risk premiums extreme (7.5–10% hull or 20–40×) | Insurer/broker commentary, monitors | Strongly against | High | Confirmed |
| MOU expired 17 Aug without deal or extension; no active US-Iran talks | Official statements (Trump, Iranian FM), Axios, GlobalSecurity | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Recent projectile strike on vessel causing crew casualty (~18 Aug) | UKMTO | Against | High | Confirmed |
| Iran maintains closure conditions (lift blockade, sanctions relief, assets, end ops); claims sovereignty/control | Iranian officials, state media | Against | High | Confirmed (claims) |
| US maintains blockade; asserts strait “open”; pauses major strikes inside Iran for weeks | CENTCOM, Trump statements | Mixed (pause helps short-term military; blockade hurts commercial) | High | Confirmed |
| Iran-Oman track on routes advancing in reporting | Bloomberg, Iranian/Omani statements, secondary | Mildly toward (if successful) | Medium | Disputed (US rejects) |
| Hardline consolidation in Iran (IRGC influence, offensive posture signals) | WSJ, ISW, Iranian appointments | Against | Medium-High | Inferred/Confirmed elements |
| Gulf states damaged early, seeking de-escalation but rejecting Iranian control claims | Reporting, GCC positions | Mildly toward (pressure for deal) | Medium | Confirmed |
| Brent >$90, energy stress ongoing | Market data | Against (market signal of risk) | High | Confirmed |
| Proxy activation (Houthis in Bab el-Mandeb) | Reporting | Against | High | Confirmed |
| US munitions drawdown concerns earlier; force posture adjustments discussed | Think-tank/military reporting | Mixed | Medium | Inferred |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

Ranked: (1) Mutual economic exhaustion and Gulf state pressure for reopening (energy revenues, reconstruction). (2) Sustained US military pause + credible enforcement reducing Iranian attack capacity. (3) Successful Iran-Oman (or broader) technical route mechanism that insurers and charterers accept. (4) Iranian internal pragmatic faction gaining enough space for limited compromise on administration without full sovereignty claim. (5) Alternative pipeline/export capacity (ADCOP, East-West, Jask) partially offsetting Hormuz dependence, reducing urgency for full reopening but also reducing leverage for prolonged closure.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

Ranked: (1) Core disagreement over who controls/administers Hormuz (Iran sovereignty claims vs. freedom of navigation + US blockade). (2) Residual Iranian missile/drone/coastal interdiction capacity and willingness to use calibrated attacks. (3) Insurer and charterer risk aversion requiring prolonged clean record, not declarations. (4) Proxy and horizontal escalation options (Houthis, others). (5) Domestic political incentives on both sides (US midterms context; Iranian hardline consolidation post-leadership losses). (6) Nuclear file linkage making pure shipping deals unstable.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate probabilities that each major component meets the operational threshold by horizon (independent estimates then adjusted for dependence):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 15%; 1m 35%; 3m 55%; 6m 70%; 1y 80%; 18m 85%  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥70–80% volume, low attack rate): 1w <5%; 1m 10%; 3m 25%; 6m 40%; 1y 55%; 18m 65%  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤2–3×): 1w <5%; 1m 8%; 3m 20%; 6m 35%; 1y 50%; 18m 60%  
- Oil/LNG export recovery (near pre-war seaborne continuity): 1w 5%; 1m 15%; 3m 30%; 6m 45%; 1y 60%; 18m 70%  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 20%; 1m 40%; 3m 55%; 6m 65%; 1y 75%; 18m 80%  
- Force posture stabilization / no major new deployments: 1w 25%; 1m 45%; 3m 60%; 6m 70%; 1y 80%; 18m 85%  
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 40%; 1m 50%; 3m 55%; 6m 60%; 1y 65%; 18m 70%  

Shipping security + insurance are the primary gating factors; military pause alone is insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 2%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~1–3%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (recent strike, MOU expiry, traffic still near zero).  
- Core rationale: Physical and commercial conditions cannot flip in days; insurers and owners require multi-week clean signals.  
- Main gating factor: Shipping volume + insurance.  
- What would raise: Immediate verified bilateral stand-down + rapid traffic surge under accepted routes.  
- What would lower: Further vessel attacks or major strike cycle.  
- Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~5–10%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight downward (stalemate locked).  
- Core rationale: Even optimistic technical progress on Iran-Oman routes would not clear residual risk for commercial actors this fast.  
- Main gating factor: Sustained low-attack transit + insurer response.  
- What would raise: Binding US-Iran (or multilateral) shipping protocol with verification + 2+ weeks clean transit.  
- What would lower: Renewed kinetic cycle or proxy surge.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~15–25%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
- Core rationale: Possible if a limited technical deal sticks and military pause holds; still requires commercial confidence rebuild that historically lags.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance + volume recovery.  
- What would raise: Verified multi-week safe transit + premium compression + Gulf state buy-in.  
- What would lower: Breakdown of Oman track or new escalation.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~30–45%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (hardline signals, mutual red lines).  
- Core rationale: Time allows for attrition, backchannel progress, or external pressure to produce a workable arrangement; commercial lag still material.  
- Main gating factor: Resolution of control/administration dispute sufficient for insurers.  
- What would raise: Formal or de-facto freedom-of-navigation arrangement + sustained enforcement.  
- What would lower: Prolonged calibrated Iranian interdiction or US escalation.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 52%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~45–60%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight downward.  
- Core rationale: Longer horizon raises chance of war fatigue, leadership adaptation, or external mediation producing functional (if imperfect) arrangements; still far from certain given core sovereignty dispute.  
- Main gating factor: Durable commercial confidence and residual proxy risk.  
- What would raise: Comprehensive package linking shipping, sanctions relief, and nuclear restraint.  
- What would lower: Regime radicalization or major horizontal escalation.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 62%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~55–70%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward.  
- Core rationale: Historical reference classes show most prolonged Gulf maritime disruptions eventually reach functional commercial recovery within this window once kinetic intensity drops, but the multi-domain bar and unresolved control issue keep it below 70–80%.  
- Main gating factor: Institutionalization of safe transit norms + insurer re-entry.  
- What would raise: Clear post-conflict security architecture or decisive degradation of Iranian interdiction capacity.  
- What would lower: Frozen conflict with intermittent attacks becoming the new normal.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low (longer horizons inherently lower precision)  

**10. Most Likely Path**

Protracted low-to-medium intensity stalemate: intermittent calibrated attacks and enforcement actions, partial technical arrangements via Oman or others that allow limited traffic under constrained conditions, elevated but gradually declining insurance, and slow volume recovery. Full multi-domain normality remains elusive until a more durable political understanding or decisive shift in capabilities/incentives. Commercial actors treat the Gulf as high-risk for an extended period.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

A pragmatic Iranian leadership prioritizes economic survival, accepts a non-sovereignty administrative formula (joint or Omani-led with Iranian consultation), US lifts or relaxes blockade in tandem, 3–4 weeks of clean transits occur, insurers rapidly reprice, and Gulf states underwrite residual risk. Probability of this path is modest but non-zero within 3–6 months if domestic Iranian pressures intensify.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Hardline consolidation, continued use of Hormuz as leverage, proxy activation, mutual red-line testing, and insurer/charterer permanent risk premium. Functional normality delayed beyond 18 months or achieved only at lower traffic/insurance levels that still fail the operational definition. Supported by current leadership signals and historical tanker-war duration.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Strongest case I am overestimating normalization: The operational definition is demanding; commercial and insurance recovery historically requires longer clean records than military pauses deliver. Iranian capacity for calibrated, deniable disruption remains high; US domestic politics and midterm pressures could produce inconsistent posture. Base rates from shorter crises may be too optimistic.

Strongest case I am underestimating: Economic pain on both sides (Iranian oil revenues, Gulf damage, global energy costs, US political costs) could force faster pragmatic deals than reference classes suggest. Alternative export routes + SPR releases + demand responses already mitigate some pressure, potentially accelerating acceptance of imperfect arrangements. US military degradation of Iranian coastal assets may be more lasting than visible.

Load-bearing assumptions: (1) Insurers remain conservative; (2) Iranian control claims are non-negotiable in the near term; (3) No sudden regime-altering internal event.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily AIS/Kpler transit counts and UKMTO incident reports.  
- War-risk premium quotes from major brokers.  
- Official language on Iran-Oman mechanism vs. US position.  
- Any sustained ≥14-day period without vessel attacks or major strikes.  
- Iranian export volumes and force-majeure status from Qatar/Kuwait/Saudi.  
- Proxy attack frequency (Bab el-Mandeb, others).  
- US force posture statements and any blockade adjustments.  
- Brent volatility and Asian buyer behavior (China tanker activity).

**15. Final Summary Table**

Horizon | Probability | Confidence  
---|---|---  
1 week | 2% | High  
1 month | 8% | Medium-High  
3 months | 22% | Medium  
6 months | 38% | Medium  
1 year | 52% | Medium  
18 months | 62% | Medium-Low  

The forecast prioritizes commercial and insurance realities over declarations or temporary kinetic pauses. Evidence as of 19 August 2026 supports a prolonged path to the full operational standard.

title: Iran War: Hormuz normality forecast
message:
**1. Forecast Question**

Estimate the probability that the Persian Gulf has returned to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War by each of these horizons: 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 18 months.

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**

“Return to functional normality” is defined as the simultaneous satisfaction of all of the following observable conditions for a sustained period of at least 14 consecutive days (to exclude transient pauses):

- Direct military activity: No confirmed Iranian or U.S./Israeli kinetic strikes on commercial vessels, energy infrastructure, or opposing military assets in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, or immediately adjacent waters (Gulf of Oman approaches). Residual air-defense or surveillance activity does not count as violation if it produces no kinetic effects.
- Proxy activity: No sustained Iranian-directed or coordinated proxy attacks (Houthis, Iraqi militias, Hezbollah maritime elements) that meaningfully degrade Gulf shipping or energy exports.
- Shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters: UKMTO/JMIC risk assessments at “moderate” or lower; no active minefields in primary traffic separation schemes; no routine IRGC turn-back orders or boardings of non-Iranian commercial vessels.
- Commercial transit levels: Daily vessel transits through Hormuz averaging ≥70% of pre-war baseline (~130 vessels/day, i.e., ≥90 vessels/day) for liquid and dry cargo combined, sustained, with non-Iranian and non-sanctioned traffic comprising a majority share.
- War-risk insurance conditions: Hull war-risk premiums for standard VLCC/Suezmax Hormuz transits ≤1.0% of hull value (pre-war baseline ~0.25%; peak crisis 5–10%+; recent multiples still elevated at ~30× in some reporting) and widely available without special consortia or state guarantees; Joint War Committee listing status no longer driving prohibitive pricing.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Combined Gulf oil + LNG exports through Hormuz and alternative pipelines (Petraline, ADCOP, Goreh-Jask) ≥85% of pre-war volumes (~20+ mb/d oil equivalent + Qatar LNG), with no force-majeure declarations remaining in force by major producers (Saudi, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Iraq).
- Energy market stress and volatility: Brent crude 30-day realized volatility ≤ pre-war average levels (or ≤25% annualized); no sustained risk premium >$10–15/bbl attributable to Hormuz risk alone; Asian and European buyers restoring normal contract volumes without large-scale force majeure or rerouting premiums.
- Force posture of major actors: U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports lifted or reduced to routine presence; no large-scale additional carrier strike group deployments or Iranian “offensive doctrine” shifts producing kinetic effects; Gulf states not under sustained missile/drone attack.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No new high-casualty strikes on population centers, nuclear facilities, or third-party states that reset the conflict trajectory.

A temporary ceasefire, partial traffic recovery, or oil-price decline alone does **not** satisfy the definition. Commercial and insurance normalization must lag and confirm military de-escalation.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 18 August 2026)**

War began 28 February 2026 with U.S.-Israeli strikes that killed Supreme Leader Khamenei and senior leadership. Iran retaliated with widespread missile/drone attacks on Gulf states, U.S. bases, and shipping. Hormuz traffic collapsed from ~130 vessels/day to single digits–teens. A 60-day U.S.-Iran MoU signed 17 June expired 17 August without successor agreement, extension, or follow-on process. Recent developments include: projectile strike on outbound vessel (UKMTO, one casualty); continued low transits (Kpler: ~6 commodity vessels on 17 Aug vs. 10-day average ~11); CENTCOM naval blockade still redirecting/disabling vessels; Iranian officials signaling shift to “fully offensive” posture and demanding blockade lift within “a few weeks”; attacks on ADNOC-affiliated vessels in prior days; Brent ~$88–92/bbl with elevated volatility; war-risk premiums still multiples of peacetime (reports of 30× or 3–10% of hull value). Pre-war oil throughput ~20+ mb/d via Hormuz; current flows severely constrained. Proxy fronts (Lebanon, Red Sea) remain active at lower intensity. Evidence base is solid on traffic and attacks but thinner on exact insurance quotes and internal Iranian decision-making.<grok:render card_id="8c5de9" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">3</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="e52816" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">4</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Relevant reference classes (3–6):

1. **Iran-Iraq Tanker War (1984–1988)**: Hundreds of attacks on shipping; Hormuz never fully closed but traffic and insurance severely disrupted. Relevance: same geography, Iranian asymmetric maritime tactics. Breaks down: multi-year attrition war with different political endgame; no U.S. carrier presence or nuclear dimension. Suggests partial stabilization only after formal ceasefire + years of residual risk; functional commercial normality took 1–3+ years post-1988.

2. **2019 Gulf shipping crisis (May–Sep)**: Iranian attacks/seizures on tankers; elevated insurance; limited duration. Relevance: same actors and waterway. Breaks down: far lower intensity, no full-scale war or leadership decapitation. Suggests 3–6 months for traffic and premiums to normalize after de-escalation.

3. **Red Sea/Houthi crisis (2023–2025/26)**: Sustained proxy attacks; massive rerouting; insurance spikes. Relevance: Iranian-linked proxies, chokepoint risk pricing, commercial caution. Breaks down: alternative route (Cape) existed; no direct state-on-state war. Suggests even after attack pauses, full traffic/insurance recovery takes 3–12+ months; residual risk persists.

4. **Black Sea grain corridor (2022 onward)**: Mined waters + ongoing conflict; insurance and escort requirements. Relevance: war-risk lag after political agreements. Suggests weeks-to-months for initial traffic, longer for insurance confidence.

5. **Suez closures / major chokepoint disruptions (historical)**: Physical or risk-driven; recovery lags political reopenings by weeks–months due to backlog, insurance, and confidence.

Base-rate prior (pre-case-specific evidence), approximate cumulative probability of functional normality:

- 1 week: 1–3%
- 1 month: 5–10%
- 3 months: 15–25%
- 6 months: 30–45%
- 1 year: 50–65%
- 18 months: 60–75%

These reflect historical lag between military pauses and commercial/insurance normalization in high-stakes energy chokepoints.

**5. Evidence Ledger**

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization**

1. Mutual economic pain (oil prices, Gulf state losses, Iranian export constraints) creating incentives for deal.  
2. Existence of diplomatic channels (Oman, prior MoU framework, Qatar mediation history).  
3. Pipeline workarounds reducing absolute dependence on Hormuz for some volumes.  
4. U.S. political preference for lower energy prices (explicit statements).  
5. Historical pattern that prolonged high-intensity Gulf disruption eventually produces negotiated off-ramps.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization**

1. Core dispute over sovereignty/control of Hormuz and U.S. blockade remains unresolved post-MoU.  
2. Iranian internal hardline shift and “offensive doctrine” signaling.  
3. Insurance and commercial confidence lag far behind any kinetic pause (historical 1–2 quarters minimum).  
4. Proxy and secondary fronts (Lebanon, Red Sea) can re-ignite.  
5. Leadership changes and domestic Iranian politics raise commitment problems.  
6. Force posture (U.S. carriers, Iranian mine/drone capabilities) remains elevated.  
7. Backlog of stranded vessels and global supply-chain rewiring create inertia against rapid return.

Ranked importance: unresolved Hormuz sovereignty + insurance lag are the highest-weight gates; kinetic intensity is secondary once a credible sustained pause exists.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate independent probabilities (then adjusted for dependence) of each component being satisfied by horizon:

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w 5%; 1m 20%; 3m 40%; 6m 55%; 1y 70%; 18m 80%.  
- Sustained safe commercial transit (≥70% volume): 1w <5%; 1m 10%; 3m 25%; 6m 40%; 1y 60%; 18m 70%.  
- Meaningful insurance normalization (≤1% hull): 1w <2%; 1m 5%; 3m 15%; 6m 30%; 1y 50%; 18m 65%.  
- Oil/LNG export recovery (≥85%): 1w <5%; 1m 15%; 3m 35%; 6m 50%; 1y 65%; 18m 75%.  
- Proxy restraint: 1w 10%; 1m 25%; 3m 40%; 6m 55%; 1y 65%; 18m 75%.  
- Force drawdown / posture de-escalation: 1w <5%; 1m 10%; 3m 25%; 6m 40%; 1y 55%; 18m 65%.  
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w 70%; 1m 50%; 3m 40%; 6m 35%; 1y 30%; 18m 25% (declining because longer windows allow more opportunity for shocks).

Gating factors are insurance + sustained safe transit + absence of new triggers. Kinetic pause is necessary but far from sufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
- Probability: 2%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~1–3%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: slightly lower (fresh attacks, MoU expiry, low traffic)  
- Core rationale: No pathway to simultaneous multi-domain satisfaction in 7 days; even a sudden deal would leave insurance, mines, and confidence unresolved.  
- Main gating factor: Insurance and commercial confidence.  
- What would raise: Immediate comprehensive deal + verified mine clearance + insurer statements of rate collapse.  
- What would lower: Further vessel strikes or Iranian offensive operations.  
- Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
- Probability: 8%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~5–10%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: modest downward (expired MoU, ongoing blockade, recent strikes)  
- Core rationale: Possible kinetic pause, but commercial and insurance lags historically require longer confirmation; current posture points to continued friction.  
- Main gating factor: Credible sustained safe transit + insurance response.  
- What would raise: Binding follow-on agreement lifting blockade and recognizing freedom of navigation + 2+ weeks clean traffic.  
- What would lower: Escalatory Iranian doctrine implementation or major new strike.  
- Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
- Probability: 22%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~15–25%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: neutral-to-slightly lower  
- Core rationale: Window long enough for a negotiated off-ramp driven by economic pain, but unresolved sovereignty dispute and insurance inertia keep probability modest.  
- Main gating factor: Political resolution of Hormuz control + insurance normalization.  
- What would raise: Durable agreement + verified demining + premium collapse to <2%.  
- What would lower: Renewed high-intensity exchanges or proxy surge.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
- Probability: 38%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~30–45%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: slight downward  
- Core rationale: Historical chokepoint recoveries often reach partial normality in this window if a political floor is reached; current case has deeper political stakes.  
- Main gating factor: Sustained multi-domain compliance after any deal.  
- What would raise: Verified force posture reductions + consistent ≥70% traffic + insurance ≤1%.  
- What would lower: Breakdown of any interim arrangement or new leadership hardline.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
- Probability: 55%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~50–65%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: neutral  
- Core rationale: Cumulative pressure and historical precedent favor eventual de-escalation, but residual risk and rewiring of supply chains keep it only modestly above coin-flip.  
- Main gating factor: Absence of new escalation triggers over long window + full commercial confidence restoration.  
- What would raise: Comprehensive settlement including nuclear and regional issues.  
- What would lower: Protracted low-intensity conflict or major third-party involvement.  
- Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
- Probability: 65%  
- Base-rate anchor: ~60–75%  
- Current-evidence adjustment: neutral  
- Core rationale: Long enough for structural adaptation or negotiated end; still well short of certainty because of commitment problems and potential for renewed cycles.  
- Main gating factor: Structural political settlement vs. frozen conflict.  
- What would raise: Verified Iranian military reconstitution limits + normalized Gulf state relations.  
- What would lower: Iranian domestic radicalization or U.S. policy reversal.  
- Confidence: Medium-Low (long-horizon uncertainty)  

Synthesis logic: Final probabilities are not mechanical averages. Insurance and sustained safe transit act as hard gates; kinetic and proxy components are necessary but insufficient. Joint satisfaction probability is therefore lower than the weakest individual component. Long-horizon figures remain below 80% because the operational definition is demanding and residual risk historically persists.

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued low-level friction and intermittent vessel incidents through autumn 2026. Economic costs eventually force limited technical arrangements (Oman-mediated corridors, partial blockade relief) by early 2027, producing partial traffic recovery (40–60% of baseline) and elevated but declining insurance. Full multi-domain normality remains elusive until mid-to-late 2027 at earliest, with residual war-risk pricing and force posture elevated. Oil markets adapt via pipelines, strategic stocks, and demand destruction rather than full Hormuz restoration.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Sudden comprehensive deal within weeks (driven by U.S. energy-price priorities + Iranian economic collapse) + rapid demining + insurer rate collapse. Probability of this path is low (~10–15% unconditional) but would lift 3- and 6-month forecasts substantially.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Iranian offensive doctrine produces sustained attacks or mining; U.S. maintains or expands blockade; proxies re-ignite; no durable political floor. Traffic stays <20% of baseline for 12+ months; insurance remains prohibitive. This path is plausible (~25–35% weight) given current signaling.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Strongest case I am overestimating normalization: The definition is correctly demanding, but I may still under-weight Iranian domestic hardline consolidation and the difficulty of restoring insurer confidence after repeated MoU failures. Historical Tanker War residual risk lasted years.  

Strongest case I am underestimating: Mutual economic pain + U.S. domestic political incentives for cheap energy could produce faster political off-ramps than pure historical base rates imply; pipeline workarounds already blunt some pressure.

Load-bearing assumptions: (1) Insurance markets require sustained clean evidence before repricing; (2) Hormuz sovereignty remains a core Iranian red line; (3) No sudden regime-altering internal Iranian change. Evidence that would prove the forecast wrong: a verified comprehensive deal + 30 consecutive days of ≥90 vessels/day at ≤1% war-risk premiums.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Daily Kpler/UKMTO transit counts and composition (Iranian vs. non-Iranian).  
- War-risk premium quotes from major brokers (Lloyd’s, Marsh, etc.).  
- Official statements on blockade status and any new MoU/follow-on text.  
- JMIC risk assessments and mine-clearance reports.  
- Iranian doctrine and force-posture announcements.  
- Gulf producer force-majeure status and actual export volumes.  
- Brent volatility and Asian buyer contract behavior.  
- Proxy attack tempo (Red Sea, Lebanon, Iraq).

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Main Gating Factor                  |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|-------------------------------------|
| 1 week    | 2%          | High         | Insurance + commercial confidence   |
| 1 month   | 8%          | Medium-High  | Sustained safe transit + insurance  |
| 3 months  | 22%         | Medium       | Political resolution of Hormuz + insurance |
| 6 months  | 38%         | Medium       | Sustained multi-domain compliance   |
