| Oil prices elevated but not at crisis peak (~$80s Brent) | Market data | Mildly positive (adaptation occurring) | High | Confirmed |
| No comprehensive ceasefire; cycle of strikes and responses continues | Multiple primary/secondary | Negative | High | Confirmed |
| Iranian oil loading disruption at Kharg under blockade | FT / shipping data | Negative for Iran (pressure to deal) | Medium-High | Reported |

**6. Key Drivers Toward Normalization** (ranked)

1. Mutual economic pain and US munitions/ political fatigue creating off-ramp pressure (highest weight).
2. Oman mediation channel producing a limited technical transit arrangement.
3. Gulf states’ strong preference for de-escalation and energy revenue recovery.
4. Adaptation already visible (partial alternative routes, Chinese/Iranian-linked traffic continuing).
5. Potential for a narrow, performance-based ceasefire that freezes kinetic activity.

**7. Key Drivers Against Normalization** (ranked)

1. Iranian insistence on formal recognition of enhanced control/sovereignty over Hormuz plus broader political/economic concessions (core load-bearing obstacle).
2. Residual IRGC operational capacity and willingness to use kinetic enforcement against non-compliant shipping.
3. Proxy networks (Houthis, Iraqi groups) that can independently or on cue disrupt without full Iranian state decision.
4. Trust deficit after multiple collapsed interim deals; each violation raises future insurance and commercial risk pricing.
5. Domestic Iranian politics (succession after Khamenei, hardliner influence) and US domestic/political constraints on concessions.
6. Second-order effects: elevated baseline risk premium, infrastructure damage, and buyer diversification that persist even after kinetic pause.

**8. Decomposed Sub-Forecasts**

Approximate independent probabilities of each major component being met by horizon (then adjusted for dependence; shipping security + insurance + transit levels are tightly coupled and act as gating factors):

- Major reduction in direct strikes: 1w ~15%, 1m ~35%, 3m ~55%, 6m ~70%, 1y ~80%, 18m ~85%
- Sustained safe commercial transit (no routine kinetic interference): 1w ~5%, 1m ~20%, 3m ~40%, 6m ~55%, 1y ~70%, 18m ~75%
- Meaningful insurance normalization: 1w <5%, 1m ~10%, 3m ~25%, 6m ~40%, 1y ~55%, 18m ~65%
- Oil/LNG export recovery ≥85%: 1w ~10%, 1m ~25%, 3m ~45%, 6m ~60%, 1y ~75%, 18m ~80%
- Proxy restraint: 1w ~20%, 1m ~40%, 3m ~55%, 6m ~65%, 1y ~75%, 18m ~80%
- Force posture drawdown/shift to defensive: 1w ~10%, 1m ~25%, 3m ~45%, 6m ~60%, 1y ~70%, 18m ~75%
- No new major escalation trigger: 1w ~60%, 1m ~50%, 3m ~45%, 6m ~40%, 1y ~35%, 18m ~30% (declining as time allows new shocks)

Gating factors are shipping security, insurance, and sustained absence of kinetic enforcement. Military pause alone is insufficient.

**9. Final Probability Forecasts by Horizon**

**1 Week**  
• Probability: 2%  
• Base-rate anchor: 1–3%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (active conditions and recent strike).  
• Core rationale: No mechanism exists for full multi-domain normalization in days; even a technical Oman deal would not clear insurance, force posture, or Iranian broader demands.  
• Main gating factor: Iranian kinetic enforcement capacity and maximalist conditions.  
• What would raise: Immediate comprehensive US-Iran ceasefire announcement with verified Hormuz free transit and insurer statements of cover restoration.  
• What would lower: New major tanker strikes or expanded US campaign.  
• Confidence: High  

**1 Month**  
• Probability: 8%  
• Base-rate anchor: 5–12%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Mild downward (conditions gap remains large).  
• Core rationale: A limited transit arrangement is plausible; full insurance + commercial recovery + proxy restraint + no new triggers is not. Historical pauses have been fragile.  
• Main gating factor: Conversion of technical deal into verified safe transit accepted by insurers and owners.  
• What would raise: Signed, implemented dual-route deal + US blockade lift + 2+ weeks zero incidents + major insurer rate cuts.  
• What would lower: Collapse of Oman talks or proxy attacks on Saudi energy.  
• Confidence: Medium-High  

**3 Months**  
• Probability: 22%  
• Base-rate anchor: 15–25%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral to slight downward.  
• Core rationale: Highest probability window for a narrow performance-based freeze that allows partial commercial recovery, but Iranian control claims and residual capacity make full definition hard to meet.  
• Main gating factor: Durability of any ceasefire against spoilers and insurance market response lag.  
• What would raise: Verified multi-week safe transit at ≥60–70% volumes + sanctions relief package + proxy stand-down.  
• What would lower: Renewed US or Iranian major strikes or formal Iranian toll regime rejection by markets.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**6 Months**  
• Probability: 35%  
• Base-rate anchor: 25–40%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Neutral.  
• Core rationale: Time allows political deals, stock rebuilding, and market adaptation, but reference classes show commercial tails are long after asymmetric maritime campaigns.  
• Main gating factor: Whether a political settlement addresses (or freezes) the sovereignty/control dispute over Hormuz.  
• What would raise: Comprehensive political agreement including sanctions path and verified force posture changes.  
• What would lower: Entrenchment of Iranian “Strait Authority” with kinetic enforcement or major proxy campaign.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**1 Year**  
• Probability: 48%  
• Base-rate anchor: 40–55%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward (deep trust deficit and succession politics).  
• Core rationale: Base rates improve with time, but second-order effects (buyer diversification, elevated baseline premiums, infrastructure repair) and potential new triggers keep probability below 50–55%. Full definition remains demanding.  
• Main gating factor: Sustained multi-domain calm long enough for insurance and commercial behavior to reset.  
• What would raise: Clear military superiority demonstration by US followed by stable settlement, or mutual exhaustion deal.  
• What would lower: Protracted low-intensity campaign or Iranian domestic hardliner consolidation.  
• Confidence: Medium  

**18 Months**  
• Probability: 58%  
• Base-rate anchor: 50–65%  
• Current-evidence adjustment: Slight downward.  
• Core rationale: Longest horizon allows structural adaptation and possible leadership or policy shifts, yet historical chokepoint and proxy campaigns show residual risk can persist. Probability stays well below levels that would imply high confidence in full normality.  
• Main gating factor: Whether the post-war equilibrium includes accepted rules of the road for Hormuz or permanent elevated risk.  
• What would raise: Durable great-power or regional security architecture that constrains spoilers.  
• What would lower: Transformation into chronic gray-zone contest similar to prolonged Red Sea disruption.  
• Confidence: Medium-Low (long-horizon uncertainty)  

Probabilities are internally consistent: rising but concave, reflecting both accumulating opportunities for deals and accumulating opportunities for spoilers/new shocks. Shipping/insurance components are the primary brakes relative to pure military pause probabilities.

**10. Most Likely Path**

Continued “no war, no peace” with intermittent technical progress on routes via Oman, periodic kinetic incidents, depressed but not zero transit (Chinese/Iranian-linked and some risk-tolerant traffic), elevated insurance, and gradual partial recovery of non-Iranian Gulf exports via alternatives or cautious Hormuz use. A narrow freeze becomes more likely in the 3–6 month window; full multi-domain normality remains a minority outcome even at 18 months. Energy markets adapt via higher prices, alternative routes, and demand destruction rather than returning to pre-war risk pricing.

**11. Faster Normalization Case**

Strongest path: US and Iran reach a performance-based package within weeks (blockade lift for verified free transit + limited sanctions relief + freeze on strikes) that Oman and Gulf states underwrite. Zero major incidents for 30+ days triggers insurer rate cuts. Proxies stand down under Iranian instruction. Probability of this path materializing enough to hit the definition by 3 months is roughly 15–20% conditional; it would raise the 3-month forecast toward 40%+.

**12. Prolonged Instability Case**

Strongest path: Iranian hardliners treat Hormuz control as non-negotiable core interest; technical talks produce only a contested dual-route regime that markets reject. Spoilers (proxies or IRGC elements) conduct periodic attacks. US is constrained by munitions and politics from decisive escalation but maintains blockade pressure. Result: chronic elevated risk, partial Chinese-dominated traffic, persistent high premiums, and Gulf export volumes recovering only slowly via non-Hormuz routes. This path keeps probabilities suppressed across all horizons.

**13. Red-Team Critique**

Possible overestimation of normalization: The forecast may underweight the speed of market adaptation and the coercive power of sustained economic pain on Iran (blockade + oil revenue loss). If a technical deal is implemented cleanly, insurance could move faster than historical analogs.  

Possible underestimation of persistence: The forecast may underweight Iranian resolve on sovereignty symbolism after leadership change and the ease with which proxies can re-escalate. Reference classes from the Tanker War and Red Sea suggest commercial tails longer than the 18-month 58% implies. Load-bearing assumption—that economic pressure eventually forces Iranian compromise on control claims—could fail if hardliners prioritize leverage over revenue. Long-horizon numbers carry the usual superforecasting discount for unforeseen shocks.

**14. Critical Signals to Monitor**

- Text and implementation details of any Iran-Oman joint statement (tolls? permits? enforcement?).  
- Actual daily transit counts by flag/ownership and corridor (Kpler, MarineTraffic, JMIC).  
- War-risk premium quotes from major brokers and P&I club circulars.  
- CENTCOM blockade accounting and any formal lift announcement.  
- Iranian loading data at Kharg and export volumes.  
- Proxy attack frequency and targeting (Saudi energy vs. pure shipping).  
- US and Iranian official statements on linkage between transit and broader political demands.  
- Munitions/stockpile reporting and any surge production announcements.  
- Gulf state force majeure status and alternative export volumes (Yanbu, etc.).

**15. Final Summary Table**

| Horizon   | Probability | Confidence   | Primary Gating Factor                  |
|-----------|-------------|--------------|----------------------------------------|
| 1 week    | 2%          | High         | Kinetic enforcement + maximalist conditions |
| 1 month   | 8%          | Medium-High  | Verified safe transit + insurer response |
| 3 months  | 22%         | Medium       | Ceasefire durability + commercial acceptance |
| 6 months  | 35%         | Medium       | Political settlement of control dispute |
| 1 year    | 48%         | Medium       | Sustained multi-domain calm            |
| 18 months | 58%         | Medium-Low   | Post-war equilibrium rules of the road |

The forecast is decision-grade for risk managers: short horizons are near-zero for full normality; medium horizons remain minority outcomes; even at 18 months the probability stays below levels that would justify treating the Gulf as low-risk again.

title: Iran War: Hormuz normality at 2%
message:
**1. Forecast Question**  
Probability that the Persian Gulf returns to functional normality following the outbreak of the 2026 Iran War, by horizons of 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, and 18 months (from 8 August 2026).

**2. Operational Definition of “Return to Functional Normality”**  
All of the following must hold simultaneously for at least 14 consecutive days (to exclude temporary pauses):

- Direct military activity: No US/Israeli or Iranian strikes on military targets, bases, ports, or energy infrastructure inside Iran, the Gulf states, or on shipping; no Iranian ballistic-missile/drone salvos against GCC states or US forces.
- Proxy activity: No Houthi attacks on Red Sea/Gulf of Aden shipping or Saudi infrastructure linked to the Iran conflict; no significant Iraqi militia or Hezbollah kinetic operations tied to the war.
- Shipping security (Strait of Hormuz and approaches): Zero confirmed attacks, boardings, mine incidents, or projectile strikes on commercial vessels for 14 days; UKMTO/JMIC report “normal” risk; AIS tracks show free choice of northern or southern corridors without IRGC coercion.
- Commercial transit levels: Daily two-way commercial transits ≥100 vessels (pre-war baseline ~130–140; recent 7-day averages ~4–8); tanker throughput ≥12–15 mb/d oil equivalent.
- War-risk insurance: Hull war-risk premiums ≤0.5% of hull value (pre-war ~0.1–0.25%; current estimates 7.5–30× baseline, often $3–10 m per VLCC transit); cargo war risk near pre-war levels; major clubs writing cover without exclusion clauses for the Gulf.
- Oil and LNG export continuity: Gulf oil exports via Hormuz ≥15 mb/d sustained; Qatari/UAE LNG loadings and transits restored to ≥80% of pre-war capacity (currently near-zero LNG crossings since mid-July in many reports); no widespread force-majeure declarations.
- Energy market stress: Brent ≤$75 sustained (current ~$82–84 range with spikes higher); realized volatility back to pre-war norms; no persistent $20+ war premium.
- Force posture: US naval blockade of Iranian ports lifted; significant drawdown of surge forces; Iranian “Persian Gulf Strait Authority” or equivalent not enforcing exclusive control/tolls; no new major minefields.
- Absence of major new escalation triggers: No assassination of remaining leadership, no nuclear-site strikes that restart cycles, no declaration of formal war expansion, no large-scale proxy mobilization.

A temporary ceasefire, partial route agreement, lower oil prices alone, or battlefield pause without commercial and insurance recovery does **not** qualify.

**3. Current Situation Snapshot (as of 8 August 2026)**  
War began 28 February 2026 with US-Israeli strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Cumulative days: ~161. June 17 MoU produced a partial, fragile reopening and traffic rebound (peak ~50–70 daily), followed by collapse after 7–8 July Iranian attacks on shipping and US retaliation (hundreds of targets).  

Current state: Hormuz traffic 3–8% of normal (recent daily counts 2–15; week of 4–7 Aug ~33 vessels vs 130–140 baseline). West-to-east tanker flows near zero some days. LNG crossings essentially halted since mid-July; Qatar force majeure extended. US naval blockade of Iranian ports active (dozens of vessels redirected). War-risk premiums still multiples of peacetime (reports of 7.5–10%+ hull value or 30× baseline). Brent ~$82–84. Sporadic incidents continue (explosions near Qeshm, Houthi claims on Saudi tankers, drone activity). Iran-Oman talks on routes/coordinates ongoing; draft reportedly includes Iranian influence over inbound traffic and possible fees/compensation; US and shipping associations resist. Trump states war “has got to end pretty soon”; Iranian hardliners and IRGC prioritize control of the strait. Proxies active. Casualties and damage substantial on all sides.<grok:render card_id="922dd1" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">0</argument></grok:render><grok:render card_id="e6b17c" card_type="citation_card" type="render_inline_citation"><argument name="citation_id">50</argument></grok:render>

**4. Reference Classes and Base-Rate Prior**

Full commercial/insurance normalization only after 1988 ceasefire (~4 years of elevated risk). Breaks down: bilateral conventional war, lower dependence on LNG, no nuclear dimension, different superpower role. Suggests multi-year elevated risk even after major combat ends.

3. **2023–25 Houthi Red Sea campaign**: Sustained asymmetric attacks; major carriers diverted for >12–18 months; insurance elevated; partial recovery only after sustained military pressure and reduced attacks. Breaks down: secondary theater, not primary oil chokepoint. Suggests 6–18+ months for full commercial confidence.  
4. **Gulf War 1990–91 / post-ceasefire**: Rapid military end; shipping and oil recovery in weeks-months under coalition control, but residual risk and force posture lingered. Breaks down: clear conventional defeat of one side.  
5. **Post-MoU June–July 2026 partial reopening (internal reference)**: Traffic rose then collapsed within weeks on first major incident. Shows commercial recovery is fragile and gated by sustained security + insurance.  

**Base-rate prior (before current evidence, probability of meeting the full operational definition):**  
- 1 week: 1–3%  
- 1 month: 5–10%  
- 3 months: 15–25%  
- 6 months: 30–45%  
- 1 year: 50–65%  
- 18 months: 60–75%  

(These reflect that pure military pauses occur faster than multi-domain commercial/insurance/force-posture normalization.)

**5. Evidence Ledger**
